0.1.title: What Is Linux? — Kernel, Distribution, Philosophy
objectives: You can explain the difference between the kernel, a distribution and the shell.
You know the two big distribution families (Debian and RHEL) and their package tools.
You find kernel version, distribution and architecture with `uname` and `/etc/os-release`.
You know the principle "everything is a file" and the purpose of the main top-level directories.
0.1.text:
title what is linux? — kernel, distribution, philosophy lead understand what linux really is: a kernel, the distributions built around it, and the ideas that make the command line so powerful. objectives you can explain the difference between the kernel, a distribution and the shell. you know the two big distribution families (debian and rhel) and their package tools. you find kernel version, distribution and architecture with `uname` and `/etc/os-release`. you know the principle \  and the purpose of the main top-level directories. sections kernel title kernel, distribution and shell body **linux** is strictly only the **kernel**: the core that talks to the hardware, schedules processes and manages memory. linus torvalds started it in 1991. alone the kernel is not usable — you need tools, libraries and a way to type commands. a **distribution** (distro) bundles the kernel with the gnu tools, a package manager, an installer and defaults. ubuntu, debian, fedora, rocky linux and almalinux are distros. the **shell** (usually `bash`) is the program that reads your commands and asks the kernel to run them. two files tell you what you are running: `uname` reports kernel and architecture, `/etc/os-release` reports the distribution. you will use both whenever you ask for help or read documentation. commands cmd uname -r what prints the kernel release. where when checking the kernel version for support or bug reports. why the kernel version decides which hardware and features you have. example uname -r cmd uname -a what prints all system information in one line. where when you paste system details into a ticket. why shows host name, kernel and architecture at once. example uname -a cmd uname -m what prints the machine architecture (x86_64, aarch64, ...). where before downloading software or an iso. why packages are built per architecture. example uname -m cmd cat /etc/os-release what shows distribution name and version. where on any modern distribution. why a standard file, same format on ubuntu, rocky, alma and others. example cat /etc/os-release tip kernel and distribution are versioned separately: ubuntu 24.04 ships kernel 6.8, rocky linux 9 ships 5.14 with many backports. family title distribution families and licences body distros group into **families**. the **debian family** (debian, ubuntu, mint) uses `.deb` packages and `apt`. the **rhel family** (red hat enterprise linux, rocky, almalinux, fedora) uses `.rpm` packages and `dnf`. commands you learn in this course work on both; only package management differs. the linux kernel is released under gpl-2.0-only; tools and applications bundled in a distribution may use different licences. this openness supports many distros, while enterprise vendors may offer support and services as well as software. the `id_like` line in `/etc/os-release` tells you the family: rocky reports `rhel fedora`, ubuntu reports `debian`. in this course your reference system is a **rocky/alma linux** vm, with ubuntu as an equal alternative. use whichever you installed in module 0.2. commands cmd grep id_like /etc/os-release what shows only the family line of the release file. where when you are unsure whether to use apt or dnf. why turns a long file into the one fact you need. example grep id_like /etc/os-release tip if `id_like` contains `debian` use `apt`; if it contains `rhel` or `fedora` use `dnf`. philosophy title philosophy and the directory tree body unix thinking in four lines: **everything is a file** (disks, devices and processes show up as paths), **small tools do one thing well**, tools are **combined** with pipes, and configuration is **plain text** you can read and edit. all files live in **one tree** starting at `/` (root directory). there are no drive letters. `/etc` holds configuration, `/home` the users' files, `/var` changing data such as logs, `/usr` programs and libraries, `/tmp` temporary files, `/dev` devices, `/proc` live kernel information. on modern systems `/bin` is just a link to `/usr/bin`. a normal user works in the home directory `/home/student`. the administrator account is **root**; you will meet it carefully in later modules. commands cmd ls / what lists the top level of the directory tree. where when getting oriented on an unknown system. why shows the standard directories described above. example ls / cmd ls /etc what lists the configuration directory. where when looking for a system setting. why nearly all system configuration is a text file here. example ls /etc cmd cat /etc/shells what lists the shells installed on the system. where when asking which shell programs exist. why shows that the shell is just a replaceable program. example cat /etc/shells tip when something is configurable, look in `/etc` first, then read the file — it is text. tasks t01 text show the kernel release with `uname -r`. hint -r means release. t02 text show the distribution information with `cat /etc/os-release`. hint note the `name` and `id_like` lines. t03 text show all system information with `uname -a`. hint -a means all. t04 text list the top level of the directory tree with `ls /`. hint find `etc`, `home`, `usr`, `var` in the output. t05 text list the configuration directory with `ls /etc`. hint these are mostly text files. t06 text show the installed shells with `cat /etc/shells`. hint `/bin/bash` should be listed. t07 text predict: which architecture will `uname -m` print on this system? then run it. hint most pcs and vms use x86_64. t08 text predict: what does `cat /etc/hostname` contain? run it to check. hint the default host name is `linux-lab`. t09 text predict: what does `echo $shell` print? run it to check. hint it is the full path to your shell program. t10 text debug: `~/distro.txt` wrongly says `id=windows`. overwrite the file so that it contains `id=linux`. hint `echo id=linux > ~/distro.txt` replaces the content; check with `cat`. t11 text mini project: create the folder `~/about_linux`. save the kernel release in `~/about_linux/kernel.txt` and the contents of `/etc/os-release` in `~/about_linux/distro.txt`. hint `uname -r > file` writes command output into a file. t12 text challenge: build `~/system_report.txt` with three lines: host name, kernel release and your user name. hint `>` creates the file, `>>` appends. commands: `hostname`, `uname -r`, `whoami`. t13 text ticket: \ hint combine `grep` for the line with `>` for the file. : { these commands are harmless and read-only. run them in the terminal of your vm (rocky/alma or ubuntu) and compare. tasks v01 title identify your system text show kernel release and distribution, and paste both outputs. blocks cmd uname -r
cat /etc/os-release expected 5.14.0-427.el9.x86_64
name=\ 
version=\ 
id=\ 
id_like=\ 
... differs on ubuntu you see `name=\ ` and a kernel like `6.8.0-...-generic` — that is correct. on wsl the kernel name contains `microsoft-standard-wsl2`. v02 title walk the directory tree text list the top level and the configuration directory and paste the output of the first command. blocks cmd ls /
ls /etc | head -n 15 expected bin  boot  dev  etc  home  lib  lib64  media  mnt  opt  proc  root  run  sbin  srv  sys  tmp  usr  var differs the exact list varies by distribution, but `etc`, `home`, `usr` and `var` must be present. `bin` appears as a link to `usr/bin` on modern systems; check with `ls -ld /bin`; `lib`, `lib64` and `sbin` may be links into `usr/` too. extra directories such as `afs` are fine. v03 title meet process 1 text every system starts one first process. find out its name. blocks cmd ps -p 1 -o comm= expected systemd differs in some containers you may see `bash` or `init`; on a normal vm it is `systemd`. if `ps` is missing, run `cat /proc/1/comm` instead. v04 title check the link and your family text check that `/bin` is a link and decide whether your system uses apt or dnf. blocks cmd ls -ld /bin
grep id_like /etc/os-release
which apt dnf expected lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 7 ... /bin -> usr/bin differs `which` prints only the tool that exists: `apt` on ubuntu, `dnf` on rocky/alma. if `which` is missing (minimal installs lack it), the shell builtin `command -v dnf` and `command -v apt` always work. quiz : { what is the linux kernel? options a complete operating system with desktop the core that manages hardware, memory and processes a text editor a package manager explain linux strictly means the kernel. a distribution adds tools, packages and an installer around it. : { which package tool belongs to the rocky linux / rhel family? options apt pacman zypper only dnf explain rhel-family systems use rpm packages managed by dnf; debian and ubuntu use apt. : { which file shows the name and version of the distribution? options /etc/os-release /etc/hostname /proc/cpuinfo /var/log/messages explain `/etc/os-release` is the standard file on all modern distributions. : { what does \  mean? options every file is a program there are no directories devices, processes and settings are reached through paths and read with the same tools files cannot be deleted explain disks appear under `/dev` and processes under `/proc`; the same tools such as `cat` and `ls` work on them. summary linux is the kernel; a distribution adds tools, packages and an installer; the shell reads your commands. debian family uses `apt`, rhel family uses `dnf`; `id_like` in `/etc/os-release` tells you which. `uname -r`, `uname -m` and `cat /etc/os-release` identify any system. one tree from `/`: `/etc` configuration, `/home` users, `/var` data, `/usr` programs. unix philosophy: everything is a file, small tools, plain text configuration. glossary term kernel meaning the core of the operating system that controls hardware, memory and processes. term distribution meaning a complete system: kernel plus tools, packages, installer and defaults. term shell meaning the program that reads and runs your commands, usually bash. term package manager meaning the tool that installs and updates software: apt or dnf. term root directory meaning the top of the file tree, written `/`. term gpl meaning a family of free-software licences; the linux kernel is licensed under gpl-2.0-only.

0.2.title: Setting up your own Linux VM
objectives: You pick the right tool for your computer (VirtualBox, UTM or WSL).
You verify the ISO with a SHA-256 checksum before installing.
You create a VM, take a snapshot and connect to it over SSH.
0.2.text: title setting up your own linux vm lead install rocky/alma linux or ubuntu in virtualbox, utm or wsl, verify the download, take a snapshot and connect over ssh. objectives you pick the right tool for your computer (virtualbox, utm or wsl). you verify the iso with a sha-256 checksum before installing. you create a vm, take a snapshot and connect to it over ssh. sections why title why your own vm? body real skills come from a **real linux**. a virtual machine (vm) is a complete computer inside your computer: you can break it, reinstall it and nothing on your real system is touched. pick the tool that fits your hardware: **virtualbox** (windows, intel mac, linux), **utm** (apple silicon macs, needs an arm64 iso) or **wsl 2** (windows 10/11, fastest to start, ubuntu only). for distributions use **rocky linux 9 / almalinux 9** (the rhel family used in companies) and optionally **ubuntu 24.04 lts**. tip plan for 2 cpu cores, 4 gb ram and 25 gb disk per vm. iso title download the iso and verify it body download the iso only from the official site of the distribution (rockylinux.org, almalinux.org, ubuntu.com). next to the iso there is a **checksum** (sha-256). compute the checksum of your file and compare: if one character differs, the file is damaged or tampered with — download again. commands cmd sha256sum (linux/macos: shasum -a 256) what computes the sha-256 checksum of a file. where on your host machine after the download. why proves the iso is complete and unmodified. example sha256sum rocky-9-latest-x86_64-minimal.iso nosim cmd get-filehash (windows powershell) what same checksum on windows. where powershell on windows hosts. why windows has no sha256sum. example get-filehash .\\rocky-9-latest-x86_64-minimal.iso -algorithm sha256 nosim warn never install from an iso whose checksum does not match, even if the installer starts. create title create the vm and install body in virtualbox/utm create a new vm, attach the iso and give it 2 cpus, 4 gb ram and 25 gb disk. start it and follow the installer: choose your language, select the disk (automatic partitioning is fine), set a root password, **create a normal user and tick \ ** (this adds the user to the `wheel`/`sudo` group). choose the **minimal** install first; you will add tools yourself. after the reboot remove the iso and log in with your normal user. finish with `cat /etc/os-release` to see which system you built. on **wsl** this is one command in powershell (administrator): `wsl --install -d ubuntu-24.04`. then restart and create your user name when asked. tip choose a short lowercase user name without spaces; you will type it a lot. snapshot title snapshots: your undo button body a **snapshot** saves the complete state of the vm. take one called `clean-install` right after the first successful boot and before every risky experiment. if you break something, restore the snapshot in seconds. in virtualbox: machine ▸ take snapshot; in utm: clone the vm or use the qemu snapshot option. for wsl export a backup: `wsl --export ubuntu-24.04 backup.tar`. danger a snapshot is not a backup of your real files; if the host disk fails, snapshots are lost with it. network title networking basics body **nat** (default) lets the vm reach the internet but hides it from your network; use port forwarding to reach it. **bridged** puts the vm on your lan with its own ip address. **host-only** connects only the vm and your computer. for learning, nat with a port-forward rule (host port 2222 → guest port 22) or bridged are both fine. inside the vm check your address with `ip -brief a`. commands cmd ip -brief a what shows interfaces with state and ip address. where inside the vm. why you need the ip address to connect over ssh. example ip -brief a nosim ssh title connect with ssh body the vm window is clumsy. connect from your host terminal over **ssh** instead: copy/paste works and it is how servers are managed in real life. first make sure the ssh service is running in the vm (`sudo systemctl enable --now sshd` on rocky/alma, `ssh` on ubuntu). then from your host: `ssh user@ip` (bridged) or `ssh -p 2222 user@127.0.0.1` (nat with port forward). accept the host key with `yes`. commands cmd ssh user@host what opens a secure remote shell. where from your host to the vm or any server. why standard way to administer linux. example ssh student@192.168.1.50 nosim cmd ssh-keygen -t ed25519 what creates a key pair for password-less login. where once on your host. why safer and more convenient than passwords. example ssh-keygen -t ed25519 nosim cmd ssh-copy-id user@host what installs your public key on the vm. where after ssh-keygen. why next logins need no password. example ssh-copy-id student@192.168.1.50 nosim tip take a snapshot after ssh works — it is the best state to return to. tasks t01 text warm-up: in the simulator read `cat /etc/os-release` to see what an installed system tells you. hint the file name has a hyphen. t02 text warm-up: run `id` and see your user, uid and groups (`wheel` means administrator). hint just `id`. t03 text guided: run `hostname` and then `uname -r` — the first facts to note after any installation. hint two separate commands. t04 text predict: what will `sudo whoami` print? think, then run it. hint sudo runs the command as root. t05 text debug: `cat /etc/os_release` fails. run it, read the error, then run the correct command. hint underscore vs hyphen; `ls /etc` helps. t06 text mini project: save the distribution name line into `~/vm-summary.txt` with `grep pretty_name /etc/os-release > ~/vm-summary.txt`. hint `>` writes the output to a file. t07 text challenge: create `~/vm-lab/snapshots` and `~/vm-lab/notes` with one `mkdir -p` command. hint brace expansion: `~/vm-lab/{snapshots,notes}`. t08 text ticket #3001 — the lab needs a vm report: write hostname, kernel version and user name (in that order) into `~/vm-report.txt`, one per line. hint first command with `>`, the next two with `>>`. : { this is the main path of this module: work through the steps on your computer. tick \  or paste an output to be checked. tasks v01 title download the iso text download rocky linux 9 or almalinux 9 (minimal iso; arm64 for apple silicon) or ubuntu 24.04 and note the published sha-256 value. blocks differs apple silicon needs the aarch64/arm64 iso; x86_64 will not boot in utm natively. v02 title verify the checksum text compute the sha-256 of your iso and paste the output. compare it manually with the published value. blocks cmd sha256sum rocky-9-latest-x86_64-minimal.iso expected 3f2b...c9a1  rocky-9-latest-x86_64-minimal.iso cmd shasum -a 256 rocky-9-latest-aarch64-minimal.iso expected (macos) 64 hex characters followed by the file name differs 64 hexadecimal characters are expected; a shorter output means the command failed. windows: `get-filehash file.iso -algorithm sha256` prints a table; paste the hash column. different from the published value? delete the file and download again. v03 title create and install the vm text create the vm (2 cpu, 4 gb ram, 25 gb disk), install the system, create an administrator user and boot into the login prompt. blocks differs boot loop or \ : check the iso is attached and the boot order starts with the optical drive. virtualbox on windows: enable virtualization (vt-x/amd-v) in the bios and disable hyper-v conflicts. v04 title first login text log in with your user and show which system you installed. paste the output. blocks cmd cat /etc/os-release expected name=\ \nversion=\ }],  : [ ubuntu\ on wsl the file exists too; the text is the same. v05 title take a snapshot text shut down cleanly with `sudo poweroff`, take a snapshot named `clean-install`, then start the vm again. blocks cmd sudo poweroff expected (the vm window closes) differs snapshots greyed out? power the vm off first (in virtualbox the snapshot button is in the machine tools). v06 title find the ip address text show your interfaces and paste the output. blocks cmd ip -brief a expected lo     unknown  127.0.0.1/8\nenp0s3 up       10.0.2.15/24 differs `10.0.2.15` means nat; use the port-forward rule to reach it from the host. no ipv4 address on enp0s3? run `nmcli device` and connect the interface, or check the vm network adapter is enabled. v07 title connect over ssh text connect from your host terminal to the vm and run the command below. paste the output. blocks cmd ssh student@192.168.1.50 expected (you get a prompt on the vm) cmd echo $ssh_connection expected 192.168.1.10 51234 192.168.1.50 22 differs `connection refused`: sshd is not running (`sudo systemctl enable --now sshd`). `connection timed out`: wrong ip or no port-forward rule (nat). `permission denied`: wrong user name or password. v08 title update the system text bring the system up to date, reboot and tick \  when the update finished without errors. blocks cmd sudo dnf -y update   # rocky/alma expected complete! cmd sudo apt update && sudo apt -y upgrade   # ubuntu expected (no e: errors) differs `could not resolve host`: the vm has no internet; check the network adapter. quiz : { what does a matching sha-256 checksum tell you? options the iso is the newest version the file is complete and unmodified the iso is free of cost the vm will boot faster explain a checksum is a fingerprint; equal fingerprints mean the file is identical to the published one. : { which network mode hides the vm from your lan but allows internet access? options bridged host-only nat none explain nat shares the host connection; use port forwarding to reach the vm. : { when should you take a snapshot? options before a risky experiment never; it wastes disk space only after deleting the vm only on wsl explain a snapshot is a quick undo point; take one before changes you may regret. : { which tool is the usual choice on an apple silicon mac? options virtualbox with x86 iso wsl 2 windows hyper-v utm with an arm64 iso explain apple silicon is arm; utm runs arm64 guests natively. summary a vm is a safe, disposable linux that you can fully control. always verify the iso checksum before installing. snapshot after a clean install and before experiments. ssh from the host terminal is the professional way to work. glossary term meaning virtual machine: a complete computer simulated by software. term iso meaning disk image file of an installation medium. term checksum meaning fingerprint of a file used to detect damage or tampering. term snapshot meaning saved state of a vm you can return to. term ssh meaning secure shell: encrypted remote terminal protocol. term nat meaning network address translation: vm shares the host connection.

0.3.title: The terminal and first steps
objectives: You can read the user, machine and directory shown in the prompt.
You run safe first commands such as whoami, hostname, pwd and ls.
You find help yourself with man, --help and error messages.
0.3.text: title the terminal and first steps lead learn to read the prompt, type your first commands and find help when you get stuck. objectives you can read the user, machine and directory shown in the prompt. you run safe first commands such as whoami, hostname, pwd and ls. you find help yourself with man, --help and error messages. sections prompt title terminal and prompt body the **terminal** is the window where you give the computer text commands. the program running inside it is the **shell**; the most common one is `bash`. the shell reads your line, runs it and prints the result. the **prompt** at the start of each line tells you three things: who you are, which machine you are on and which directory you are in. example: `student@linux-lab:~$` — user `student`, machine `linux-lab`, `~` means the home directory. a trailing `$` marks a normal user, `#` marks the administrator (root). tip nothing runs until you press enter. use backspace to fix typos. first title first commands: who am i, where am i? body before touching a system you must know who you are and where you are. the commands below only read information and change nothing. click a box to paste the command into the terminal. commands cmd whoami what prints the user you are working as. where after login, and before and after using sudo. why prevents actions with the wrong user. example whoami cmd hostname what prints the machine's name. where when you connect to several servers. why makes sure you are on the right machine. example hostname cmd pwd what prints the full path of the current directory. where whenever you feel lost. why knowing your location prevents mistakes in file operations. example pwd cmd what lists files and folders in the current directory. -l adds details. where everywhere — the most used command. why look around before you act. example ls -l cmd echo what prints the text you give it and expands variables like $user. where in scripts and for quick experiments. why the simplest way to see a variable's value. example echo $user help title getting help and reading errors body every linux command has a manual: `man command` shows it in full, `command --help` shows a short summary. if you type an unknown command the shell says `command not found` — that is information, not a disaster: you probably made a typo. the shell also saves time: **tab** completes commands and file names, **↑ / ↓** recalls earlier commands, `history` lists them all with numbers, `clear` wipes the screen. commands cmd man what shows a command's manual page. where when you want to look up a command's options. why you get the right information straight from your own system. example man ls cmd --help what prints a short usage summary. where for a quick refresher. why shorter than man and often enough. example ls --help cmd history what lists earlier commands with numbers. where to find an old command again. why you don't have to retype everything. example history tip pressing tab twice lists all possible completions. try typing `whoa` and press tab. preview title symbols you will see later body in this course some commands and symbols appear in tasks before their own module. for now just know what they do; you will learn the details in the matching module. `cd dir` changes your current directory (details: module 1.1). `>` writes a command's output into a file instead of the screen, `>>` appends to the end of a file (module 3.2). `cat file` prints a file's content (module 2.6). `|` (pipe) feeds one command's output into the next (module 3.2). `&&` and `;` run commands one after another (module 1.4). `sudo` runs a command with administrator rights (module 4.3). `mkdir` and `touch` create folders and empty files (module 2.3); `grep`, `head`, `tail`, `wc` filter and count text (modules 3.4–3.5). tip do not memorize this list. come back here when a task puzzles you; you will work with full cards for the same symbols when you reach their module. tasks t01 text type `whoami` and read which user you are working as. hint just type the command name and press enter. t02 text use `hostname` to find the machine's name. hint the output matches the word after the @ in the prompt. t03 text use `pwd` to print the full path of the current directory. hint the path starts with / — an absolute path. t04 text print this text with `echo \ hint put the text inside double quotes. t05 text list the directory in detail with `ls -l`. what does the `d` in the first column mean? hint d means directory, - means a regular file. t06 text open the manual of `ls` with `man ls`. hint the command name follows man. t07 text show the short help with `ls --help`. hint two dashes, no space: --help t08 text deliberately type a command that does not exist (e.g. `lss`) and read the error. hint the message is command not found — a sign of a typo. t09 text show the running kernel version with `uname -r`. hint -r stands for release. t10 text type `echo $user`. is the output the same as `whoami`? hint the dollar sign expands the variable to its value. t11 text run in order: `pwd`, `ls`, `cd documents`, `pwd`. how did your location change? hint four separate lines, each with enter. t12 text list the commands you typed in this session with `history`. hint a numbered list appears. t13 text clear the screen with `clear`. hint shortcut: ctrl+l t14 text challenge: in your home directory create a file with `echo hello > first.txt`, then read it with `cat first.txt`. hint the > writes output into a file, `cd` changes directory, `cat` reads a file (see \ ). first return home with `cd ~`. t15 text predict: `cd ~/documents`, then `cd ..`, then `pwd`. predict which path you will see before running it, then check. hint `..` means the parent directory. t16 text debug: a colleague typed `cat nots.txt` and got an error. find the correct name with `ls` in your home directory and read the file with `cat`. hint a misspelled file name gives 'no such file'; use the name from the `ls` output. t17 text mini project: write your user name into a file with `whoami > hello.txt`, then read it with `cat hello.txt`. hint `>` redirects output into a file (see \ ). `cd ~` first. t18 text ticket #1001 — support needs system info: in your home directory write the kernel version (`uname -r`) and then the host name (`hostname`) into `info.txt`. the file must have 2 lines. hint use `>` for the first and `>>` (append) for the second; otherwise the first line is lost. see \  for these symbols. quiz : { your prompt ends with `#`. what does that mean? options the command was written as a comment you are working as the administrator (root) the file is hidden the terminal is broken explain `$` means a normal user, `#` means root. a wrong command as root can do great damage — be careful. : { how do you open a command's manual? options help command manual command man command read command explain `man command` opens the full manual; `command --help` gives a short summary. : { what does `command not found` usually mean? options the command name is misspelled or the command is not installed the computer will shut down the disk is full there is no internet explain check the spelling first; then check whether the command is installed. : { which key completes a partly typed command or file name? options esc ctrl+z tab alt explain tab completes; pressed twice it lists the options. summary the prompt shows user, machine and directory; `$` is normal, `#` is root. `whoami`, `hostname`, `pwd`, `ls` are safe exploration commands. for help use `man command` and `command --help`; error messages are clues. tab, ↑/↓ and `history` save time. glossary term terminal meaning the window where you type commands. term shell meaning the program that runs your commands, e.g. bash. term prompt meaning the user@machine:directory info at the start of each line. term home directory meaning the user's own folder, written as ~. : { do the tasks below on your own linux vm (rocky/alma or ubuntu). if you do not have a vm yet, see module 0.2 first. tasks v01 title find your kernel version text open a terminal in your vm and print the version of the running kernel. paste the output below. blocks cmd uname -r expected 5.14.0-427.13.1.el9_4.x86_64 differs your version number may differ; what matters is a dotted version such as `5.14.0`. if you see `command not found`, check spelling (lower case, spaces). v02 title identify your distribution text the file `/etc/os-release` tells you the distribution name and version. blocks cmd cat /etc/os-release expected name=\ \nversion=\ \nid=\ }],  : [ ubuntu\ on `no such file` make sure you are on a real distribution, not a bare container. v03 title your first file text write and read a file in your home directory. the output must contain `hello`; then press \ blocks cmd cd ~ && echo hello > first.txt && cat first.txt expected hello differs if nothing shows, check with `ls -l first.txt` that the file was created.

1.1.title: Navigating the Terminal: pwd, ls, cd
objectives: You see your current directory with `pwd` and know that the `~` in the prompt is the home directory.
You list directory contents with `ls` and its options (`-l`, `-a`, `-h`) and find hidden files.
You move between directories with `cd` using the shortcuts `~`, `-`, `..` and `.`.
You know the difference between absolute and relative paths, read the columns in `ls -l` output and use Tab completion.
1.1.text:
title navigating the terminal: pwd, ls, cd lead see where you are, get to know your surroundings, reach your target: move around the file system safely with `pwd`, `ls` and `cd`. objectives you see your current directory with `pwd` and know that the `~` in the prompt is the home directory. you list directory contents with `ls` and its options (`-l`, `-a`, `-h`) and find hidden files. you move between directories with `cd` using the shortcuts `~`, `-`, `..` and `.`. you know the difference between absolute and relative paths, read the columns in `ls -l` output and use tab completion. sections where title where am i? pwd and the home directory body in linux everything lives in a single tree whose root is `/`. in the terminal you are always somewhere in this tree: your **current working directory**. most commands act there unless told otherwise. `pwd` (print working directory) prints your current directory as a **full path**. a command run in the wrong directory can cause data loss, so check with `pwd` especially before deleting or copying. when you log in you land in your **home directory**, such as `/home/student`. it is written `~` for short; that is the `~` in the prompt. commands cmd pwd what shows your current directory as a full path. where before any operation, especially deleting and copying. why prevents wrong operations in the wrong directory. example pwd cmd echo ~ what prints the expansion of the `~` shortcut, i.e. the full path of your home directory. where when you want to know the path of your home directory. why `~` is expanded by the shell; commands see the real path. example echo ~ tip a `~` in the prompt means you are in your home directory; in any other directory only the last folder name, such as `documents`, is shown. title what is inside? ls body `ls` lists the contents of your current directory. if you give it a directory as a path, it lists that one without entering it: `ls /etc`. look first, then decide. options start with `-` and can be combined: `-l` detailed list, `-a` including hidden files, `-h` human-readable sizes (k, m, g). `ls -lah` gives all three at once. commands cmd what lists the files and folders in your current directory. where after entering a directory or when checking whether something exists. why working where you don't know what is there is dangerous. example }, { ls /etc what lists the contents of the given directory without entering it. where to look at another directory. why you look without changing your working directory. example ls /etc cmd ls -a what also shows hidden files whose names start with a dot. where when looking for configuration files. why hidden files do not appear in normal `ls` output. example ls -a cmd ls -lh what detailed list; prints sizes as k/m/g. where when looking at file sizes. why easier than reading byte counts. example ls -lh ~ tip if `ls` output is long in a directory with many files, use `ls -l | head` to see the first lines. (`|` feeds the first command's output to the second and `head` shows the first 10 lines; details in modules 3.2 and 2.6.) title reach your target: cd body `cd` (change directory) changes your working directory. on success it prints nothing; you see the result in the prompt or with `pwd`. if the directory does not exist, you get an error. shortcuts: `cd` (without an argument) and `cd ~` take you to your home directory, `cd ..` goes up one directory, `cd -` returns to the previous directory. `.` is the current directory; `cd .` stays where you are. case matters: `documents` and `documents` are different names. if a name contains a space, use quotes: `cd \ ],  : [{ cd documents what enters the `documents` folder in your current directory. where when going down into a subfolder. why relative path: starts from where you are. example cd documents cmd cd .. what goes up one directory. where when leaving a folder. why `..` points to the parent directory in every directory. example cd .. cmd cd ~ what goes to the home directory. where when you are lost. why works wherever you are. example cd ~ cmd cd - what returns to the previous directory and prints its path. where when switching back and forth between two directories. why saves you from retyping long paths. example cd - cmd what typed without an argument, goes to the home directory. where to get home quickly. why same as `cd ~`, but shorter. example }],  if you get lost, type `cd`, then check with `pwd`: you are back in your home directory. paths title absolute and relative paths body an **absolute path** starts with `/` and is the full address from the root: `/usr/bin`. it always leads to the same place regardless of where you are. `~/documents` also counts as absolute, because `~` expands to a full path. a **relative path** does not start with `/` and is computed from your current directory: `documents`, `../downloads`, `./notes.txt`. the same spelling leads to different places in different directories. `..` is the parent directory and `.` is the current directory; they can be chained: `cd ../..` goes up two directories. when you are in `/usr/bin`, `cd ../..` takes you to the root `/`. commands cmd cd /usr/bin what goes straight to `/usr/bin` using an absolute path. where when heading to a target regardless of where you are. why the result is always the same. example cd /usr/bin cmd cd ../.. what goes up two directories. where when leaving a deep folder quickly. why in relative paths `..` can be chained. example cd ../.. tip if you are unsure, type the absolute path; for short distances a relative path is faster. hidden title hidden files body files and folders whose names **start with a dot** are hidden: `.bashrc`, `.profile`, `.config`. normal `ls` does not show them, `ls -a` does. settings are usually kept in these files. in `ls -a` output you see two special entries: `.` (the current directory) and `..` (the parent directory). they are not real files but shortcuts present in every directory. commands cmd ls -a ~ what lists everything in the home directory, including hidden files. where when looking for configuration files. why files like `.bashrc` only show up this way. example ls -a ~ cmd ls -a what shows hidden files without `.` and `..`. where for a cleaner list (on a real vm). why same as `-a`, but without the two shortcut entries. example ls -a ~ nosim warn do not delete or damage configuration files such as `.bashrc` and `.profile`; your shell environment may break. longlist title reading ls -l output body `ls -l` gives one line per file. example: `-rw-r--r-- 1 student student 35 nov 12 10:32 notes.txt`. from left to right: **1st character:** type. `-` regular file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link. **next 9 characters:** permissions (`rw-r--r--`: owner reads/writes, group and others read). **number:** link count. **two names:** owner user and group. **number:** size in bytes. **date:** last modification. **last:** name. the `total` line at the top is the sum of disk blocks used. you will see the details of permissions in later modules. commands cmd ls -l what detailed list showing type, permissions, owner, size, date and name. where when checking a file's owner or permissions. why all the basic information about a file in one line. example ls -l cmd ls -ld ~ what shows a directory itself (not its contents) in detail. where when checking a directory's permissions or owner. why without `-d`, `ls` looks inside the directory. example ls -ld ~ tip if the line starts with `d` it is a folder, if it starts with `-` it is a file. tab title tab completion body don't type long names by hand in the terminal: type the first letters of the name and press **tab**. if there is a single match, the shell completes the name. if there are several matches, press tab **twice**; the options are listed. it works for commands as well as file and folder names. it saves time and prevents typos: if tab does not complete, that name does not exist or you are in the wrong directory. extra shortcut: the **↑/↓** keys recall previous commands. these features work in a real shell (on your vm). commands cmd cd doc + tab what typing `doc` and pressing tab completes it to `documents/`. where in every command, when typing file and folder names. why you type less and make fewer mistakes. example cd doc nosim tip make it a habit: press tab before typing a name from start to finish. tasks t01 text show your current directory with `pwd`. hint the output is a full path starting with `/`. t02 text list the contents of your home directory with `ls`. hint `ls` without an argument looks at your current directory. t03 text enter the `documents` folder with `cd documents`. hint the directory name in the prompt should change. t04 text list in detail with `ls -l`. hint `-l` is a lowercase l. t05 text list including hidden files with `ls -a`. hint `.hidden_notes.txt` should be visible. t06 text go to the `~/projects/website` directory using an absolute path. hint `cd ~/projects/website`. t07 text enter the `css` subfolder using a relative path. hint you are already inside `website`: `cd css`. t08 text while inside `css`, use `..` to move to the sibling folder `images`. hint first up, then down: `cd ../images`. t09 text return to the previous directory with `cd -`. hint don't forget the dash character. t10 text return to your home directory with `cd` without an argument. hint `cd` or `cd ~`. t11 text predict: if you type `cd /usr/bin/../..` from a command in `/usr/bin`, where do you end up? think first, then run the command and verify with `pwd`. hint each `..` goes up one directory: `/usr/bin` → `/usr` → `/`. t12 text predict: what are the type, owner and permissions of the file `/etc/hostname`? verify with `ls -l /etc/hostname`. hint if the first character is `-` it is a regular file; the owner will be `root`. t13 text debug: a friend types `cd ~/downloads` and gets `no such file or directory`. go to the `downloads` folder using the correct name. hint case matters in linux: `downloads`. t14 text mini project: go to the `~/projects/website/css` directory, list its contents, then go up two directories and finish in `~/projects`. hint `cd ~/projects/website/css`, `ls -l`, `cd ../..`. t15 text challenge: list the contents of both `~/documents` and `~/projects/website`, including hidden files, with a single `ls` command. hint `ls` can take multiple paths; use it together with `-a`. t16 text ticket #1101 — a colleague wants the full path of the `images` folder in the `website` project. go to the folder, show the path with `pwd`, then return to your home directory. hint `cd ~/projects/website/images`, `pwd`, `cd`. : { run these tasks on your own vm (ubuntu, rocky, alma or wsl). they are all read-only; they change nothing. tasks v01 title where am i? text open the terminal; print your current directory and the path of your home directory, and paste the output. blocks cmd pwd
echo ~ expected /home/student
/home/student differs if your username is not `student`, your own name appears in the path; that is normal. if the output is `/root`, you are running as root; switch to a normal user. v02 title find hidden files text list your home directory including hidden files and find the `.bashrc` file. blocks cmd ls -a ~ expected .  ..  .bash_logout  .bashrc  .profile  desktop  documents ... differs you may see many hidden folders (`.cache`, `.config`); that is normal. on wsl, `.bashrc` is still in the home directory; make sure you look under `~`. v03 title absolute, relative and cd - text go to `/var/log` using an absolute path, go up with `..`, return with `cd -` and print the paths. blocks cmd cd /var/log
pwd
cd ..
pwd
cd -
cd /etc
pwd expected /var/log
/var
/var/log
/etc differs `cd -` also prints the previous path by itself; seeing an extra line is normal. if `/var/log` does not exist (very minimal image), try `cd /usr/bin` instead. v04 title read ls -l text list the file `/etc/passwd` in detail; read its type, permissions, owner and size. blocks cmd ls -l /etc/passwd expected -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 1234 nov 12 10:32 /etc/passwd differs a `.` or `+` at the end of the permissions (selinux/acl) is normal. size and date vary depending on your system. v05 title tab completion text type `cd doc` and press tab without pressing enter; it should complete to `documents/`. then type `cd ~/` and press tab twice to see the list. when done, say \ blocks cmd cd doc<tab> differs if it does not complete, the `documents` folder does not exist or you are not in your home directory; check with `pwd`. on some minimal systems the `bash-completion` package is needed for completion. quiz : { what does the `pwd` command do? options lists files shows the current directory as a full path changes directory changes the password explain `pwd` (print working directory) prints the working directory. : { what does `cd ..` do? options goes to the home directory stays in place goes up one directory returns to the previous directory explain `..` is the parent directory; use `cd ~` for home and `cd -` for the previous one. : { which one is used to see hidden files? options ls -a ls -l ls -h ls -r explain `-a` shows files whose names start with a dot. : { in `ls -l` output, what does it mean if a line starts with `d`? options deleted file executable file symbolic link directory explain the first character shows the type: `d` directory, `-` file, `l` symbolic link. summary `pwd` tells you where you are, `ls` what is there, `cd` where to go. `~` is the home directory, `..` the parent directory, `.` the current directory, `cd -` the previous directory. an absolute path starts with `/`; a relative path is computed from your current directory. `ls -a` shows hidden files, `ls -l` shows type, permissions, owner, size and date. complete with tab; mind upper and lower case. glossary term working directory meaning the directory you are currently in, where commands run by default. term home directory meaning the directory that belongs to the user; abbreviated `~`, for example `/home/student`. term absolute path meaning a full address starting from the `/` root. term relative path meaning a path starting from your current directory. term hidden file meaning a file whose name starts with a dot, visible with `ls -a`. term tab completion meaning typing the start of a name and pressing tab to have the shell complete it.

1.2.title: Identity and System — whoami, id, uname
objectives: You read your user identity, UID/GID values and group memberships with `whoami`, `id` and `groups`.
You find the machine name, kernel version and architecture with `hostname` and `uname`.
You identify the distribution and its version with `/etc/os-release`.
You see the time and how long the system has been running with `date` and `uptime`.
You read disk and memory usage with `df -h` and `free -h`.
You use environment variables with `env` and `$USER`.
1.2.text:
title identity and system — whoami, id, uname lead before you touch a system, answer two questions: who am i? which machine am i on? this module teaches you how, using safe read-only commands. objectives you read your user identity, uid/gid values and group memberships with `whoami`, `id` and `groups`. you find the machine name, kernel version and architecture with `hostname` and `uname`. you identify the distribution and its version with `/etc/os-release`. you see the time and how long the system has been running with `date` and `uptime`. you read disk and memory usage with `df -h` and `free -h`. you use environment variables with `env` and `$user`. sections identity title who am i? whoami, id, groups body before you run a command you should know which account you are using: a normal user or an administrator? a command run with the wrong account either fails or does more damage than intended because of excess privileges. `whoami` prints only the user name. `id` says more: the numeric user id **uid**, the primary group id **gid** and all groups you belong to. linux permissions look at these numbers, not at names. uid 0 is always **root** (the administrator); normal users usually start at 1000. `groups` lists the same groups, names only. in this course the user `student` belongs to the groups `student`, `wheel` and `devs`. `wheel` is the administrator group that allows `sudo` on the rhel family (on ubuntu this group is called `sudo`). commands cmd whoami what prints the current user name. where after logging in, after using `sudo`, or inside a script. why prevents actions with the wrong user. example whoami cmd what shows uid, gid and all groups. where when investigating `permission denied` errors. why permissions are checked by numbers and group membership. example }, { groups what lists the names of the groups you belong to. where to check whether you can reach a file through a group. why shorter and easier to read than `id`. example groups cmd id -u what prints only the uid number. where in scripts, to test whether you are root (0 = root). why a single number is easy to compare in a script. example id -u nosim tip `whoami` gives a name, `id` gives the numbers the system really uses. when in doubt, run `id`. host title which machine? hostname and uname body when you have several servers or vms, their command lines all look alike. `hostname` tells you the machine's name on the network; it is the cheapest way to confirm you are on the right machine before a destructive command. `uname` reports on the kernel. `uname -r` prints the kernel release, `uname -m` the architecture (`x86_64` = 64-bit intel/amd, `aarch64` = arm) and `uname -a` everything in one line. you are asked for these values when opening a support ticket or downloading software. commands cmd hostname what prints the machine's name. where to tell servers apart, when writing a ticket. why prevents working on the wrong machine. example hostname cmd uname -r what prints the running kernel version. where for bug reports or driver compatibility checks. why the kernel version decides which features exist. example uname -r cmd uname -m what prints the machine architecture. where before downloading a package or iso. why packages are built per architecture. example uname -m cmd uname -a what prints all system information on one line. where to paste into a support request. why name, kernel and architecture at once. example uname -a cmd hostname -i what prints the machine's ip address(es). where when you want to connect to your vm via ssh. why the shortest way to find the address. example hostname -i nosim tip the `student@linux-lab` part of the prompt is user@machine; `whoami` and `hostname` give the same information. distro title which distribution? /etc/os-release body even with the same kernel, distributions differ. the distribution name and version are stored as plain text in `/etc/os-release`, in the same format on ubuntu, rocky, alma and others. you read it with `cat`; you do not change it. `name` and `version` give the readable name, `pretty_name` a one-line summary, and `id_like` the family (`debian` or `rhel fedora`). the family tells you which package manager to use: `apt` or `dnf`. commands cmd cat /etc/os-release what shows the complete distribution information. where as the first step on a new system. why decides which commands and packages apply. example cat /etc/os-release cmd grep pretty_name /etc/os-release what shows only the readable distribution name. where to put a single line into a ticket. why filters the one line you need out of a longer file. example grep pretty_name /etc/os-release cmd grep id_like /etc/os-release what shows the family the distribution belongs to. where when you are unsure whether to use `apt` or `dnf`. why the family determines the package manager. example grep id_like /etc/os-release tip wsl has the same file; it shows the linux distribution inside, not windows. time title time and uptime: date, uptime body `date` prints the system time and time zone. you need it when reading logs and when putting dates in backup file names. you can change the format with a pattern starting with `+`: `date +%f` → `2026-11-12`. `uptime` gives three things on one line: the time, how long the system has been running and the **load average** for the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. if the load is far above the number of cpu cores, the system is slow. you also notice unexpected reboots here. commands cmd date what prints the current date and time. where when matching log entries to times. why a wrong clock is a common cause of certificate and log problems. example date cmd date +%f what prints the date as yyyy-mm-dd. where when adding a date to file names (`backup-2026-11-12`). why a consistent format that sorts alphabetically. example date +%f nosim cmd uptime what shows uptime and load average. where the first place to look when the system is slow. why quickly shows load and the last reboot. example uptime cmd uptime -p what prints uptime in readable form (`up 2 days, 3 hours`). where to report the duration briefly. why gives only the duration, without load figures. example uptime -p nosim tip compare the load average with the core count: on 4 cores, 4.0 means fully busy. resources title disk and memory: df -h, free -h body `df` (disk free) shows how full the mounted file systems are. `-h` (human-readable) uses units like `g` and `m` instead of bytes. if the `use%` column goes above 90%, take care: a full disk makes services crash. `free` shows memory (ram) and swap. the important column is `available`: the memory that can be given to new programs. a small `free` value is normal, because linux uses spare memory as cache (`buff/cache`). both only read; neither changes anything. commands cmd df -h what shows size and usage of all file systems. where on a `no space left on device` error. why finds out which partition is full. example df -h cmd df -h / what shows only the root file system. where when checking a single partition. why keeps the output short. example df -h / cmd free -h what shows memory and swap usage in readable units. where when the system is slow. why the `available` column shows the memory that is really free. example free -h warn `df` measures file systems, `du` measures folders; do not mix them up. you find a full disk with `df -h` and look for the cause with tools you will meet in later modules. tip do not worry about a small value in the `free` column of `free` output; look at `available`. env title environment variables: env and $user body the shell stores information in **environment variables**. `$user` holds the user name, `$home` the home directory, `$shell` the shell and `$hostname` the machine name. you use a value by putting `$` in front: `echo $user`. `env` lists all variables as `name=value`. to pick a single one from the long output, combine it with `grep` using `|` (pipe): `env | grep user`. (`|` and `grep` are covered in modules 3.2 and 3.4.) variables are handy in scripts: `echo \ ` combines the user and the machine. the output of the command inside `$(...)` is inserted in its place. commands cmd env what lists all environment variables. where when investigating where a setting comes from. why shows the values you are running with. example env cmd echo $user what prints the value of the user name variable. where in scripts and file names. why you do not have to type the user name by hand. example echo $user cmd echo $home what prints the path of the home directory. where to write portable paths. why works for every user instead of a fixed `/home/student`. example echo $home cmd env | grep user what filters the variables whose name contains user. where to find one variable in a long list. why a pipe and `grep` narrow down the output. example env | grep user cmd echo \ what combines user and machine name. where when building a report line or log message. why shows how a variable and command output are combined. example echo \ }, { printenv user what prints the value of a single variable. where in a script when you need only the value. why no `grep` needed, the output is just the value. example printenv user nosim tip variable names are case-sensitive: `$user` works, `$user` is empty. tasks t01 text find out which user you are with `whoami`. hint just type `whoami` and press enter. t02 text find out the machine's name with `hostname`. hint it should match the part after `@` in the prompt. t03 text print the kernel version with `uname -r`. hint `-r` stands for release. t04 text run `id` to see uid, gid and all groups. hint if `uid=` is 1000 you are a normal user, if 0 you are root. t05 text list your groups with `groups` and compare with the `id` output. hint `groups` prints names only, no numbers. t06 text read the distribution information with `cat /etc/os-release`. hint the `pretty_name` line is the summary. t07 text see how long the system has been running and the load average with `uptime`. hint the last three numbers are the 1, 5 and 15 minute load. t08 text run `df -h` to see disk usage in readable units. hint look at the `use%` column. t09 text show the memory status with `free -h`. hint the really free memory is in the `available` column. t10 text among the environment variables, filter only those containing user: `env | grep user`. hint the `|` sign passes the output of `env` to `grep`. t11 text predict: is the user `student` in the group `devs`? then verify with `groups`. hint say your guess first, then run the command. t12 text predict: what does `echo \ ` print? verify by running it. hint `$user` and `$(hostname)` are replaced by their values before the command runs. t13 text the file `~/kernel.txt` contains an old kernel version. fix it so it holds the real kernel version. hint `uname -r > ~/kernel.txt` overwrites the old content. then check with `cat ~/kernel.txt`. t14 text create `~/me.txt` containing, in order, the output of `whoami`, `id` and `hostname` (3 lines). hint use `>` for the first and `>>` for the others: `whoami > ~/me.txt`, `id >> ~/me.txt`. (`>` writes output to a file, `>>` appends; details in module 3.2.) t15 text write the readable distribution name, without the `pretty_name=` prefix, into `~/distro.txt`. hint `grep pretty_name /etc/os-release | cut -d= -f2 > ~/distro.txt`: `cut` takes what follows the `=` sign. (`cut` is covered in module 3.5, `grep` and `|` in modules 3.4 and 3.2.) t16 text write only the major number (first number) of the kernel version into `~/major.txt`. hint take the output of `uname -r`, split it at the dot with `cut -d. -f1` and keep the first field. (`cut` is covered in module 3.5.) t17 text ticket: support wants system information. write the machine name, kernel version, user name and the `df -h` output, in that order, into `~/sysinfo.txt`. hint start with `hostname > ~/sysinfo.txt`, then append the other four outputs with `>>`. t18 text ticket: the administrator asks whether the account `student` is in the `wheel` group. as evidence, save only the output containing `wheel` into `~/admin_check.txt`. hint `id | grep wheel > ~/admin_check.txt` (`|` passes output to the next command, `grep` filters; details in modules 3.2 and 3.4.) : { all commands in this section are read-only; you can run them safely on your vm. output may differ by distribution; what matters is that you recognise the structure. tasks v01 title find your identity text show your user name, uid/gid values and groups; paste the `id` output. blocks cmd whoami
id
groups expected student
uid=1000(student) gid=1000(student) groups=1000(student),10(wheel)
student wheel differs on ubuntu the administrator group is called `sudo`, not `wheel`; in the `id` output you see `27(sudo)`. your user name may not be `student`; that is fine, just see your own name. v02 title machine and kernel text show the machine name and the full kernel information; paste the `uname -a` output. blocks cmd hostname
uname -r
uname -m
uname -a expected linux-lab
5.14.0-427.el9.x86_64
x86_64
linux linux-lab 5.14.0-427.el9.x86_64 #1 smp preempt_dynamic ... x86_64 gnu/linux differs your kernel version may differ (`6.8...` on ubuntu 24.04); what matters is that the output starts with `linux`. on a vm on apple silicon the architecture shows `aarch64`. v03 title know your distribution text read the distribution information and paste the output. blocks cmd cat /etc/os-release
grep id_like /etc/os-release expected name=\ 
version=\ 
pretty_name=\ 
id_like=\ }],  : [ some distributions have no `id_like` line at all (for example debian itself); `grep` then prints nothing. v04 title time and uptime text show the date and how long the system has been running; paste the `uptime` output. blocks cmd date
date +%f
uptime expected thu nov 12 10:28:55 cet 2026
2026-11-12
 10:28:55 up 2 days,  3:12,  1 user,  load average: 0.08, 0.03, 0.01 differs on a freshly started vm the uptime is shown in minutes (`up 12 min`). the date format and time zone can vary with the system language. v05 title disk and memory text show disk and memory status in readable units; paste both outputs together. blocks cmd df -h
free -h expected filesystem      size  used avail use% mounted on
/dev/mapper/rhel-root  20g  4.1g  16g  21% /
...
               total        used        free  ...
mem:           3.8gi       612mi       2.4gi ... differs on wsl the `df -h` output also lists the windows drives (`c:\`). the memory columns show different numbers depending on your vm settings. v06 title environment variables text print the user variable and filter it from the `env` output. blocks cmd echo $user
echo $home
env | grep user
echo \ expected student
/home/student
user=student
student@linux-lab differs `env | grep user` may return several lines (for example ones matching `xdg_session_...`); look for the `user=` line. on some systems `$user` is empty (for example inside a container); `whoami` still works. v07 title see the administrator identity text run `whoami` with `sudo`: the command now runs as root. if it asks for a password, type your account's password (it is not shown while typing). `sudo` is covered in module 4.3. blocks cmd whoami
sudo whoami
whoami expected student
root
student differs if you get `student is not in the sudoers file`, your account is not in the administrator group; try the user you created during installation. `root` must appear in the middle; `sudo` elevates only that one command, afterwards you are a normal user again. quiz : { you see `uid=0(...)` in the `id` output. what does it mean? options the account is disabled the user is root (administrator) the user is a guest the user belongs to no group explain uid 0 always belongs to root. normal users usually get a uid of 1000 or higher. : { which command shows the running kernel version? options `hostname` `whoami` `uname -r` `df -h` explain `uname -r` prints the kernel version. `hostname` shows the machine name, `whoami` the user, `df -h` the disk. : { which command shows disk usage in readable units (gb, mb)? options `df -h` `free -h` `uptime` `id` explain `df -h` shows file systems. `free -h` shows memory, `uptime` the running time. : { which environment variable holds the current user's name? options `$host` `$name` `$who` `$user` explain `$user` holds the user name; `$home` holds the home directory, `$shell` the shell. summary `whoami`, `id`, `groups`: show who you are and which permissions you have; uid 0 = root. `hostname` and `uname -r/-m/-a`: machine name, kernel version and architecture. `/etc/os-release`: distribution name, version and family (`id_like`). `date` and `uptime`: the time, and the uptime with the load average. `df -h` and `free -h`: disk and memory status; for memory look at the `available` column. `env`, `$user`, `$home`: environment variables; you use a value with `$`. before starting any task, check who you are and which machine you are on. glossary term uid meaning user number; permission checks use this number, not names. 0 = root. term gid meaning group number; identifies the user's primary group. term wheel meaning the administrator group that grants `sudo` on the rhel family (`sudo` on ubuntu). term kernel meaning the linux core that manages the hardware; its version is shown by `uname -r`. term hostname meaning the machine's name on the network. term load average meaning average system load over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes; shown by `uptime`. term environment variable meaning a `name=value` pair kept by the shell, for example `user` or `home`.

1.3.title: Help and discovery
objectives: You open a man page, navigate it, search it and quit; you recognise the section numbers (1, 5, 8).
You get a quick summary with --help and help, and read SYNOPSIS notation ([ ], | and ...).
You find where a command is and what type it is with which and type, and search for files with find.
You review old commands with history and systematically resolve 'command not found' errors (exit code 127).
1.3.text:
title help and discovery lead use man, --help, which, type, find and history to research an unfamiliar command on your own, without the internet. objectives you open a man page, navigate it, search it and quit; you recognise the section numbers (1, 5, 8). you get a quick summary with --help and help, and read synopsis notation ([ ], | and ...). you find where a command is and what type it is with which and type, and search for files with find. you review old commands with history and systematically resolve 'command not found' errors (exit code 127). sections man title man: manual pages body linux has hundreds of commands; even professionals don't memorise them all, they **know where to look**. the most reliable source is the system's own manual, the `man` pages: `man ls`. the page opens in a pager: **space** goes down a page, **b** goes up, **/kernel** + enter searches the text, **n** jumps to the next match, **q** quits. page headings are always the same: name (short name), synopsis (usage form), description, options, examples, see also. the manual is split into **sections**: 1 = user commands, 5 = file formats (e.g. `/etc/passwd`), 8 = administration commands. the same name can appear in several sections: `man passwd` shows the command, `man 5 passwd` shows the file format. in the simulator the pages are short and section numbers are not supported; on a real vm you see the full page. commands cmd man what opens the manual page of a command. where when learning a new command or option. why it is accurate information that ships with your system and matches its version. example man ls cmd man <section> what opens a specific manual section. where when the same name is both a command and a file format. why you reach the right page directly. example man 5 passwd nosim cmd whatis what gives a one-line description of a command. where to quickly remember what a command does. why you get a summary without opening the page. example whatis ls nosim cmd apropos what searches manual pages by keyword. where when you don't know the command's name but know what it does. why searching for 'copy file' lets you find cp. example apropos copy nosim tip if you get lost in a page, leave with `q`. to search, type `/`, enter the word, press enter; the next match is `n`. warn `whatis` and `apropos` rely on an index (mandb); on freshly installed minimal systems they may return nothing. in that case run `sudo mandb`. help title --help and help: quick summary body if you don't want to read the whole manual, `ls --help` prints a short usage summary. if the output is long, limit it with `| head` or `| less`: `ls --help | head -n 5`. **shell built-in** commands like `cd` have no separate program, so `man cd` sometimes doesn't exist. for them bash has the `help` command: `help cd`. on its own, `help` lists the known commands (in the simulator this list is short). quick rule: for an external program use `--help` first, `man` for details; for a shell built-in use `help`. commands cmd --help what prints a short usage summary of the command. where to quickly recall an option. why it is much faster than man. example ls --help cmd help what gives help about bash's own (built-in) commands. where for commands like cd, type, history. why these commands may not have a separate man page. example help cmd less what shows long output page by page. where for long --help or file output. why the navigation keys are the same as in man. example ls --help | less nosim tip when help is printed, don't miss the top line: the `usage:` line gives you the usage form. synopsis title reading synopsis notation body the synopsis line gives the command's 'pattern'. example: `ls [option]... [file]...`. read it like this: anything inside `[ ]` is **optional**. `...` means the previous part can be written **more than once**. `a | b` means **either a or b**. `< >` or uppercase (file, dir) is a value you substitute. parts written in bold are typed exactly as shown. example: `cp [option]... source... dest` → options are optional, at least one source and one destination are required. `ls` also works with no arguments because everything is in square brackets. commands cmd ls --help what shows the usage pattern (usage). where to learn the order of arguments. why if you can read the pattern, you can figure out any new command. example ls --help cmd man cat what opens the page that contains the synopsis section. where a simple example to practise with. why you see square brackets and ... in a real page. example man cat tip to find what is mandatory, look at the parts outside the square brackets. where title which and type: where is the command? body when you type a command, the shell searches the directories in the `path` variable in order. `which ls` prints the **path** it finds (e.g. `/usr/bin/ls`). `type` is more informative: it tells you whether the command is an **external program**, a **shell built-in (builtin)**, an alias or a function. `type cd` → `cd is a shell builtin`. use it to understand which one runs when several commands share the same name. to see the contents of `path`, use `echo $path`. `alias` and `command -v` also work on a real vm, but not in the simulator. commands cmd which what shows the file path of the command. where to find out where a program is installed. why you verify that you are running the right version. example which ls cmd type what tells the type of the command (program, builtin, alias). where when investigating unexpected behaviour. why you tell a builtin from an external program. example type cd cmd echo $path what prints the directories where commands are searched. where when investigating 'command not found'. why you see whether the program's directory is in path. example echo $path cmd command -v what prints the path/name if the command exists; stays silent otherwise. where in scripts, to check 'is it installed?'. why it is a portable existence check. example command -v ls nosim cmd alias what lists defined shortcuts. where to understand where commands like `ll` come from. why you see the source of what type calls an 'alias'. example alias nosim tip if a command behaves strangely, first check its type with `type command`. find title find: file search basics body `find <start> <conditions>` walks a directory tree and prints what matches the conditions. the two most common conditions: `-name` (by name) and `-type` (`f` file, `d` directory). put the wildcard **in quotes**: `find . -name \ `. without quotes the shell expands the pattern itself first and the result is misleading. the start point `.` is the current directory, `~` is home. you can count the result with `| wc -l` and save it with `> file` (`|` and `>` are covered in module 3.2, `wc` in modules 3.4–3.5; for now: `|` passes output to the next command, `wc -l` counts lines, `>` writes to a file). `-maxdepth 1` limits the depth on a real system (the simulator ignores it). commands cmd find what searches the directory tree for files matching a condition. where when you forgot where a file is. why it scans the tree by name, type or size. example find . -name \ }, { find -type what finds only files (f) or directories (d). where to count directories separately. why you narrow the result. example find ~ -type d cmd find | wc -l what gives the number of items found. where to know how many matches there are. why you get a number without reading a long list. example find ~ -name \  | wc -l tip to hide error messages on a real system, add `2>/dev/null`. warn don't delete with `find ... -delete` or `-exec rm`; first view the list with plain `find`, then decide. history title history: past commands body `history` lists the commands you typed in this and earlier sessions with numbers. if it is long, take the last ten commands with `history | tail -n 10` (`|` and `tail` are covered in modules 3.2 and 3.4–3.5). in real bash, **up arrow** brings back the previous command, **ctrl+r** searches the history, `!!` re-runs the last command, `!42` re-runs command number 42. the simulator does not support `!!`; the arrow keys work. commands that contain secrets (passwords) are written to the history; don't forget that. commands cmd history what lists past commands with numbers. where to remember what you typed earlier. why you find a long command without retyping it. example history cmd history | tail what shows only the most recent commands. where in a long history. why the list stays short. example history | tail -n 5 cmd what re-runs the last command. where `sudo !!` for a privileged retry. why it saves time. example nosim tip press ctrl+r and type part of the command: bash brings back the match. notfound title dealing with 'command not found' body if you type a command that doesn't exist you get `nosuchcmd: command not found` and the exit code is **127**: `nosuchcmd; echo $?` → `127`. code 127 means 'command not found'. systematic check: (1) is it a typo? (`ls` instead of `lss`) (2) upper/lower case: linux is case-sensitive. (3) check whether it exists with `type command`. (4) if the program isn't installed, install the package (ubuntu `sudo apt install`, rocky/alma `sudo dnf install`). (5) if it is installed, check the directory with `echo $path`. this differs from the 'no such file or directory' error: there the command was found but the file you gave doesn't exist. commands cmd echo $? what prints the exit code of the last command. where when checking whether a command succeeded. why 0 means success, 127 means command not found. example nosuchcmd; echo $? cmd type what does the command exist, and where? where the first check after an error. why it weeds out typos. example type nosuchcmd tip on a real system ubuntu sometimes suggests 'command 'x' not found, did you mean...'; read the suggestion carefully. tasks t01 text open the manual page of the `ls` command with `man ls`. hint the sim page is short; look at name, synopsis and description. t02 text show the short usage summary with `ls --help`. hint double dash: --help. t03 text type `type cd`. does the output say 'builtin'? what does that mean? hint builtin: inside bash, not a separate program. t04 text find the path of the `ls` command with `which ls`. hint the output starts with /usr/bin/. t05 text open `man cat` and read the synopsis line: which part is optional? hint anything inside square brackets is optional. t06 text type `help` and see the list of known commands. hint type it without arguments. t07 text find all `.txt` files under the current directory with `find . -name \ hint put the pattern in quotes. t08 text list the commands you have typed so far with `history`. hint a numbered list appears. t09 text show only the first three lines of the page with `man ls | head -n 3`. hint pipe: | (passes output to the next command; see module 3.2). t10 text predict: what number does `nosuchcmd; echo $?` print? then run it to verify. hint no such command → exit code 127. t11 text predict: how many directories does `find ~ -type d | wc -l` count under home (including home)? run it and verify. hint desktop, documents, downloads and home itself. t12 text debug: `man mkdirr` gives an error ('no manual entry'). open the manual of the correct command with `man mkdir`. hint typo: an extra r. t13 text mini: find where the `todo.txt` file is with `find` and save the path to the file `~/path.txt`. hint `find ~ -name todo.txt > ~/path.txt`; then check with `cat ~/path.txt`. (`>` writes output to a file; see module 3.2.) t14 text challenge: in a single command, count the `.txt` files under home and write the number to `~/count.txt`. hint `find`, pipe, `wc -l` (counts lines; modules 3.4–3.5) and redirection (`>`, module 3.2). the result is the file count; .txt files you created yourself are counted too. t15 text ticket #4410 — support: 'where is ls installed, and what kind of command is cd?' save the path to `~/ls_path.txt` and the type of `cd` to `~/cd_type.txt`. hint `which ls > ...` and `type cd > ...`. (`>` writes output to a file; see module 3.2.) t16 text ticket #4411 — the teacher wants to see what you tried: first run `which ls`, then save the history to `~/hist.txt`. hint `history > ~/hist.txt`. (`>` writes output to a file; see module 3.2.) : { run the following commands on your vm (ubuntu, rocky, alma or wsl). there is no destructive command; still, remember to leave the pager (man) with `q`. tasks v01 title open a manual page text open `man ls`, search for `long` with `/`, leave with `q`. then paste the first lines. blocks cmd man ls | head -n 5 expected ls(1)    user commands

name
       ls - list directory contents differs if your language is turkish/german the headings may be translated. if you get 'no manual entry', the manual package is missing: `sudo apt install man-db` or `sudo dnf install man-db`. v02 title --help summary text paste the first lines of the `ls --help` output. blocks cmd ls --help | head -n 5 expected usage: ls [option]... [file]...
list information about the files (the current directory by default). differs on macos or busybox the `--help` format may differ; run it on a linux vm. v03 title command types text paste the type and path of the `cd`, `ls` and `which ls` commands. blocks cmd type cd
type ls
which ls expected cd is a shell builtin
ls is aliased to `ls --color=auto'
/usr/bin/ls differs `ls` may be an alias (for colour on ubuntu/rocky); this is normal. on some distributions you get `/bin/ls` (`/bin` is linked to `/usr/bin`). v04 title search with find text find the `.txt` files in your home. since the output is personal, just say 'done'. blocks cmd find ~ -maxdepth 2 -name \  2>/dev/null differs if there is no output, you have no .txt files in your home: first create one with `touch ~/notes.txt`. v05 title whatis and apropos text search for the one-line description of `ls` and for commands containing 'copy'. blocks cmd whatis ls
apropos copy | head -n 5 expected ls (1) - list directory contents
cp (1) - copy files and directories differs if you see 'nothing appropriate', there is no index: run `sudo mandb` and try again. on ubuntu/rocky the `apropos` output may have a different number of lines. v06 title command not found text run a command that doesn't exist and paste the exit code. blocks cmd nosuchcmd; echo $? expected bash: nosuchcmd: command not found
127 differs ubuntu may suggest 'command 'nosuchcmd' not found, did you mean...'; the last line should still be 127. if you use zsh the message is 'zsh: command not found: nosuchcmd'. v07 title look at the history text list your last five commands. blocks cmd history | tail -n 5 expected   498  which ls
  499  nosuchcmd
  500  history | tail -n 5 differs the numbers will be different; this is normal. in a freshly opened terminal the list may be short. v08 title manual sections text open the section 5 page describing the format of the `/etc/passwd` file and paste the first lines. blocks cmd man 5 passwd | head -n 5 expected passwd(5)   file formats manual

name
       passwd - password file differs `man passwd` (section 1) is a different page: the password-changing command. if the page is missing, the `man-db` or `man-pages` package is absent. quiz : { which keys are used to search for text in a man page and to quit the page? options `f` and `x` `/` and `q` `s` and `e` `?` and `esc` explain `/word` searches, `n` goes to the next match, `q` quits. : { in the pattern `ls [option]...
