[file]...`, what do `[ ]` and `...` mean? options mandatory and forbidden the part in square brackets is hidden optional and can be written more than once just a comment line explain square brackets mean optional, the three dots show that the previous part can be repeated. : { what is the number in the output of `nosuchcmd; echo $?`? options 127 255 explain in the 'command not found' case bash returns 127 as the exit code. : { with which command do you see that `cd` is not an external program? options `find cd` `ls cd` `man -f cd` `type cd` explain the output of `type cd` is `cd is a shell builtin`; that is, it is inside bash. summary `man command` is the detailed manual, `command --help` a short summary, `help` is for shell built-ins. in man: `/` searches, `n` next, `q` quits; sections: 1 commands, 5 file formats, 8 administration. synopsis: `[ ]` optional, `...` repetition, `|` or. `which` shows the path, `type` shows the type; `find . -name \ ` searches for files. `history` lists the past; `command not found` has exit code 127. glossary term man page meaning the manual page of a command that ships with the system. term synopsis meaning the man section showing the command's usage pattern. term builtin meaning a command embedded in bash that has no separate program. term path meaning the list of directories where commands are searched. term exit code meaning the number a command leaves when it finishes; 0 is success, 127 is command not found. term pager meaning a program that shows long text page by page (less).

1.4.title: Command success: $?, &&, || and error messages
objectives: You read the last command's exit status with `echo $?` and tell 0 from non-zero.
You chain commands conditionally with `true`, `false`, `&&`, `||` and `;`.
You know the difference between stdout and stderr and separate errors with `2>`.
You read `Permission denied`, `No such file or directory` and `command not found` and find the cause.
You test files, numbers and strings with `test` and `[ ]`.
sol: test -f notes.txt && echo yes || echo no
mkdir -p project && cd project && touch main.txt && echo built
cp notes.txt backup/ && echo saved > status.txt || echo failed > status.txt
grep hello notes.txt > /dev/null && echo found || echo missing
1.4.text:
title command success: $?, &&, || and error messages lead no output does not mean an error. every command leaves an exit status; in this module you learn to read it, chain commands based on it and understand error messages. objectives you read the last command's exit status with `echo $?` and tell 0 from non-zero. you chain commands conditionally with `true`, `false`, `&&`, `||` and `;`. you know the difference between stdout and stderr and separate errors with `2>`. you read `permission denied`, `no such file or directory` and `command not found` and find the cause. you test files, numbers and strings with `test` and `[ ]`. sections status title exit status: $? body when a command finishes it produces an **exit status**. **0 = success**, any other number = failure. a silent command (such as `mkdir`) may have succeeded or failed; to be sure, type `echo $?`. common codes: `1` general error, `2` misuse or missing path (`ls`), `126` not executable, `127` command not found, `130` interrupted with ctrl+c. careful: `$?` is overwritten after every command. an `echo $?` typed right afterwards leaves its own result (0); read the code **immediately after the command in question**. commands cmd echo $? what prints the exit status of the last command. where checking commands that print nothing. why shows with a number whether the command really worked. example pwd; echo $? cmd true what does nothing and always ends with 0. where testing chains and loops when you need a 'successful' command. why easily produces the success state. example true; echo $? cmd false what does nothing and always ends with 1. where trying the error path. why easily produces the failure state. example false; echo $? tip no output is not an error. most unix commands are silent on success. chain title chaining: &&, || and ; body `a && b`: b runs only if a **succeeded** (0). `a || b`: b runs only if a **failed**. `a ; b`: b runs in every case. the classic pattern: `mkdir lab && cd lab` (enter the folder if it was created). `a && b || c` acts like an if/else, but if b fails c runs too, so use it only for simple cases. commands cmd what runs the right side if the left side succeeded. where steps that depend on each other. why prevents carrying on after a failed step. example mkdir lab && cd lab cmd what runs the right side if the left side failed. where error messages or fallback plans. why reacts to failure automatically. example cd /nonexistent || echo failed cmd what runs commands in order regardless of success. where writing independent commands on one line. why keeps the order, ignores the result. example pwd; whoami; hostname warn in chains like `rm -r old_project ; ...` using `;` runs the destructive command even if the previous step failed. join destructive steps with `&&`. streams title stdout and stderr body every command has two output channels: **stdout** (channel 1, normal output) and **stderr** (channel 2, error messages). both appear on screen, but they can be redirected separately. `>` sends only stdout to a file; the error stays on screen. `2>` sends errors to a file. `2>/dev/null` throws errors away. `2>&1` sends stderr to wherever stdout goes. note: redirection **does not change the exit status**; even if the error is hidden, the command still failed. commands cmd what writes error messages (stderr) to a file. where inspecting errors later. why separates normal output from errors. example ls /nonexistent 2> errors.txt cmd 2>/dev/null what discards error messages. where silencing expected, harmless errors. why keeps output clean, but also hides real problems. example ls /nonexistent 2>/dev/null; echo $? cmd 2>&1 what redirects stderr to the same place as stdout. where collecting output and errors in one file or pipeline. why keeps the complete record in one place. example ls ~ /nonexistent > all.txt 2>&1 errors title reading error messages body an error message usually looks like `program: argument: reason`. the first word is the program that failed, the second the problem path, the last the reason. **no such file or directory**: the path does not exist or has a typo; check where you are with `ls` and `pwd`. **permission denied**: the path exists but you lack permission; look at `ls -l`. **command not found** (code 127): wrong command name or not installed; check with `type` / `which`. **is a directory**: you gave a folder to a command that expects a file. commands cmd ls -l what shows file permissions and owner. where looking for the cause of permission denied. why you see which permission is missing. example ls -l locked.txt cmd type what tells you whether a name is a command, builtin or alias. where on command not found errors. why shows whether the command exists. example type ls danger when you see permission denied, do not reflexively type `sudo` or `chmod 777`. understand the cause first; needlessly wide permissions are a security hole. test title testing conditions: test and [ ] body `test` (and its equivalent `[ ... ]`) checks a condition and prints nothing; it reports the result only through its exit status: 0 if true, 1 if false. that is why it fits so well with `&&` / `||`. common ones: `-f` regular file, `-d` directory, `-e` exists, `-r`/`-w`/`-x` readable/writable/executable, `-z` string empty. for numbers `-eq -ne -gt -lt`, for strings `=` and `!=`. inside `[ ]` the **spaces** next to the brackets are mandatory. commands cmd test -f what succeeds if the path exists and is a regular file. where checking that a file exists. why you avoid running a command on a missing file and getting an error. example test -f notes.txt && echo yes cmd [ -d ] what succeeds if the path is a directory. where e.g. creating a folder only if it is missing. why lets you act conditionally. example [ -d documents ] && echo dir cmd [ -gt ] what compares numbers (-eq -ne -gt -lt). where numeric checks. why turns numeric conditions into an exit status. example [ 3 -gt 2 ] && echo gt tip classic pattern: `test -d backup || mkdir backup`. it creates the folder if missing and leaves it alone otherwise. tasks t01 text run `pwd` first, then read its exit status right away with `echo $?`. hint type two separate lines; the code should be 0. t02 text list a path that does not exist: `ls /nonexistent`, and read the error message. hint the error goes to stderr; it still shows on screen. t03 text run `false`, then read its status with `echo $?`. what number do you get? hint `false` always fails. t04 text in a single line write `mkdir lab && cd lab` to create the folder and enter it. hint `&&` runs the second command only if the first succeeded. (`mkdir` creates a folder, module 2.3; `cd` is module 1.1.) t05 text type `cd /nonexistent || echo failed` and think about why `failed` is printed. hint when `cd` fails, `||` runs the right-hand side. t06 text predict: what does `cat missing.txt; echo $?` print and what is the code? then run it to verify. hint `cat` prints an error when it cannot find the file and exits with 1. t07 text predict: what does `test -f notes.txt && echo yes || echo no` print? run it to verify. hint `notes.txt` exists in home and is a regular file. t08 text `cat locked.txt` gives 'permission denied'. understand why, fix it with `chmod` and read the file. hint give yourself read permission: `chmod u+r locked.txt`. (`chmod` changes permissions, covered in module 4.4; `cat` in module 2.6.) t09 text `cp notes.txt backup/` fails because `backup` does not exist. chain it: create the folder and copy the file. hint `mkdir backup && cp notes.txt backup/`. (`cp` copies, module 2.4; `mkdir` module 2.3.) t10 text mini project: (1) write the error of `ls /nonexistent` to `errors.txt`, (2) write the output of `ls ~` to `files.txt`, (3) read the last command's status with `echo $?`. hint use `2>` for the error and `>` for the output. (`>` writes output to a file; details in module 3.2.) t11 text mini project: in one line create the `project` folder, enter it, create the file `main.txt` and finally print `built`. hint join four commands with `&&`; you can use `mkdir -p project`. (`touch` creates an empty file, module 2.3.) t12 text challenge: create the `backup` folder if it is missing; copy `notes.txt` into it; if the copy succeeded write `saved` into `status.txt`, otherwise `failed`. hint `test -d backup || mkdir backup` and `cp ... && echo saved > status.txt || echo failed > status.txt`. (`cp` module 2.4, `>` module 3.2.) t13 text challenge: does `notes.txt` contain `hello`? test it in one line and print `found` or `missing`; discard grep's own output to `/dev/null`. hint `grep hello notes.txt > /dev/null && echo found || echo missing`. (`grep` searches text, module 3.4.) t14 text ticket: a colleague says 'i cannot read my report' and tried `cat documents/raport.txt`. find the right name with `ls documents`, read the file with `cat` and write the exit status to `exit.txt`. hint the right name is `report.txt`. `cat documents/report.txt; echo $? > exit.txt`. : { run the following commands on your own vm (ubuntu/rocky/alma or wsl); we only use safe, read-only commands. paste the output and check it. tasks v01 title success and failure codes text run one successful and one failing command and read the code after each. paste the whole output. blocks cmd ls /
echo $?
ls /nonexistent
echo $? expected bin  boot  dev  etc ...
0
ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': no such file or directory
2 differs a failing `ls` gives 2 (gnu ls); other commands may give 1. that is fine, what matters is that it is not 0. if the message is localised it may be in another language; the code is the same. v02 title command not found: 127 text run a command that does not exist and read the exit status. blocks cmd nonexistentcmd
echo $? expected bash: nonexistentcmd: command not found
127 differs ubuntu sometimes suggests a package with 'command not found'; the code is still 127. if you type `echo $?` twice the second gives 0; read it only right after the first command. v03 title how && and || behave text try the chains and see which side runs. blocks cmd true && echo ok
false && echo never
false || echo fallback
true ; echo always expected ok
fallback
always differs if `never` appears you may have typed `;` instead of `&&`. if nothing prints, look for a quote or spacing mistake. v04 title permission denied text open a file you cannot read as a normal user and paste the error and status (read-only, nothing changes). blocks cmd cat /etc/shadow
echo $? expected cat: /etc/shadow: permission denied
1 differs if you are root the file opens; switch to a normal user (`su - student` or a new user). on older systems you can try `/etc/sudoers` instead of `/etc/shadow`. v05 title conditions with test text test file and directory conditions. paste the result as `yes` / `no`. blocks cmd test -d /etc && echo yes || echo no
test -f /etc/nonexistent && echo yes || echo no expected yes
no differs if both print `yes` you may have typed `-e` instead of `-f`. when you write `[ -d /etc ]`, do not forget the spaces around `[` and `]`. quiz : { what is the exit status of a command that finished successfully? options 127 255 explain 0 means success; every non-zero value indicates a failure. : { when does b run in the line `a && b`? options always only if a fails only if a succeeds (0) never explain `&&` acts like and; b runs only if a ends with 0. : { what does exit status 127 indicate? options command not found permission denied interrupted with ctrl+c file not found explain 127 = command not found. a permission problem is 126, ctrl+c is 130. : { what does `ls /nonexistent 2>/dev/null; echo $?` do? options shows the error message and prints 0 creates the folder prints nothing at all hides the error message but the status stays non-zero explain `2>/dev/null` only discards the message; the command still failed and `$?` is not 0. summary exit status: 0 is success, anything else is an error. read it immediately with `echo $?`. `&&` continues on success, `||` on failure, `;` in every case. stdout is redirected with `>`, stderr with `2>`; redirection does not change the exit status. error message: program, path, reason. 127 = no such command, permission denied = no permission. `test` and `[ ]` turn conditions into an exit status. glossary term exit status meaning the number a command leaves when it finishes; 0 = success. term stdout meaning standard output (channel 1); normal results. term stderr meaning standard error (channel 2); error messages. term meaning operator that runs the right side if the left side succeeded. term meaning operator that runs the right side if the left side failed. term /dev/null meaning a special file that swallows everything written to it.

1.5.title: Shell Tools and Environment
objectives: You reuse old commands with history, !! and Ctrl+R.
You work fast with Tab completion and the Ctrl+C/L/A/E shortcuts.
You know the difference between double quotes, single quotes and the backslash.
You define variables, pass them on with export, and read and extend PATH.
You shorten commands with wildcards (*, ?, []), brace expansion and $().
1.5.text:
title shell tools and environment lead make the shell work for you: history, completion, shortcuts, quoting, variables, path, wildcards and command substitution. objectives you reuse old commands with history, !! and ctrl+r. you work fast with tab completion and the ctrl+c/l/a/e shortcuts. you know the difference between double quotes, single quotes and the backslash. you define variables, pass them on with export, and read and extend path. you shorten commands with wildcards (*, ?, []), brace expansion and $(). sections history title command history body the shell remembers what you type. `history` shows a numbered list; `history 5` shows only the last 5 commands. the up arrow (↑) recalls the previous command. `!!` runs the previous command again. its most common use is `sudo !!`, which adds the `sudo` you forgot. `ctrl+r` **searches** the history: type a few letters, the matching old command appears, press enter to run it. commands cmd history what lists the commands you ran, with numbers. where when you want to recall a long command from yesterday. why saves retyping and shows what you did. example history cmd history 5 what shows only the last 5 commands. where when a short overview is enough. why you don't drown in a long list. example history 5 cmd what runs the previous command again, unchanged. where like `sudo !!` after a permission error. why no need to retype the same command. example echo hello nosim cmd ctrl+r what searches backwards through the history. where finding a very old, long command. why much faster than scrolling with the arrow key. example history nosim tip after pressing ctrl+r, press ctrl+r again to jump to the next older match. shortcuts title tab completion and shortcuts body the `tab` key completes command, file and folder names. with one match it completes; with several, press tab twice to list the options. it saves time and prevents typos. a few shortcuts cover half of daily work: `ctrl+c` stops a running command, `ctrl+l` clears the screen (same as `clear`), `ctrl+a` jumps to the start of the line, `ctrl+e` to the end. with `alias` you can give long commands a short name. commands cmd tab what completes the name you typed or lists the options. where long file and folder names. why speed and accuracy. example ls doc nosim cmd ctrl+c what interrupts the running command (sends sigint). where a command that hangs or never ends. why you leave the command without closing the terminal. example sleep 100 nosim cmd ctrl+a / ctrl+e what moves the cursor to the start / end of the line. where editing a long command. why faster than stepping with the arrow keys. example ls -l documents nosim cmd clear what clears the screen; ctrl+l does the same. where when the screen gets cluttered. why keeps output readable. example clear cmd alias what gives a command a short alias. where commands you type often. why less typing. to make it permanent, put it in `~/.bashrc`. example alias ll='ls -l' nosim tip never type a long file name by hand; type the first letters and press tab. quoting title quotes and escaping body before running a command the shell interprets special characters. quotes control that. inside **double quotes** `$variable` and `$(command)` are expanded. inside **single quotes** everything stays literal. a **backslash** (`\`) removes the special meaning of one character. file names with spaces also need quotes: `cat \ `. without quotes the shell sees two separate arguments. commands cmd echo \ what double quotes: variables expand, spaces are kept. where messages with variables. why flexible and safe. example echo \ }, { echo '...' what single quotes: nothing expands, text is printed literally. where fixed text that contains `$`. why stops the shell from interfering. example echo 'hello $user' cmd what removes the special meaning of the next character. where protecting a single `$` or space. why a short alternative to quotes. example echo \$home tip when in doubt, put variables in double quotes: `\ ` also works with names containing spaces. variables title variables and export body define a variable with `name=alice`; **no spaces around the equals sign**. read it with `$name`. a variable defined this way lives only in this shell. to let programs you start see it, use `export name=alice`. `env` shows all exported **environment variables** (`home`, `user`, `path`, `shell`...). changes made with `export` are lost when the terminal closes; to keep them, write them into `~/.bashrc`. commands cmd name=alice what defines a shell variable (no spaces). where values you will reuse. why you don't retype the same value. example name=alice cmd echo $name what prints the value of the variable. where checking a value. why confirms what the shell sees. example echo $home cmd export what passes the variable on to child programs. where settings that programs read. why without export the variable stays in this shell only. example export greeting=hello cmd env what lists environment variables. where inspecting or debugging the environment. why shows which setting is active. example env | grep greeting cmd unset what removes a variable. where dropping a variable you no longer need. why keeps the environment clean. example unset greeting nosim tip don't write `name = alice` (with spaces): the shell looks for a command called `name` and fails. path title path: where commands are found body when you type a command, the shell searches the folders in the `path` variable in order. folders are separated by `:`. `which ls` shows the path found, `type ls` shows the kind of command (program, builtin). to add a folder with your own tools, append it to `path`. keep the old value: `export path=$path:~/bin`. if you only write `path=~/bin`, even `ls` can no longer be found. commands cmd echo $path what shows the search folders. where first place to look on 'command not found'. why you see why a command isn't found. example echo $path cmd which what shows the full path of a command. where finding out which program runs. why avoids mixing up programs with the same name. example which ls cmd type what tells whether a command is a program or a builtin. where builtins such as `cd`. why explains differences in behaviour. example type cd cmd export path=$path:~/bin what adds `~/bin` to the search path. where calling your own scripts by name. why no need to type the full path each time. example export path=$path:~/bin warn never assign something like `path=/new/dir` that throws away the old value; no command, `ls` included, will be found. close and reopen the terminal to recover. tip to make it permanent, add the same `export` line to `~/.bashrc`. globbing title wildcards (globbing) body the **shell** expands wildcards, not the command. `*` matches anything (including nothing), `?` exactly one character, `[abc]` one of the characters in brackets. for `ls *.txt` the shell first turns the pattern into file names, then hands them to `ls`. if nothing matches, the shell leaves the pattern as it is. before delete commands, test the pattern with `echo`: `echo *.log`. patterns and quoting are covered in depth in module 3.3. commands cmd what any sequence of characters. where selecting files of the same type. why many files with one command. example echo lab/*.txt cmd what exactly one character. where names of fixed length. why matches more narrowly than `*`. example echo lab/?.txt cmd [ ] what one of the characters in brackets. where selecting a few specific files. why gives full control. example echo lab/[ab].txt warn `rm *` deletes every file in the current folder. first check what matches with `echo *`, then run `rm`. tip hidden files (starting with `.`) are not matched by `*`. expansion title brace expansion and command substitution body brace expansion generates text: `file{1,2,3}.txt` becomes three names, `f{1..3}` becomes `f1 f2 f3`. the files don't have to exist, which makes it ideal for bulk `touch` and `mkdir`. `$(command)` runs the command and substitutes its **output**: `echo \ `. you can also store output in a variable: `username=$(whoami)`. commands cmd {a,b,c} what multiplies a comma-separated list. where creating many files and folders. why three files in one line. example touch ~/lab/file{1,2,3}.txt cmd {1..3} what generates a number or letter range. where numbered names. why no manual typing. example echo f{1..3} cmd $(...) what puts a command's output inside another command. where dynamic values like date, user, host name. why you use the live value instead of hard-coding it. example echo \ }],  the old `` `command` `` form works too, but `$()` is far more readable when nested. output title echo, printf and exit code body `echo` prints text and variables. for formatted output use `printf`: `%s` is text, `%d` a number, `\n` a newline. `printf` adds no newline automatically. every command leaves an **exit code**: `0` means success, anything else an error. read the last one with `$?`. in scripts this is how you check for success. commands cmd echo what prints text or a variable's value. where giving messages and quick checks. why the simplest output tool. example echo \ }, { printf what produces formatted output. where aligned output or exact control over newlines. why more predictable than echo. example printf \  alice cmd echo $? what prints the exit code of the last command. where telling whether a command succeeded. why `0` is success, non-zero is an error. example echo $? tasks t01 text print a message with `echo \ hint put the text in double quotes. t02 text show the command history. hint type `history`. t03 text print the `home` variable, which holds your home directory, with `echo`. hint put `$` in front of the variable: `echo $home`. t04 text export the variable `greeting=hello` with `export`, then find it in the `env` output with `grep`. hint `export greeting=hello`, then `env | grep greeting` (`|` passes output to the next command, `grep` searches lines; modules 3.2 and 3.4). t05 text list the `.txt` files in the `lab` folder with a wildcard: run `echo lab/*.txt`. hint `*` matches any name; don't forget the `.txt` suffix. t06 text with brace expansion, create `file1.txt`, `file2.txt` and `file3.txt` in `lab` with one command. hint `touch ~/lab/file{1,2,3}.txt` (`touch` creates empty files; module 2.3). t07 text create the folder `~/bin` and add it to `path` while keeping the old value. hint `mkdir ~/bin` (creates a folder; module 2.3), then `export path=$path:~/bin`. t08 text predict: what does `echo '$home'` print? run the single-quoted version to check. hint variables are not expanded inside single quotes. t09 text predict: what does `echo \ ` print? run it to check. hint the output of the command inside `$()` is substituted. t10 text predict: what does `echo f{1..3}` print? run it to check. hint brace expansion produces three words separated by spaces. t11 text debug: your home folder contains a file called `my notes.txt`, and `cat my notes.txt` fails. show the file's content with the correct syntax. hint quote the name: `cat \ },  : { mini project: create the folder `~/projects`, create `a.txt` and `b.txt` in it with one command, then write the output of `$(whoami)` into `owner.txt`. hint `mkdir ~/projects`, `touch ~/projects/{a,b}.txt`, `echo \  > ~/projects/owner.txt` (`>` writes output to a file; module 3.2). t13 text challenge: write exactly `host: linux-lab user: student` into `~/info.txt`. produce the values with `$(hostname)` and `$(whoami)`. hint `echo \  > ~/info.txt` (`>` writes output to a file; module 3.2). t14 text ticket: the team wants to call the scripts in `~/tools` by name. add the folder to `path` in this session and append the setting to the end of `~/.bashrc` so it is permanent. hint (`>>` appends to a file; module 3.2) `export path=$path:~/tools`, then append the same line with single quotes and `>>` to `~/.bashrc`. t15 text print the line `name: alice` with `printf`; use `%s` and `\n`. hint `printf \  alice`. t16 text list a file that doesn't exist (`ls nofile`), then show the exit code with `echo $?`. hint after an error `$?` is a non-zero number. : { run the commands below on your own vm (ubuntu, rocky, alma or wsl). the commands in this module are harmless; still, extend `path` with `export` and never overwrite it with `path=`. tasks v01 title explore the history text run a few commands, then show the last lines of the history. then try `!!` and `ctrl+r`. blocks cmd echo one
echo two
history | tail -n 5 expected   101  echo one
  102  echo two
  103  history | tail -n 5 cmd # press ctrl+r, type 'echo', press enter; then:
!! differs the numbers will differ with your history; the order of the lines matters. if `!!` doesn't work, make sure you are in bash: `echo $shell`. v02 title variable and export text define a variable, export it, and check whether a child shell can see it. blocks cmd myvar=hello
bash -c 'echo \ '
export myvar
bash -c 'echo \ '
env | grep myvar expected child: []
child: [hello]
myvar=hello differs if the first line isn't `child: []`, `myvar` was exported earlier; reopen the terminal. copy all three lines when pasting the output. v03 title quote difference text print the same text with double and single quotes and see the difference. blocks cmd echo \ 
echo 'hello $user'
echo hello \$user expected hello student
hello $user
hello $user differs if your user isn't `student`, your own name appears; that is normal. if `$user` is empty, try `echo $logname`. v04 title wildcards and braces text in a safe folder, create files with braces and match them with wildcards. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/lab
touch ~/lab/{a,b,c}.txt ~/lab/d.log
echo ~/lab/*.txt
echo ~/lab/?.log
echo ~/lab/[ab].txt expected /home/student/lab/a.txt /home/student/lab/b.txt /home/student/lab/c.txt
/home/student/lab/d.log
/home/student/lab/a.txt /home/student/lab/b.txt differs if your home isn't `/home/student`, the path looks different; the file names must be the same. in `wsl`, `~` is your linux home, not the windows side. v05 title add your own tool to path text write a tiny script, add its folder to `path` and call it by name. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/tools
printf '#!/bin/bash\necho tool works\n' > ~/tools/hello
chmod +x ~/tools/hello
export path=$path:~/tools
hello
which hello expected tool works
/home/student/tools/hello differs on `command not found`, check with `echo $path` that the `tools` path was added. on `permission denied`, run `chmod +x ~/tools/hello` again. v06 title try the shortcuts text type `sleep 100` and stop it with `ctrl+c`. then type a long command and move around with `ctrl+a` and `ctrl+e`, clear the screen with `ctrl+l`. type `~/doc` and complete it with tab. when finished, press \ blocks cmd sleep 100
# ctrl+c
ls ~/doc
# tab differs if your terminal emulator grabs ctrl+l, type `clear` instead. if tab does nothing, press it twice; with several matches they are listed. quiz : { what does `!!` do? options deletes the history lists the history runs the previous command again closes the shell explain `!!` is replaced by the previous command; `sudo !!` is very common. : { what does `echo '$home'` print? options /home/student $home an empty line an error explain variables are not expanded inside single quotes; the text is printed as is. : { which command makes a variable visible to child programs? options export unset echo history explain `export` puts the variable into the environment; `env` then shows it. : { what is the output of `echo f{1..3}`? options f{1..3} f1f2f3 f1 f2 f3 explain the shell performs brace expansion and produces three separate words. summary `history`, `!!` and `ctrl+r` let you reuse commands. `tab` completes; `ctrl+c` interrupts, `ctrl+l` clears, `ctrl+a/e` move within the line. `$` expands in double quotes, not in single quotes, and `\` protects one character. `name=value` has no spaces; child programs need `export`. `path` holds the folders searched for commands; extend it with `export path=$path:...`. `*`, `?`, `[]` are wildcards; `{a,b}` is brace expansion; `$()` substitutes command output. glossary term history meaning the list of commands the shell remembers. term environment variable meaning a variable carrying settings for the shell and child programs (home, path, user). term path meaning a `:`-separated list of folders searched for commands. term globbing meaning expansion of `*`, `?`, `[]` patterns into file names. term command substitution meaning replacing `$(command)` with the command's output. term exit code meaning the number a command leaves behind; `0` is success, anything else an error.

2.1.title: The Linux Directory Tree
objectives: You explain that Linux has no C: or D: drive and everything branches under one root directory `/`.
You tell apart the roles of `/etc`, `/home`, `/root`, `/var/log`, `/usr`, `/bin`, `/dev`, `/tmp`, `/proc` and `/opt`.
You move safely through the system with `ls`, `cd` and `cat` and build the "ID card" of a server.
2.1.text:
title the linux directory tree lead in linux everything has its place: fixed directories for configuration, logs, user files and programs. learn where to look for which file. objectives you explain that linux has no c: or d: drive and everything branches under one root directory `/`. you tell apart the roles of `/etc`, `/home`, `/root`, `/var/log`, `/usr`, `/bin`, `/dev`, `/tmp`, `/proc` and `/opt`. you move safely through the system with `ls`, `cd` and `cat` and build the \  of a server. sections root title the root of the tree: / body windows has drives like `c:` and `d:`. linux has just **one** tree whose root is `/` (the root directory). even a new disk or usb stick is **mounted** onto a branch of this tree. where things live is defined by the **fhs** (filesystem hierarchy standard). that is why you find config files in the same place on ubuntu and rocky. you see the root directory with `ls /`; you change nothing by doing so. quick map: `/etc` configuration, `/home` users, `/var` variable data (logs), `/usr` programs, `/tmp` temporary files, `/proc` and `/sys` virtual kernel files, `/dev` devices. commands cmd ls / what lists the folders inside the root directory. where when you first enter a system. why you get to know the main branches of the tree. example ls / cmd cd / what moves to the root directory. where as the starting point for absolute paths. why paths starting with `/` work from anywhere. example cd / cmd pwd what prints the full path of the current directory. where after navigating, to be sure where you are. why prevents actions in the wrong directory. example pwd tip a path starting with `/` is **absolute** (`/etc/hostname`); without it, the path starts in the current directory. config title configuration and users: /etc, /home, /root body `/etc` holds the **configuration files** of the system and installed programs: `/etc/passwd` (users), `/etc/hostname` (machine name), `/etc/fstab` (disks), `/etc/os-release` (distribution). they are plain text files you read with `cat`. personal files of normal users live under `/home/<user>`, for example `/home/student`. the administrator `root` has its own home, `/root`; only root may enter, others get `permission denied`. `/etc/shadow` stores password hashes and is readable by root only. `cat /etc/shadow` as a normal user fails; that is not a fault but protection. commands cmd cat /etc/os-release what shows the name and version of the distribution. where to find out which linux you are on; same path on every distribution. why you pick the right commands for that distribution. example cat /etc/os-release cmd cat /etc/hostname what shows the machine's name. where when working with several servers, to confirm you are on the right one. why reduces the risk of working on the wrong server. example cat /etc/hostname cmd ls /home what lists the home directories of normal users. where to quickly see which users exist. why you see where user data lives. example ls /home tip always make a backup before changing a config file; in this module you only read. variable title logs and virtual files: /var, /proc, /sys body `/var` holds data that **changes** while the system runs. most important is `/var/log`: system and service logs live here. on rhel, rocky and alma the main log is `/var/log/messages`, on ubuntu it is `/var/log/syslog`. do not look for logs in `/etc`: configuration is in `/etc`, logs in `/var/log`. `/proc` and `/sys` are not real files on disk. the kernel generates them in ram on the fly. the numbers in `ls /proc` are the ids of running processes (pids). `cat /proc/cpuinfo` shows live cpu data, `cat /proc/meminfo` memory data. use these files for **reading** only. browsing around in them or writing to them is not a safe habit. commands cmd ls /var/log what lists the log files. where the first place to look when troubleshooting. why you follow the trail of a problem in the logs. example ls /var/log cmd cat /proc/cpuinfo what reads the cpu information from the kernel. where for hardware and resource checks. why as a virtual file it is always up to date. example cat /proc/cpuinfo cmd find what searches for files by name below a directory. where when you do not know which directory a file is in. why instead of guessing, you find the exact path. example find /etc -name sshd_config tip is the file called `messages` or `syslog`? it depends on the distribution; look first with `ls /var/log`. danger writing to files under `/proc` and `/sys`, or opening `/proc/kcore` with `cat`, can make the system unstable. only read known files such as `cpuinfo`, `meminfo` or `version`. programs title programs and devices: /usr, /bin, /dev, /tmp, /opt body `/usr` is the big library of installed programs. most commands live in `/usr/bin`. on modern distributions `/bin` is not a separate directory but a **symbolic link** (symlink) to `/usr/bin`: `ls -ld /bin` shows `bin -> usr/bin`. `/dev` holds device files: `/dev/sda` is a disk, `/dev/null` is a \  that swallows everything written to it. in `ls -l` their lines start with `c` (character device) or `b` (block device). `/tmp` is for temporary files and is usually cleared on reboot. `/opt` is for third-party software, `/srv` for data the server publishes. if you cannot find an application, look in `/opt`, `/usr/local` and `/etc` in turn. commands cmd ls -ld /bin what shows the `/bin` entry itself; the link target appears after `->`. where to tell whether a path is a directory or a link. why explains why the tree can look different between distributions. example ls -ld /bin cmd ls -l /dev/null what shows the type and permissions of a device file. where when examining how hardware appears as a file. why you see that in linux everything is a file. example ls -l /dev/null cmd ls /opt what lists the directory for third-party software. where when looking for a manually installed application. why software outside the package manager often lives here. example ls /opt tip to learn where a command lives, you can type `which ls`. warn `/tmp` is accessible to everyone. do not store secrets such as passwords there, and read the path twice before using `rm -r` even in `/tmp`. tasks t01 text go to the root directory: `cd /`. hint type just a single slash. t02 text list the configuration directory: `ls /etc`. hint you will see files like `passwd` and `hostname`. t03 text read the distribution info: `cat /etc/os-release`. hint the `version_id` line gives the version. t04 text list the log directory: `ls /var/log`. hint this virtual machine has a file called `messages`. t05 text list the home directories of the users: `ls /home`. hint `student` and `alice` should appear. t06 text read the machine name: `cat /etc/hostname`. hint the output should be `linux-lab`. t07 text read the cpu information from the virtual file: `cat /proc/cpuinfo`. hint this file takes no disk space; the kernel generates it. t08 text predict: is `/bin` a directory or a link? verify with `ls -ld /bin`. hint look for `->` in the output; the arrow marks a symlink. t09 text predict: can a normal user read the password hashes? try `cat /etc/shadow`. hint expect `permission denied`; the protection is deliberate. t10 text predict: what does `ls /root` tell a normal user? try it. hint `/root` is only the home of root. t11 text debug: a user wanted to read logs, typed `cd /etc/log` and got `no such file or directory`. go to the correct directory. hint logs are not under `/etc` but under `/var`. t12 text mini project: build a small fhs tree under `~/mini-root`. with one `mkdir -p` create the folders `etc`, `var/log` and `tmp`, create the file `etc/app.conf` with `touch`, and write a log line with `echo started > ~/mini-root/var/log/app.log`. hint braces: `~/mini-root/{etc,var/log,tmp}`; you write into the log file with the redirect `>`. (`mkdir`/`touch` are covered in module 2.3, `>` in module 3.2.) t13 text challenge: write the server's id card into `~/idcard.txt`: machine name (`/etc/hostname`), users (`ls /home`) and distribution name (the `pretty_name` line). use `>` for the first, `>>` for the others. hint `grep pretty_name /etc/os-release >> ~/idcard.txt` appends the distribution line. (`>` writes, `>>` appends: module 3.2; `grep`: module 3.4.) t14 text challenge: you do not know the path of `sshd_config`. search for it by name under `/etc`: `find /etc -name sshd_config`. hint `-name` expects the file name; the path turns out to be under `/etc/ssh/`. t15 text ticket #2410 — \  the third-party software is under `/opt`. find the `error` line in its log file and save it to `~/ticket-2410.txt`. hint first `ls /opt`, then `ls /opt/shopapp/logs`; then `grep error ... > ~/ticket-2410.txt` (`grep` module 3.4, `>` module 3.2). : { in this section you only read; no command changes system files. output may differ slightly by distribution (ubuntu / rocky / alma / wsl); that is normal. tasks v01 title explore the root directory text list the contents of the root directory and paste the output. blocks cmd ls / expected bin  boot  dev  etc  home  lib  opt  proc  root  run  sbin  srv  sys  tmp  usr  var differs the number and order of folders depend on the distribution; `etc`, `var` and `usr` must appear. if the output is a single column, widen the terminal; the content is the same. v02 title which distribution am i on? text read the distribution info and paste the output. blocks cmd cat /etc/os-release expected name=\ 
version=\ 
id=\ 
... differs on ubuntu you see `name=\ ` and `id=ubuntu`; the lines differ but `name=` and `id=` are always there. if the file is missing the system is very old; try `cat /etc/issue`. v03 title is /bin really a link? text list `/` in long format and look at the `bin` line. blocks cmd ls -l / | grep ' bin' expected lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 7 ... bin -> usr/bin differs if the output is empty try `ls -ld /bin`; on very old distributions `/bin` is a real directory. if the line starts with `l` it is a symbolic link. v04 title virtual files: /proc text read the first lines of the kernel's cpu information. blocks cmd head -n 5 /proc/cpuinfo
ls /proc | head -n 10 expected processor	: 0
vendor_id	: genuineintel
...
1
10
... differs on arm cpus (utm on apple silicon) the fields differ; the `processor` line still appears. on wsl the contents of `/proc` may be somewhat restricted. v05 title look at the log directory text list the log files and paste the output. blocks cmd ls /var/log expected anaconda  audit  dnf.log  messages  secure  wtmp ... differs on ubuntu you see `syslog` and `auth.log`, on rocky `messages` and `secure`. some files need `sudo` to read; listing does not. v06 title a file in the temporary directory text create a test file in `/tmp`, look at it and delete it right away. deleting a single file is safe. blocks cmd echo test > /tmp/lab-test.txt
ls -l /tmp/lab-test.txt
rm /tmp/lab-test.txt expected -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 5 ... /tmp/lab-test.txt differs if you mistyped the name, `rm` says \ ; the name must be `lab-test.txt`. do not use `-r` or wildcards (`*`) with `rm`. v07 title a device file text list `/dev/null` in long format and paste the output. blocks cmd ls -l /dev/null expected crw-rw-rw-. 1 root root 1, 3 ... /dev/null differs if the line starts with `c` it is a character device; other permission letters are no problem. if the file is missing you may be in a container; a normal vm always has it. quiz : { in which directory do you look for system logs? options /etc /home /var/log /proc explain logs are constantly growing data and live under `/var/log`. `/etc` is for configuration files. : { why is `/proc` a \  directory? options because only root may see it they are not real files on disk; the kernel generates the information in ram because its files are encrypted because it is downloaded from the internet explain `/proc` and `/sys` are a live interface of the kernel and take no disk space. : { in which directory are the configuration files of the system and programs? options /etc /tmp /dev /opt explain `/etc` is the standard place for configuration files (`passwd`, `hostname`, `fstab`...). : { where are the personal files of `student`, and where those of `root`? options `/root` and `/home` `/etc/student` and `/etc/root` both under `/home` `/home/student` and `/root` explain normal users live under `/home/<name>`; root's home is separately `/root`. summary linux has a single tree; the root is `/` and everything hangs below it. `/etc` configuration, `/var/log` logs, `/home` and `/root` home directories, `/usr` programs. `/proc` and `/sys` are virtual kernel files; `/dev` is for devices, `/tmp` for temporary files, `/opt` for third-party software. when searching, first think about what a directory is for, then verify with `ls`, `cat` and `find`. glossary term fhs meaning filesystem hierarchy standard: defines what each directory is used for. term root directory meaning the top of the tree, `/`; all paths branch from here. term absolute path meaning a full path starting with `/`, independent of where you are. term symbolic link meaning a special file pointing to another path; shown with `->` in `ls -l`. term pid meaning the numeric id of each running process; appears as a directory name under `/proc`.

2.2.title: Paths and Types
objectives: You tell absolute (start with `/`) from relative paths and use the shortcuts `.`, `..` and `~`.
You read the file type from the first letter of `ls -l` (`-`, `d`, `l`, `c`, `b`).
You create a symbolic link with `ln -s` and see what it points to.
2.2.text:
title paths and types lead read absolute and relative paths correctly, recognise file types with ls -l and create symbolic links (shortcuts). objectives you tell absolute (start with `/`) from relative paths and use the shortcuts `.`, `..` and `~`. you read the file type from the first letter of `ls -l` (`-`, `d`, `l`, `c`, `b`). you create a symbolic link with `ln -s` and see what it points to. sections paths title absolute and relative paths body on linux the only way to reach a file is to give a **path**. an **absolute path** starts at the root directory (`/`) and points to the same place from anywhere: `/etc/hostname`. a **relative path** does not start with `/` and is worked out **from the current directory**. inside `/etc`, `hostname` is enough; in your home directory the same name fails, because no such file is there. check where you are with `pwd` first. the meaning of a relative path always depends on the current directory. commands cmd pwd what prints the absolute path of the current directory. where before using relative paths. why so you do not work in the wrong directory. example pwd cmd what changes the working directory; takes absolute or relative paths. where when moving between directories. why afterwards short relative paths are enough. example cd /etc cmd cat what prints the contents of a file. where when reading small text files. why to test that a path points to the right file. example cat /etc/hostname tip when unsure, type the absolute path; it works from every directory. shortcuts title special path shortcuts: . .. ~ body `.` is the current directory, `..` the parent directory, `~` your home directory (`/home/student`). you can combine them in paths: `../config.txt`, `~/documents/report.txt`. files whose name starts with `.` are **hidden**; `ls` does not show them, `ls -a` does. every directory also lists the entries `.` and `..`. commands cmd cd .. what moves up to the parent directory. where when returning from a subdirectory. why go up quickly without typing the full path. example cd .. cmd ls -a what lists all files including hidden ones. where when looking for configuration files. why hidden files do not appear otherwise. example ls -a ~ types title reading file types body on linux everything is a file: text, folders, devices, shortcuts. in `ls -l` output the **first letter** of the line tells the type. `-` regular file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link, `c` character device (`/dev/null`), `b` block device (disk), `s` socket, `p` named pipe. the next nine characters are permissions (covered in later modules). commands cmd ls -l what long listing: type, permissions, owner, size, date, name. where to find out what something is. why you know what it is before deleting or reading it. example ls -l /dev/null cmd stat what shows detailed information and the type of a file. where when you need the type or timestamps. why gives the type as a word instead of a letter. example stat /etc/hostname tip files under `/dev` are hardware interfaces, not real data; do not read them randomly with `cat`. links title symbolic links body a **symbolic link** is a small shortcut file that points to another path. `ls -l` shows it with `l` and as `link -> target`. reading the link means reading the target. if the target is deleted or moved, the link stays behind **broken**. a relative target (`../docs/readme.txt`) is resolved **from the link's directory**, not from your current one. commands cmd ln -s what creates a symbolic link: `ln -s target link`. where to reach a long path under a short name. why you keep the file in one place without copying. example ln -s ~/documents/report.txt ~/link.txt cmd readlink what prints the target of a link. where to see where a link leads. why just the target instead of the whole `ls -l` line. example readlink ~/link.txt nosim warn argument order for `ln -s`: target first, then link. swapped, you get a broken link. `ln -sf` overwrites an existing file; be careful. danger if a link points to a directory, `rm -r link/` (with a trailing `/`) can delete the contents of the target directory. to remove the link type `rm link` and check with `ls -l` first. tasks t01 text run `cat /etc/hostname` using the absolute path. hint works from any directory. t02 text move to `/etc` with `cd /etc`. hint an absolute path starts with `/`. t03 text while in `/etc`, type the relative path `cat hostname`. hint the file is in the current directory. t04 text go home with `cd ~` and run `cat hostname` again. what happens and why? hint there is no hostname file in home; expect an error. t05 text from `/home/student` go up one directory with `cd ..`. hint confirm with `pwd` that it shows `/home`. t06 text now type relatively: `cd student/documents`. hint no `/` at the start. t07 text run `ls -l /etc/hostname`. what is the first character? hint `-` means regular file. t08 text run `ls -l /dev/null` and predict first: which letter comes first? hint `c` for character device. t09 text create the symbolic link `~/link.txt` with `ln -s ~/documents/report.txt ~/link.txt`. hint target first, then the link name. t10 text inspect the link with `ls -l ~/link.txt`. what is after the arrow (`->`)? hint the line starts with `l`. t11 text what does `cat ~/link.txt` print? predict first, then run it. hint the link reads its target. t12 text debug: inside `~/projects/app`, `config.txt` is not found; the file is one level up. read it with `cat` using a relative path with `../`. hint first `cd ~/projects/app`, then `cat ../config.txt`. t13 text mini project: create `~/lab/docs` and `~/lab/bin`, write a file with `echo hello linux > ~/lab/docs/readme.txt`, and create `~/lab/bin/readme-link` as a symbolic link to it. hint `mkdir -p`, `echo ... >` and `ln -s target link`. (`mkdir` is covered in module 2.3; `>` writes output to a file, covered in module 3.2.) t14 text challenge: go into `~/lab/bin` and create the link `rel-link` with a **relative target** (`../docs/readme.txt`); then read it with `cat rel-link`. hint a relative target is resolved from the link's directory. t15 text ticket: the application looks for its configuration at `~/app/current/config.txt`, but the real file is in `~/releases/v2/config.txt`. create `~/app/current` as a symbolic link to `~/releases/v2` and verify with `cat ~/app/current/config.txt`. hint `mkdir -p ~/app`, then `ln -s ~/releases/v2 ~/app/current`. t16 text run `ls -la ~` to see hidden files too. hint `-a` shows hidden files, `-l` the details. : { on your vm, try absolute/relative paths, look at the file types in `/dev` and create a symbolic link. all commands are harmless. tasks v01 title absolute and relative path text try the same file relatively, then from the wrong directory, and paste the output. blocks cmd pwd
cd /etc
pwd
cat hostname
cd ~
cat hostname expected /home/student
/etc
linux-lab
cat: hostname: no such file or directory differs if your host is not called `linux-lab` that is fine; you see your own host name. if `cat hostname` in home does not fail, you created a file named `hostname` there. v02 title read file types text look at the type of a file, a directory and a device; watch the first letters. blocks cmd ls -ld /etc /etc/hostname /dev/null expected drwxr-xr-x. ... /etc
-rw-r--r--. ... /etc/hostname
crw-rw-rw-. ... /dev/null differs some distributions have no `/etc/hostname`; try `/etc/os-release` instead. a `.` or `+` after the permissions is the selinux/acl marker, not important. v03 title create a symbolic link text create a file in home and a link to it, then read the link. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/practice
echo hello linux > ~/practice/notes.txt
ln -s ~/practice/notes.txt ~/practice/link.txt
ls -l ~/practice
cat ~/practice/link.txt expected lrwxrwxrwx. 1 student student ... link.txt -> /home/student/practice/notes.txt
hello linux differs if `->` is missing or `link.txt` is red you may have swapped the arguments: target first, then link. on `file exists`, `~/practice/link.txt` is already there; remove it first with `rm ~/practice/link.txt`. v04 title type name with stat text show the type as a word with `stat`, then delete the practice folder. blocks cmd stat -c '%f' /etc /etc/hostname /dev/null ~/practice/link.txt
# cleanup: look first with ls -l ~/practice, then
rm -r ~/practice expected directory
regular file
character special file
symbolic link differs on macos or bsd tools `-c` does not exist; this belongs on a linux vm. if you see `rm: cannot remove ... is a directory`, you forgot `-r`. quiz : { which is an absolute path? options documents/report.txt /home/student/documents/report.txt ../report.txt ~report.txt explain an absolute path starts with `/` at the root and points to the same file from anywhere. : { a line in `ls -l` starts with `l`. what is it? options regular file directory device symbolic link explain `l` means symbolic link; `-` is a regular file, `d` a directory. : { where are you after `cd ..` from `/etc`? options /home /etc/.. ],  `..` is the parent directory; from `/etc` you go up to `/`. : { what happens when the target of a symbolic link is deleted? options the link is deleted too the link copies the target the link stays broken the target comes back explain the link only stores a path; when the target disappears the link remains but is broken. summary absolute paths start with `/`; relative paths are resolved from the current directory. `.` is current, `..` parent, `~` your home directory. the first letter of `ls -l` gives the type: `-`, `d`, `l`, `c`, `b`. `ln -s target link` creates a symbolic link; if the target goes away the link breaks. glossary term absolute path meaning full address starting at the root directory (`/`). term relative path meaning address worked out from the current directory. term symbolic link meaning shortcut file that points to another path. term device file meaning special file under `/dev` that represents hardware.

2.3.title: Creating and deleting files and folders
objectives: You create folders and nested structures with mkdir and mkdir -p.
You create empty files with touch, several at once using brace expansion.
You know the difference between rmdir and rm -r and check before deleting.
2.3.text:
title creating and deleting files and folders lead use mkdir, touch, rmdir and rm to build and clean up a file structure in a safe practice area. objectives you create folders and nested structures with mkdir and mkdir -p. you create empty files with touch, several at once using brace expansion. you know the difference between rmdir and rm -r and check before deleting. sections create title creating: mkdir and touch body first make a safe **practice area**: a folder `practice` in your home directory. mistakes then only affect it. as a normal user you cannot write to system directories like `/etc` — that is a protection mechanism. `mkdir` creates folders, `touch` creates empty files. brace expansion produces several names: `touch {a,b,c}.txt` creates `a.txt b.txt c.txt`. commands cmd mkdir what creates a new folder. where for projects, backups or practice areas. why keeps your files organised. example mkdir practice cmd mkdir -p what also creates missing parent folders; no error if the folder exists. where when building nested structures. why one command builds the whole tree. example mkdir -p project/src/code cmd touch what creates an empty file or updates an existing file's timestamp. where when you quickly need an empty file. why a starting point for scripts and test files. example touch file1.txt cmd ls -r what lists the tree including subfolders. where when verifying the structure. why you see what will be affected before deleting or moving. example ls -r project tip always verify the result with ls after an action. delete title deleting: rm and rmdir body linux has **no trash can** on the command line: files removed with `rm` are gone. so check with `ls` what you are about to delete. `rmdir` removes only **empty** folders; for a non-empty one it fails and protects you. to delete a folder with its contents you need `rm -r`. using `rm` on a folder without `-r` gives 'is a directory'. in this simulator dangerous commands such as `rm -rf /` are refused. commands cmd what deletes files (no undo). where when cleaning up unneeded files. why for space and tidiness — but use with care. example rm delete_me.txt cmd rmdir what removes only empty folders. where when removing empty folders. why stops you from accidentally deleting a full folder. example rmdir project cmd rm -r what deletes a folder together with its contents. where when removing non-empty folders. why clears the tree in one command; use after checking. example rm -r project tip make it a habit: first `ls -r folder`, then `rm -r folder`. warn before pressing enter, re-read which folder `rm -r` will delete. in the wrong directory it destroys your whole project. danger on a real system never type `rm -rf /` or `rm -rf ~`. it causes irreversible data loss; only the simulator refuses it here. safedelete title safe deleting: a checklist body scenario: you want to clear old logs in `~/practice/logs`. step 1 `ls logs` (what is in there?), step 2 `rm -i logs/old.log` (confirm each file), step 3 `ls logs` (is it gone?). only then think about `rm -r`. `rm -i` asks before every file (`y` = yes). `rm -i` asks only once when deleting more than three files or recursively: less noisy, still a safety net. commands cmd rm -i what asks for confirmation before each deletion. where when deleting by hand in an important folder. why a typo costs you one 'n', not your data. example rm -i old.log cmd rm -i what asks once before deleting more than three files or recursively. where for bulk deletions such as `rm -i *.tmp`. why fewer prompts than `-i`, but still a last warning. example rm -i *.tmp cmd rmdir -p what removes an empty folder and its empty parents. where when tidying empty nested folders. why cleans up a whole empty chain; stops at the first non-empty folder. example rmdir -p a/b/c tip run the same pattern with `ls` first (`ls *.tmp`), then replace `ls` with `rm`: you delete exactly what you saw. warn wildcards such as `rm *` expand before the command runs. a stray space (`rm * .tmp`) deletes everything. tasks t01 text in your home directory create a practice folder with `mkdir practice`. hint make sure you are home first with `cd ~`. t02 text enter the folder with `cd practice`. hint the directory in the prompt changes. t03 text create an empty file with `touch file1.txt`. hint you can check with ls -l. t04 text create a subfolder with `mkdir folder1`. hint in ls -l the line starts with d. t05 text build the nested structure in one command with `mkdir -p project/src/code`. hint -p also creates the intermediate folders. t06 text list the structure with its subfolders using `ls -r project`. hint -r is a capital letter. t07 text create three files in one command with `touch {a,b,c}.txt`. hint separate with commas inside the braces, no spaces. t08 text create `delete_me.txt` with `touch`, then delete it with `rm`. hint two commands; check with ls that it is gone. t09 text try to delete the non-empty folder with `rmdir project`. did it fail? why? hint rmdir only removes empty folders. t10 text delete the folder with its contents using `rm -r project`. hint look inside first with ls -r proje. t11 text run `rm folder1` on the folder without `-r` and read the error. hint expect 'is a directory'. t12 text challenge: `mkdir -p ~/practice/final_project`, `touch report.txt` inside it, `ls -r final_project` one level up, then `rm -r final_project`. hint to create the file, `cd ~/practice/final_project` first, then leave with `cd ..`. t13 text as a normal user, try to create a folder in a system directory: `mkdir /etc/practice`. what happens? hint expect permission denied; system directories are protected. t14 text debug: the folder `~/old_project` cannot be removed (`rmdir` fails). remove it together with its contents. hint it contains files; `rmdir` is not enough, you need `rm -r`. t15 text mini project: under `~/web` create the folders `css`, `js`, `img` with a single `mkdir -p` and the file `index.html` with `touch`. hint brace: `~/web/{css,js,img}`. t16 text ticket #2310 — accounting expects `jan.txt`, `feb.txt`, `mar.txt` in `~/archive/2026/q1`. build the structure. hint `mkdir -p` for the folders, `touch` with brace for the files. quiz : { what is true for a file deleted with `rm`? options it goes to the trash it is kept for 30 days it cannot be recovered it is only hidden explain the command line has no trash can; deletion is permanent. : { what does `-p` do in `mkdir -p a/b/c`? options asks for a password also creates missing parent folders hides the folder makes the folder read-only explain -p (parents) builds the whole path at once and does not complain if the folder already exists. : { what happens if you run `rmdir` on a non-empty folder? options it fails and the folder stays the folder is deleted with its contents the folder is emptied the folder is moved explain rmdir only removes empty folders. for non-empty ones use `rm -r`. : { which command is most commonly used to create an empty file? options mkdir touch explain `touch file` creates an empty file or updates its timestamp. summary `mkdir` creates folders, `mkdir -p` nested folders, `touch` empty files. `touch {a,b,c}.txt` uses brace expansion to create several files. `rmdir` removes only empty folders, `rm -r` non-empty ones; there is no trash. check with `ls` before and after every action. glossary term directory / folder meaning a structure that holds files; the same concept. term recursive meaning an operation that includes subfolders; -r or -r. term brace expansion meaning the shell turns patterns like {a,b,c} into several words. term timestamp meaning the time a file was last modified. : { on your vm, first create a safe practice folder; never try `rm -r` where real data lives. tasks v01 title build a project tree text build a nested structure in the practice folder and paste the `ls -r` output. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/practice/project/{src,test}
touch ~/practice/project/src/main.c
ls -r ~/practice expected /home/student/practice:
project

/home/student/practice/project:
src  test
... differs the order of `ls -r` may differ; `src` and `test` must appear. empty folders are separated by a blank line in `ls -r` output. v02 title see the protection text as a normal user try to create a folder in a system directory and paste the error. blocks cmd mkdir /etc/practice expected mkdir: cannot create directory ‘/etc/practice’: permission denied differs on a localised system the message may be translated. if the folder was created you are root; use a normal user and remove it with `sudo rmdir /etc/practice` (`sudo` runs a command with admin rights; details in module 4.3). v03 title clean up text look inside first, then delete the practice folder. if no errors, press \ blocks cmd ls -r ~/practice
rm -r ~/practice
ls ~/practice expected ls: cannot access '/home/student/practice': no such file or directory differs if you see `rm: cannot remove ... is a directory`, you forgot `-r`.

2.4.title: Copy and Move
objectives: You copy files and (with -r) folders using cp; for backups you use cp -a.
You move or rename files and folders with mv.
You think about whether the target exists and control overwriting with -i, -n and -v.
2.4.text:
title copy and move lead copy files and folders with cp, move or rename them with mv, and protect yourself from overwrite traps with -i, -n and -v. objectives you copy files and (with -r) folders using cp; for backups you use cp -a. you move or rename files and folders with mv. you think about whether the target exists and control overwriting with -i, -n and -v. sections copy title copying: cp body `cp source target` creates a **copy** of the source; the source stays where it is. if the target is an existing folder, the copy goes inside it; otherwise the target becomes the new file name. copying folders needs **`-r`** (recursive); without it `cp` skips the folder and prints an error. if you also want to keep ownership, permissions and timestamps, use `cp -a` (archive), the safest choice for backups. commands cmd what copies a file; the source is unchanged. where to make a backup before editing a file or to put it elsewhere. why if the original breaks, you still have a copy. example cp draft.txt draft_copy.txt cmd cp -r what copies a folder including its contents. where when backing up a project or photo folder. why without -r a folder is not copied. example cp -r photos backup/ cmd cp -a what archive copy: keeps subfolders, permissions, owner and timestamps. where for real backups and when copying system files. why the copy is as identical to the original as possible. example cp -a photos backup/ tip after copying, check both the source and the target with `ls`. move title moving and renaming: mv body `mv source target` **moves** a file: the source disappears and shows up at the target. linux has no separate 'rename' command; moving within the same folder is renaming (`mv old.txt new.txt`). folders need no `-r`. with several sources the last argument must be an existing **folder**: `mv a.txt b.txt folder/`. within one filesystem `mv` does not copy data, it only changes the entry, so it is very fast. commands cmd what moves a file or folder to another folder. where when organising files or fixing a misplaced file. why leaves no copy behind and takes no extra space. example mv wrong/report.txt inbox/ cmd mv old new what renames in the same folder (if the target does not exist). where to fix a file or folder name. why renaming = moving within the same place. example mv todo.txt tasks.txt cmd mv a b folder/ what moves several files into a folder in one command. where bulk organising. why one command, fewer mistakes. example mv inbox/mail1.txt inbox/mail2.txt backup/ tip make sure the target folder exists before moving: if it does not, `mv a.txt folder` renames the file to `folder`! safety title overwriting and safety options body if a file with the same name exists at the target, `cp` and `mv` **overwrite it without asking**; the old content does not come back. this is the most common way to lose data silently. three safety options: **`-i`** (interactive) asks before overwriting, **`-n`** (no-clobber) leaves existing files alone, **`-v`** (verbose) prints what it does line by line. on many distributions `cp` and `mv` are aliased to `-i` for root, but not for a normal user. commands cmd cp -i what asks for confirmation (y/n) before overwriting an existing target. where when you are not sure whether the target exists. why prevents accidental data loss. example cp -i tasks.txt draft.txt nosim cmd cp -n what never overwrites an existing file. where in bulk copies, to protect older files. why quiet but safe: the target stays unchanged. example cp -n tasks.txt draft.txt nosim cmd cp -v what prints every file that is copied. where in multi-file operations to see what happened. why makes it easy to verify the result. example cp -v tasks.txt tasks_v.txt cmd mv -i what asks before overwriting when moving. where when moving into a folder that may hold a file with the same name. why the file at the target is not lost. example mv -i draft.txt backup/ nosim warn `cp a b` and `mv a b` **overwrite `b` without asking** if it exists. look with `ls b` first or add `-i` / `-n`. danger typing a wrong target (for example `mv notes.txt /etc/hosts`) can destroy an important system file. take a vm snapshot before experimenting near system folders; without privileges the command simply fails. tip for permanent safety you can define `alias cp='cp -i'` and `alias mv='mv -i'` (added to your shell configuration file). preserve title preserving and updating: -p, -u, rsync body scenario: you refresh a backup folder. a plain `cp` gives the copy a new timestamp and owner; `cp -p` keeps mode, owner and time, so you can still see when the original was changed. `cp -u` and `mv -u` copy or move only if the source is newer than the target or the target is missing. for large folders that you sync repeatedly, a dedicated tool (`rsync`, see module 2.8) is the better fit. commands cmd cp -p what copies and preserves mode, owner and timestamps. where when backing up `notes.txt` and the modification time must stay. why without `-p` every copy looks brand new, which hides history. example cp -p notes.txt notes.bak cmd cp -u what copies only if the source is newer or the target is missing. where when refreshing `~/backup` with `cp -u *.txt backup/`. why skips unchanged files and never overwrites a newer target. example cp -u notes.txt backup/ cmd mv -u what moves only if the source is newer or the target is missing. where when merging two folders of reports. why protects the newer file from being replaced by an older one. example mv -u report.txt archive/ tip combine flags: `cp -pv a b` preserves attributes and prints what it did. warn `-u` compares timestamps only, not content. a file with a wrong clock can be skipped. tasks t01 text enter the working folder: `cd lab`. hint all following tasks happen in `~/lab`. t02 text make a copy of `draft.txt` called `draft_copy.txt`: `cp draft.txt draft_copy.txt`. hint source first, then target. use `ls` to see both still exist. t03 text rename `todo.txt` to `tasks.txt`: `mv todo.txt tasks.txt`. hint renaming is moving within the same folder; `todo.txt` must be gone. t04 text create a backup folder: `mkdir backup`. hint it is the target of the next steps. t05 text copy `draft.txt` into the `backup` folder: `cp draft.txt backup/`. hint the trailing `/` makes clear the target is a folder. t06 text copy the `photos` folder with its contents into `backup`: `cp -r photos backup/`. hint `-r` is required for folders. t07 text move and rename at once: `mv draft_copy.txt backup/draft_old.txt`. hint giving a new name in the target renames while moving. t08 text predict: what does `cp photos backup` (without `-r`) do? run it to verify. hint expect an error: the folder is skipped ('-r not specified'). t09 text predict: what does `cat backup/draft.txt` show? run it to verify. hint the copy has the same content as the original: `draft v1`. (`cat` prints file contents; details in module 2.6.) t10 text predict: try to move a file that does not exist: `mv ghost.txt backup`. does it succeed? hint expect 'no such file or directory'. t11 text debug: `report.txt` was left in the `wrong` folder by mistake. move it to the `inbox` folder. hint `mv wrong/report.txt inbox/`. then check with `ls wrong inbox`. t12 text mini project: create `archive/2026` with `mkdir -p`, then move `inbox/mail1.txt` there under the name `jan.txt`. hint two commands: `mkdir -p archive/2026`, then `mv inbox/mail1.txt archive/2026/jan.txt`. t13 text challenge: rename the `photos` folder to `pictures`, then copy the `pictures` folder with its contents into `~/documents`. hint first `mv`, then `cp -r`; the target `~/documents` is an existing folder. t14 text ticket #2410 — accounting wants a backup of the `inbox` folder named `backup/inbox_2026`. the original `inbox` must stay in place and complete. hint folder copy: `cp -r inbox backup/inbox_2026`. the target does not exist, so it becomes the new name. t15 text copy with `-v` and see what happens: `cp -v tasks.txt tasks_v.txt`. hint -v prints every copied file; verify the result with `ls`. t16 text predict: `cp tasks.txt draft.txt` overwrites the target. run it, then read the content with `cat draft.txt`. what do you see? hint `draft v1` is gone; `buy milk` took its place. on a real system `-i` would have prevented this. : { on your vm work in a safe folder called `~/vmlab`; never experiment with `cp` and `mv` in folders that hold real data. tasks v01 title copy a file text create a file, copy it and paste the `ls -l` output. (`echo ... > file` writes text to a file, `mkdir` creates a folder; details in modules 3.2 and 2.3.) blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/vmlab && cd ~/vmlab
echo \  > original.txt
cp original.txt copy.txt
ls -l expected total 8
-rw-r--r--. 1 student student 17 jan 10 10:00 copy.txt
-rw-r--r--. 1 student student 17 jan 10 10:00 original.txt differs date, time and owner may differ; `copy.txt` and `original.txt` must appear. the `.` mark (selinux) appears only on rocky/alma, not on ubuntu. v02 title copy a folder text create a project folder, back it up with `cp -r` and paste the `ls -r` output. blocks cmd cd ~/vmlab
mkdir -p project/src
touch project/src/main.c
cp -r project project_backup
ls -r expected .:
copy.txt  original.txt  project  project_backup

./project:
src
... differs if you get `cp: -r not specified` you forgot `-r`. the order may differ; both `project` and `project_backup` must appear. v03 title move and rename text rename the file, then move it into a new folder and paste the result. blocks cmd cd ~/vmlab
mv copy.txt renamed.txt
mkdir moved
mv renamed.txt moved/
ls . moved expected .:
moved  original.txt  project  project_backup

moved:
renamed.txt differs if you see `mv: cannot stat` the source name is wrong; look with `ls` first. without creating `moved/` first, `mv renamed.txt moved/` fails. v04 title prevent overwriting text show with `-n` that an existing file is kept. careful: without `-n` the content would be lost. blocks cmd cd ~/vmlab
echo \  > keep.txt
echo \  > other.txt
cp -n other.txt keep.txt
cat keep.txt expected keep me differs if you see `new`, `-n` was not typed or your `cp` is very old; try `cp -i` and answer `n`. with `-i`, answer the `overwrite 'keep.txt'?` question with `n`. v05 title clean up text delete the working folder. look inside first; if no errors, press \ blocks cmd ls -r ~/vmlab
rm -r ~/vmlab
ls ~/vmlab expected ls: cannot access '/home/student/vmlab': no such file or directory differs if you see `rm: cannot remove ... is a directory`, you forgot `-r`. quiz : { why does `cp photos backup/` fail for a folder? options the backup folder is protected copying folders needs -r cp only copies .txt files the folder must be renamed first explain `cp` skips folders by default; use `cp -r` (or `cp -a`) to copy them with their contents. : { which command renames a file within the same folder? options rename touch explain on linux renaming is moving within the same folder: `mv old new`. : { what does `cp -i a b` do when the target already exists? options asks before overwriting silently deletes the target merges the files ignores the target and does not copy explain `-i` (interactive) asks for confirmation before overwriting. to never overwrite without asking, use `-n`. : { which option best keeps permissions and timestamps when making a backup? options cp -v cp -n cp -i cp -a explain `cp -a` (archive) copies recursively and preserves permissions, owner and timestamps. summary `cp source target` copies, `cp -r` copies folders, `cp -a` also keeps permissions. `mv source target` moves; in the same folder it renames, and folders need no `-r`. if the target exists, `cp` and `mv` overwrite without asking; `-i` asks, `-n` protects, `-v` shows. check with `ls` whether the target exists and where things end up. glossary term source / target meaning the item being copied or moved / where it goes. term recursive (-r) meaning processing a folder with its subfolders and contents. term overwrite meaning replacing the content of a same-named target file with new content. term archive copy (-a) meaning a recursive copy that preserves permissions, owner and timestamps. term rename meaning changing a name with mv within the same folder.

2.5.title: File information
objectives: You know that on Linux an extension is just a name and `file` shows the real type.
You read size, permissions, owner and times with `stat` and `ls -l`.
You create symbolic links and find their target with `ls -l`, `readlink` and `realpath`.
2.5.text:
title file information lead use file, stat, ls -l, ln -s, readlink and realpath to read a file's real type, size, times and link target. objectives you know that on linux an extension is just a name and `file` shows the real type. you read size, permissions, owner and times with `stat` and `ls -l`. you create symbolic links and find their target with `ls -l`, `readlink` and `realpath`. sections type title real type: file body on windows you tell the type from the extension. on linux `.jpg` is only a name; the content can be something else entirely. `file` ignores the extension and looks at the first bytes of the content. this helps with downloaded files: a file called `image.jpg` may really be an executable program. commands cmd file what tells the real file type from its content. where on downloaded or suspicious files. why exposes wrong extensions and disguised files. example file /etc/hostname nosim cmd file -i what prints the type as a mime type (e.g. text/plain). where in scripts and web server configuration. why gives a short, machine-readable type. example file -i /etc/hostname nosim tip in the output, `ascii text` means text, `elf` an executable program and `directory` a folder. details title details: stat and ls -l body `ls -l` shows type, permissions, owner, size and date on one line. `stat` gives more: inode, link count and three timestamps. times: **access** last read, **modify** last change of the content, **change** last change of metadata such as permissions or owner. the first character shows the type: `-` file, `d` folder, `l` symbolic link. commands cmd stat what shows all technical details of a file. where when you need exact size, permissions and times. why more detailed than `ls -l`. example stat ~/info/data.txt cmd ls -l what prints a long-format listing. where for a quick look into a folder. why type, permissions, owner, size and date on one line. example ls -l ~/info cmd ls -lh what shows sizes in readable kb/mb. where with larger files. why a readable size instead of a byte count. example ls -lh ~/info cmd ls -ld what lists the folder itself, not its contents. where when checking a folder's permissions. why folder info without opening it. example ls -ld ~/info tip `ls -lh` rounds;
