for exact bytes use `stat` or `wc -c`. lscols title reading ls -l output column by column body sample line: `-rw-r--r-- 1 ayse dev 2048 mar 5 10:12 notes.txt`. columns in order: type and permissions (`-` file, `d` directory, `l` link; then `rwx` triplets for owner/group/others), link count, owner (`ayse`), group (`dev`), size in bytes (`2048`), modification time and name. the permission triplets are covered in detail in module 4.x; for now `r` means read, `w` write, `x` execute. on a directory, `x` means you may enter it. commands cmd ls -lt what sorts the long listing by modification time, newest first. where when looking for the most recently changed file in a folder. why shows at a glance what was just modified. example ls -lt nosim cmd ls -ls what sorts the long listing by size, largest first. where when hunting the file that fills the disk. why big files appear at the top. example ls -ls nosim tip `ls -lhs` shows human-readable sizes (k, m), largest first. warn for directories the size column is the directory entry itself, not the total of its contents; use `du` for that. links title symbolic links and the real path body a symbolic link (symlink) is a small file that points to another path. `ls -l` shows it as `link.txt -> data.txt`. if the target is missing the link is **broken**: it exists, but opening it gives an error. deleting a link does not delete the target; `rm link.txt` removes only the link. `readlink` prints the target one step, `realpath` the fully resolved absolute path. commands cmd ln -s what creates a symbolic link: target first, then link name. where for shortcuts or version markers. why access under a second name without copying. example ln -s data.txt ~/info/link.txt cmd readlink what prints the target a link points to. where when you want to know where a link goes. why in scripts you get the target cleanly. example readlink ~/info/link.txt nosim cmd realpath what prints the absolute path with all links resolved. where with relative paths or chains of links. why shows the file's real location on disk. example realpath ~/info/link.txt nosim warn the target path is relative to the link's folder. `ln -s data.txt ~/info/link.txt` works; `ln -s data.txt ~/link.txt` from another folder creates a broken link. names title name and size: basename, dirname, wc body `basename` returns the last part of a path, `dirname` the folder part. both are common in scripts for splitting paths. `wc -c` gives the size in bytes, `wc -l` the number of lines. commands cmd basename what prints the last component (file name) of a path. where in scripts when you only need the name. why no need to cut the path by hand. example basename ~/info/data.txt cmd dirname what prints the folder part of a path. where to find the folder of a file. why you get the folder without the file name. example dirname ~/info/data.txt cmd wc -c what prints the byte count of a file. where when you need the exact size. why exact size without rounding. example wc -c ~/info/data.txt tasks t01 text run `stat` on `~/info/data.txt` and find the size and modify lines. hint `stat ~/info/data.txt` t02 text list the folder `~/info` in long format. hint `ls -l ~/info` t03 text print only the file name of the path `~/info/data.txt` with `basename`. hint the output must be `data.txt`. t04 text print the folder part of the same path with `dirname`. hint the output must be `/home/student/info`. t05 text list the contents of `~/info` with readable sizes. hint `ls -lh ~/info` t06 text how many bytes is `data.txt`? find out with `wc -c`. hint three lines: alpha, beta, gamma; each has a line ending. t07 text find the number of lines of `data.txt` with `wc -l`. hint `wc -l ~/info/data.txt` t08 text create the symbolic link `~/info/link.txt` with the target `data.txt`. hint `ln -s data.txt ~/info/link.txt`; the target is relative to the link's folder. t09 text predict: how does the link look in the output of `ls -l ~/info`? run it and check. hint you see `link.txt -> data.txt` and an `l` at the start. t10 text read the link's type with `stat ~/info/link.txt`. hint the output says `symbolic link`. t11 text predict: which letter does the line of `ls -ld ~/info` start with? run it. hint a folder starts with `d`: `drwx...`. t12 text predict: what does `stat` do for the non-existent `~/info/missing.txt`? run it. hint it fails: no such file or directory. t13 text try a broken link: create a link without target using `ln -s nothing.txt ~/broken`, then run `cat ~/broken`. hint the link exists, the target does not; `cat` reports an error. (`cat` prints a file to the screen; details in module 2.6.) t14 text debug: `~/info/picture.jpg` is really plain text. rename it to `picture.txt`. hint look inside with `cat`, then rename with `mv`. (`cat` is in module 2.6, `mv` in module 2.4.) t15 text mini project: create the folder `~/inventory`, write a file with `echo version1 > ~/inventory/v1.txt`, create the link `current` with target `v1.txt` and verify with `ls -l ~/inventory`. hint order: `mkdir`, `echo >`, `ln -s v1.txt ~/inventory/current`, `ls -l`. (`>` redirects output to a file, details in module 3.2; `mkdir` in module 2.3.) t16 text hard task: create `~/shortcut` as a link to `~/info/data.txt`, inspect it with `ls -l ~/shortcut` and `stat ~/shortcut`, then delete the link. `data.txt` must remain. hint `rm` removes only the link and does not touch the target. t17 text ticket #2520: the audit team wants the size of `~/info/data.txt` in bytes in the file `~/size.txt`. redirect the output into the file. hint `wc -c ~/info/data.txt > ~/size.txt` (`>` redirects output to a file; details in module 3.2.) : { try it on your vm. there are no destructive commands here; you only create small test files in your home directory. tasks v01 title find the real type text run `file` on a text file, a program and a folder and paste the output. blocks cmd file /etc/hostname /usr/bin/ls /etc expected /etc/hostname: ascii text
/usr/bin/ls:  elf 64-bit lsb pie executable, x86-64, ...
/etc:         directory differs the location of `ls` depends on the distribution; find it with `which ls`. if `file` is missing, install it with `sudo apt install file` on ubuntu or `sudo dnf install file` on rocky/alma. v02 title the lying extension text give a text file the name `.jpg` and see what `file` says. blocks cmd echo hello > ~/fake.jpg
file ~/fake.jpg expected /home/student/fake.jpg: ascii text differs your path may be `/home/alice/fake.jpg`; the word `text` is what matters. v03 title details with stat text find the size, modify and change lines in the `stat` output. blocks cmd stat ~/fake.jpg expected   file: /home/student/fake.jpg
  size: 6   blocks: 8   regular file
access: (0644/-rw-r--r--) ...
modify: 2026-01-01 10:00:00 ... differs on a localised system labels may be translated; `lang=c stat ~/fake.jpg` prints english. the birth line is `-` on some file systems. v04 title link and real path text create a symbolic link and find the target with `ls -l`, `readlink` and `realpath`. blocks cmd ln -s fake.jpg ~/pic_link
ls -l ~/pic_link
readlink ~/pic_link
realpath ~/pic_link expected lrwxrwxrwx 1 student student 8 ... /home/student/pic_link -> fake.jpg
fake.jpg
/home/student/fake.jpg differs if `->` is missing in the `ls -l` output, check the order of `ln -s` (target first, then link name). if `realpath` is missing, `readlink -f ~/pic_link` does the same. v05 title clean up text delete the test files. if there were no errors, press \ blocks cmd ls -l ~/fake.jpg ~/pic_link
rm ~/pic_link ~/fake.jpg differs `rm` removes the link first, then the target file. in reverse order the link stays broken, which is harmless. quiz : { what does `file image.jpg` use to determine a file's type? options its extension the first bytes of its content its size its owner explain on linux the extension is only a name; `file` checks the content. : { what does the modify time in `stat` output show? options the last read the last permission change the last content change the deletion of the file explain modify is the content time, change the metadata time, access the last read. : { what happens when you run `rm link.txt` on a symbolic link? options only the link is deleted the target file is deleted both are deleted it gives an error explain a link is its own entry; deleting it does not touch the target. : { which command prints the absolute path with all links resolved? options basename dirname wc -c realpath explain `realpath` resolves relative paths and link chains into the real absolute path. summary an extension is only a name; use `file` for the real type. `ls -l` is the quick overview, `stat` the details; modify is content time, change metadata time. `ln -s target link` creates a symbolic link; `ls -l` shows `->`. `readlink` shows the target, `realpath` the full absolute path; `rm link` does not delete the target. glossary term symlink meaning a special file that points to another path. term inode meaning the metadata record of a file in the file system. term dangling link meaning a symbolic link whose target does not exist. term mime type meaning a label for the content type, e.g. text/plain.

2.6.title: Reading files: cat, less, head, tail, wc
objectives: You choose the right tool by file size (cat, less, head, tail).
You read the start and end of a file with head and tail and the -n option.
You count lines, words and bytes with wc and do a small log analysis with grep -c and |.
2.6.text:
title reading files: cat, less, head, tail, wc lead there is a right tool for every file: cat for small files, less for large ones; head for the start, tail for the end and live logs, wc for counting. objectives you choose the right tool by file size (cat, less, head, tail). you read the start and end of a file with head and tail and the -n option. you count lines, words and bytes with wc and do a small log analysis with grep -c and |. sections choose title choosing the right tool body on linux, settings, logs and notes are mostly plain text files. there is no single command to read them; you choose by the **size and purpose** of the file. small file: `cat`. large file: `less`. start: `head`. end: `tail`. follow live: `tail -f`. estimate size: `wc`. checking the size with `wc -l` first is a good habit. tip when in doubt, run `wc -l notes.txt` for the line count first, then decide. cat_less title reading everything: cat and less body `cat` prints the whole file at once; fast and handy for short files. `cat -n` numbers the lines. `less` opens the file page by page and does not flood the terminal. inside: **space** one page down, **b** one page up, `/word` searches, **q** quits. in the simulator `less` behaves like `cat`; try the real effect on your vm. commands cmd cat what prints the whole file. where short files (notes, /etc/hostname). why the fastest way, but it cannot be paused. example cat notes.txt cmd cat -n what prints the file with line numbers. where when you talk about a line (error on line 7). why line numbers make discussion and debugging easier. example cat -n notes.txt cmd less what opens the file page by page; space, b, /search, q. where long texts and logs. why does not fill the terminal, and you can search inside. example less /var/log/messages nosim warn if you open a huge file with `cat`, the screen scrolls for minutes. press `ctrl+c` to stop it and use `less` next time. danger never print program (binary) files with `cat`: the terminal becomes garbled. type `reset` to recover. if you are unsure it is text, look with `less`. head_tail title start and end: head and tail body `head` shows the first 10 lines, `tail` the last 10. change the number with `-n`: `head -n 3 notes.txt`. new log entries are added at the end, so `tail` shows the newest events. `tail -f` **follows** the file and prints new lines instantly; quit with `ctrl+c`. with several files each one gets a header `==> name <==`. commands cmd head -n what shows the first n lines. where for header lines or the top of a configuration. why a quick look into a big file. example head -n 3 logs/app.log cmd tail -n what shows the last n lines. where for the newest log entries. why errors are usually at the end. example tail -n 4 logs/app.log cmd tail -f what follows the file and prints new lines live. where watching the log of a running service. why you catch the problem the moment it happens. example tail -f logs/app.log nosim tip `tail -f` never ends on its own; it waits even if no new lines arrive. quit with `ctrl+c`. title counting: wc body `wc` (word count) gives lines, words and bytes. `-l` counts only lines, `-w` only words, `-c` only bytes. without an option all three appear side by side: `3 6 33 notes.txt`. checking `wc -l` before opening a file prevents `cat` accidents. commands cmd wc -l what prints the line count. where to learn the length of a log or list. why a quick idea of the file size. example wc -l logs/app.log cmd wc -w what prints the word count. where text length, one-word files. why measures the size of the content. example wc -w notes.txt cmd what prints lines, words and bytes together. where when you need an overview. why three measures with one command. example wc documents/report.txt combine title combining: pipe and redirection body `|` (pipe) feeds the output of one command into the next: `head -n 6 app.log | tail -n 3` gives lines 4-6. `>` writes the output to a file instead of the screen. `grep error app.log` shows only lines containing error; `grep -c` counts them. details come in later modules; here we combine it with the reading tools. commands cmd head | tail what selects the middle lines of a file. where when you need a specific line range. why chaining both tools gives you a range. example head -n 6 logs/app.log | tail -n 3 cmd grep -c what counts lines that contain the pattern. where when asking how many errors there are. why saves you counting by hand. example grep -c error logs/app.log cmd what writes the output to a file. where when keeping a result or attaching it to a ticket. why the output is preserved. example grep error logs/app.log > errors.txt warn `>` erases the contents of the target file if it exists. think twice before naming an existing file; use `>>` to append. danger if you read and write the same file as in `cat notes.txt > notes.txt`, the file is emptied and the data is lost. always redirect to a different file. paths title log paths by distribution body the main system log is `/var/log/syslog` on debian/ubuntu and `/var/log/messages` on rhel/rocky/alma. a missing file gives `no such file or directory`; the problem is the path, not the command. many logs can only be read with `sudo` (for example `sudo less /var/log/secure`). look first with `ls /var/log`. tip if the file is missing, find the real name with `ls /var/log`. as a fallback `sudo journalctl -n 20` shows the latest entries. tasks t01 text read a small file with `cat notes.txt`. hint the file is short, so cat fits. t02 text how many lines does `logs/app.log` have? find out with `wc -l logs/app.log`. hint the option is a lowercase l. t03 text show the first 3 lines of the log with `head -n 3 logs/app.log`. hint the line count follows -n. t04 text show the last 4 lines with `tail -n 4 logs/app.log`. hint the last line should be 'shutdown complete'. t05 text read the file with line numbers using `cat -n notes.txt`. hint -n adds line numbers. t06 text find the word count with `wc -w notes.txt`. hint three lines with two words each. t07 text see lines, words and bytes together with `wc documents/report.txt`. hint without an option three numbers appear. t08 text show the start of two files with one command: `head -n 2 documents/list.csv documents/report.txt`. hint each file gets a header `==> name <==`. t09 text predict: what does `wc -l notes.txt` show? run it and check. hint think of the line count you saw with `cat -n`. t10 text predict: what happens with `cat logs`? run it and read the error. hint logs is a directory, not a file; expect 'is a directory'. t11 text predict: which line does `head -n 6 logs/app.log | tail -n 1` print? run it and check. hint the last of the first 6 lines, so line 6. t12 text debug: a colleague typed `tail 5 logs/app.log` and got an error because `5` is treated as a file. show the last 5 lines with the correct command. hint the line count needs `-n`. t13 text mini project: write all errors to `errors.txt` with `grep error logs/app.log > errors.txt`, then count them with `wc -l errors.txt`. hint there should be three error lines. t14 text challenge: write only lines 4, 5 and 6 of `logs/app.log` to the file `middle.txt`. hint take the first 6 lines, then the last 3 of those, and redirect the result with `>`. t15 text ticket: 'how many errors are on the server, and which are the first two?' save the first two error lines in `first_errors.txt` and show the total number of error lines with `grep -c`. hint `grep error logs/app.log | head -n 2 > first_errors.txt`, then `grep -c error logs/app.log`. : { on your vm you only read; nothing is deleted. reading system files is safe, but be careful not to overwrite files with redirection. tasks v01 title read a small file with cat text print the distribution information and paste the output. blocks cmd cat /etc/os-release expected name=\ 
version=\ 
... differs on rocky/alma you see `name=\ `; the fields may differ. if you get `no such file` you may be in wsl or a container; try `cat /etc/hostname`. v02 title read the start and end text show the first 5 and last 3 lines of the user file. blocks cmd head -n 5 /etc/passwd
tail -n 3 /etc/passwd expected root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
... differs the second line is `daemon` on ubuntu and may be `bin` on rhel. the first line must always start with `root:x:0:0`. v03 title count lines text find the line count of `/etc/passwd` and the three measures of `/etc/hostname`. blocks cmd wc -l /etc/passwd
wc /etc/hostname expected 32 /etc/passwd
 1  1 10 /etc/hostname differs your line count depends on the installation; what matters is that a number and the file name appear. in `wc /etc/hostname` the first number is lines, the second words, the third bytes. v04 title browse with less text open the main log: `/var/log/syslog` on ubuntu, `/var/log/messages` on rhel/rocky/alma. try space, b, /error and q. when done press \ blocks cmd # ubuntu
sudo less /var/log/syslog
# rocky / alma
sudo less /var/log/messages differs if the file is missing, look for its name with `ls /var/log`; some systems only have `sudo journalctl -n 50`. if you cannot leave less, press `q`. v05 title follow live (tail -f) text open two terminals. in the first follow the file; in the second append a line. when you see the new line, quit the first with `ctrl+c` and paste the output. blocks cmd # terminal 1
touch ~/live.log
tail -f ~/live.log cmd # terminal 2
echo \  >> ~/live.log expected new entry differs terminal 1 stays empty and waits; that is normal until a line is appended. with only one terminal do not pause `tail -f` with `ctrl+z`; open a second tab or window. quiz : { which tool is suitable for safely viewing a 5 gb log file? options cat: prints everything at once less: shows it page by page mkdir: creates a folder rm: deletes the file explain less shows only what fits the screen and lets you search; cat streams the whole file across the screen. : { what does `-f` do in `tail -f`? options force-deletes the file hides the file name reads faster follows the file and shows new lines live explain -f means 'follow'; quit with ctrl+c. : { which command gives only the number of lines in a file? options wc -l notes.txt wc -w notes.txt head notes.txt cat -n notes.txt explain wc -l counts lines; -w counts words. : { what does `head -n 3 notes.txt` show? options the last 3 lines the 3 words in the file the first 3 lines everything except line 3 explain head shows the start; -n 3 means the first three lines. for the end use tail. summary small file: `cat`; large file: `less` (space, b, /search, q). `head -n` shows the start, `tail -n` the end; `tail -f` follows live (quit with ctrl+c). `wc -l`, `wc -w`, `wc` count lines, words and bytes. `|` chains tools, `>` writes the result to a file; `>` overwrites existing files. the log path depends on the distribution: syslog or messages. glossary term log meaning a file where a program or system writes events in order. term pager meaning a program that shows text page by page, such as less. term pipe meaning the | symbol; makes the output of one command the input of the next. term redirection meaning writing output to a file instead of the screen; > or >>. term follow meaning watching the end of a file live with tail -f.

2.7.title: Editors
objectives: You open, edit, save and close files with nano.
You know vim's modes and can always get out of vim (:q!, :wq).
You use basic vim commands: insert, delete a line, undo, search.
You edit config files safely: backup first, sudo only when needed.
2.7.text:
title editors lead edit text files in the terminal: nano for a quick start, vi/vim when it has to be everywhere and fast. objectives you open, edit, save and close files with nano. you know vim's modes and can always get out of vim (:q!, :wq). you use basic vim commands: insert, delete a line, undo, search. you edit config files safely: backup first, sudo only when needed. sections nano title nano: the easy editor body `nano` is beginner friendly: you start typing right away and the shortcuts are listed at the bottom of the screen. `^` means the **ctrl** key, so `^x` is ctrl+x. if the file does not exist, `nano file` opens an empty buffer and creates the file when you save. on ubuntu nano is usually preinstalled; on rocky/alma install it with `sudo dnf install nano` if needed. commands cmd nano file what opens a file in the nano editor (creates it on save if missing). where for quick edits of text and config files. why simple, with visible help at the bottom. example nano todo.txt nosim cmd ctrl+o what writes out (saves) the file; confirm the name with enter. where inside nano, whenever you want to save. why saves your work without leaving the editor. example nano todo.txt nosim cmd ctrl+x what exits nano; asks to save if there are unsaved changes (y/n). where inside nano, when you are done. why the way out: y saves, n discards. example nano todo.txt nosim cmd ctrl+k / ctrl+u what cuts the current line / pastes it back. where to delete, move or duplicate lines. why fast line editing without a mouse. example nano todo.txt nosim tip more nano keys: `ctrl+w` search, `ctrl+g` help, `alt+u` undo, `ctrl+_` go to line number. vim title vi / vim: modes body `vi` is installed on practically every linux system, `vim` is its improved version (on some minimal systems `vi` is simply vim). learn the basics once and you can fix a server in any situation. the key idea: vim has **modes**. in **normal mode** (default at start) keys are commands — typing `dd` deletes a line instead of writing text. with `i` you enter **insert mode** and type normally; `esc` takes you back. with `:` you enter **command-line mode** for `:w`, `:q`, `:wq`, `:q!`. beginner mistake number one: typing text while in normal mode. if strange things happen, press `esc` once or twice, then continue. commands cmd vim file what opens a file in vim (starts in normal mode). where for config files, scripts and on servers without nano. why available everywhere and very fast once learned. example vim todo.txt nosim cmd i / esc what `i` enters insert mode, `esc` returns to normal mode. where whenever you switch between typing and commanding. why without `i` you cannot type text; without `esc` you cannot give commands. example vim todo.txt nosim cmd :wq what writes the file and quits (also `zz` or `:x`). where from normal mode after typing `:`. why saves and leaves in one step. example vim todo.txt nosim danger stuck in vim? press `esc`, then type `:q!` and enter to quit without saving, or `:wq` to save and quit. ctrl+c or ctrl+x do not exit vim. vimcmds title essential vim commands body these normal-mode commands cover most daily work. arrow keys work, but `h j k l` (left, down, up, right) keep your hands on the home row. many commands take a number: `3dd` deletes three lines, `5j` moves five lines down. `gg` jumps to the top, `g` to the end, `:42` to line 42. use `:set number` to show line numbers. commands cmd what deletes (cuts) the current line; `p` pastes it below. where in normal mode. why remove, move or duplicate lines (`yy` copies). example vim todo.txt nosim cmd what undoes the last change; `ctrl+r` redoes it. where in normal mode. why fixes accidental edits. example vim todo.txt nosim cmd /text what searches forward for `text`; `n` jumps to the next match. where in normal mode. why find settings in long config files. example vim server.log nosim cmd :q! what quits and discards all unsaved changes. where from normal mode when you made a mess or just looked. why the emergency exit; plain `:q` refuses if there are changes. example vim todo.txt nosim tip run `vimtutor` once (about 30 minutes) — the best interactive vim course, installed with vim. safe title editing safely body system config files live in `/etc` and belong to root. as a normal user you can read them but not save changes: use `sudo nano /etc/file` only when you must. **make a backup first** so you can restore after a typo. non-interactive alternatives need no editor: `echo \  >> file` appends a line, `echo \  > file` **overwrites** the whole file. with `cp file file.bak` you create a backup in one second. if vim crashed or the terminal closed, a leftover swap file (`.file.swp`) may remain and vim warns on the next start. if nobody else is editing the file, you can delete the swap file. commands cmd cp file file.bak what creates a backup copy before editing. where before every change to an important file. why you can restore the old state with `cp file.bak file`. example cp app.conf app.conf.bak cmd sudoedit what edits a root-owned file with your own editor via a temporary copy. where for files in `/etc`. why safer than running the whole editor as root. example sudoedit /etc/hosts nosim cmd export editor what sets the default editor used by tools such as `sudoedit` and `crontab -e`. where in your shell or in `~/.bashrc`. why tools then open nano instead of an editor you do not know. example export editor=nano nosim cmd cat file what shows the file content without opening an editor. where to verify the result of an edit. why quick check that the file contains what you expect. example cat todo.txt warn before editing a file under `/etc`, make a backup (`sudo cp file file.bak`). a broken `/etc/fstab` or `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` can make the machine unbootable or unreachable. tip `>` overwrites, `>>` appends. one missing `>` can empty a file — check with `cat` afterwards. tasks t01 text create a file without an editor: `echo \  > hello.txt`. hint `>` creates or overwrites the file (details in module 3.2). t02 text show the content of the file with `cat hello.txt`. hint you should see hello editor. t03 text back up `todo.txt` before editing it: `cp todo.txt todo.txt.bak`. hint source first, then the backup name. t04 text append a line to `todo.txt` without an editor: `echo \  >> todo.txt`. hint use two `>` characters to append (`>>` details in module 3.2). t05 text show `todo.txt` with line numbers using `cat -n todo.txt`. hint in vim you would see them with `:set number`. t06 text find the line with `report` and show its number: `grep -n report todo.txt`. hint `-n` prints the line number in front. `grep` is covered in detail in module 3.4. t07 text predict: how many lines does `todo.txt` have now? check with `wc -l todo.txt`. hint it had 3 lines and you appended one. t08 text predict: what happens when a normal user runs `echo test > /etc/motd`? try it. hint expect permission denied; editing system files needs sudo (and a backup). t09 text debug: a bad edit broke `app.conf` (it says `mode=debug`). restore the old version from `app.conf.bak`. hint copy the backup over the file with `cp`. t10 text debug: vim keeps warning about a leftover swap file `.todo.txt.swp` in your home folder. nobody is editing the file; delete the swap file. hint hidden file: `rm .todo.txt.swp`; list it with `ls -a`. t11 text mini project: create the folder `scripts`, write `scripts/hello.sh` containing the lines `#!/bin/bash` and `echo hello` (use `printf` with `\n`), then make it mode 755. hint `printf '#!/bin/bash\necho hello\n' > scripts/hello.sh`, then `chmod 755 scripts/hello.sh`. `chmod` details in module 4.4. t12 text challenge: first back up `notes.txt` as `notes.txt.bak`, then append the line `meeting at 10` to `notes.txt`. hint order matters: `cp` before the edit, then `echo ... >>`. t13 text challenge: from `server.log` save only the lines containing `error` into `errors.txt`. hint `grep` pattern file, with the output redirected using `>`. `grep` → module 3.4, `>` → module 3.2. t14 text ticket #2705 — new hires need a welcome note. create `~/welcome.txt` containing `welcome to linux-lab`, put a copy into `~/documents/welcome.txt`, and make the copy read-only for everyone (mode 444). hint `echo`, `cp`, `chmod 444`. `chmod` details in module 4.4. quiz : { you are in vim and want to leave without saving. what do you type? options ctrl+x esc, then :q! ctrl+c esc, then :wq explain `:q!` quits and discards changes; `:wq` would save them. ctrl+x is nano's exit key, not vim's. : { in vim you type `dd` right after starting and a line disappears. why? options vim is broken you were in insert mode dd is a typo in the file you were in normal mode where dd deletes a line explain vim starts in normal mode where keys are commands. `dd` deletes the current line; `u` undoes it. : { what does `ctrl+x` do in nano? options exits nano and asks to save changes cuts a line opens help searches text explain ctrl+x exits; with unsaved changes nano asks y/n. ctrl+k cuts, ctrl+g is help, ctrl+w searches. : { what should you do before editing `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`? options delete the file and create a new one run the editor as a normal user make a backup copy of it nothing, the file can be regenerated explain a backup (`sudo cp file file.bak`) lets you restore quickly after an error. summary `nano file` to edit, `ctrl+o` saves, `ctrl+x` exits. vim has modes: normal (commands), insert (`i`, text), command line (`:`). `esc` returns to normal. exit vim: `:wq` (save) or `:q!` (discard). basics: `dd`, `u`, `/text`, `gg`/`g`. back up system files before editing; use `sudo` only when needed. `>` overwrites, `>>` appends. glossary term normal mode meaning vim's default mode in which keys are commands. term insert mode meaning vim mode for typing text, entered with i, left with esc. term swap file meaning a hidden .file.swp that vim creates while editing; it remains after a crash. term buffer meaning the in-memory copy of the file you edit until you save. term editor meaning environment variable naming the default editor for other tools. : { on your vm you now use the real editors. do all steps in your home directory with test files; take a snapshot before touching files in /etc. tasks v01 title first file with nano text open nano, type the text, save with ctrl+o and enter, exit with ctrl+x. then show the file. blocks cmd nano nano_test.txt
# type: hello nano   -> ctrl+o, enter, ctrl+x
cat nano_test.txt expected hello nano differs `command not found`: install nano with `sudo apt install nano` (ubuntu) or `sudo dnf install nano` (rocky/alma). if nano asks 'save modified buffer?' on exit, press `y` and enter. v02 title cut and paste lines in nano text in nano write `line one` and `line two`, save and exit. reopen, cut the first line with ctrl+k, paste it twice with ctrl+u, save. paste the result. blocks cmd nano lines.txt
# type two lines, save, exit
nano lines.txt
# ctrl+k once, ctrl+u twice, ctrl+o, enter, ctrl+x
cat -n lines.txt expected      1	line two
     2	line one
     3	line one differs if the order differs, it depends on where the cursor was when pasting; `line one` and `line two` must both appear. no numbering shown? you forgot `-n` in `cat -n`. v03 title first file with vim text open vim, press `i`, type the text, then esc and `:wq` enter. show the file. blocks cmd vim vim_test.txt
# i  -> type: hello vim  -> esc  -> :wq  -> enter
cat vim_test.txt expected hello vim differs typed text is missing or odd? you did not press `i` first. press esc, `:q!`, and start again. `vim: command not found`: use `vi vim_test.txt` or install vim (`sudo apt install vim` / `sudo dnf install vim-enhanced`). v04 title quit without saving text write `keep` into a file, then open it in vim, add a line `lose` and leave with `:q!`. the file must still contain only `keep`. blocks cmd echo keep > discard.txt
vim discard.txt
# i -> type: lose -> esc -> :q! -> enter
cat discard.txt expected keep differs if `lose` is in the file, you used `:wq` instead of `:q!`. if vim refuses to quit with `:q`, that is the protection for unsaved changes: use `:q!`. v05 title delete a line and undo text create a 20-line file, delete line 5 with `5g` then `dd`, press `u` to undo, then `dd` again and save. count the lines. blocks cmd seq 1 20 > numbers.txt
vim numbers.txt
# 5g -> dd -> u -> dd -> :wq
wc -l numbers.txt expected 19 numbers.txt differs result 20: the final `dd` or the save did not happen; result 18: you deleted twice without `u`. `seq` is missing? use `for i in $(seq 1 20); do echo $i; done > numbers.txt` or install coreutils. v06 title set the default editor text set nano as default editor for this session and check the variable. blocks cmd export editor=nano
echo $editor expected nano differs to make it permanent add `export editor=nano` to `~/.bashrc`; it takes effect in a new shell. v07 title backup before editing /etc text back up `/etc/hosts` with sudo, check the backup, and open the original with sudoedit or `sudo nano`. look, change nothing, exit without saving. blocks cmd sudo cp /etc/hosts /etc/hosts.bak
ls -l /etc/hosts.bak
sudoedit /etc/hosts
# look around, then ctrl+x (nano) or :q! (vim) expected -rw-r--r--. 1 root root 158 ... /etc/hosts.bak differs `sudoedit` complains about the editor? run `export editor=nano` first, or use `sudo nano /etc/hosts`. if `sudo` asks for a password, enter your own (nothing is displayed while typing).

2.8.title: Disk and network health
objectives: Find which partition is full with `df -h` and which folder takes the space with `du`.
Read memory and load with `free -h` and `uptime`.
Narrow down a network problem layer by layer with `ip`, `ping` and `ss`.
Save health output to a file and prepare a report for a support ticket.
2.8.text:
title disk and network health lead when a server slows down, check two things first: disk usage and the network. do a quick health check with df, du, free, uptime, ip, ping and ss. objectives find which partition is full with `df -h` and which folder takes the space with `du`. read memory and load with `free -h` and `uptime`. narrow down a network problem layer by layer with `ip`, `ping` and `ss`. save health output to a file and prepare a report for a support ticket. sections disk title disk usage: df and du body when a disk hits 100%, writes fail with `no space left on device`; services and logs stop. so first ask **which partition** is full: `df -h`. columns: `size` total, `used`, `avail` free, `use%` percentage, `mounted on` the mount point. once you know the partition, find **which folder** uses the space with `du`. `du -sh folder` gives a total; `du -h --max-depth=1 folder | sort -h` lists subfolders from small to large. sometimes space looks free but files cannot be created: inodes ran out, check with `df -i`. commands cmd df -h what shows size and usage of partitions in readable units. where first command on slowness or 'disk full' errors. why shows at a glance which mount point has the problem. example df -h cmd du -sh what shows the total size of a folder. where after df shows the full partition. why narrows down the culprit folder. example du -sh /var/log nosim cmd du --max-depth=1 what lists sizes of folders one level down; sort with sort -h. where when hunting the biggest folder. why drills down without walking the whole tree. example du -h --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h nosim cmd df -i what shows inode (file count) usage. where space is free but files cannot be created. why millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes. example df -i nosim tip `df` finds the partition, `du` finds the folder. do df first, then du. warn check what a file is with `ls -l` before deleting. for a log of a running service, truncating it (`: > file`) is often better than deleting; if unsure, ask your administrator. mem title memory and load: free and uptime body `free -h` shows ram and swap. watch the `available` column: memory that can really be given to new programs. even if `free` looks small, cache (`buff/cache`) is released when needed, so do not panic. `uptime` shows how long the system has been up and the **load average** (1, 5, 15 minutes). if load constantly exceeds your cpu core count, work is queuing up. commands cmd free -h what shows ram and swap usage in readable units. where when you suspect memory pressure. why available tells the real free memory. example free -h cmd uptime what shows uptime, user count and load average. where quick check on a slow server. why load average shows a trend, not a snapshot. example uptime tip to make a report, use `df -h > report.txt`, and `>>` to append. (details on `>` and `>>` in module 3.2.) net title network: ip, ping and ss body narrow a network problem from the bottom up: 1) is the interface up and does it have an ip? `ip -br a`. 2) is there a default route (gateway)? `ip route`. 3) is the gateway reachable? `ping -c 3 <gateway>`. 4) an internet ip? `ping -c 3 1.1.1.1`. 5) name resolution? `ping -c 3 example.com`. if ping works for an ip but not for a name, the problem is **dns** (`/etc/resolv.conf`). if nothing works, check the cable, vm network setting or gateway. `ss -tuln` shows which ports the machine listens on (e.g. 22 for ssh). commands cmd ip -br a what lists interfaces, their state and ip addresses briefly. where first step in a network problem. why without an ip there is no point checking higher layers. example ip -br a nosim cmd ip route what shows the routing table and default gateway. where when you cannot reach the outside. why without a default via line, traffic cannot leave. example ip route nosim cmd ping -c 3 what sends 3 test packets to a target; reports loss and latency. where testing connectivity and dns. why without -c, ping runs forever. example ping -c 3 1.1.1.1 nosim cmd ss -tuln what lists listening tcp/udp ports numerically. where to see if a service listens on its port. why checks the server side of 'i cannot connect'. example ss -tuln nosim danger on a remote server, commands like `ip link set eth0 down` cut your ssh connection and lock you out. make sure you have console access before changing network settings. tasks t01 text look at partition usage with `df -h`. hint -h gives readable units (g, m). t02 text show memory status with `free -h`. hint look at the available column. t03 text show the load average with `uptime`. hint three numbers: 1, 5, 15 minutes. t04 text read the sample report `~/reports/df_sample.txt` with `cat` and find the use% column. hint `cat ~/reports/df_sample.txt` t05 text save the output of `df -h` to `~/disk_report.txt` with `>`. hint `df -h > ~/disk_report.txt`. a single `>` overwrites the file. (details on `>` in module 3.2.) t06 text append the output of `free -h` to the same file (`>>`). hint `>>` appends, `>` overwrites; if you overwrote it, repeat t05. (details in module 3.2.) t07 text append the output of `uptime` to `~/disk_report.txt` too. hint use `>>` again. t08 text predict: which mount point is the line with 95% in `~/reports/df_sample.txt`? then verify with `grep 95% ~/reports/df_sample.txt`. hint the mounted on column at the end of the line. (details on `grep` in module 3.4.) t09 text predict: what does `~/reports/ping_sample.txt` say about the network? see the loss rate with `grep loss ~/reports/ping_sample.txt`. hint 100% packet loss means the target was never reached. (details on `grep` in module 3.4.) t10 text predict: what is the ip of interface eth0 in `~/reports/ip_sample.txt`? verify with `grep eth0 ~/reports/ip_sample.txt`. hint the /24 is the netmask, not part of the ip. (details on `grep` in module 3.4.) t11 text the disk is bloating. look with `ls -l ~/logs`; the old debug log `old_debug.log` is useless, delete it but do not touch `app.log`. hint `rm ~/logs/old_debug.log`. check the exact name with ls before deleting. t12 text mini project: build the report `~/health.txt`. it should contain, in order, the heading `== disk ==`, the `df -h` output, the heading `== memory ==` and the `free -h` output. hint first line `echo \  > ~/health.txt`, the rest with `>>`. (details on `>` / `>>` in module 3.2.) t13 text challenge: from `~/reports/df_sample.txt` write only the 95% line to `~/alert.txt` and the number of such lines to `~/alert_count.txt`. hint `grep` filters the line, `grep -c` counts; redirect both with `>`. (`grep` â†’ module 3.4, `>` â†’ 3.2.) t14 text ticket: \  find the full mount point in `~/reports/df_sample.txt` and write its name to `~/full_mount.txt`. also delete the useless `~/logs/core.dump`. hint the full one is the 95% line. the mount point is `/var`: `echo /var > ~/full_mount.txt`. (details on `>` in module 3.2.) : { the commands here only read information, so they are safe on your vm. paste the output and we will check it automatically. tasks v01 title disk usage text run `df -h` and paste the output. note the usage percentage of the root (`/`) partition. blocks cmd df -h
df -i / expected filesystem      size  used avail use% mounted on
/dev/sda2        19g  4.1g   14g  23% / differs the partition may be `/dev/vda1`, `/dev/mapper/...` or `/dev/nvme0n1p2`; the use% column is what matters. many `tmpfs`/`loop` lines are normal (ubuntu snap); focus on the `/` line. v02 title space hunt text sort the sizes of your home directory and of the folders under /var. paste the largest 5 lines. blocks cmd du -sh ~
sudo du -xh /var --max-depth=1 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -5 expected 120m	/var/cache
1.1g	/var/lib
1.4g	/var differs if `sort -h` is missing (very old system) use `sort -n` and `du -k`. if sudo asks for a password, enter your vm user password; it is not shown while typing. v03 title ip and routing text show your interfaces and default gateway; paste the output. blocks cmd ip -br a
ip route expected lo      unknown  127.0.0.1/8
enp0s3  up       10.0.2.15/24
default via 10.0.2.2 dev enp0s3 differs the interface name may be `eth0`, `enp0s3` or `ens160`. on virtualbox nat the ip is usually 10.0.2.15; with bridged networking it comes from your router's range. if there is no ip at all, check that the vm network card is connected and set to nat/bridged. v04 title connectivity and dns test text ping an ip first, then a name. paste both outputs. blocks cmd ping -c 3 1.1.1.1
ping -c 3 example.com expected 3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss differs if the ip works but the name does not, it is a dns problem; look at `cat /etc/resolv.conf`. some networks block icmp; if ping fails but the web works, the problem is ping itself. v05 title listening ports text list the ports your machine listens on and paste the output. blocks cmd ss -tuln expected tcp   listen  0  128  0.0.0.0:22  0.0.0.0:* differs if ssh is not installed, 22 will not appear; that is fine for this module. if `ss` is missing, try `netstat -tuln` on old systems. quiz : { which command shows which partition is full? options du -sh df -h free -h uptime explain `df` shows partition usage, `du` shows folder sizes. : { `/var` is 95% full. how do you find the biggest subfolder? options ping -c 3 /var df -i du -h --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h ip route explain du gives subfolder sizes, sort -h orders them small to large. : { `ping 1.1.1.1` works but `ping example.com` does not. most likely problem? options dns (name resolution) unplugged cable disk full not enough ram explain the ip is reachable but names are not resolved: check dns settings. : { which command shows the ports the machine listens on? options ip -br a ping -c 3 df -h ss -tuln explain `ss -tuln` lists listening tcp/udp ports numerically. summary `df -h` answers which partition, `du -sh` / `du --max-depth=1` which folder is full. in `free -h` watch `available`; in `uptime` the load average. narrow network problems bottom-up: `ip -br a`, `ip route`, ping an ip, ping a name. turn output into a report with `>` and `>>`; check with `ls -l` before deleting. glossary term inode meaning a record holding information about a file; their number is limited. term load average meaning average number of runnable jobs over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. term gateway meaning the exit from the local network to the outside (usually the router). term dns meaning the system that translates names into ip addresses.

2.9.title: Disk management
objectives: Read disks, partitions, file systems, and UUIDs with `lsblk` and `lsblk -f`.
Learn what `fdisk -l` and `blkid` display.
Distinguish the roles of `mkfs`, `mount`, `umount`, and `/etc/fstab`.
Verify the target and recovery path before running destructive disk commands.
sol: echo "Check lsblk and df -hT before changing a disk." > ~/reports/disk-ticket.txt
2.9.text: title disk management lead identify a new disk, distinguish partitions from file systems, and inspect mount points safely. backups and verifying the target device are essential before changing a real disk. objectives read disks, partitions, file systems, and uuids with `lsblk` and `lsblk -f`. learn what `fdisk -l` and `blkid` display. distinguish the roles of `mkfs`, `mount`, `umount`, and `/etc/fstab`. verify the target and recovery path before running destructive disk commands. sections inventory title identify disks and partitions body device names vary by machine: a disk may be `/dev/sda`, `/dev/vda`, or `/dev/nvme0n1`; a partition may look like `/dev/sda1`. do not trust the name alone; verify size, type, and mount point. `lsblk` displays a tree. `lsblk -f` adds file system type, uuid, and mount points. `fdisk -l` lists partition tables; `blkid` displays file-system identifiers. commands cmd lsblk what lists disks and partitions as a tree. where when identifying a new device or inspecting disk status. why shows the relationship between disks, partitions, and mount points. example lsblk nosim cmd lsblk -f what lists file-system types, uuids, and mount points. where when matching a partition to an fstab entry. why shows identifiers such as uuids for persistent references. example lsblk -f nosim cmd fdisk -l what lists partition tables without changing them. where when inspecting a partition layout before opening an interactive menu. why provides an overview of disk capacity and partition boundaries. example sudo fdisk -l nosim cmd blkid what displays file-system types and uuid values. where when verifying a partition's identity. why uuids reduce dependence on device-name ordering in fstab. example sudo blkid nosim tip start with `lsblk -f`, then use `sudo fdisk -l` if needed. a device name alone is not reliable identification. filesystem title partitions and file systems body partitioning divides free disk space into partitions; formatting writes a file system to a selected partition. `mkfs.ext4` and `mkfs.xfs` are common examples. a formatted partition is not automatically accessible as a directory. in the interactive `fdisk` menu, `p` prints the table, `n` creates a partition, and `w` writes changes. writing to the wrong disk can destroy data. practice only on a disposable virtual disk with a recovery plan. commands cmd mkfs.ext4 what creates an ext4 file system on a partition and erases existing data. where only on a verified, empty partition with a backup. why linux needs a file system to store files on the partition. example sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1 nosim cmd mkfs.xfs what creates xfs on a partition and erases existing data. where on an empty test partition when xfs is intended. why choose a file-system type that fits the workload and distribution. example sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1 nosim danger `mkfs` or `w` in `fdisk` can destroy data. never try these on the system disk, a real usb drive, or an unverified device. the vm tasks in this module only read information and do not format anything. mount title mounting and persistent configuration body `mount` attaches a file system to a directory; `umount` detaches it. create the mount point first. `findmnt` shows current mounts, while `df -ht` shows file-system type and usage. use `/etc/fstab` for mounts that should persist across reboots. prefer uuids over device names. its fields are source, target, type, options, dump, and fsck order. `nofail` can keep a missing optional disk from blocking boot; choose options for the actual situation. commands cmd mount what shows mounted file systems; with a device and directory, it mounts one. where when inspecting current mounts or performing an approved mount operation. why linux exposes disk contents through directories. example findmnt / nosim cmd umount what detaches a mounted file system. where before removing external storage or beginning maintenance. why allows writes to finish and the file system to be detached safely. example sudo umount /mnt/archive nosim cmd findmnt what lists mounted file systems with their source and target. where when verifying where a partition is mounted. why presents the mount table in a readable form. example findmnt / nosim tip back up `/etc/fstab` before editing. afterward, use `sudo mount -a` to check the syntax instead of rebooting immediately; it can perform mounts. tasks t01 text list the sample disk workspace in the simulator with `ls ~/disklab`; inspect the real disk tree in your own vm. hint `lsblk` shows the real device tree; here you are only listing sample files. t02 text run `df -h` in the simulator and inspect the disk usage report. hint `-h` displays readable sizes. t03 text read the sample disk tree with `cat ~/disklab/lsblk.txt`. what is the second disk called? hint look for the `sdb` line. t04 text create `~/disklab/archive` as a mount-point directory. hint `mkdir -p ~/disklab/archive` t05 text predict: which uuid does the sample fstab use for `/data`? verify with `grep data ~/disklab/fstab.sample`. hint the uuid follows `uuid=` at the start of the line. (`grep` searches line by line for a pattern; details in module 3.4.) t06 text remove the incorrect or temporary sample entry in `~/disklab/fstab.tmp`. hint check the path and name, then run `rm ~/disklab/fstab.tmp`. t07 text mini project: write a mount plan for `/data` with a uuid and the `nofail` option to `~/disklab/mount-plan.txt`. hint save one line with `echo \  > ~/disklab/mount-plan.txt`. (`>` redirects output to a file; details in module 3.2.) t08 text challenge: make a backup of the sample fstab at `~/disklab/fstab.backup`. hint `cp ~/disklab/fstab.sample ~/disklab/fstab.backup` t09 text ticket: \  write in the support note that `lsblk` should be checked first, followed by `df -ht`. hint save both commands in a text line with `echo`. (`>` writes to a file; details in module 3.2.) t10 text show only the header line of `~/disklab/lsblk.txt` with `head -n 1`. which columns are listed? hint `head -n 1 ~/disklab/lsblk.txt` t11 text predict: which uuid does the xfs file system in `lsblk-f.txt` have? verify with `grep xfs ~/disklab/lsblk-f.txt`. hint the line with `xfs` also shows uuid and mount point. t12 text prepare a nested mount-point directory `~/disklab/mnt/data` in one command. hint `mkdir -p` creates missing parent folders too. t13 text mini project: note the root file system's uuid and type (`1111-2222`, `xfs`) in `~/disklab/uuid-note.txt`. hint write both values in one line with `echo ... > file`. (details in module 3.2.) t14 text challenge: count how many entries (lines) the sample fstab has with `wc -l ~/disklab/fstab.sample`. hint one mount entry per line; `wc -l` counts lines. : { these tasks only read disk information; they do not change partition tables or file systems. run them in your vm and review the output before sharing device names. tasks v01 title disk and file-system tree text list disks, partitions, and file-system types. check mount points instead of guessing which disk is the system disk from its name. blocks cmd lsblk -f expected name fstype fsver label uuid fsavail fsuse% mountpoints differs columns and device names vary by distribution; you may see `sda`, `vda`, or `nvme0n1`. a blank extra disk may have empty fstype and mountpoints columns. v02 title mounted space usage text show the size and usage of mounted file systems, including their types. blocks cmd df -ht expected filesystem type size used avail use% mounted on differs containers and wsl may show multiple `overlay` or `tmpfs` lines. pay particular attention to the use% value for mount point `/`. v03 title verify the root mount text find the source and file-system type used to mount the root directory (`/`). blocks cmd findmnt -no source,fstype,target / expected /dev/vda2 xfs / differs the source may be `/dev/mapper/...` or `/dev/nvme0n1p...`; the sample output need not match exactly. this command does not change the disk. quiz : { which command displays disks and partitions as a tree? options mkfs.ext4 lsblk umount du -sh explain `lsblk` lists disks and their partitions. : { which command can destroy existing data? options findmnt df -ht mkfs.ext4 lsblk -f explain `mkfs` writes a new file system to the selected device and erases existing data. : { what do we call the directory through which a mounted file system is accessed? options mount point uuid inode cron entry explain a mount point is the path in the linux directory tree where a file system is accessible. : { which identifier is generally more persistent in fstab than a device name? options size mount name disk order uuid explain a uuid identifies the file system even if device names change. summary `lsblk -f` shows the disk tree along with file-system types and uuids. `mkfs` erases data; use it only on a verified empty test device with a backup. `mount` attaches, `umount` detaches; `findmnt` and `df -ht` are read-only checks. use uuids in `/etc/fstab`, back up the file, and verify changes carefully. glossary term partition meaning a region of a physical or virtual disk defined in its partition table. term file system meaning the structure that defines how files and directories are stored on a partition. term mount point meaning the directory through which a mounted file system is accessed. term uuid meaning a unique identifier for a file system.

2.10.title: Remote connections and file transfer
objectives: Use the SSH client with the correct user, host, and port.
Explain the different purposes of host keys and user keys.
Distinguish one-off copies with `scp` from synchronization with `rsync`.
Protect private keys and never blindly accept an unknown host key.
sol: echo "Use scp for a simple copy; use rsync for repeatable synchronization." > ~/ops/transfer-ticket.txt
echo "Create keys with ssh-keygen and never share the private key." > ~/ops/key-ticket.txt
2.10.text: title remote connections and file transfer lead use ssh for encrypted access to remote linux systems, scp for file copies, and rsync for repeatable synchronization. verify host keys and protect your private key before connecting. objectives use the ssh client with the correct user, host, and port. explain the different purposes of host keys and user keys. distinguish one-off copies with `scp` from synchronization with `rsync`. protect private keys and never blindly accept an unknown host key. sections ssh title a secure session with ssh body `ssh user@host` opens an interactive shell on a remote machine. the default port is 22; use `-p` for a different port. `ssh -g host` displays the effective client configuration without connecting. on first connection, verify the server's host-key fingerprint. compare it with the fingerprint provided by the server administrator through a trusted channel; do not accept a key just because a prompt appears. a saved host record helps detect identity changes on later connections. commands cmd ssh user@host what opens an encrypted terminal session on a remote machine. where when administering remote servers. why runs remote commands securely over the network. example ssh student@linux-lab nosim cmd ssh -p port what connects ssh to the specified tcp port. where when the server uses a non-default ssh port. why directs the client to the correct service. example ssh -p 2222 student@linux-lab nosim cmd ssh -g host what prints effective ssh client settings without connecting. where when verifying an entry in `~/.ssh/config`. why shows the resolved host, user, and port. example ssh -g linux-lab | grep -e '^(hostname|user|port) ' nosim tip do not dismiss a host-key-changed warning. if a server was reinstalled, verify its fingerprint through an authorized channel. keys title key pairs and access security body an ssh key consists of a private and a public key. keep the private key in your own account, never share it, and protect it with suitable file permissions. add the public key to the target account. a key does not magically eliminate passwords: a passphrase protects the private key. `ssh-keygen` creates a key pair. `ssh-copy-id` adds the public key to a remote account; use it only for accounts and servers you are authorized to access. changing server authentication can lock out access. commands cmd ssh-keygen -t ed25519 what generates an ed25519 public/private key pair. where in your own account when preparing key-based login. why allows key-based authentication instead of repeated password entry. example ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -a 64 nosim cmd ssh-keygen -lf what displays the fingerprint of a public key. where when comparing a key with a trusted reference. why provides a short, comparable identity for the public key. example ssh-keygen -lf ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub nosim cmd ssh-copy-id what adds a public key to the remote user's authorized-key list. where only for your own account and an authorized server. why enables key authentication on later connections. example ssh-copy-id student@linux-lab nosim warn never send the private-key file (`id_ed25519`) to anyone. only the `.pub` file may be shared; get permission from the server and account owner. transfer title copy with scp, synchronize with rsync body `scp` copies a file or directory over ssh to or from a remote host. the source/destination form is `user@host:/path`; directories require `-r`. check in advance whether a destination file will be overwritten. `rsync` can transfer only changed parts, preserve file attributes, and be run repeatedly. the trailing `/` matters: copying the contents of a source directory to a destination differs from copying the directory itself. preview the plan with `--dry-run`; `--delete` can remove extra destination files. commands cmd scp what transfers copies over ssh. where when sending or retrieving a small number of files. why provides a simple encrypted transfer command. example scp report.txt student@linux-lab:/home/student/ nosim cmd scp -r what copies a directory and its contents recursively. where when sending a directory to a remote system. why transfers a directory tree in one command. example scp -r reports/ student@linux-lab:/home/student/ nosim cmd rsync -av what transfers files in archive mode, synchronizes changes, and shows progress. where for repeated backups and directory synchronization. why avoids copying every file on every run. example rsync -av --dry-run reports/ student@linux-lab:/home/student/reports/ nosim cmd rsync --delete what also deletes destination files that do not exist in the source. where only when the destination must exactly match the source. why removes stale target files; data is lost if the target is wrong. example rsync -av --delete source/ backup/ nosim danger `rsync --delete` and a misdirected `scp`/`rsync` command can delete or overwrite destination files. check the target, make a backup, and use `--dry-run`. tasks t01 text list the sample transfer files in the simulator with `ls ~/transfer`. hint this command only lists files. t02 text list the sample ssh files in the simulator with `ls ~/.ssh`. hint this virtual directory contains only a sample configuration and host-key record. t03 text read the sample manifest with `cat ~/transfer/manifest.txt`. which file is being transferred? hint find the `report.txt` entry in the manifest. t04 text model a one-file transfer: copy `report.txt` as `report.remote.txt`. hint `cp ~/transfer/report.txt ~/transfer/report.remote.txt` t05 text predict: which key type does the sample host record use? check with `grep linux-lab ~/.ssh/known_hosts.sample`. hint the line contains `ssh-ed25519`. (`grep` searches text lines; details in module 3.4.) t06 text remove the old local copy `~/transfer/old_copy.txt`, not the source file. hint give `rm` only the exact path of the old copy. t07 text mini project: copy the sample ssh configuration to `~/ops/connection-plan.txt` and verify the `host linux-lab` and `port 22` lines. hint first run `cp ~/ops/ssh-config.sample ~/ops/connection-plan.txt`, then read it with `cat`. t08 text challenge: prepare a synchronized copy of the report at `~/transfer/sync-copy.txt`. hint copy it with `cp`, then verify its contents with `cat`. t09 text ticket: \  recommend `scp` for the file and `rsync` for synchronization in the support note. hint write both tool names to a note file. (`>` redirects output to a file; details in module 3.2.) t10 text show the first line of `~/ops/ssh-config.sample` with `head -n 1`. which host alias is defined? hint `head -n 1 ~/ops/ssh-config.sample` t11 text predict: which address does `linux-lab` point to? verify with `grep hostname ~/ops/ssh-config.sample`. hint `192.0.2.x` is a documentation range, not a real server. t12 text create the receiving folder `~/transfer/incoming` for downloaded files. hint `mkdir ~/transfer/incoming` t13 text mini project: keep a backup of the manifest as `~/ops/manifest.bak` before a transfer. hint `cp source target`; the source stays unchanged. t14 text ticket: \  note that a key is created with `ssh-keygen` and the private key is never shared. hint include `ssh-keygen` and the word `private` in the line. : { these commands display the client version and configuration. they do not connect to a remote host or transfer files; use only authorized servers for real connections. tasks v01 title ssh client version text verify that the ssh client is installed; do not start a connection to a remote system. blocks cmd ssh -v expected openssh_9.6p1 differs the version number varies by distribution; seeing `openssh` is enough. the output is often written to stderr, but it is visible in the terminal. v02 title effective ssh settings text display the resolved host, user, and port values for `localhost` without opening a connection. blocks cmd ssh -g localhost | grep -e '^(hostname|user|port) ' expected user student\nhostname localhost\nport 22 differs your user name may not be `student`; that is normal. settings in `~/.ssh/config` can affect the output. v03 title rsync version text display the rsync version and feature summary; this command does not start a transfer. blocks cmd rsync --version expected rsync  version 3 differs the version varies by distribution. if the command is missing, rsync may not be installed. follow administrator policy for installation; installing a package is not required for this exercise. quiz : { which tool opens a remote linux shell? options rsync ssh mkfs crontab explain `ssh` opens an encrypted interactive remote session. : { which item must remain secret and must not be shared? options private key public key host name port number explain the private key stays with its owner; the public key can be added to the target account. : { which option previews an rsync operation without making changes? options --delete --dry-run ],  `--dry-run` shows the planned transfer without making changes. : { which tool is better suited to repeated, changing file transfers and synchronization? options fdisk scp mkfs rsync explain `rsync` is designed for incremental, repeatable synchronization. summary ssh opens an encrypted terminal session; inspect settings without connecting using `ssh -g`. protect the private key and verify the host-key fingerprint through a trusted source. use `scp` for straightforward copies and `rsync` for repeated synchronization. check direction and target; always use `--dry-run` and a backup before `rsync --delete`. glossary term ssh meaning an encrypted network protocol for remote shells and transfers. term host key meaning a key the server uses to prove its identity to the client. term public key meaning the shareable part of a key pair added to the remote account. term private key meaning the secret part of a key pair that must remain protected by its owner. term dry run meaning a preview of planned changes without applying them.

2.11.title: Scheduled tasks
objectives: Know the five cron fields in order: minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week.
Inspect and edit user jobs with `crontab -l` and `crontab -e`.
Use absolute paths, PATH, and log redirection in cron's limited environment.
Account for distribution differences and the impact of deleting jobs.
sol: echo "Edit with crontab -e; verify with crontab -l." > ~/schedule/job-notes.txt
echo "Use absolute paths, set PATH explicitly, and redirect output to a log." > ~/reports/cron-ticket.txt
2.11.text: title scheduled tasks lead use cron to run commands repeatedly at specific times. read the five time fields correctly, define the environment explicitly, and monitor generated output. objectives know the five cron fields in order: minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. inspect and edit user jobs with `crontab -l` and `crontab -e`. use absolute paths, path, and log redirection in cron's limited environment. account for distribution differences and the impact of deleting jobs. sections syntax title cron time and expression format body a user crontab line has five time fields and a command: minute (0–59), hour (0–23), day of month (1–31), month (1–12), and day of week (0–7; both 0 and 7 mean sunday). `*` means every value, `*/15` every 15 intervals, and `1-5` a range. `0 3 * * *` runs every day at 03:00; `*/15 * * * 1-5` runs every 15 minutes on weekdays. combining day-of-month and day-of-week can create unexpected matches; verify the schedule you intend. commands cmd crontab -l what lists the current user's cron table. where when checking whether a job is already scheduled. why helps you avoid adding a duplicate without inspecting existing schedules. example crontab -l nosim cmd crontab -e what opens the user's cron table in the default editor. where when adding or changing a user's scheduled tasks. why manages cron entries without directly editing the system file. example crontab -e nosim cmd crontab -r what removes the current user's entire crontab. where only when all schedules for that user should deliberately be removed. why deletes every scheduled job; accidental use can cause an outage. example crontab -r nosim warn `crontab -r` deletes all jobs for the current user. to remove one job, delete only that line in `crontab -e`; save the output of `crontab -l` first. environment title cron environment, paths, and logs body cron does not run in an interactive terminal. profile files may not be loaded, path may be limited, and the working directory may not be what you expect. use absolute paths for executables and files; define `path=...` at the top of the crontab if needed. redirect standard output and errors to a log file, and manage its growth separately. the time zone depends on system configuration. test the script manually as the same user first, then verify its permissions and dependencies. commands cmd command -v what shows the full path of a command. where when finding the path of a program for a cron entry. why prevents command-not-found errors caused by cron's limited path. example command -v date nosim cmd date what shows the system's local date and time. where when investigating schedule or time-zone problems. why lets you compare the system clock that cron uses. example date cmd systemctl status cron what shows the cron service status on debian/ubuntu. where when scheduled user jobs do not appear to run. why jobs cannot start if the scheduler service is not running. example systemctl status cron nosim tip use an absolute log path such as `>> /home/student/cron.log 2>&1`; `>` overwrites the file each run, while `>>` appends (`>`, `>>`, and `2>&1` are covered in module 3.2). manage title observe and manage jobs safely body a user crontab applies only to that user. system-wide cron directories and the root crontab are separate and privileged; do not change their files without authorization. the service is usually `cron` on debian/ubuntu and `crond` on rhel-based systems. a schedule alone does not prove that a job succeeded: check its log file, service logs, and expected result. a test job that runs every minute creates noise and uses resources; remove it after testing. commands cmd crontab -l what displays the user's scheduled jobs again. where when verifying an entry after editing. why confirms the entry that was actually saved. example crontab -l nosim cmd systemctl status crond what shows the cron service status on rhel-based systems. where when checking the service and distribution differences. why reminds you that the service name varies across distributions. example systemctl status crond nosim cmd journalctl -u cron what displays logs for the specified systemd unit. where when service logs are written to the systemd journal. why shows scheduler errors and startup records. example sudo journalctl -u cron --since today nosim danger commands in the root crontab run with administrator privileges. do not run an unfamiliar line; verify its owner and target files. cron jobs are not suitable for password prompts or interactive input. tasks t01 text list the sample schedule files in the simulator with `ls ~/schedule`. hint inspect the real crontab and service in the vm task. t02 text read the sample schedule with `cat ~/schedule/cron.sample`. at what time does the daily backup run? hint read the first five fields, then the command. t03 text show the header with `head -n 1 ~/schedule/cron.sample` and identify the five field names in order. hint minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. t04 text predict: how often does the sample status check run? verify with `grep check-status ~/schedule/cron.sample`. hint `*/15` means every 15 minutes. t05 text read the incorrect schedule with `cat ~/schedule/wrong-entry.txt`. find the hour or minute values outside the allowed range. hint hours go up to 23; minutes go up to 59. t06 text remove the file containing the incorrect sample entry: `~/schedule/wrong-entry.txt`. hint check the path, then run `rm ~/schedule/wrong-entry.txt`. t07 text mini project: write a backup entry that runs daily at 03:00 to `~/schedule/backup-plan.txt`. hint save the line `0 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup`. t08 text challenge: write a job note containing the commands to edit and inspect a schedule to `~/schedule/job-notes.txt`. hint `crontab -e` edits; `crontab -l` lists. t09 text ticket: \  recommend setting path, using absolute paths, and redirecting output to a log in the support note. hint use the words `path` and `log` in the note. t10 text count the lines of the sample schedule with `wc -l ~/schedule/cron.sample`. hint the comment line counts too. t11 text predict: which job is the last line of the sample? verify with `tail -n 1 ~/schedule/cron.sample`. hint `tail -n 1` shows the last line. t12 text read the job script with `cat ~/schedule/backup.sh`. what message does it print? hint the `printf` line prints the message. t13 text mini project: back up the schedule as `~/schedule/cron.backup` before changing it. hint `cp source target` t14 text challenge: write an entry that runs `/usr/local/bin/report` every monday at 06:30 to `~/schedule/weekly-plan.txt`. hint order: minute hour day month weekday. monday = 1. : { these tasks inspect the current scheduler; they do not add or remove cron jobs. the service name may differ by distribution. tasks v01 title user crontab text list the current user's crontab. if no jobs exist, the message is normal; you do not need to add a job. blocks cmd crontab -l expected 0 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup differs a `no crontab for ...` message means this user has no entries; you have not done anything wrong. only the current user's table is read. v02 title cron service text check the status of your distribution's `cron` or `crond` service. blocks cmd systemctl status cron expected active: active (running) differs debian/ubuntu usually use `cron`; the rhel family uses `crond`. some wsl/container installations may not run systemd; this is an environment difference. v03 title scheduler logs text on systems using the systemd journal, inspect today's cron service records. blocks cmd sudo journalctl -u cron --since today expected cron differs the service may be called `crond` on your system; adjust the command. no log records alone do not prove that a scheduled task failed. quiz : { what is the order of the five cron time fields? options hour, minute, month, day, command minute, month, hour, command, day minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week day, hour, minute, month, user explain a user crontab uses minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. : { when does `0 3 * * *` run? options every day at 03:00 every three minutes on the third day of every month at 03:00 on weekdays explain minute `0`, hour `3`, and all other time fields `*` means daily at 03:00. : { what is a good first approach if a cron job cannot find `date`? options retry every minute use the absolute command path or set path explicitly run `crontab -r` format the file system explain cron may have a limited path; use an absolute command path or set path explicitly. : { what is the safe way to remove one incorrect job? options delete all jobs with `crontab -r` run `rm /etc/crontab` stop the service and leave it stopped remove only that line in `crontab -e` explain removing one line with `crontab -e` leaves the user's other jobs intact. summary a user cron entry contains minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week, and command. use `crontab -e` to edit and `crontab -l` to list and verify. absolute paths, an explicit path, and log redirection matter in cron's environment. `crontab -r` deletes all user jobs; edit one line carefully and monitor its output. glossary term crontab meaning a table of scheduled jobs for a user or the system. term cron field meaning a time field specifying a minute, hour, day, or month. term path meaning the list of directories where the shell searches for commands. term redirection meaning sending command output to a file or another stream.

3.1.title: Streams: stdin, stdout, stderr
objectives: You tell stdin (0), stdout (1) and stderr (2) apart.
You redirect output and errors to files with `>`, `>>` and `2>`.
You merge or discard streams with `2>&1` and `/dev/null`.
3.1.text:
title streams: stdin, stdout, stderr lead every linux command has three standard channels: input, output and error. understanding them is the foundation of redirection and pipes. objectives you tell stdin (0), stdout (1) and stderr (2) apart. you redirect output and errors to files with `>`, `>>` and `2>`. you merge or discard streams with `2>&1` and `/dev/null`. sections streams title the three standard channels body a running program has three open channels: **stdin** (0) reads input, **stdout** (1) writes the normal result, **stderr** (2) writes error messages. by default input comes from the keyboard, output and errors go to the screen. because both land on the same screen they look mixed, yet they are separate channels. that separation lets you send errors to their own file. commands cmd echo what writes text to stdout. where for tests and simple output. why the simplest stdout example. example echo hello cmd cat what writes a file to stdout. where to see file contents. why reads a file and feeds the channel. example cat lab/names.txt cmd what when asked to list a missing path, the error goes to stderr. where to see the error channel. why the message appears on screen but is not on stdout. example ls lab/missing.txt tip channel numbers: 0 = input, 1 = output, 2 = error. you use them in redirections. redirect title redirecting to files body `>` writes stdout to a file and **truncates** it. `>>` **appends**. `2>` redirects only stderr. `<` feeds a file as stdin. if output and errors should go to the same file write `> file 2>&1`: stdout goes to the file first, then stderr is attached to wherever stdout goes. order matters. `/dev/null` is a special file that discards everything written to it. commands cmd what writes stdout to a file; an existing file is emptied. where to save output. why you keep the result for later. example echo hello > out.txt cmd what appends stdout to the end of a file. where when keeping logs. why preserves the old content. example echo world >> out.txt cmd what writes only error messages to a file. where to collect errors separately. why output stays on screen, errors are saved. example ls lab/missing.txt 2> errors.txt cmd what makes a file the command's input. where for commands that read input. why reads from a file instead of the keyboard. example cat < lab/names.txt cmd 2>&1 what sends stderr to wherever stdout goes. where to collect everything in one file. why output and errors are saved together. example ls lab missing_dir > all.txt 2>&1 cmd 2>/dev/null what discards errors. where to silence harmless errors. why keeps the screen clean. example ls lab missing_dir 2>/dev/null tip safe habit: decide first whether you need `>>` or `>`. a wrong `>` silently wipes an existing file. warn `>` empties the target file before the command runs. `sort file > file` destroys the file's content. streamsplit title redirecting each stream separately body read a command line left to right: `ls data yok > out.txt 2> err.txt` -> `ls` runs;
