**1>** (`>`) writes normal output to `out.txt`, **2>** writes the error message to `err.txt`. nothing is left on screen. rule: `n>` redirects only stream n; with no number, `>` means 1. each redirection has its own file. commands cmd what redirects stdout explicitly (same as `>`). where when writing output and errors as a readable pair. why `1>` and `2>` together show clearly which stream goes where. example ls data yok 1> out.txt 2> err.txt cmd what writes stdout and stderr together to one file (bash). where when everything should land in one log. why short form of `> file 2>&1`. example ls data yok &> all.txt cmd <<< what feeds a string to the command's stdin (here-string). where quick tests without creating a file. why no temp file or `echo |` needed. example wc -w <<< \ }],  if it gets confusing, read the line stream by stream: which number, which file? mind the order with `2>&1`: file first, then 2>&1. tasks t01 text write text to the screen (stdout) with `echo hello`. hint the output appears directly on screen. t02 text print the file's content to stdout with `cat lab/names.txt`. hint you should see three names. t03 text list the missing path `lab/missing.txt` with `ls` and read the error message. hint that message comes from stderr. t04 text write the text to the file `out.txt` with `echo hello > out.txt`. hint you see no output; check with `cat out.txt`. t05 text append a second line to the same file with `echo world >> out.txt`. hint `>>` appends, `>` overwrites. t06 text put the error into `errors.txt` with `ls lab/missing.txt 2> errors.txt`. hint the error no longer shows on screen. t07 text feed the file as stdin with `cat < lab/names.txt`. hint `<` reads input from a file. t08 text predict: when `ls lab/missing.txt > result.txt` runs, does the error appear on screen? is `result.txt` filled? run it to verify. hint `>` redirects stdout only; the error is on stderr. t09 text predict: what does `cat lab/names.txt | wc -l` print? run it to verify. hint `wc -l` counts lines; how many lines does the file have? (`|` passes output to the next command; module 3.2. `wc`: module 3.5.) t10 text debug: `ls lab missing_dir > all.txt` prints the error on screen and it does not reach `all.txt`. make `all.txt` contain both the listing and the error. hint add `2>&1` at the end of the command. t11 text mini project: build `build.log`. 1) `echo start > build.log` 2) `ls lab >> build.log` 3) `ls nothing 2>> build.log`. the file must have 3 lines. hint the first uses `>`, the others `>>` and `2>>`. t12 text challenge: discard the errors of `ls lab missing_dir` into `/dev/null` and save the normal output to `found.txt`. hint two redirections: `2>/dev/null` and `> found.txt`. t13 text ticket: the auditor wants the number of users in `lab/names.txt` in `~/count.txt` (number only). hint `wc -l < file` prints the count without a file name; save with `>`. (`wc` counts lines; module 3.5.) : { these commands run in your vm's home directory and only write files you create yourself; still, do not reuse the name of an important file. tasks v01 title separate output and errors text list an existing file and a missing path; write output and errors to separate files, then show both. blocks cmd ls /etc/hostname /nonexistent > out.txt 2> err.txt
cat out.txt err.txt expected /etc/hostname
ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': no such file or directory differs the error text varies slightly by distribution and language; `nonexistent` must appear. if `out.txt` is empty, `/etc/hostname` does not exist on your system; use `/etc/hosts`. v02 title overwrite and append text create a file with `>`, append a line with `>>` and show the result. blocks cmd echo \  > ~/streams.txt
echo \  >> ~/streams.txt
cat ~/streams.txt expected line one
line two differs if only `line two` appears you used `>` in both commands. v03 title silence errors text list a directory you cannot read as a normal user together with a file; discard the errors to `/dev/null`. blocks cmd ls /root /etc/hostname 2>/dev/null expected /etc/hostname differs if `hostname` is missing your system has no such file; as long as no error message appears on screen it worked. quiz : { which channel number is stderr? options ],  0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr. : { what does `echo x > file` do when the file already exists? options appends to it gives an error empties it and overwrites it asks for confirmation explain `>` truncates the file; use `>>` to append. : { which command saves errors to a file and keeps normal output on screen? options `ls x 2> err.txt` `ls x > err.txt` `ls x >> err.txt` `ls x | err.txt` explain `2>` redirects only stderr. : { what is `/dev/null` for? options stores logs it is the keyboard input a temp directory it discards everything written to it explain `/dev/null` is a black hole: whatever you write there vanishes. summary three channels: stdin (0), stdout (1), stderr (2). `>` overwrites, `>>` appends, `2>` redirects errors, `<` supplies input. `2>&1` merges errors into output; order matters in `> file 2>&1`. `/dev/null` discards data. glossary term stdin meaning standard input, channel 0; keyboard by default. term stdout meaning standard output, channel 1; screen by default. term stderr meaning standard error, channel 2; error messages. term redirection meaning connecting a channel to a file or another channel. term /dev/null meaning special file that discards what is written.

3.2.title: Redirection and Pipes
objectives: You chain commands with `|` into pipelines.
You count, sort and deduplicate with `wc`, `sort` and `uniq`.
You combine pipes and redirection, and split a stream with `tee`.
cmds: grep ERROR logs/app.log | tee all_errors.txt | wc -l
grep ERROR logs/app.log | tee -a all_errors.txt | wc -l
sol: grep ERROR logs/app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn > report.txt
grep ERROR logs/app.log | tee all_errors.txt | wc -l
3.2.text:
title redirection and pipes lead a pipe connects the output of one command to the input of the next. small tools combined this way solve big problems. objectives you chain commands with `|` into pipelines. you count, sort and deduplicate with `wc`, `sort` and `uniq`. you combine pipes and redirection, and split a stream with `tee`. sections pipe title the pipe: command | command body `|` connects **stdout** of the left command to **stdin** of the right one. nothing is written to disk in between. each tool does one thing; the pipe combines them. only stdout travels through a pipe. error messages (stderr) still go to the screen unless you add `2>&1` before the pipe. commands cmd wc -l what counts lines. where at the end of a pipeline to count results. why answers 'how many?'. example cat logs/app.log | wc -l cmd grep what keeps only lines that match a pattern. where to filter logs and lists. why reduces a big stream to the interesting lines. example grep error logs/app.log | wc -l cmd head / tail what shows the first / last lines. where to see the top or bottom of a result. why keeps output short. example sort -n data/nums.txt | tail -n 1 tip build a pipeline step by step: run the first command, check the output, then add the next `|`. sortuniq title sort, uniq and tee body `uniq` only collapses **adjacent** duplicate lines, so you almost always run `sort` first. `uniq -c` prefixes each line with its count; `sort -rn` then ranks them by that number. `sort` compares text by default, so `10` comes before `9`. use `sort -n` for numbers. `tee file` writes the stream to a file **and** passes it on, like a t-junction. commands cmd sort what sorts lines; `-n` numeric, `-r` reverse, `-u` unique. where before `uniq` or to rank values. why brings similar lines together. example sort data/fruits.txt cmd uniq -c what collapses adjacent duplicates and counts them. where to build frequency tables. why shows how often each line occurs. example sort data/fruits.txt | uniq -c cmd tee what saves the stream to a file and also passes it on. where to keep an intermediate result of a pipeline. why you see and store the data in one go. example grep error logs/app.log | tee all_errors.txt | wc -l tip the classic ranking: `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`. warn `uniq` without `sort` leaves duplicates that are not next to each other. pipeerr title error stream and pipelines body a pipe only carries stdout. with `ls missing 2>&1 | wc -l` the error line is counted too; `2>&1` sends stderr to wherever stdout goes. order matters: `2>&1` comes **before** the pipe. `tee` normally overwrites the file; `tee -a` appends. in a long pipeline, saving an intermediate result with `tee` lets you inspect it when a stage looks wrong without rerunning everything. commands cmd 2>&1 | what feeds error messages into the pipe as well. where when filtering output and errors as one stream. why errors do not vanish on screen; `grep`/`wc` see them too. example ls data missing 2>&1 | wc -l cmd tee -a what appends the stream to a file and passes it on. where when accumulating a record of a repeated job. why older records are not erased. example grep error logs/app.log | tee -a all_errors.txt | wc -l cmd sort -u what sorts and removes duplicates in one step. where when you want a unique value list and no counts. why shorter than `sort | uniq`. example sort -u data/fruits.txt tip when debugging: first `cmd 2>&1 | head`, then silence unwanted errors with `2>/dev/null`. tasks t01 text count the lines of `logs/app.log` with `cat logs/app.log | wc -l`. hint the pipe feeds the file content to `wc -l`. t02 text sort `data/fruits.txt` alphabetically with `sort`. hint equal lines appear next to each other. t03 text count how many entries the `data` folder has with `ls -1 data | wc -l`. hint `-1` writes each name on its own line; `wc -l` counts the lines. t04 text count the error lines of `logs/app.log` with `grep error logs/app.log | wc -l`. hint grep filters, `wc -l` counts. t05 text remove duplicates from `data/fruits.txt` with `sort data/fruits.txt | uniq`. hint sort first so duplicates are adjacent. t06 text count each fruit with `sort data/fruits.txt | uniq -c`. hint the number in front is the count. t07 text save all error lines of the log to `errors.txt` with `grep error logs/app.log > errors.txt`. hint check with `cat errors.txt`. t08 text predict: what is the first line of `sort data/nums.txt | head -n 1`? `2` or `10`? run it to verify. hint plain `sort` compares text, not numbers. t09 text predict: which number does `sort -n data/nums.txt | tail -n 1` print? run it to verify. hint `-n` sorts numerically; the last line is the largest. t10 text debug: `uniq data/unsorted.txt` still shows duplicates. write the unique lines (`a`, `b`) to `~/unique.txt`. hint `sort data/unsorted.txt | uniq > unique.txt`. t11 text mini project: build the report `report.txt` with the error lines of the log counted and ranked: `grep error logs/app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn > report.txt`. hint four stages: filter, sort, count, rank; then redirect. t12 text challenge: in a single pipeline save all error lines to `all_errors.txt` and also print how many there are (use `tee`). hint `grep ... | tee all_errors.txt | wc -l`. t13 text ticket: management wants to know how many different users appear in `data/access.txt`. write only the number into `~/users_count.txt`. hint `sort | uniq | wc -l`, then redirect with `>`. : { on your vm these pipelines only read; the only files written are ones you create in your home directory. tasks v01 title count with a pipe text count how many entries `/etc` has and paste the number. blocks cmd ls /etc | wc -l expected 187 differs the number depends on your system; any number is fine. v02 title extract and sort users text take the first field of `/etc/passwd`, sort it and show the first five names. blocks cmd cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd | sort | head -n 5 expected _apt
backup
bin
daemon
games differs names differ per distribution; only the alphabetical order matters. use `| grep root` to check that `root` exists. `cut` is covered in detail in module 3.5; here it is enough to know `-d:` (delimiter) and `-f1` (1st field). v03 title frequency table text count which login shells are used in `/etc/passwd` and rank them. blocks cmd cut -d: -f7 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn expected      24 /usr/sbin/nologin
      3 /bin/bash
      1 /bin/sync differs counts and shells vary per system. if you see only one line, check that `sort` comes before `uniq -c`. `cut -d: -f7` takes the seventh field (login shell); `cut` is covered in module 3.5. v04 title keep a copy with tee text save a listing with `tee` while counting it; check the file. if it worked press \ blocks cmd ls /etc | tee ~/etc_list.txt | wc -l
head -n 3 ~/etc_list.txt differs if `etc_list.txt` is empty, check that you wrote `~/etc_list.txt` after `tee`. quiz : { what does the pipe `|` connect? options stdout of the left command to stdin of the right command a file to a command stderr to stdout two files explain the pipe feeds the left command's stdout into the right command's stdin. : { why is `sort` used before `uniq`? options `uniq` needs a file `sort` makes it faster `uniq` only works on numbers `uniq` only collapses adjacent duplicates explain sorting makes identical lines adjacent. : { what does `tee out.txt` do in a pipeline? options deletes the stream writes the stream to a file and passes it on only shows errors sorts the stream explain `tee` splits the stream like a t-piece. : { which command prints the largest number of a file with one number per line? options `sort file | head -n 1` `sort -r file | tail -n 1` `sort -n file | tail -n 1` `uniq -c file` explain `sort -n` ranks numerically; the last line is the largest. summary `cmd1 | cmd2` passes stdout of cmd1 as stdin to cmd2. `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` builds a frequency ranking. `sort -n` sorts numerically; plain `sort` sorts as text. `tee` stores a stream in a file while passing it on. glossary term pipe meaning connects the output of one command to the input of another. term pipeline meaning a chain of commands joined by pipes. term filter meaning a command that reads stdin and writes a changed stream to stdout. term tee meaning writes a stream to a file and to stdout.

3.3.title: Wildcards and Quoting
objectives: Match filenames with `*`, `?` and `[]`.
Distinguish brace expansion from glob expansion.
Explain how single quotes, double quotes and backslashes behave.
Check matching names before running a bulk operation.
3.3.text:
title wildcards and quoting lead before a command runs, the shell expands wildcard patterns and treats spaces as separators. select groups of files safely by using patterns and quotes correctly. objectives match filenames with `*`, `?` and `[]`. distinguish brace expansion from glob expansion. explain how single quotes, double quotes and backslashes behave. check matching names before running a bulk operation. sections globbing title wildcards: *, ? and [] body the shell matches wildcard patterns against names in the current directory before running a command. `*` matches zero or more characters, while `?` matches exactly one. `img?.jpg` matches names with one character in that position; `img*.jpg` also includes longer names. `[12]` matches exactly one of the characters in the brackets; `[0-9]` matches one digit. if nothing matches, bash usually leaves the pattern unchanged. you can notice this in the command output. the shell expands wildcards, not `ls`. when you run `ls *.txt`, the shell passes matching names to `ls` as separate arguments. commands cmd ls *.jpg what lists names that match `*.jpg`. where when you want to inspect files with a particular extension together. why you can see all matches without typing every name. example ls *.jpg cmd ls img?.jpg what lists `.jpg` names with exactly one character after `img`. where when a specific part and length of a name should match. why `?` represents one character, so `img10.jpg` does not match. example ls img?.jpg cmd ls img[12].jpg what matches names such as `img1.jpg` and `img2.jpg`. where when only certain individual characters are allowed. why it limits the pattern to characters inside the brackets. example ls img[12].jpg cmd ls *.{jpg,png} what expands the brace options into separate patterns. where when you want to perform the same operation on multiple extensions. why you can write similar patterns briefly and clearly. example ls *.{jpg,png} tip if you are unsure what matches, first display the expansion with `printf '%s\n' *.jpg`. do not run a command that changes files yet. quoting title quotes and escaping body quotes control how the shell interprets spaces and special characters. without quotes, a name containing a space is split into multiple arguments. `\ ` keeps it together as one argument. characters inside single quotes stay literal; variables such as `$home` are not expanded. double quotes preserve spaces but still expand variables and command substitutions. a backslash removes the special meaning of the character immediately after it. commands cmd ls \ what passes a name containing a space as one argument. where when listing names with spaces or passing them to commands. why it prevents the shell from splitting the name into two parts. example ls \ }, { echo '$home' what prints the literal `$home` text inside single quotes. where when you want to display special characters without expansion. why you see the text as written, not the variable's value. example echo '$home' cmd echo \ what expands the variable inside double quotes and prints its value. where when using a variable value while preserving spaces. why the value stays together while the shell still expands the variable. example echo \ }, { ls my\ file.txt what uses a backslash to remove the special meaning of the space. where when you need to protect one special character. why it keeps the name as one argument without using quotes. example ls my\ file.txt tip when a filename contains a variable, usually quote it as `\ `; this also preserves any spaces in its value. safe title use wildcards safely body a wildcard pattern can match multiple names. before a delete command such as `rm *.tmp`, run the same pattern with `ls` and check which names are selected. in particular, `*` can match a broad set of names. first use `pwd` to confirm the current directory, then list the matches. do not test an unfamiliar pattern with a destructive command on a real system. commands cmd ls *.tmp what shows matching names ending in `.tmp` before deletion. where immediately before a bulk operation using wildcards. why you can confirm which names the command would affect. example ls *.tmp cmd rm -i *.tmp what asks for confirmation before deleting each matching file. where when removing only temporary files you have checked. why you get a chance to cancel if a match is wrong. example rm -i *.tmp nosim warn never use wildcards in delete commands blindly. first confirm the directory and matches with `pwd` and `ls`; test destructive commands only in a safe environment. regex title regex basics (bre / ere) body globs are for file names; a **regular expression** (regex) matches text content. `grep` uses bre by default and `grep -e` uses ere. careful: `*` means 'anything' in a glob but 'zero or more of the previous item' in a regex. core patterns: `^` start of line, `$` end of line, `.` any character, `*` zero or more of the previous, `[abc]` a set. ere adds `+` (one or more), `?` (zero or one), `|` (or) and `()` (group); bre needs `\+`, `\?`, `\|` for these. put patterns in single quotes so the shell does not interpret them: `grep -e 'a|b' file`. commands cmd grep '^img' what selects lines that start with `img`. where when anchoring to the start or end of a line. why rules out partial matches. example ls | grep '^img' cmd grep -e what uses extended regex (ere). where when you need `|`, `+` or `()`. why gives readable patterns without escapes. example ls | grep -e '^(img|doc)[0-9]+' cmd grep '\.txt$' what matches the extension at the end. where use `\.` when the dot must be a real dot. why a bare `.` matches any character. example ls | grep '\.txt$' tip `sed -e` and `awk` use the same ere pattern language; you will meet them in module 3.6. practice title apply patterns in practice tasks body this module uses english ascii names such as `img1.jpg`, `img2.jpg`, `img10.png`, `doc1.txt` and `doc2.txt`. the command examples can be tried safely in the virtual lab. brace expansion is not the same as globbing: `{1,2}` is split into separate strings by the shell, while `*` and `?` match existing names. predict which names a command receives, then verify in the lab. commands cmd echo *.txt what prints matching names with the `.txt` extension. where when testing a pattern before changing anything. why you can see how the shell expands the pattern. example echo *.txt cmd touch log_{1,2,3}.txt what creates three separate names using brace options. where when you need similar test names. why it avoids repeating nearly identical commands. example touch log_{1,2,3}.txt tip names containing spaces in the lab exist only in the virtual filesystem; you do not need to try the same commands on your real system. tasks t01 text the lab is already set up with mixed names. run `ls *.jpg` and observe that only names ending in `.jpg` are listed. hint `*` matches zero or more characters; the dot and `jpg` suffix stay fixed in the pattern. t02 text use `ls img?.jpg` to list `.jpg` names with exactly one character after `img`. hint `?` matches exactly one character. leave the pattern unquoted so the shell expands it. t03 text use `ls doc*` to list names that start with `doc`. hint `*` allows zero or more characters after `doc`. t04 text run `echo *.txt`. how does the shell pass matching names to `echo`? hint the shell first expands the pattern to matching names; `echo` prints those names. t05 text use `ls img[12].jpg` to list images whose character after `img` is `1` or `2`. hint each option inside the brackets represents one character. t06 text use `ls *.{jpg,png}` to match `.jpg` and `.png` names in one command. hint the `jpg` and `png` brace options produce separate patterns. t07 text create a `texts` directory and copy names that start with `doc` and end in `.txt` into it. do not copy `notes.md`. hint run `mkdir texts`, then `cp doc*.txt texts`. (`mkdir` is covered in module 2.3, `cp` in module 2.4.) t08 text predict: does `echo '$home'` print the variable's value or the literal `$home` text? run it to check. hint text inside single quotes is not expanded. t09 text predict: what does `echo *.xyz` print if no names match `*.xyz`? verify in the lab. hint by default, bash leaves an unmatched pattern unchanged. t10 text debug: target the name `old report.txt` as one argument and remove that file. hint quote the name containing a space: `rm \ `. (`rm` is covered in module 2.3.) t11 text mini project: create a `backup` directory and copy only `.jpg` and `.png` files into it. hint use `mkdir backup`, followed by `cp *.jpg *.png backup`. (`mkdir` is covered in module 2.3, `cp` in module 2.4.) t12 text challenge: create the names `log_1.txt`, `log_2.txt` and `log_3.txt` with brace expansion, then remove all three with the `log_?` pattern. hint run `touch log_{1,2,3}.txt` first, then `rm log_?.txt`. (`touch` and `rm` are covered in module 2.3.) t13 text ticket: rename `my file.txt`, which contains a space, to `my_file.txt`. make sure the original name stays one argument. hint use `mv \  my_file.txt`. (`mv` is covered in module 2.4.) : { you can run the commands in this section in your own vm. create files only inside `glob-lab` in your home directory; do not test wildcard deletions elsewhere. tasks v01 title single-character wildcard text create `glob-lab` in your home directory. add the names `a1.txt` and `a2.txt` inside it, then list the `a?.txt` pattern. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/glob-lab && cd ~/glob-lab && touch a1.txt a2.txt && ls a?.txt expected a1.txt
a2.txt differs `a?.txt` matches exactly one character; both names should appear. if the names appear on one line, use `ls -1 a?.txt` to show each on its own line. v02 title single and double quotes text in the same terminal session, first set `name=linux`. then print the variable with double quotes and with single quotes. the output should contain both `linux` and `$name`. blocks cmd name=linux
echo \ 
echo '$name' expected linux
$name differs if both lines show `linux`, you may have used double quotes instead of single quotes. the `name=linux` assignment and `echo` commands must run in the same shell session. v03 title preserve a name with spaces text create a directory named `my docs` inside `glob-lab`. then list it with quotes; the output should contain `my docs`. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/glob-lab && cd ~/glob-lab && mkdir -p \  && ls -d \ expected my docs differs if the name is split, check the quotes in both the creation and listing commands. `ls -d` displays the directory name instead of its contents. v04 title check matches before deleting text create two temporary files inside `glob-lab`. first list the `*.tmp` matches and confirm that only those two names appear. delete them only if you confirmed the correct directory and matches. blocks cmd cd ~/glob-lab && touch sample1.tmp sample2.tmp && ls *.tmp differs if other names appear, do not run the delete command; check `pwd` and the list first. if there are no matches, confirm you are in `glob-lab` and that the names end in `.tmp`. quiz : { what does the `?` wildcard match? options zero or more characters only one file extension all characters inside square brackets exactly one character explain `?` represents exactly one character; `*` can match zero or more. : { which form prints `$home` without expanding it? options `echo '$home'` `echo \ `echo $home` `echo \$home` explain everything inside single quotes stays literal. in this example, a backslash also escapes the `$` character. : { in bash, what does `echo *.xyz` do by default when no names match `*.xyz`? options deletes all files prints nothing prints the unmatched `*.xyz` pattern unchanged changes the current directory explain by default, bash passes an unmatched glob pattern to the command unchanged. : { how do you correctly list the name `my file.txt`? options `ls my file.txt` `ls \ `ls my-file.txt` `ls *.txt` explain the quotes preserve the space and pass the name to `ls` as one argument. summary `*` matches zero or more characters; `?` matches exactly one. `[abc]` matches one of the listed characters; `{a,b}` expands options into separate strings. single quotes preserve everything literally; double quotes preserve spaces while expanding variables. protect names with spaces using quotes or a backslash. check the directory and matches before running a destructive command with wildcards. glossary term glob meaning a wildcard pattern that the shell matches against filenames. term wildcard meaning a special character representing one or more characters in filename patterns. term quoting meaning controlling how the shell interprets spaces and special characters. term escape character meaning a backslash (`\`) that removes the special meaning of the character after it.

3.4.title: Searching: grep and find
objectives: Search file contents with `grep`.
Explain the effects of `-i`, `-n`, `-v` and `-c`.
Find files by name and type with `find`.
Use search results with pipes and redirection.
3.4.text: title searching: grep and find lead grep searches lines inside files, while find searches for files and directories in a directory tree. combine them to inspect logs and project files quickly. objectives search file contents with `grep`. explain the effects of `-i`, `-n`, `-v` and `-c`. find files by name and type with `find`. use search results with pipes and redirection. sections grep title search file contents with grep body `grep pattern file` prints matching lines. the pattern can be plain text or a regular expression. use `-i` to ignore case, `-n` to show line numbers, `-v` to select non-matching lines and `-c` to count matching lines. `grep` can also read text from a pipe when no filename is given. this lets you filter long output with `command | grep pattern`. commands cmd grep -n what shows line numbers alongside matching lines. where when locating a match in a file. why makes it easier to find and inspect the result. example grep -n error logs/app.log cmd grep -i what ignores upper- and lowercase differences. where when log messages use different capitalization. why `error`, `error` and `error` all match. example grep -i error logs/app.log cmd grep -v what shows lines that do not match the pattern. where when excluding unwanted lines from results. why filters the inverse of a match. example grep -v info logs/app.log cmd grep -c what prints the number of matching lines. where when counting events in a log. why gives a total without printing every line. example grep -c error logs/app.log tip pass the pattern and filename as separate arguments. quote a search string that contains special characters. find title search the file system with find body `find start ...` searches downwards from the given directory. `-name` selects a name pattern, `-type f` selects regular files and `-type d` selects directories. quote filename patterns so the shell does not expand `*` before find receives it. `find` can search by more than name, and its output can be piped to another command. `locate` searches a prebuilt filename index; it is fast, but newly created files may not be indexed yet. starting from a focused directory avoids scanning unrelated system paths. commands cmd find . -name what searches by name in a directory tree. where when you know a filename or extension inside a project. why it also searches subdirectories. example find project -name \ }, { find . -type f what selects regular files only. where when you need to distinguish files from directories. why limits results to one kind of filesystem object. example find project -type f -name \ }, { find . -type d what selects directories only. where when locating folders inside a project. why keeps directory names separate from filenames. example find project -type d cmd locate what searches an indexed database of filenames quickly. where when looking for the path of a known file across the system. why it is fast when the index is current; new files may not appear yet. example locate sshd_config nosim warn `find /` can scan the entire system and produce permission warnings. start with a narrow path such as your project or home directory. combine title combine searches and save results body `grep` and `find` answer different questions: grep finds text inside files, while find locates files by name and path. save results with `>` or pass them to another filter with `|`. inspect search results before changing important files. the commands in this module search and read; redirection creates a report only in your working directory. commands cmd grep -r what searches file contents recursively in a directory. where when finding where a setting or word appears in a project. why avoids opening files one by one. example grep -r todo project cmd find . -type f -name \  > list.txt what writes paths of matching text files to a list. where when you want to inspect search results later. why keeps results in a reusable report. example find project -type f -name \  > text_files.txt tip run a search and inspect its output first; then redirect it to a report if needed. tasks t01 text show the `error` lines in `logs/app.log` with `grep`. hint pass the pattern and file: `grep error logs/app.log`. t02 text search `logs/app.log` for `warn`, ignoring letter case. hint use `grep -i warn logs/app.log`. t03 text find the `404` line in the access log and include its line number. hint use `grep -n 404 logs/access.log`. t04 text find names ending in `.conf` in the `project` tree. hint use `find project -name \ `; quote the pattern. t05 text find only regular `.txt` files under `project`. hint use `find project -type f -name \ },  : { predict how many matching lines `grep -c error logs/app.log` reports, then verify. hint the command prints the count, not the matching lines. t07 text predict how to filter only `200` lines from the access log. use a pipe. hint try `cat logs/access.log | grep 200`. (`cat` is in module 2.6, `|` in module 3.2.) t08 text debug: save the `error` lines to `errors.txt` in your home directory. hint redirect stdout with `grep error logs/app.log > errors.txt` (`>` is covered in module 3.2). t09 text show log lines that do not contain `info`. hint `-v` selects non-matching lines: `grep -v info logs/app.log`. t10 text mini task: search project files for lines containing `todo`. hint search a directory recursively with `grep -r todo project`. t11 text mini task: find regular files ending in `.log` under `logs`. hint use `find logs -type f -name \ },  : { challenge: search `project` for `todo`, ignoring case and showing line numbers. hint combine options with `grep -rin todo project`. t13 text ticket: save all `.txt` file paths in the project to a `text_files.txt` report. hint use `find . -type f -name \  > text_files.txt` (`>` is covered in module 3.2). : { read existing text and paths on your own vm. these commands do not change system files; use your home directory when creating a report. tasks v01 title search a log text search a system log for `error`, ignoring case, and paste one matching line. blocks cmd grep -i error /var/log/messages | head -n 3 expected error differs if that log does not exist, choose a log on your distribution or create `~/lab/app.log` with sample lines. v02 title show line numbers text find the `root` line in `/etc/passwd` and include its line number. blocks cmd grep -n '^root:' /etc/passwd expected 1:root: differs the line number may vary by system; the output should contain `root` with a number before it. v03 title search by filename text find the file named `hostname` under `/etc`. blocks cmd find /etc -type f -name hostname expected /etc/hostname differs the output should contain the full path. `find` takes the starting directory and name as separate arguments. v04 title save results safely text create `lab` in your home directory, make a report listing `.txt` files there, and inspect the report. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/lab && cd ~/lab && touch notes.txt readme.txt && find . -type f -name '*.txt' > files.txt && cat files.txt differs if the report is empty, check that `cd ~/lab` succeeded and the filenames are correct. do not search the whole system. (`mkdir`/`touch` are in module 2.3, `>` in module 3.2.) quiz : { what does `grep -i error file` do? options shows only the first line deletes the file shows matching lines regardless of letter case renames the file explain `-i` makes the search case-insensitive. : { what does `grep -n` add to its output? options line numbers file sizes owner names modification times explain `-n` shows the line number for each match. : { what does `find project -type f -name '*.txt'` search for? options directories only logs across the whole system lines containing txt regular files ending in .txt under project explain the starting path is `project`, the type is regular file, and the name pattern ends in `.txt`. : { which command searches file contents recursively for `todo`? options `find project -type d` `grep -r todo project` `sort todo project` `cut todo project` explain `grep -r` searches file contents recursively in a directory tree. summary `grep` searches file contents; `find` locates files and directories in a tree. `grep -i` ignores case, `-n` shows line numbers, `-v` inverts matches and `-c` counts them. `find -name` selects a name pattern; `-type f` selects regular files and `-type d` directories. quote filename patterns so the shell does not expand `*` before the search. start from a narrow directory instead of searching a large tree unnecessarily. glossary term grep meaning a search tool that finds matching lines in text files. term find meaning a filesystem search tool that starts at a directory and descends through its tree. term regular expression meaning a pattern syntax for matching text. term recursive search meaning a search that also visits subdirectories.

3.5.title: Text Filtering: sort, uniq, cut and tr
objectives: Sort text and numbers with `sort`.
Collapse or count consecutive duplicates with `uniq`.
Select fields from delimited text with `cut`.
Transform characters with `tr` and combine tools in pipelines.
3.5.text:
title text filtering: sort, uniq, cut and tr lead turn raw text into a useful report by sorting lines, counting duplicates, selecting fields and transforming characters. objectives sort text and numbers with `sort`. collapse or count consecutive duplicates with `uniq`. select fields from delimited text with `cut`. transform characters with `tr` and combine tools in pipelines. sections sort title sort lines with sort body `sort file` sorts lines alphabetically or lexically. `-r` reverses the order; `-n` sorts numeric values rather than text. for example, a plain text sort may place `100` before `2`. `sort` prints its result and does not change the source file. redirect the output to a different file if you want to keep the sorted result. commands cmd sort what sorts lines as text. where when putting a list in alphabetical order. why groups similar lines together. example sort data/fruits.txt cmd sort -r what reverses the sort order. where when you want later values first. why produces the reverse of the same ordering. example sort -r data/fruits.txt cmd sort -n what sorts lines by numeric value. where for files with one number per line. why places values such as `2` and `100` in numeric order. example sort -n data/numbers.txt tip by default, `sort` compares text. use `-n` for numbers, and check the first lines with `head` if needed. uniq title collapse duplicates with uniq body `uniq` collapses only identical adjacent lines. if duplicates occur in different parts of a file, sort them first to bring them together. `uniq -c` prefixes each unique line with its count. this is useful for simple frequency reports. commands cmd uniq what collapses consecutive identical lines into one. where when removing duplicates from a sorted list. why leaves one copy of each value. example sort data/fruits.txt | uniq cmd uniq -c what collapses consecutive duplicates and prints their counts. where when calculating how often each value occurs. why shows each value and its frequency together. example sort data/fruits.txt | uniq -c warn `uniq` does not search for duplicates across the whole file; it catches only adjacent repeats. the common pattern is `sort | uniq`. cuttr title select fields with cut and transform characters with tr body `cut -ddelimiter -ffield` selects fields from delimited lines. csv uses commas, while `/etc/passwd` uses colons. select multiple fields with a comma-separated list such as `-f1,3`. `tr set1 set2` transforms characters from standard input. for example, you can convert ascii lowercase letters to uppercase. `cut`, `sort`, `uniq` and `tr` use stdin and stdout, so they can be combined with pipes. commands cmd cut -d, -f1 what selects the first field from comma-separated lines. where when extracting a column from a csv file. why removes columns you do not need. example cut -d, -f1 data/employees.csv cmd cut -d, -f1,3 what selects the first and third fields. where when you need more than one column. why keeps only the required data. example cut -d, -f1,3 data/employees.csv cmd tr 'a-z' 'a-z' what converts ascii lowercase letters to uppercase. where when standardizing the letter case of text. why transforms characters within a pipeline. example echo hello | tr 'a-z' 'a-z' tip for text separated by variable amounts of whitespace, `awk` may be more flexible than `cut`; here we focus on fixed delimiters. pipeline title combine tools in a pipeline body text filters are small and focused. for example, select a status-code field from a log, sort it and count it with `uniq -c`. check the result on screen, then save it to a report with `>`. order matters: `sort | uniq -c` counts duplicates, then `sort -rn` sorts by count from highest to lowest. commands cmd sort | uniq -c | sort -rn what counts values and sorts them from most to least frequent. where when finding common values in logs or lists. why combines small tools into a report. example cut -d' ' -f2 data/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn cmd cut -d, -f2 what passes the selected field from csv into a pipe. where when preparing one column for another filter. why keeps each tool focused on one task. example cut -d, -f2 data/employees.csv | sort | uniq warn `>` overwrites the existing contents of its target. do not write over the source file; choose a separate report filename. tasks t01 text sort the lines in `data/fruits.txt` alphabetically. hint use `sort data/fruits.txt`. t02 text show the same fruit list in reverse order. hint use `sort -r data/fruits.txt`. t03 text sort the numbers in `data/numbers.txt` numerically. hint use `sort -n data/numbers.txt`. t04 text remove duplicate fruit lines; remember to sort first. hint use `sort data/fruits.txt | uniq`. t05 text count how many times each fruit occurs. hint use `sort data/fruits.txt | uniq -c`. t06 text extract only employee names, the first column of the csv. hint the delimiter is a comma: `cut -d, -f1 data/employees.csv`. t07 text predict the frequency of each department in the employee csv. the header in the second field is included. hint use `cut -d, -f2 data/employees.csv | sort | uniq -c`. t08 text predict the first line from a text sort of the numbers, then run it. hint plain `sort` compares text; `10` may come first. t09 text debug: write the sorted unique lines from `data/mixed.txt` to `unique.txt`. hint sort first, then use `uniq` and redirect the result. t10 text mini task: convert `hello` to uppercase with `tr`. hint use `echo hello | tr 'a-z' 'a-z'`. t11 text mini task: write the unique department names from the employee csv to `reports/departments.txt`. hint extract the second csv field, sort it, then redirect `uniq` output to the report. t12 text challenge: sort the access log's status codes by frequency, highest first. hint extract the second field with `cut`, then use `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`. t13 text ticket: write counts of access-log status codes to `reports/status_count.txt`. hint extract the second field, sort, use `uniq -c`, then redirect to the report. : { these filters only read input on your vm. use separate filenames in your home directory for output reports. tasks v01 title numeric sort text sort the user ids in `/etc/passwd` numerically and paste the first few lines. blocks cmd cut -d: -f3 /etc/passwd | sort -n | head -n 5 expected 0
1
2 differs the ids depend on the distribution; they should be in increasing numeric order. v02 title select a csv field text extract the name field from the report csv in your home directory. if it is not present, replace the path with one of your csv files. blocks cmd cut -d, -f1 ~/documents/list.csv expected name
alice
bob differs if your csv uses a different delimiter, change `-d`. the first line may be a header. v03 title count frequencies text count login shell fields in `/etc/passwd` and paste the frequency table. blocks cmd cut -d: -f7 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn expected \d+\s+\s+ differs counts vary by distribution. make sure `sort` comes before `uniq -c`. v04 title create a small report text prepare sample status codes in your home directory, sort and count them, then show the report. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/lab && cd ~/lab && printf '200\n404\n200\n500\n200\n' > status.txt && sort status.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn > status_report.txt && cat status_report.txt differs if `status_report.txt` is empty, check `status.txt` and the redirection order. do not overwrite the source. quiz : { which option sorts numeric lines by their numeric values? options `sort -r` `sort -n` `uniq -c` `cut -n` explain `sort -n` sorts numerically. : { why is `uniq` usually used after `sort`? options `uniq` reads only csv `sort` makes a backup `uniq` converts all text to uppercase `uniq` collapses only adjacent duplicates explain sorting brings identical values next to each other so `uniq` can collapse them. : { what does `cut -d, -f2 file.csv` select? options the second comma-delimited field the second line the second character the file size explain `-d,` sets the delimiter to a comma and `-f2` selects the second field. : { what does `tr 'a-z' 'a-z'` do? options sorts lines in reverse counts duplicates converts lowercase ascii letters to uppercase extracts the second column explain `tr` transforms character sets; this example converts ascii lowercase letters to uppercase. summary `sort` sorts text; use `sort -n` for numbers and `sort -r` for reverse order. `uniq` collapses only adjacent duplicates, so sorting first is usually necessary. `uniq -c` reports the count for each unique line. `cut -ddelimiter -ffield` selects fields from delimited lines. `tr` transforms characters; combine small tools with pipes and write reports to separate files. glossary term filter meaning a command that reads input and writes selected or transformed output. term delimiter meaning a character that separates fields in a line. term field meaning one column of a line split by a delimiter. term frequency table meaning a list showing how often each value occurs.

3.6.title: sed and awk
objectives: You use sed with `s/old/new/`, the `g` flag, `-n` + `p`, addresses/ranges and `d`.
You know that `sed -i` changes a file permanently and make a backup first (`-i.bak`).
You select fields with awk (`$1`, `$NF`, `-F`), write conditions and compute sums and averages with `BEGIN`/`END`.
You count values in log files with awk arrays and combine awk in pipelines with `cut`, `sort`, `uniq`.
cmds: awk '{c[$2]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}'
awk '{c[$2]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' access.log | sort
3.6.text:
title sed and awk lead use sed to replace, delete and select text line by line; use awk to split lines into fields (columns), calculate and summarize log files. objectives you use sed with `s/old/new/`, the `g` flag, `-n` + `p`, addresses/ranges and `d`. you know that `sed -i` changes a file permanently and make a backup first (`-i.bak`). you select fields with awk (`$1`, `$nf`, `-f`), write conditions and compute sums and averages with `begin`/`end`. you count values in log files with awk arrays and combine awk in pipelines with `cut`, `sort`, `uniq`. sections sed-sub title sed: substitution (s///) body `sed` (stream editor) reads text line by line, applies a command and prints the result. it **does not change the file**; only `-i` does that (third section). the most common command is `s/search/replace/`. by default only the **first** match on each line is replaced; add `g` (global) for all of them: `s/cat/dog/g`. the delimiter does not have to be `/`. for paths like `/usr/local` use `|`: `s|/usr/local|/opt|`. a `&` in the replacement stands for the match itself; write `\&` for a literal `&`. commands cmd sed 's/old/new/' what replaces the first match on each line. where for a quick text fix. why you see the result without touching the file. example sed 's/cat/hamster/' pets.txt cmd sed 's/old/new/g' what replaces all matches on the line. where when a word must change everywhere. why without `g` the second match on a line stays. example sed 's/cat/dog/g' pets.txt cmd sed 's|a|b|' what uses `|` as delimiter; readable for paths containing `/`. where when replacing paths and urls. why no `\/` escapes needed. example sed 's|/usr/local|/opt|' paths.txt cmd sed -e ... -e ... what applies several sed commands in order. where when one pass needs several changes. why the file is read only once. example sed -e 's/it/it/g' -e 's/hr/hr/g' employees.csv tip with `-e` (extended regex) `+`, `?`, `|` and `( )` work without escapes: `sed -e 's/[0-9]+/n/g' access.log`. warn the pattern is a **regular expression**: `.` means any character. to match a dot write `\.`, otherwise `s/1.2/x/` also replaces `102`. sed-lines title sed: selecting and deleting lines body by default sed prints every line. `-n` turns that off; then `p` (print) prints only the lines you want. you pick lines with an **address**: a number (`2p`), a range (`1,3p`), the last line (`$p`) or a regex (`/404/p`). `d` (delete) drops the line from the output. `/^#/d` removes comment lines, `/^$/d` blank lines, `1d` the header line. all of this affects only the **output**; the file stays the same. to save the result, redirect: `sed '/^#/d' server.conf > clean.conf`. commands cmd sed -n 'np' what prints only line n. where to view a specific line of a big file. why shorter than `head | tail`. example sed -n '2p' pets.txt cmd sed -n 'a,bp' what prints lines a through b; `$` is the last line. where to look at one section of a file. why you get the range with one command. example sed -n '2,4p' employees.csv cmd sed '/regex/d' what deletes matching lines from the output. where when stripping comment or blank lines. why produces the clean version of a config file. example sed '/^#/d' server.conf cmd sed '1d' what skips the first line (e.g. a csv header). where before processing data that has a header. why later tools do not mistake the header for data. example sed '1d' employees.csv tip `-n` and `p` always go together. alone, `sed '2p'` prints line 2 **twice** (once automatically, once by `p`). sed-inplace title sed -i: editing a file in place body `sed -i` writes the result not to the screen but **into the file itself**. there is no undo and no trash can: a wrong regex damages the file permanently. rule: run without `-i` first and check the output, then run with a backup. `sed -i.bak '...' file` keeps the original as `file.bak` and works in both gnu (linux) and bsd (macos) sed. **gnu/bsd difference:** on linux `sed -i 's/a/b/' f` is enough. on macos `-i` requires a suffix; for no backup write `sed -i '' 's/a/b/' f`. if the same command behaves differently on two systems, this is why. commands cmd sed -i.bak what edits the file in place and saves the original as `.bak`. where when changing configuration files. why if something goes wrong you restore from the backup. example sed -i.bak 's/8080/9090/' server.conf cmd cp file file.bak what makes a manual backup. where before changing several files. why leaves you a way back after `-i`. example cp app.conf app.conf.bak nosim cmd diff old new what shows the difference between two files. where when verifying the change. why you see whether only the intended line changed. example diff server.conf.bak server.conf nosim warn `sed -i` cannot be undone. on production systems take a **backup** first. for several files (`sed -i ... *.conf`) test on one file without `-i` first. danger with a wrong pattern, `sed -i 's/.*//' file` empties the whole file. take a **snapshot** of your vm before destructive experiments. awk-basics title awk: fields and conditions body `awk` splits each line into **fields** at whitespace: `$1` is the first, `$2` the second, `$nf` the last field, `$0` the whole line. change the separator with `-f`: for csv use `-f,`. a program has the form `pattern { action }`. without a pattern it applies to every line; with one, only to matching lines: `$3 > 5000` or `/404/`. without an action the line is printed. `nr` is the line number, `nf` the field count; `nr>1` skips the header. `begin { }` runs once before the first line, `end { }` once after the last. ideal for sums and averages: `{ s += $3 } end { print s }`. use `printf` for formatted output; you write the line ending yourself (`\n`). commands cmd awk '{print $1}' what prints the first field of each line. where to take a column from logs or command output. why `cut` trips over varying spaces, awk does not. example awk '{print $1}' access.log cmd awk -f, '...' what sets the field separator to `,`. where for csv and `:`-separated files. why the only way to get the values into the right fields. example awk -f, 'nr>1 {print $1, $3}' employees.csv cmd awk 'condition' what prints only lines that satisfy the condition. where when selecting values over a threshold or error codes. why allows numeric comparisons `grep` cannot do. example awk -f, 'nr>1 && $3 > 5000 {print $1}' employees.csv cmd awk '... end {...}' what prints the result after the last line. where for sums, averages, counters. why one pass gives you the summary. example awk -f, 'nr>1 {s+=$3} end {print s}' employees.csv tip always put the awk program in **single quotes**; otherwise the shell expands `$1` itself and awk gets an empty program. awk-arrays title awk: counting and log analysis body awk arrays are **associative** (key → value) and need no declaration. `c[$2]++` increments the counter for each status code; in the `end` block `for (k in c)` prints them all. the order is undefined, so append `sort`. the pattern combines with pipes: `ps aux | awk 'nr>1 {print $1}' | sort | uniq -c` shows how many processes each user has. `cut -d' ' -f2 access.log | sort | uniq -c` works too, but with irregular spacing awk is safer. commands cmd awk '{c[$2]++} end {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' what counts how often each value in field two occurs. where when counting per http status code or ip. why summarizes a log with one command. example awk '{c[$2]++} end {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' access.log | sort cmd awk '{print $nf}' what prints the last field of each line. where for lines with a varying number of fields. why you do not need to know the last column's number. example awk '{print $nf}' access.log cmd awk 'begin {...}' what runs once before the file is read. where for headings or initial values. why adds a title to the report output. example awk 'begin {print \ } {print $1, $2}' access.log cmd awk '{printf ...}' what c-style formatted output. where for aligned or decimal numbers. why `print` does not give you control of format and line ending. example awk -f, 'nr>1 {printf \ , $1, $3}' employees.csv tip average: `end {print s/(nr-1)}` (with a header) or a separate counter (`n++`). watch out for division by zero on an empty file. tasks t01 text print only line 2 of `pets.txt` with sed: `sed -n '2p' pets.txt`. hint `-n` turns off automatic printing, `2p` prints only line 2. the simulator does not run sed ('not supported'); your command is still recorded. t02 text print only the first column (the ip addresses) of `access.log` with awk. hint `awk '{print $1}' access.log` — the program belongs in single quotes. t03 text predict: which names does `cut -d, -f1 employees.csv` print (same as `awk -f, '{print $1}'`)? think first, then run it. hint the first column is the `name` header and four names (anna, ben, cara, dan). t04 text you are changing the port in `server.conf`. first back it up with `cp server.conf server.conf.bak`, then run `sed -i 's/8080/9090/' server.conf`. hint order matters: backup first, then `-i`. alternatively `sed -i.bak` makes the backup itself; but here the file `server.conf.bak` must exist. t05 text print `server.conf` without comment lines (those starting with `#`): `sed '/^#/d' server.conf`. hint `^#` means # at line start, `d` removes the line. the file stays unchanged. t06 text broken command: `sed 's/usr/local/bin/opt/bin/' paths.txt` fails because the `/` in the path collides with the delimiter. fix it: replace `/usr/local` with `/opt` (use `|` as delimiter). hint `sed 's|/usr/local|/opt|' paths.txt`. the first character after `s` is the delimiter; `|`, `#` and `,` are common. t07 text predict: how often does the department `it` appear in the output of `cut -d, -f2 employees.csv | sort | uniq -c`? then run the command. hint `uniq -c` prefixes each distinct line with its count. the `dept` header is a line too. t08 text mini project: create the folder `reports`, copy `employees.csv` into it and compute the average salary in the copy with awk (skip the header): `awk -f, 'nr>1 {s+=$3; n++} end {print s/n}' reports/employees.csv`. hint steps: `mkdir reports`, `cp employees.csv reports/`, then awk. `nr>1` skips the header, `n` counts the rows. t09 text mini project: create the folder `backup`, copy `app.conf` to `backup/app.conf`, then change `mode=dev` to `mode=prod` in `app.conf` with `sed -i`. hint `mkdir backup`, `cp app.conf backup/app.conf`, `sed -i 's/mode=dev/mode=prod/' app.conf`. make the backup before `-i`. t10 text predict: which animal does `sed -n '3p' pets.txt` print? verify with the equivalent `head -n 3 pets.txt | tail -n 1`. hint lines: cat, dog, bird, cat, fish. `head -n 3` takes the first three, `tail -n 1` the last of them. t11 text challenge: with awk select only the lines of `access.log` whose status code is 404 (condition: second field is 404). hint `awk '$2 == 404' access.log` — the pattern alone is enough; without an action the line is printed. t12 text challenge: in one sed call make two replacements in `employees.csv` (with two `-e`): `it` to `it`, `hr` to `hr`. just print, do not change the file. hint `sed -e 's/it/it/g' -e 's/hr/hr/g' employees.csv`. t13 text debug: a wrong `sed -i` broke `db.conf` (only `host=` is left). the backup `db.conf.bak` is still there. restore the file from the backup. hint `cp db.conf.bak db.conf`. check with `cat db.conf`: it should show `host=localhost` and `port=5432`. t14 text ticket #3601 — 'the live server needs a clean configuration: prepare a copy without comment lines as `server.live`, and keep the original as `server.conf.orig`.' (the simulator has no sed: produce the output without comments using `grep -v`; on a real system `sed '/^#/d'` does the same.) hint `cp server.conf server.conf.orig` and `grep -v '^#' server.conf > server.live`. t15 text ticket #3602 — 'write the distribution of status codes in access.log to the file `status_report.txt`.' (one count per code, e.g. `3 200`.) hint take the second column, sort, count: `cut -d' ' -f2 access.log | sort | uniq -c > status_report.txt`. an awk array would do the same. t16 text ticket #3603 — 'calculate the total salary of the it department.' write it with awk: separator `,`, rows whose second field is `it`, sum the third field, print with `end`. hint `awk -f, '$2==\  {s+=$3} end {print s}' employees.csv` (result 11300). : { run these commands on your own ubuntu/rocky/alma vm. everything stays in `~/lab` and your own test files. sed and awk come preinstalled on these distributions (gnu versions). tasks v01 title create the test files text create the following four test files in `~/lab` with `printf` and paste the line counts. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/lab && cd ~/lab
printf 'cat\ndog\nbird\ncat\nfish\n' > pets.txt
printf 'name,dept,salary\nanna,it,5200\nben,hr,4100\ncara,it,6100\ndan,ops,3900\n' > employees.csv
printf '# server config\nport=8080\n# debug off\ndebug=false\nhost=localhost\n' > server.conf
printf '10.0.0.1 200\n10.0.0.2 404\n10.0.0.1 200\n10.0.0.3 500\n10.0.0.2 200\n' > access.log
wc -l pets.txt employees.csv server.conf access.log expected   5 pets.txt
  5 employees.csv
  5 server.conf
  5 access.log
 20 total differs if a count is not 5, a `printf` line is missing or has too much; check the file with `cat` and run the command again. if you see a literal `n` instead of a newline, check the single quotes. v02 title sed: replace, select, delete text run three sed commands. the files stay unchanged, only the output differs. paste the output. blocks cmd cd ~/lab
sed 's/cat/hamster/' pets.txt
sed -n '2,3p' pets.txt
sed '1d' employees.csv expected hamster
dog
bird
hamster
fish
dog
bird
anna,it,5200
ben,hr,4100
cara,it,6100
dan,ops,3900 differs if `cat pets.txt` still shows `cat` that is correct: without `-i` the file does not change. no output at all? `cd ~/lab` may have failed; repeat v01. v03 title sed -i with a backup text change the port in `server.conf` with a backup and show the difference. paste the output. blocks cmd cd ~/lab
# gnu sed (ubuntu/rocky/alma); -i.bak makes a backup
sed -i.bak 's/8080/9090/' server.conf
grep port server.conf
diff server.conf.bak server.conf expected port=9090
2c2
< port=8080
---
> port=9090 differs on macos/bsd `-i.bak` works too; without a suffix you need `sed -i '' ...`. if the `diff` output is empty nothing changed; check the spelling of `8080`. to undo: `cp server.conf.bak server.conf`. v04 title awk: column, condition, sum text run three awk commands on `employees.csv`: two columns, salaries over 5000, total and average. blocks cmd cd ~/lab
awk -f, 'nr>1 {print $1, $3}' employees.csv
awk -f, 'nr>1 && $3 > 5000 {print $1}' employees.csv
awk -f, 'nr>1 {s+=$3} end {printf \ , s, s/(nr-1)}' employees.csv expected anna 5200
ben 4100
cara 6100
dan 3900
anna
cara
total=19300 avg=4825.0 differs depending on the locale the decimal separator may be `4825,0`. if you see `total=0`, `-f,` is missing or the shell expanded `$3`; put the program in single quotes. v05 title log analysis: counting text count the status codes in `access.log` with an awk array, find the 404 line with sed and paste the output. optionally count running processes per user. blocks cmd cd ~/lab
awk '{c[$2]++} end {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' access.log | sort
sed -n '/404/p' access.log
ps aux | awk 'nr>1 {print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3 expected 200 3
404 1
500 1
10.0.0.2 404
    120 root
     35 student
      4 www-data differs the numbers and users of the last command depend on your system; what matters is the `count user` format on each line. (`ps` is covered in module 5.1.) the order of `for (k in c)` is undefined, which is why we added `sort`. quiz : { what does `sed 's/a/b/' file` do without the `g` flag? options replaces every a in the file with b replaces only the first a on each line with b changes only the first line edits the file in place explain without `g` only the first match per line is replaced; and without `-i` the file is not changed at all. : { what is the safest way to edit a configuration file in place? options `sed -n 's/a/b/p' file` `sed -e 's/a/b/' file` `sed -i 's/a/b/' file` (no backup) `sed -i.bak 's/a/b/' file` explain `-i.bak` keeps the original as `file.bak`; `-i` alone cannot be undone. : { what does `awk -f, '{print $nf}' employees.csv` print? options the first field of each line the number of fields on the line the last field of each line the whole line explain `nf` is the field count, `$nf` is the value of the last field. : { what is `nr>1` for in `awk -f, 'nr>1 {s+=$3} end {print s}'`? options skips the first line (the header) processes only the first line sets the field count to 1 sorts the file explain `nr` is the line number; `nr>1` runs the action on every line except the header. summary `sed 's/old/new/g'` substitutes; `-n` + `p` selects, `d` deletes. without `-i` the file never changes. `sed -i` is permanent: use `-i.bak` for a backup. on macos you need `-i ''`. awk splits lines into fields: `$1`, `$nf`, `-f,`; calculate with `nr`, `nf`, `begin`, `end`. with the associative array `c[$2]++` you count values in logs; sort the output with `sort`. always put programs in single quotes and check the result on screen first. glossary term sed meaning stream editor that processes text line by line. term awk meaning text-processing language that splits lines into fields and supports conditions, calculations and reports. term field meaning a part of a line that awk splits off at the separator: `$1`, `$2`, … `$nf`. term address meaning a number, range or regex that selects which lines a sed command applies to. term in-place editing meaning with `sed -i` the result is written into the file itself instead of the screen. term associative array meaning an awk array holding key-value pairs; typical for counters. term regex meaning a regular expression describing a text pattern; sed and awk use it for matching.

3.7.title: Comparison: diff, cmp, comm, patch
objectives: You read `diff` output (normal and `-u` unified), including `@@` hunks and `+`/`-` lines.
You compare directories and files quickly with `diff -r`, `diff -q`, `cmp` and `sha256sum -c`.
You find differences between sorted lists with `comm`, and common or unique lines with `sort | uniq -d/-u`.
You create patches with `diff -u`, apply them with `patch`, undo them with `-R`, and check exit codes (0/1/2).
sol: sort list_a.txt list_b.txt list_b.txt | uniq -u > only_a.txt
3.7.text:
title comparison: diff, cmp, comm, patch lead compare two files, two directories and two lists, read the difference, create and apply patches, and use exit codes in scripts. objectives you read `diff` output (normal and `-u` unified), including `@@` hunks and `+`/`-` lines. you compare directories and files quickly with `diff -r`, `diff -q`, `cmp` and `sha256sum -c`. you find differences between sorted lists with `comm`, and common or unique lines with `sort | uniq -d/-u`. you create patches with `diff -u`, apply them with `patch`, undo them with `-r`, and check exit codes (0/1/2). sections diff title diff: line-by-line differences body `diff old new` compares two text files line by line and prints the changes needed to turn the old file into the new one. in normal output you see a command line such as `2c2` (line 2 changed); `<` marks lines from the first file, `>` lines from the second. in practice the **unified** format (`-u`) is the standard: `---` is the first file, `+++` the second; the hunk `@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@` means three lines starting at line 1 in the first file and four lines starting at line 1 in the second. lines starting with `-` exist only in the old file, lines with `+` only in the new one; lines starting with a space are context. git and patch tools use this format. **exit code:** `0` files identical, `1` differences found, `2` trouble (file missing, unreadable). so `diff` reports 'failure' when it finds differences; that is not an error. in the simulator `diff`, `cmp`, `comm` and `patch` do not run; try them on your own vm. here the simulator only checks that you typed the command, plus the prepared files. commands cmd diff what shows the difference between two files in normal format (with `<` and `>` lines). where when comparing two versions of a configuration file. why you see what changed without reading the whole file. example diff v1.txt v2.txt nosim cmd diff -u what unified format: `---`/`+++` header, `@@` hunks and `+`/`-` lines. where when sharing changes, in code review, when creating patches. why context lines make clear where the change is. example diff -u v1.txt v2.txt nosim cmd diff -q what prints only 'files ... differ', or nothing. where when only 'same or not' matters; in scripts. why no long output, the exit code is still 0/1. example diff -q v1.txt v2.txt nosim cmd diff -y what shows two columns side by side; differences marked with `|`, `<`, `>`. where when comparing short files by eye. why you see both versions next to each other. example diff -y v1.txt v2.txt nosim cmd diff -w what ignores whitespace differences (indentation, trailing spaces). where for files that were only reformatted. why noise disappears, real content differences remain. example diff -w v1.txt v2.txt nosim tip which file is 'old' and which is 'new'? order matters: `diff old new`. swap them and `+` and `-` swap too. warn files created on windows carry `\r` (crlf) at each line end, so every line looks different. clean up with `tr -d '\r' < win.txt > fixed.txt` or use `diff --strip-trailing-cr`. dirs title comparing directories body `diff -r dir_a dir_b` compares two directory trees recursively. for files that exist in only one directory it prints `only in dir_a: extra.txt`; for files with different content it prints the diff. with `-q` (or `-rq`) you see only which files differ; ideal for checking a backup with many files. you can also compare the output of two commands: `diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt)` (process substitution, a **bash** feature) hands the outputs over like temporary files. it does not work in plain `sh`. commands cmd diff -r what compares two directories including subdirectories. where when comparing two project versions or a backup. why missing, extra and changed files in one go. example diff -r dir_a dir_b nosim cmd diff -rq what lists only files that differ or exist on one side only. where for backup verification, in large trees. why a short overview; look at single files in detail afterwards. example diff -rq dir_a dir_b nosim cmd diff <( ) what compares the output of two commands like files (bash). where for sorted lists or comparing two environments. why no intermediate files needed. example diff <(sort list_a.txt) <(sort list_b.txt) nosim tip direction does not matter, but for readability always write the 'reference' directory first. bytes title cmp and checksums body `cmp` compares files **byte by byte** and reports the byte and line number of the first difference. for binary files `diff` only says 'binary files differ'; `cmp` shows the exact position. `cmp -s` prints nothing, only the exit code (0 same, 1 different, 2 trouble). in scripts: `if cmp -s a b; then echo same; fi`. if the files are on different machines you cannot compare them directly; compute a **checksum**. `sha256sum notes.txt` produces a hash; identical content gives an identical hash. `sha256sum -c sums.txt` recomputes stored hashes and prints `ok` or `failed`. this is how you verify a download is intact. `md5sum` is outdated; use `sha256sum` for security. commands cmd cmp what compares two files byte by byte and reports the position of the first difference. where for binary files and to verify copies. why gives a definite answer even for non-text files. example cmp v1.txt v2.txt nosim cmd cmp -s what silent comparison; the result is only in the exit code. where in scripts as an `if` condition. why decides 'same?' without output. example cmp -s v1.txt v1.bak; echo $? nosim cmd sha256sum what computes the sha-256 hash of a file. where for verifying downloads and backups. why you compare contents without having the files side by side. example sha256sum v1.txt nosim cmd sha256sum -c what checks a hash list; prints `ok` or `failed` per file. where for iso images or backups. why shows automatically whether anything is corrupted or changed. example sha256sum -c sums.txt nosim tip see the exit code with `echo $?` right after the command; if another command runs in between, the value is gone. lists title comparing lists: comm, uniq body `comm a b` shows two **sorted** files in three columns: column 1 only in a, column 2 only in b, column 3 in both. `-1`, `-2`, `-3` hide that column: `comm -12` = common lines, `comm -23` = only in a, `comm -13` = only in b. **pitfall:** if the input is not sorted, `comm` gives wrong results and warns 'file 2 is not in sorted order'. sort first: `sort list_b.txt > sorted_b.txt`. without `comm`, `sort a b | uniq -d` gives lines present in both lists (duplicated ones) and `sort a b | uniq -u` gives lines that appear only once. each list should be free of duplicates itself, otherwise the counting breaks. both commands also work in the simulator. commands cmd comm what compares two sorted files in three columns. where when comparing user, package or ip lists. why separates common and unique lines in one command. example comm list_a.txt sorted_b.txt nosim cmd comm -12 what shows only lines present in both files. where when you need the intersection. why hides columns 1 and 2, the common one remains. example comm -12 list_a.txt sorted_b.txt nosim cmd comm -23 what shows only lines present in the first file. where for the question 'i have it, you don't'. why finds missing or surplus entries. example comm -23 list_a.txt sorted_b.txt nosim cmd sort | uniq -d what from merged sorted lines, prints the duplicated (common) ones. where without `comm`, or for a quick intersection. why works everywhere with standard tools. example sort list_a.txt list_b.txt | uniq -d cmd sort | uniq -u what prints only lines that occur exactly once (symmetric difference). where when looking for lines that are in only one of the lists. why eliminates the common lines. example sort list_a.txt list_b.txt | uniq -u tip rule of thumb: always `sort` before `comm`; and use the same locale (`lc_all=c`) afterwards, otherwise the sort order may not match. patch title create and apply patches: patch body `diff -u old new > change.patch` writes the difference to a file. someone else applies it with `patch` to their old copy: `patch work.txt < change.patch`. for directory trees you create `diff -run old/ new/ > all.patch`; when applying, `-p1` strips the first path component (`old/`), `-p0` uses paths unchanged. before applying, try `patch --dry-run < change.patch`: it changes nothing and tells you whether the hunks fit. on failures a `.rej` file is created. `patch -r < change.patch` undoes the patch. a patch relies on context lines; if the file was changed elsewhere in the meantime, applying can fail or shift (`fuzz`). commands cmd diff -u > file.patch what writes the difference in unified format to a patch file. where to hand a change to someone else. why only the changed lines are transported, not the whole file. example diff -u v1.txt v2.txt > change.patch nosim cmd patch what applies the changes in a patch file to a file. where when working a received patch into your copy. why applies only the difference instead of replacing the whole file. example patch work.txt < change.patch nosim cmd patch --dry-run what tests the patch without actually applying it. where before patching important files. why you spot mismatches without changing anything. example patch --dry-run work.txt < change.patch nosim cmd patch -r what reverses the patch (undoes it). where when an applied patch causes problems. why restores the state before the patch. example patch -r work.txt < change.patch nosim tip if the patch is for a directory tree, run it from the project root and try `--dry-run` first. warn `patch` modifies files in place. for important files make a backup first with `cp work.txt work.txt.orig`, and on your vm take a snapshot first. danger do not apply patches to the root directory (`/`) or system configuration; work only in your practice folder. a wrong `-p` value changes the wrong files. tasks t01 text compare `v1.txt` and `v2.txt` with `diff v1.txt v2.txt`. hint the simulator has no diff; typing the command is enough. you will see the real output on your vm. t02 text compare the same files in unified format: `diff -u v1.txt v2.txt`. hint `-u` means unified; the output contains `@@` hunks. t03 text compare byte by byte with `cmp v1.txt v2.txt`. hint cmp reports the byte and line number of the first difference. t04 text copy `v1.txt` with `cp v1.txt v1.bak` and verify they are identical with `diff -q v1.txt v1.bak`. hint if identical, `diff -q` prints nothing and the exit code is 0. t05 text compare the directories `dir_a` and `dir_b` with `diff -rq dir_a dir_b`. hint `-r` recursive, `-q` short summary. `-r dir_a dir_b` is accepted too. t06 text `list_b.txt` is not sorted. for `comm`, create a sorted copy with `sort list_b.txt > sorted_b.txt`. hint the redirect `>` writes the sorted output into a new file. t07 text use `comm -12 list_a.txt sorted_b.txt` to show the lines present in both lists. hint `-12` hides columns 1 and 2; the common column remains. t08 text predict, then run: `sort list_a.txt list_b.txt | uniq -d`. which names appear? hint `uniq -d` prints only lines that occur more than once. t09 text predict, then run: `sort list_a.txt list_b.txt | uniq -u`. which names appear? hint `-u` prints only lines that occur once: names that are in only one of the two lists. t10 text predict: what does `grep -q debug v1.txt ; echo $?` print? run it to check. hint `grep -q` returns 0 if found, 1 if not; `v1.txt` contains no debug. t11 text debug: `win.txt` looks different on every line because it has windows line endings (`\r`). create a clean copy with `tr -d '\r' < win.txt > fixed.txt`. hint `tr -d` deletes the given character; redirect input with `<`, output with `>`. t12 text mini project: copy with `cp v1.txt work.txt`, create a patch with `diff -u v1.txt v2.txt > change.patch`, then apply it with `patch work.txt < change.patch`. hint three commands in order; diff and patch do not run in the simulator, try them on your vm. t13 text challenge: write only the names that are in `list_a.txt` (not in `list_b.txt`) to the file `only_a.txt`. without `comm`; hint: pass `list_b.txt` twice. hint `sort list_a.txt list_b.txt list_b.txt | uniq -u > only_a.txt`: names from b occur at least twice, names only in a occur once. t14 text copy with `cp v1.txt same.txt`, run `cmp -s v1.txt same.txt` and type `echo $?` right after. hint in one line this also works: `cmp -s v1.txt same.txt ; echo $?`. t15 text predict, then run: `cut -d= -f1 v1.txt`. which keys are listed? hint `-d=` is the delimiter, `-f1` the first field: everything before the `=`. t16 text ticket #3701 — change review: back up `v2.txt` as `v2.bak`, save the difference to `v1.txt` with `diff -u v1.txt v2.txt > review.patch`, and write `review done` into `report.txt`. hint three steps: `cp`, `diff -u ... > review.patch`, `echo review done > report.txt`. quiz : { with which exit code does `diff a b` end when the files differ? options 127 explain 0 identical, 1 differences, 2 trouble. a difference is not an error, but it is not zero either. : { what does `comm` need from its input files to work correctly? options that they are sorted root privileges the same size that they are binary explain comm expects sorted input; otherwise the result is wrong. apply `sort` first. : { what does a line starting with `+` mean in unified diff output? options the line existed only in the old file the line is a comment the line is only in the new file (added) the line was moved elsewhere explain `-` was removed from the old file, `+` added to the new one; lines starting with a space are context. : { which command undoes an applied patch? options diff -r change.patch patch -u change.patch cmp -r change.patch patch -r < change.patch explain `patch -r` reverses the patch; the patch file is read from standard input. summary `diff -u old new` shows the change; exit code 0 same, 1 different, 2 trouble. `diff -rq` checks directories, `cmp` compares bytes, `sha256sum -c` verifies content integrity. `comm` works only on sorted input; alternatives: `sort | uniq -d` (common) and `uniq -u` (unique). create a patch with `diff -u > change.patch`, test with `patch --dry-run`, apply with `patch`, undo with `patch -r`. pitfalls: unsorted `comm`, crlf line endings, `diff` on binary files. glossary term hunk meaning a change block in unified diff that starts with `@@` and includes context lines. term unified diff meaning the `diff -u` format: `---`/`+++` header, `@@` hunks, `+`/`-` lines. term patch meaning a file holding diff output; the `patch` command applies it to files. term exit code meaning a command's final status, read with `$?`. for diff: 0 same, 1 different, 2 trouble. term checksum meaning a hash value computed from content; if the content changes, the value changes. term crlf meaning windows line ending (`\r\n`); linux uses only `\n`. : { run the following commands on your own vm in the `~/lab` folder. they only create files in this practice folder and do not touch system settings. tasks v01 title diff: normal and unified text create two small files and see the difference in both formats. paste the unified output. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/lab && cd ~/lab
printf 'port=80\nhost=linux-lab\nmode=prod\n' > v1.txt
printf 'port=8080\nhost=linux-lab\nmode=prod\ndebug=on\n' > v2.txt
diff v1.txt v2.txt
diff -u v1.txt v2.txt expected 1c1
< port=80
---
> port=8080
3a4
> debug=on
--- v1.txt	2026-11-12 10:00:00
+++ v2.txt	2026-11-12 10:00:01
@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@
-port=80
+port=8080
 host=linux-lab
 mode=prod
