+debug=on differs date and time will differ; what matters are the `@@`, `-` and `+` lines. if there is no output, the files are identical; re-check the `printf` lines. v02 title exit codes text see `diff -q`, `cmp -s` and the exit codes. paste the output. blocks cmd cd ~/lab
diff -q v1.txt v2.txt; echo \ 
cp v1.txt same.txt
cmp -s v1.txt same.txt; echo \ 
diff v1.txt missing.txt; echo \ expected files v1.txt and v2.txt differ
exit=1
exit=0
diff: missing.txt: no such file or directory
exit=2 differs if your system language differs, the message may be translated; the `exit=` values must match. if you see `exit=0` on the first line, `v2.txt` was not created; run v01 again. v03 title comm and uniq text compare two name lists. first see the warning for unsorted `comm`, then the right way. blocks cmd cd ~/lab
printf 'alice\nbob\ncarol\ndave\n' > list_a.txt
printf 'erin\nbob\ncarol\n' > list_b.txt
comm -12 list_a.txt list_b.txt
sort list_b.txt > sorted_b.txt
comm -12 list_a.txt sorted_b.txt
comm -23 list_a.txt sorted_b.txt
sort list_a.txt list_b.txt | uniq -d
diff <(sort list_a.txt) <(sort list_b.txt) expected comm: file 2 is not in sorted order
bob
carol
alice
dave
bob
carol
1d0
< alice
... differs with unsorted input the `comm` warning may not appear or the output may be incomplete; the result is undefined, so always `sort` first. if `diff <(...)` gives a `syntax error`, your shell is not bash; type `bash` and try again. v04 title create, test, apply and undo a patch text turn a copy of `v1.txt` into `v2.txt` with a patch and undo it. paste the output. blocks cmd cd ~/lab
diff -u v1.txt v2.txt > change.patch
cp v1.txt work.txt
patch --dry-run work.txt < change.patch
patch work.txt < change.patch
cat work.txt
patch -r work.txt < change.patch
cat work.txt expected checking file work.txt
patching file work.txt
port=8080
host=linux-lab
mode=prod
debug=on
patching file work.txt
port=80
host=linux-lab
mode=prod differs if you see `patch: command not found`: on ubuntu `sudo apt install patch`, on rocky/alma `sudo dnf install patch`. (`sudo` is in module 4.3, `apt`/`dnf` in module 5.5.) if `--dry-run` is not supported (very old version), skip that line. if you see `hunk #1 failed`, `work.txt` is not identical to `v1.txt`; start over with `cp v1.txt work.txt`. v05 title checksums text compute hashes, then modify a file and catch the corruption with `sha256sum -c`. paste the output. blocks cmd cd ~/lab
sha256sum v1.txt same.txt
sha256sum v1.txt > sums.txt
sha256sum -c sums.txt
echo 'x' >> v1.txt
sha256sum -c sums.txt expected <64 hex characters>  v1.txt
<64 hex characters>  same.txt
v1.txt: ok
v1.txt: failed
sha256sum: warning: 1 computed checksum did not match differs the first two hashes must be identical (`v1.txt` and `same.txt` have the same content). on a non-english system the warning text may be translated; `ok` and `failed` stay the same. if `same.txt` is missing, run the step from v02.

3.8.title: Archiving and compression
objectives: You explain the difference between archiving (tar: bundling) and compression (gzip, bzip2, xz).
You create archives with `tar -czf`, list them with `tar -tf` and extract into a new directory with `tar -xzf -C`.
You know the risks of tar bombs and overwriting, and always list before extracting.
You use `gzip -k` and `zip`/`unzip` and compare compression ratios.
You make a dated backup and verify it with `sha256sum`.
3.8.text:
title archiving and compression lead bundle files with tar, gzip and zip, compress them, restore them safely and verify your backups. objectives you explain the difference between archiving (tar: bundling) and compression (gzip, bzip2, xz). you create archives with `tar -czf`, list them with `tar -tf` and extract into a new directory with `tar -xzf -c`. you know the risks of tar bombs and overwriting, and always list before extracting. you use `gzip -k` and `zip`/`unzip` and compare compression ratios. you make a dated backup and verify it with `sha256sum`. sections concept title archiving and compression are different things body **archiving** means **bundling** many files and directories, with their paths and permissions, into **one** file; the size does not shrink. `tar` (tape archive) does this. **compression** shrinks a single file: `gzip` (fast, common), `bzip2` (smaller, slower), `xz` (smallest, slowest). in practice you use both: `tar` bundles, then gzip compresses. the result is a `.tar.gz` or `.tgz` file. `tar` does both in one command with `-z` (gzip), `-j` (bzip2) or `-j` (xz). important detail: `gzip notes.txt` **deletes** the original file and leaves only the `.gz` file. use `-k` (keep) to preserve the original. commands cmd gzip -k what compresses a file and keeps the original (adds `.gz`). where for large logs or text files. why without `-k` the original is deleted; with `-k` you can experiment safely. example gzip -k logs/app.log nosim cmd gunzip what decompresses a `.gz` file and deletes the `.gz` file (same as `gzip -d`). where when you restore a single compressed file. why `gunzip -k` keeps the `.gz` as a safety copy. example gunzip logs/app.log.gz nosim cmd zcat what prints the content of a compressed file without decompressing it on disk. where when reading old compressed logs or searching them with `grep`. why no disk space or extra time spent on unpacking. example zcat logs/app.log.gz | head nosim tip compare sizes with `ls -lh`. text and logs compress very well; already compressed jpg, mp4 or zip files barely shrink. warn `gzip notes.txt` deletes the original. back up data that exists only once first, or use `-k`. tar title tar: create, list, extract body `tar` options can be combined in one word: **c** (create), **x** (extract), **t** (list), **v** (verbose), **f** (file, the archive name; **always the last letter**, the name follows immediately), **z/j/j** (gzip/bzip2/xz). always add **relative paths** to an archive (`project`, not `/home/student/project`). gnu tar strips a leading `/` and warns, so extracting cannot overwrite system files. `-c directory` makes tar change into that directory first: when extracting it is the destination, when creating it is the root of the source. the target directory must already exist. commands cmd tar -czf what bundles a directory into one gzip-compressed archive. where when making backups and before sending a project. why one file is much easier to copy, transfer and store. example tar -czf backups/project.tar.gz project nosim cmd tar -tf what lists the paths inside the archive without extracting (`-z` not needed, tar detects the type). where before extracting, to see the content. why prevents tar bombs and overwrite surprises. example tar -tf backups/project.tar.gz nosim cmd tar -xzf -c what extracts the archive into the given (existing) directory. where when restoring, to keep the current directory clean. why always extract into a new, empty directory, then check. example tar -xzf backups/project.tar.gz -c restore nosim cmd tar -xzf ... member what extracts only the named file or directory from the archive. where when rescuing a single file from a backup. why you do not extract everything or overwrite current files. the path must be written as in the `tar -tf` output. example tar -xzf backups/project.tar.gz -c restore project/notes.txt nosim cmd tar --exclude what leaves files matching the pattern out of the archive. where to keep logs, temporary files or `.git` out of a backup. why the backup gets smaller and faster. put `--exclude` before the path to archive. example tar -czf backups/lab-nologs.tar.gz --exclude='*.log' . nosim cmd tar -cjf what creates an archive with xz compression, the strongest level (`-j` is for bzip2). where for archives that are rarely used and kept long. why smaller file, but slower and more cpu load. example tar -cjf backups/project.tar.xz project nosim tip mnemonic: **c**reate, e**x**tract, lis**t**; then `f` and the file name. tar detects the compression type itself when extracting, so `tar -xf` is often enough. warn the archive name must directly follow `f`. with `tar -cfz backup.tgz project`, `z` is taken as the archive name and the file ends up wrongly named. safe title extracting safely: tar bombs and overwriting body some archives have no top-level directory; extracting dumps hundreds of files straight into your current directory (a **tar bomb**). cleaning up is painful because you cannot tell which files came from the archive. solution: list first with `tar -tf` (or `tar -tvf`), then extract into a new, empty directory. `tar -x` **silently overwrites** existing files with the same name. never extract directly into your working directory. permissions and owners: `tar` stores permissions in the archive. as **root**, owners and permissions are restored faithfully; as a normal user the `umask` applies. use `-p` to explicitly preserve permissions. restoring files owned by another user requires `sudo`. commands cmd tar -tvf what lists the archive verbosely: permissions, owner, size, date and path. where before extracting, to check permissions and whether there is a top-level directory. why you spot tar bombs and absolute paths in advance. example tar -tvf backups/project.tar.gz nosim cmd tar -xpf what extracts the archive and preserves file permissions. where for backups where permissions matter. why stops the `umask` from altering permissions. example tar -xpf backups/project.tar.gz -c restore nosim cmd sudo tar -xpf what extracts as root; owner and group are restored too. where for system backups or files belonging to other users. why ownership is kept, but root also magnifies mistakes. example sudo tar -xpf backups/project.tar.gz -c restore nosim tip habit: look with `tar -tf backup.tar.gz | head`, run `mkdir restore`, then `tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -c restore`. danger never extract an archive you do not trust as root, least of all with target `/` (`-c /`). members with absolute paths or `..` can overwrite system files. snapshot first, list first. zip title zip and unzip body `zip` bundles and compresses at once and is compatible with windows/macos; ideal for exchanging files. directories need `-r` (recursive). install with `sudo apt install zip unzip` on ubuntu or `sudo dnf install zip unzip` on rocky/alma. difference from `.tar.gz`: zip compresses each file separately, so extracting single files is fast; but it preserves linux permissions and owners less reliably than `tar`. for linux backups prefer `tar`. commands cmd zip -r what adds a directory with its subdirectories to a zip archive. where when sending files to windows/macos users. why opens everywhere; without `-r` the directory content is not added. example zip -r backups/project.zip project nosim cmd unzip -l what lists the content of a zip archive without extracting. where for checking before extracting. why the same safety habit as `tar -tf`. example unzip -l backups/project.zip nosim cmd unzip -d what extracts the zip archive into the given directory (created if needed). where when restoring. why you do not scatter files into the current directory. example unzip backups/project.zip -d restore nosim backup title a simple backup and verification body a simple backup: a name with the date, one command to bundle, plus a checksum. `date +%f` prints today as `2026-11-12`, so each backup gets its own name and never overwrites an older one. `$(...)` inside the command runs first and its output becomes part of the name. `sha256sum` produces a file's fingerprint. if you check the backup with `sha256sum -c` after copying it, you know it is intact. a backup only counts once a copy lives **on another disk or machine**; also try a restore once. automatic backups use a scheduler (`cron` or a systemd timer). that is a topic for another module; here we run the command by hand. commands cmd sha256sum what prints the sha-256 checksum of a file. where when verifying backups or downloaded files. why even one changed bit changes the sum, so corruption shows up. example sha256sum backups/project.tar.gz > backups/sha256sums nosim cmd sha256sum -c what compares stored sums with the files; prints `ok` or `failed`. where after copying a backup or before restoring it. why you find a broken backup right away, not in a crisis. example sha256sum -c backups/sha256sums nosim cmd tar -czf ... $(date +%f) what creates a backup archive with today's date in its name. where for regular, manually made backups. why old backups are not overwritten and versions stay distinguishable. example tar -czf backups/project-$(date +%f).tar.gz project nosim cmd date +%f what prints today's date as `2026-11-12`. where for date stamps in file names. why produces names that sort by date. example date +%f tip the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 off-site. tasks t01 text you are in the `lab` directory. look at the project tree to archive with `ls -r project`. hint -r is uppercase; it lists subdirectories too. t02 text create the `backups` directory for the backups: `mkdir backups`. hint create it inside `lab`. t03 text bundle `project` with gzip into the archive `backups/project.tar.gz` (`tar -czf ...`). the simulator does not run `tar`; the command's correctness is checked. hint order: `tar -czf <archive> <source>`; the archive name follows `f`. t04 text list the archive's content without extracting: `tar -tzf backups/project.tar.gz`. hint `t` = list. `-tf` is accepted too. t05 text create the `restore` directory, then extract the archive there with `-c`: `tar -xzf backups/project.tar.gz -c restore`. hint `mkdir restore` first; the `-c` target must exist. t06 text compress `logs/app.log` and keep the original: `gzip -k logs/app.log`. hint `-k` = keep. without it the original is deleted. t07 text extract only `project/notes.txt` from the archive into `restore`. hint the member name goes at the end of the command, as shown by `tar -tf`: `project/notes.txt`. t08 text predict: what total line count does `wc -l logs/*.log` show? guess first, then run it. hint three files: `app.log`, `web.log`, `db.log`; the last line is `total`. t09 text predict: which two `backups/project-$(date +%f).tar.gz`. hint `$(date +%f)` is command substitution; you can use it inside the name. t12 text debug: a tar bomb dumped `bomb1.txt`, `bomb2.txt`, `bomb3.txt` into `lab`. with `cp -r`, check with `ls -r staging`, then bundle `staging` as `staging.tar.gz`. hint steps: `mkdir staging`, `cp -r project staging/`, `ls -r staging`, `tar -czf staging.tar.gz staging`. t14 text challenge: add `project` recursively to `backups/project.zip` (`zip -r`), list it with `unzip -l`, then create its sum with `sha256sum`. all three in this order. hint `zip -r backups/project.zip project`, `unzip -l backups/project.zip`, `sha256sum backups/project.zip`. t15 text ticket #3801 — the auditors want compressed copies of the logs, but the originals in `logs` must stay. create -1 project/src | wc -l` print? run it to verify. hint `src` contains two `.c` files. : { run the commands below on your own vm (ubuntu/rocky/alma). everything stays in `~/lab`; your real data is untouched. no step is destructive, but archives overwrite files of the same name: do not experiment outside lab. taking a snapshot before bigger experiments is a good habit. tasks v01 title set up the test project text create a small project and a big log file under `~/lab`, then list the project files. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/lab/project/{src,docs}
cd ~/lab
echo 'int main(void) { return 0; }' > project/src/main.c

tar -czf backup.tar.gz project

mkdir restore restore2
tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -c restore

ls -r restore restore2 expected restore:
project
...

notes.txt differs if you see `cannot open: no such file or directory`, the `-c` directory is missing; create it with `mkdir` first. if tar says `not found in archive`, write the path as shown by `tar -tf`. v04 title compare compression ratios text compress `big.log` with gzip, bzip2 and xz, keeping the original. compare the sizes. blocks cmd cd ~/lab
gzip -k big.log

(`sudo` is in module 4.3, `apt`/`dnf` in module 5.5.) if an old `gzip` does not know `-k`, make a copy first with `cp big.log big2.log`. v05 title dated backup and checksum text make a dated backup, save its checksum and verify it. optionally try zip. blocks cmd cd ~/lab
tar -czf backup-$(date +%f).tar.gz project
sha256sum backup-*.tar.gz > sha256sums
sha256sum -c sha256sums expected backup-2026-11-12.tar.gz: ok cmd # optional (without zip: sudo apt install zip unzip or sudo dnf install zip unzip)

options `tar -xzf backup.tar.gz` `tar -tf backup.tar.gz` `tar -czf backup.tar.gz` `gzip -d backup.tar.gz` explain `t` lists (list). `x` extracts, `c` creates; `gzip -d` decompresses. : { what happens after `gzip notes.txt`? options both `notes.txt` and `notes.txt.gz` remain a `.zip` file is created `notes.txt.gz` is deleted `notes.txt` is deleted and replaced by `notes.txt.gz` explain gzip replaces the original with the compressed file. use `gzip -k` to keep it. : { why do you list an archive with `tar -tf` before extracting? options to see tar bombs and files that would be overwritten beforehand to make extraction faster because `tar -x` does not work without listing to compress the archive explain without a top-level directory the files scatter into the current directory, and existing files can be overwritten. : { what does `-c restore` do in `tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -c restore`? options compresses the archive under the name `restore` excludes files named `restore` changes into `restore` before extracting and extracts there checks the archive's checksum explain `-c` (change directory) sets the target directory; it must exist beforehand. summary archiving (`tar`) bundles, compression (`gzip`, `bzip2`, `xz`) shrinks; `.tar.gz` is the combination. create: `tar -czf backup.tar.gz project`; list: `tar -tf`; extract: `tar -xzf ... -c restore`. list first, then extract into a new directory: protects against tar bombs and overwriting. `gzip` deletes the original, `gzip -k` keeps it; zip is compatible with windows/macos. make dated backups, verify them with `sha256sum` and test a restore. glossary term archive meaning many files and directories, with their paths, bundled into one file (`tar`). term compression meaning reducing the size of data; `gzip`, `bzip2`, `xz`. term tarball meaning an archive made with `tar`, usually `.tar.gz`. term tar bomb meaning an archive without a top-level directory that scatters files into the current directory when extracted. term relative and absolute path meaning absolute paths start with `/`; relative paths are preferred inside archives. term checksum meaning a file's fingerprint (`sha256sum`); makes corruption visible.

3.9.title: Advanced Basics
objectives: Find files with `find` by name, type, size, time and permissions
Know the difference between `-exec ... {} \;`, `-exec ... {} +` and `xargs`; list first before `-delete`
Redirect stdout/stderr: `>`, `>>`, `2>`, `2>&1`, `/dev/null`, here-document and `tee`
Summarise logs with pipelines such as `sort | uniq -c | sort -nr`
Recognise the pitfalls of quoting (`'...'` and `"..."`), globs and brace expansion
Use exit codes, `&&`/`||`, shebang, `chmod +x` and `./script.sh` to run small scripts
cmds:
cat > notes2.txt <<'EOF'
line one
line two
EOF
sol: cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 1 > top.txt
