title advanced basics lead work in bulk, not one by one: find files with `find`, process them with `xargs`, redirect streams, build pipelines and write your first small script. objectives find files with `find` by name, type, size, time and permissions know the difference between `-exec ... {} \;`, `-exec ... {} +` and `xargs`; list first before `-delete` redirect stdout/stderr: `>`, `>>`, `2>`, `2>&1`, `/dev/null`, here-document and `tee` summarise logs with pipelines such as `sort | uniq -c | sort -nr` recognise the pitfalls of quoting (`'...'` and `\ `), globs and brace expansion use exit codes, `&&`/`||`, shebang, `chmod +x` and `./script.sh` to run small scripts sections find title find: searching in depth body `find <start> <conditions> <action>` walks the directory tree and processes every path that meets the conditions. with no conditions it lists everything. with no action the default is `-print`. key rule: **quote your patterns**. if you type `find . -name *.log`, the shell expands `*.log` against files in the current directory before `find` even starts, and the result will surprise you. list first, act later: before a dangerous action (`-delete`, `-exec rm`) run the same command without the action and read the output. commands cmd find -name / -iname what searches file names by pattern; `-iname` ignores upper/lower case. where when looking for files with a certain extension in a project. why you scan the whole tree in seconds without browsing by hand. example find . -name \ }, { find -type what filters by type: `f` file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link. where when you only want directories or only files. why lets you set permissions for directories and files separately instead of a blanket `chmod -r`. example find . -type d cmd find -size / -mtime / -perm / -user what filters by size (`-size +1m`), modification day (`-mtime +7` = older than 7 days), permissions (`-perm 644`) or owner (`-user alice`). where in clean-ups, security audits, hunting old logs. why finding the right file is cheaper than deleting the wrong one. example find /var/log -name \  -mtime +7 nosim cmd find -exec ... {} \; what runs the command for each match separately; `{}` is replaced by the path. end it with `+` and the paths are collected and passed to a single call. where when applying `chmod`, `ls -l`, `wc` and the like to every file. why bulk processing without a loop; the `+` form starts far fewer processes. example find project -name \  -exec ls -l {} \; nosim cmd find -delete what deletes matches directly; there is no undo. where when cleaning up temporary files. why faster than `-exec rm` (one process). put conditions before `-delete`, otherwise everything is deleted. example find project -name \  -delete nosim tip habit: first `find ... -print`, read the output, then append `-delete` or `-exec`. danger `find . -delete` with no condition deletes everything in the current tree. order matters: `-name` first, `-delete` last. xargs title xargs and command substitution body `rm`, `cp`, `wc` expect file names as **arguments** and do not read them from a pipe (stdin). `xargs` turns the lines on stdin into arguments for that command. file names may contain spaces or newlines. the safe way: `find ... -print0 | xargs -0 ...`; names are separated by the nul character. a plain `| xargs rm` hits the wrong file when names contain spaces. `$(command)` inserts a command's output into the command line. it is an alternative to `xargs` but can hit the argument-length limit on very long lists. commands cmd xargs what runs a command and passes it the input from stdin as arguments. where when feeding the output of `find` or `grep -l` into `rm`, `wc`, `chmod`. why fills the gap of the pipe: output becomes arguments. example find . -name \  | xargs wc -l nosim cmd find -print0 | xargs -0 what separates names with nul and hands them to xargs; safe with spaces and odd characters. where for irreversible bulk jobs such as deleting and moving. why a file called `my file.txt` is not split into two arguments. example find . -name \  -print0 | xargs -0 rm nosim cmd $(...) what command substitution: the inner command's output becomes part of the outer command. where when adding a date to a file name or `hostname` to a message. why you build commands with dynamic values. example echo \ }],  `xargs` may run the command once even on empty input (gnu: prevent with `-r`). for dangerous commands first use `xargs echo rm` to see what would run. stream title streams, redirection and pipelines body every process has three streams: 0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr. `>` redirects stdout (1), `2>` redirects stderr. `2>&1` means \ ; **order matters**: `cmd > f 2>&1` writes both to the file, `cmd 2>&1 > f` leaves errors on screen. throw noise into `/dev/null`: `cmd 2> /dev/null`. in bash, `&>` redirects both stdout and stderr; the portable form is `> f 2>&1`. the classic log-summary pattern: `cut -d' ' -f2 run.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr`. `uniq` only merges adjacent lines, which is why `sort` must come first. commands cmd 2> and 2>&1 what `2> f` writes errors to a file; `> f 2>&1` writes output and errors to the same file. where when collecting script output in a log file. why you record errors without losing them; the order is essential. example ls missing.txt notes.txt > both.txt 2>&1 cmd > /dev/null what throws the output away. where when you only care about the exit code, not the output. why keeps the screen clean: `grep -q` or `cmd 2> /dev/null`. example ls missing.txt 2> /dev/null cmd <<eof (here-document) what feeds several lines into the command's stdin; ends when `eof` stands alone on a line. where when creating scripts or configuration files. why with a quoted `<<'eof'` variables are not expanded; the text goes in literally. example cat > notes2.txt <<'eof'
line one
line two
eof nosim cmd tee what writes stdin to the screen and to a file; `-a` appends. where when saving an intermediate result in the middle of a pipeline. why you see and store at once. `| sudo tee f` solves the permission problem of `sudo cmd > f`. example grep error run.log | tee errors.txt cmd sort | uniq -c | sort -nr what counts lines and sorts them from most to least frequent. where in log, ip and error-frequency analysis. why one line answers \ ; add `| head -n 3` for the top three. example cut -d' ' -f2 run.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr tip `wc -l` counts lines; `head -n 1` gives the first line, `tail -n 5` the last five. combined they make quick log checks. quoting title quoting, expansion and exit codes body the shell expands before running: `$variable`, `$(...)`, globs (`*.log`) and braces (`{a,b}`). quotes control this expansion. double quotes `\ ` expand variables and `$(...)` but block globbing. single quotes `'...'` expand nothing. always protect values with spaces using double quotes. every command returns an exit code: 0 means success, anything else an error. `$?` shows the last one. `&&` continues only on success, `||` only on failure. commands cmd '...' and \ what single quotes leave text unchanged; double quotes allow `$` expansion. where when writing variables, names with spaces and patterns. why `echo \ ` prints the path, `echo '$home'` prints the text `$home`. example echo \  '$home' cmd * ? [ ] glob what the shell expands the pattern to file names; `*` is anything, `?` one character. where when selecting several files with one command. why unquoted, the pattern arrives mangled at `find -name`; if `*.log` matches nothing it stays as typed. example ls logs/*.log cmd {a,b} brace expansion what the shell turns `{a,b,c}` into three words; it does not look at files, it only generates text. where when creating several files or directories. why `mkdir -p project/{src,docs}` creates two directories with one command. example touch report_{1,2,3}.txt cmd && and || what `a && b`: b only if a succeeded. `a || b`: b only if a failed. `;` always continues. where for tasks with a precondition: `cd dir && rm ...`. why if `cd` fails, the following delete does not run in the wrong directory. example grep -q fatal run.log || echo none warn write `cd logs && rm *.tmp` instead of `cd logs; rm *.tmp`: if `cd` fails, `;` still runs `rm` in the directory you are in. script title your first script: shebang and running it body a script is a text file containing commands. the first line, the **shebang** (`#!/bin/bash`), names the interpreter. to run it the file needs the `x` permission. `./script.sh` runs the file from the current directory. if you type just `script.sh`, the shell only searches the directories in `path`; the current directory is deliberately not in it (security). `bash script.sh` works even without `x`. script arguments are `$1`, `$2` …, the exit code is `$?`. in small scripts you can set a default with `name=\ ],  : [{ #!/bin/bash what first line of the script; tells the kernel the interpreter. where at the top of every executable script. why it is clear which shell runs the script, keeping behaviour consistent across distributions. example printf '#!/bin/bash\necho \ \n' > greet.sh cmd chmod +x what adds the execute permission to the file. where before running your script directly. why without `x`, `./script.sh` says \ example chmod +x greet.sh cmd ./script.sh what runs the script by path; arguments follow. where for scripts in the current directory. why no `path` lookup; exactly the file you chose runs. example ./greet.sh alice cmd echo $? what shows the exit code of the last command (0 = success). where when checking a command's success by hand or in a script. why `&&`, `||` and `if` all use this code. example grep -q error run.log; echo $? tip for your own scripts you can add `~/bin` to `path`: `export path=\ `. make it permanent in `~/.bashrc`. tasks t01 text in the `lab` directory list all `.tmp` files with `find`: `find . -name \ hint put the pattern in double quotes. t02 text count the `error` lines in `run.log` and write the number to the file `count.txt`: `grep -c error run.log > count.txt`. hint `-c` gives the number of matching lines. t03 text write `host: ` and the machine name into the file `who.txt`: `echo \  > who.txt`. hint inside double quotes `$(hostname)` is expanded. t04 text create the directory `backup`, then use a glob to copy all `.log` files from `logs` into it: `cp logs/*.log backup/`. hint first `mkdir backup`; `cp` takes the target last. t05 text first write the error to `err.txt`: `ls missing.txt 2> err.txt`. then write output and error of `ls missing.txt notes.txt` together into `both.txt`. hint `> both.txt 2>&1`; order: `>` first, then `2>&1`. t06 text with `printf` write the script `greet.sh` (shebang + `echo \ `), make it executable with `chmod +x greet.sh` and run `./greet.sh alice > greet.out`. hint `printf '#!/bin/bash\necho \ \n' > greet.sh`; use single quotes, otherwise `$1` is expanded immediately. t07 text predict: which level does `cut -d' ' -f2 run.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr` show most often, and how many times? guess first, then run it. hint the second field is the level (`info`, `warn`, `error`). count the lines. t08 text predict: what does `echo \  '$home'` print? guess, then run it. hint double quotes expand, single quotes do not. t09 text predict: what does `grep -q fatal run.log || echo none` print? guess, then run it. hint without `fatal`, `grep` returns 1; then `||` runs the right-hand command. t10 text debug: someone typed `find . -name *.log` and got only `run.log`; the files under `logs/` are missing. fix the command and write the full list to `all_logs.txt`. hint first run `find . -name *.log` and see: the shell expanded `*.log` to `run.log`. quote the pattern. t11 text debug: `./hello.sh` says \ . fix it and run it; the result must end up in `hello.out`. hint check the permissions with `ls -l hello.sh`; then `chmod +x hello.sh`. (`chmod` is covered in module 4.4.) t12 text mini project: filter the `error` lines, show them and save them to `errors.txt` at once (`tee`), then append the output of `wc -l errors.txt` to `summary.txt` with `>>`. hint `grep error run.log | tee errors.txt`, then `wc -l errors.txt >> summary.txt`. t13 text challenge: delete all `.tmp` files under `project` using `find` and `-exec rm {} \;`. (the simulator does not run `-exec`; the correct syntax is checked.) hint `find project -name \  -exec rm {} \;`; the `\;` matters. on a real vm test with `-print` first. t14 text challenge: get the line count of all `.txt` files the safe way: `-print0` with `xargs -0` and `wc -l`. (`xargs` is not in the simulator; the syntax is checked.) hint `find . -name \  -print0 | xargs -0 wc -l`. t15 text challenge: in `access.log` find the most frequent ip with its count and write only that single line to `top.txt`. hint `cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 1 > top.txt`. t16 text ticket #3901 — support: \  write `check.sh` (shebang + `grep -e ... | sort > problems.txt`), make it executable and run it. hint write it with `printf` or `echo` in single quotes, `chmod +x check.sh`, `./check.sh`. (`chmod` is covered in module 4.4.) : { do the following steps on your own vm (ubuntu, rocky or alma). try everything under `~/adv`; never use `-delete` or `rm -r` where real data lives. tasks v01 title set up a practice area and search with find text build a practice tree, then search with `find` by name, type and size. paste the output. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/adv/logs ~/adv/project/src
touch ~/adv/logs/app.log ~/adv/logs/old.log ~/adv/project/a.tmp ~/adv/project/src/b.tmp
echo data > ~/adv/project/src/main.txt
find ~/adv -name \ 
find ~/adv -type d
find ~/adv -type f -size -1k expected /home/student/adv/logs/app.log
/home/student/adv/logs/old.log
/home/student/adv
/home/student/adv/logs
... differs the order of `find` output depends on the file system; what matters is that all `.log` files appear. if your user is not `student`, the start of the path differs; that is fine. v02 title -exec, + and xargs text apply first `-exec ... \;`, then `-exec ... +` and `xargs -0` to the same files. notice: `\;` starts one command per file, `+` batches. blocks cmd find ~/adv -name \  -exec ls -l {} \;
find ~/adv -name \  -exec ls -l {} +
find ~/adv -name \  -print0 | xargs -0 ls -l expected -rw-r--r-- 1 student student 0 nov 12 10:00 /home/student/adv/project/a.tmp
-rw-r--r-- 1 student student 0 nov 12 10:00 /home/student/adv/project/src/b.tmp differs with `+` the `ls -l` output usually comes sorted by path, with `\;` in find order. the content is the same. the message `find: missing argument to '-exec'` means the trailing `\;` or `+` is missing. v03 title list first, then delete text first take a **snapshot** of your vm. `-delete` is irreversible: see what would be deleted, then delete only inside `~/adv`. press \  afterwards. blocks cmd # dry run first
find ~/adv -name \  -print
# if correct, delete (condition before -delete)
find ~/adv -name \  -delete
find ~/adv -name \ expected (the last command prints nothing) differs if the last command still lists files, `-delete` may be missing or you are in the wrong directory; check with `pwd`. v04 title log analysis: here-document and pipeline text write a sample log with a here-document, then count the levels and redirect the error stream. blocks cmd cat > ~/adv/run.log <<'eof'
10:01 info start
10:02 error disk full
10:03 warn slow disk
10:04 info retry
10:05 error timeout
10:06 info ok
eof
cut -d' ' -f2 ~/adv/run.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
ls /nonexistent ~/adv/run.log > ~/adv/both.txt 2>&1
cat ~/adv/both.txt expected       3 info
      2 error
      1 warn
ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': no such file or directory
/home/student/adv/run.log differs if numbers or spacing differ, check the log lines: the second field of each line must be the level. on a localised system the error message is translated; you will see local text instead of `no such file`. v05 title your first script text write the script, try to run it without `x`, grant the permission, run it again and look at the exit code. blocks cmd cd ~/adv
cat > hello.sh <<'eof'
#!/bin/bash
name=\ 
echo \ 
eof
./hello.sh
chmod +x hello.sh
./hello.sh student
echo $? expected bash: ./hello.sh: permission denied
hello, student
0 differs if the first `./hello.sh` works, your file system (e.g. some wsl mounts) already grants `x`. (`chmod` is covered in module 4.4.) if you see `hello.sh: command not found`, you forgot the `./` prefix; the current directory is not in `path`. quiz : { what is the difference between `find ... -exec rm {} \;` and `find ... -exec rm {} +`? options `\;` applies only to directories, `+` only to files `\;` runs the command once per file, `+` collects the paths and passes them to a few calls `+` never runs the command, it only lists there is no difference, only a style explain `\;` starts one process per match; `+` collects arguments and gets by with far fewer processes. : { why is `find . -name *.log` (unquoted) a problem? options `find` does not accept patterns `-name` only works with capital letters the shell expands `*.log` to names in the current directory before `find` starts the command deletes the whole disk explain the shell does the expanding. quote the pattern as `\ ` so it reaches `find` unchanged. : { which command writes both output and errors to `out.txt`? options `cmd > out.txt 2>&1` `cmd 2>&1 > out.txt` `cmd 2> out.txt 1> out.txt` `cmd | out.txt` explain stdout is redirected to the file first, then stderr goes \ . in the reverse order the error stays on screen. : { how do you safely pass `find` results to `rm` when file names contain spaces? options `find . | xargs rm` `rm $(find .)` `find . -name x | rm` `find ... -print0 | xargs -0 rm` explain `-print0` and `xargs -0` separate names with nul; names containing spaces or newlines are not split. summary `find` walks trees; quote patterns, list first, then add `-delete`/`-exec`. `-exec ... \;` per file, `-exec ... +` and `xargs` in batches; the safe pair: `-print0 | xargs -0`. `>` stdout, `2>` stderr, `2>&1` merges (order matters), `/dev/null` is the bin, `tee` shows and saves. `sort | uniq -c | sort -nr` finds the most frequent entries; combine with `head`/`tail`/`wc -l`. double quotes expand, single quotes do not; `&&` on success, `||` on failure. script = shebang + `chmod +x` + `./script.sh`; exit code `$?`. glossary term glob meaning file name patterns like `*`, `?`, `[...]` that the shell expands. term stdout / stderr meaning standard output (1) and standard error (2) streams. term here-document meaning passing multi-line text as a command's input with `<<eof`. term pipe meaning `|` connects the output of one command to the input of the next. term shebang meaning the first script line `#!/bin/bash`; it names the interpreter. term exit code meaning number a command returns when it ends; 0 success, otherwise error. read with `$?`. term nul separator meaning the `\0` byte that separates names; `-print0` and `xargs -0` use it.

4.1.title: User information: who, where, when?
objectives: You read your own identity (UID, GID, groups) with `whoami`, `id` and `groups`.
You know what `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/group` and `/etc/shadow` hold and what their fields mean.
You see who is connected now with `who` and `w`, successful logins with `last` and failed ones with `lastb`.
You query accounts with `getent`, no matter whether they live in a file or a central directory (LDAP/SSSD).
4.1.text:
title user information: who, where, when? lead use whoami, id, who, w, last, lastb and getent to see who exists on the system, who is logged in, and where accounts are stored. objectives you read your own identity (uid, gid, groups) with `whoami`, `id` and `groups`. you know what `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/group` and `/etc/shadow` hold and what their fields mean. you see who is connected now with `who` and `w`, successful logins with `last` and failed ones with `lastb`. you query accounts with `getent`, no matter whether they live in a file or a central directory (ldap/sssd). sections title who am i? whoami, id, groups body linux is a multi-user system. every process runs as some user and permissions depend on it. to understand why a command fails, first find out **who you are** and which groups you belong to. the `id` output looks like `uid=1000(student) gid=1000(student) groups=...`. the uid is the numeric identity of the user; the kernel works with **numbers**, not names. `root` is always uid 0. usually uids from 1000 up belong to human users and lower ones to system accounts. commands cmd whoami what prints the effective user name. where to confirm who you are after sudo or su. why prevents working as the wrong user. example whoami cmd what shows uid, primary gid and all groups. where for permission problems and checking new accounts. why shows which groups give a user access. example id alice cmd groups what lists the names of the groups you belong to. where for a quick group check. why gives a more readable summary than id. example groups tip `id username` also works for other users; if the account does not exist you get `no such user`. it is the quickest way to test whether an account exists. files title account files: passwd, group, shadow body local accounts live in three plain-text files. **/etc/passwd** is world-readable; each line has 7 colon-separated fields: `name:x:uid:gid:comment:home:shell`. the `x` means the password is not stored here. password hashes are in **/etc/shadow**, readable only by root. **/etc/group** holds group name, gid and members. the `/sbin/nologin` shell means the account cannot log in interactively (a service account). `getent` queries the same information from all configured sources (files, ldap, sssd). in corporate environments users may not be in `/etc/passwd` at all, so scripts should prefer `getent passwd` over `cat /etc/passwd`. commands cmd cat /etc/passwd what shows the local account list. where when you need home directory and shell information. why shows how accounts are defined. example cat /etc/passwd cmd cut -d: -f1 what extracts field 1 (user name) from colon-separated data. where to list only the names. why pulls the column you need from large files. example cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd cmd grep what finds the line of one specific user. where when checking a single account record. why faster than reading the whole list. example grep student /etc/passwd cmd getent passwd what looks the account up in all sources (file, ldap, sssd). where on corporate servers and in scripts. why also finds users from the central directory. example getent passwd student nosim cmd getent group what queries a group and its members. where to check who is in which group. why helps solve access problems. example getent group devs nosim tip `cut -d: -f1,7 /etc/passwd` shows user name and shell side by side; entries with `nologin` are service accounts. warn do not edit `/etc/passwd` or `/etc/shadow` by hand in a text editor. one wrong character can break everyone's login. manage accounts with tools like `useradd` and `usermod` (module 4.2). online title who is connected now? who and w body before maintenance, a reboot or stopping a service, check whether someone else is working on the server. `who` shows connected users, their terminal (`tty1`, `pts/0`) and login time; for remote logins the ip appears in parentheses. `w` is more detailed: the first line shows uptime and the **load average**, then for each session the idle time (idle) and the command being run (what). commands cmd who what shows logged-in users, terminals and times. where before maintenance. why you will not interrupt someone's work by accident. example who nosim cmd what shows sessions, idle time, running command and load average. where when the server is slow or you look for suspicious sessions. why answers who is doing what in one command. example nosim tip if only one session is open on your vm, only you appear. open a second terminal tab and run `who` again; the count goes up. history title login history: last and lastb body `last` reads `/var/log/wtmp` and lists **successful** logins, logouts and reboots (`reboot`). a common mistake: searching `last` for failed attempts. failed logins do not appear in `last`. failed login attempts are stored in `/var/log/btmp` and read with `lastb`; only root can read it. if you suspect brute-forcing, run `sudo lastb | head` first. on some distributions the btmp file may not exist and the command errors; that can simply mean no failed attempts were ever recorded. commands cmd last what lists successful logins/logouts and reboot records. where when investigating who logged in at night. why reveals account misuse. example last -n 10 nosim cmd lastb what lists failed login attempts (needs root). where during security audits. why shows attack attempts. example sudo lastb -n 10 nosim tip `last -n 5 student` shows only the last 5 logins of the `student` account. warn login records are sensitive (user names, ip addresses). remove ips and names before sharing output on public forums. tasks t01 text find out which user you are running as with `whoami`. hint the output should be `student`. t02 text show your uid, gid and group list with `id`. hint groups are in the `groups=` part. t03 text print your groups with the `groups` command. hint the `wheel` group means sudo rights. t04 text look at another user's identity with `id alice`. hint pass the user name as the argument. t05 text read the account file with `cat /etc/passwd`. hint the file is readable by everyone. (`cat` → module 2.6.) t06 text find only the line of the `student` account with `grep student /etc/passwd`. hint field 6 of the line is the home directory. (`grep` → module 3.4, `cut` → 3.5.) t07 text list only the user names with `cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd`. hint -d sets the delimiter, -f the field number. (`cut` → module 3.5.) t08 text count how many accounts exist with `wc -l /etc/passwd`. hint -l counts lines; each line is one account. (`wc` → module 2.6.) t09 text predict: how many lines (groups) does `/etc/group` have? guess first, then verify with `wc -l /etc/group`. hint count the groups root, wheel, student, alice, devs. t10 text predict: what does `cat /etc/shadow` do as a normal user? think first, then run it. hint password hashes are root-only: permission denied|erişim engellendi|zugriff verweigert. t11 text predict: what does `id bob` return for a user that does not exist? run it and read the error. hint expect a `no such user` error; the exit code is not 0. t12 text debug: a ticket says `alice` cannot log in. in `~/documents/accounts.txt` find alice's line and write her shell (field 7) into `~/alice_shell.txt`. hint `grep alice file | cut -d: -f7 > target`. a `nologin` shell blocks interactive login. (`grep`, `cut` → module 3.4/3.5; `>` → 3.2.) t13 text mini project: write the names of accounts whose shell ends in `/bin/bash` in `/etc/passwd` into `~/shell_users.txt`. hint `grep '/bin/bash$' /etc/passwd | cut -d: -f1 > ~/shell_users.txt`; `$` means end of line. (`grep`, `cut` → module 3.4/3.5; `>` → 3.2.) t14 text challenge: put your user name (`whoami`) and then the `id` output into `~/me.txt`. it must show `student`, `uid=1000` and `wheel`. hint use `>` for the first command and `>>` for the second. (`>` and `>>` → module 3.2.) t15 text challenge: how many accounts in `/etc/passwd` have the `nologin` shell? write the number into `~/nologin_count.txt`. hint `grep -c` counts matching lines; redirect the output with `>`. (`grep`, `cut` → module 3.4/3.5; `>` → 3.2.) t16 text ticket #4107: the auditor wants the uid and groups of `alice`. save the information in `~/alice_info.txt`. hint `id alice > ~/alice_info.txt`; the output must contain `uid=1001` and `devs`. (`>` and `>>` → module 3.2.) : { these commands only read, so you can run them safely on your vm. `lastb` needs `sudo`. remove ips and user names before sharing output. tasks v01 title who is connected? text paste the output of `who` and `w`. blocks cmd who
w expected student  pts/0   2026-11-12 09:00 (192.168.1.10)
 09:20:01 up 1 day,  2:30,  1 user,  load average: 0.00, 0.01, 0.05
user     tty      from      login@   idle   what
... differs if there are no lines you may be in a graphical session's fake terminal; try a real terminal. on wsl `who` may be empty; the load average line of `w` is enough. v02 title successful logins text list the latest logins and paste the output. blocks cmd last -n 5 expected student  pts/0  192.168.1.10  wed nov 12 09:00   still logged in
reboot   system boot  5.14.0  wed nov 12 08:55 still running

wtmp begins mon nov 10 08:00:00 2026 differs if you see `command not found`: `sudo apt install util-linux` (ubuntu) or `sudo dnf install util-linux` (rocky/alma). in containers or wsl wtmp may be empty; the final `wtmp begins` line is enough. v03 title failed logins text look at the `lastb` output. the list may be empty; that is normal. then press \ blocks cmd sudo lastb -n 5 expected (if empty) btmp begins wed nov 12 08:55:00 2026 differs `no such file or directory` (no btmp): no failed login was ever recorded. you can generate an entry by entering a wrong password in a second terminal (e.g. `su - alice`) and looking again. v04 title query an account with getent text get the record of the `student` account; numbers and home directory must be visible. blocks cmd getent passwd student expected student:x:1000:1000:student:/home/student:/bin/bash differs if your user name is not `student`, use your own: `getent passwd $(whoami)`. if the output is empty that account does not exist; check your name with `whoami`. v05 title your identity text paste your `id` output. blocks cmd expected uid=1000(student) gid=1000(student) groups=1000(student),10(wheel) differs on ubuntu the sudo group is called `sudo`; on rocky/alma it is `wheel`. if the uid is 0 you are running as root; switch to a normal user. v06 title account list and shells text list user name and shell side by side (first 8 lines). blocks cmd getent passwd | cut -d: -f1,7 | head -n 8 expected root:/bin/bash
bin:/sbin/nologin
daemon:/sbin/nologin
... differs on ubuntu the shell path may be `/usr/sbin/nologin`. if `cut` fails, make sure you wrote the delimiter as `-d:` (no space). quiz : { which command shows failed login attempts? options last lastb who ],  `last` shows only successful logins; failed attempts are in `/var/log/btmp` and read with `lastb`. : { what does field 7 of a `/etc/passwd` line show? options the home directory the login shell the password hash the uid explain fields: name, x, uid, gid, comment, home, shell. field 7 is the shell (e.g. /bin/bash or /sbin/nologin). : { in which file are password hashes stored? options /etc/passwd /etc/shadow /etc/group /var/log/wtmp explain hashes are in /etc/shadow, readable only by root; the x in passwd indicates this. : { why do scripts prefer `getent passwd`? options it also finds ldap/sssd users besides the local file it is always faster it needs no permissions and shows passwords it only works as root explain getent queries all sources through nss, so it returns users from the central directory too. summary `whoami`, `id` and `groups` show who you are and which groups you are in. `/etc/passwd` has 7 fields (name, x, uid, gid, comment, home, shell); password hashes are in `/etc/shadow`. `who` and `w` show current sessions, `last` successful and `lastb` failed past logins. `getent` queries accounts without caring whether they come from a file or a central directory. glossary term uid / gid meaning numeric identity of a user and a group; root has uid 0. term nologin meaning a shell that blocks interactive login; used for service accounts. term wtmp / btmp meaning log files of successful and failed logins (`last` / `lastb`). term load average meaning average system load over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. term nss / getent meaning the layer that resolves account info from files or directory services, and the command to query it.

4.2.title: User management: add, modify, lock, delete
objectives: You create an account with a home directory and shell using `useradd -m -s` and set its password with `passwd`.
You add users to groups with `usermod -aG` and know what happens if the `-a` is forgotten.
You lock accounts with `usermod -L` and manage password policy with `chage`.
You know the difference between `userdel` and `userdel -r` and think about preserving data before deleting.
4.2.text:
title user management: add, modify, lock, delete lead manage the lifecycle of an account safely with useradd, passwd, usermod, groupadd, chage and userdel. objectives you create an account with a home directory and shell using `useradd -m -s` and set its password with `passwd`. you add users to groups with `usermod -ag` and know what happens if the `-a` is forgotten. you lock accounts with `usermod -l` and manage password policy with `chage`. you know the difference between `userdel` and `userdel -r` and think about preserving data before deleting. sections create title creating accounts: useradd and passwd body when a new employee arrives you create an account for them. these actions change system files (`/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/group`), so they need **root privileges**, i.e. `sudo`. `useradd` does **not create a home directory on every distribution by default**, so add `-m`. `-s /bin/bash` sets the login shell. the new home is filled with template files from `/etc/skel`. `passwd` sets the password; nothing is shown while you type, which is normal. debian/ubuntu also have the interactive `adduser` wrapper; rocky/alma do not (use `useradd` there). in scripts prefer `useradd`, which works everywhere. commands cmd useradd what creates a new user account. where when adding a new employee or service account. why everyone gets separate files and permissions. example sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash testuser nosim cmd passwd what sets or changes the account's password. where after the account is created. why an account without a password cannot log in. example sudo passwd testuser nosim cmd chage what manages password aging (`-d 0` forces a change at first login). where to force a new account to change its password at first login. why the temporary password set by the admin does not become permanent. example sudo chage -d 0 testuser nosim cmd getent passwd what verifies that the account exists. where after every addition. why catches typos immediately. example getent passwd testuser nosim tip keep account names lowercase ascii (`alice`, `testuser`). spaces, accented characters and capitals cause trouble. warn adding users on a real vm changes the system. take a snapshot of your vm first (module 0.2). do not type passwords on the command line (`chpasswd` leaves them in history). modify title modifying: usermod, groupadd, groups body `usermod` changes an existing account. most used: `-ag group` (**append** to group), `-s` (shell), `-l` (lock), `-u` (unlock). use `groupadd` to create a group; after a group change the user must **log in again**. the classic mistake: `usermod -g devs alice` without `-a`. it wipes all of alice's supplementary groups and leaves only `devs`, including `wheel`. the user loses sudo rights. always use `-ag`. sudo rights come from membership in `wheel` on rocky/alma and `sudo` on ubuntu. do not edit `/etc/sudoers` by hand; use `visudo`, which checks the syntax. commands cmd groupadd what creates a new group. where when creating a shared group for a project team. why you grant access to the group, not to each person. example sudo groupadd labteam nosim cmd usermod -ag what adds the user to a group while keeping existing groups. where when putting someone in a team or the sudo group. why without `-a` the old groups are removed. example sudo usermod -ag labteam testuser nosim cmd usermod -l what locks the account (password login is disabled); `-u` unlocks. where when an employee leaves or an account looks suspicious. why cuts access at once while data stays intact. example sudo usermod -l testuser nosim cmd passwd -s what shows account status (l/lk = locked). where to verify the lock. why confirms the lock was really applied. example sudo passwd -s testuser nosim cmd what verifies the group change. where after each usermod. why shows the membership was added and old ones were not removed. example id testuser tip after a group change an open session keeps using the old groups; the user must log out and back in. danger `usermod -g` (without `-a`) removes all of a user's supplementary groups. on an admin account this can remove sudo access and lock you out of the system. always write `-ag` and check with `id`. delete title deleting: userdel and the home directory body `userdel name` removes the account from `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow` and `/etc/group`, but **leaves the home directory and its files**. the directory then belongs to a uid with no owner. `userdel -r` also deletes the home directory and mail spool permanently. the safe order in real life: (1) lock with `usermod -l`, (2) check running processes and cron jobs, (3) back up the home directory, (4) only then delete. you can find files of a deleted user with `find / -user uid`. if the user has a session or running process, `userdel` errors out; end the session first. commands cmd userdel what deletes the account, keeps the home directory. where after the employee left and data was backed up. why closes the account without risk of data loss. example sudo userdel testuser nosim cmd userdel -r what deletes account, home directory and mail spool permanently. where only when the data is truly not needed. why cleans up disk space and leftovers. example sudo userdel -r testuser nosim cmd ls -ld what shows the home directory still exists. where after userdel. why you see that leftover directories remain ownerless. example ls -ld /home/testuser warn `userdel -r` cannot be undone: photos, documents and keys are gone. back up first, snapshot your vm, lock the account, and re-read the user name before pressing enter. danger with `sudo rm -r /home/name`, a wrong path (a stray space or missing name) deletes other data. run it only for the `testuser` you created and type the full path. tasks t01 text try your sudo rights with `sudo whoami`. the output must be `root`. hint `student` is in the wheel group, so sudo works. (`sudo` → module 4.3.) t02 text show alice's account record with `grep alice /etc/passwd`. hint field 6 is the home directory. t03 text list which users have a home directory with `ls /home`. hint each user has one folder. t04 text read the password hashes with `sudo cat /etc/shadow`. the file is root-only. hint put `sudo` first; hashes start with `$6$...`. t05 text see the permissions and owner of alice's home directory with `sudo ls -ld /home/alice`. hint `-d` lists the directory itself, not its content. t06 text read all groups with `cat /etc/group`. hint line format: group:x:gid:members. t07 text find the members of the `devs` group with `grep devs /etc/group`. hint members are in field 4, comma-separated. t08 text list alice's home content (including hidden files) with `sudo ls -la /home/alice`. hint reading another user's home needs root. t09 text predict: what does `cat /etc/shadow` do as a normal user? run it and verify. hint expect permission denied|erişim engellendi|zugriff verweigert. t10 text predict: how do the permissions of alice's home directory look? guess first, then verify with `sudo ls -ld /home/alice`. hint a private home: `drwx------` (700). t11 text predict: what does `id carol` return for an account that does not exist yet? run it. hint expect a `no such user` error. t12 text debug: the `userdel -r alice` in `~/offboard.sh` deletes the home directory that must be kept for the audit. rewrite the script so it contains `sudo userdel alice` without `-r`. hint `echo 'sudo userdel alice' > ~/offboard.sh`. use single quotes. (`>` and `>>` → module 3.2.) t13 text mini project: write a three-line plan into `~/new_user_plan.txt`: `sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash carol`, `sudo passwd carol` and `sudo usermod -ag devs carol`. hint use `>` on the first line and `>>` on the rest. (`>` and `>>` → module 3.2.) t14 text challenge: the script `~/onboard.sh` must create `dave` with `-m -s /bin/bash -g devs`, then force a password change at first login with `chage -d 0 dave`. make the script `chmod 750`. hint two `echo` commands and one `chmod`; use `sudo`. (`chmod` → module 4.4.) t15 text ticket #4210: `eve` has left the company. first lock the account, then delete it (keeping the home directory). write the commands in order into `~/offboard_eve.txt`. hint `sudo usermod -l eve` and `sudo userdel eve`; do not use `-r`. t16 text ticket #4211: `frank` will become an administrator on the server (rocky/alma). write the command into `~/frank.txt`. hint `sudo usermod -ag wheel frank`; do not forget `-a`. : { this section changes the system. take a snapshot of your vm first. work only on `testuser` and `labteam` from this section; do not touch your own account. tasks v01 title create an account text create the `testuser` account with a home directory and bash shell and paste its record. blocks cmd sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash testuser
getent passwd testuser expected testuser:x:1001:1001::/home/testuser:/bin/bash differs if you see `user already exists` the account was created earlier; `getent passwd testuser` is enough. on ubuntu the uid may be a number other than 1001. v02 title set a password text set a password for `testuser`. nothing is shown while typing. paste the success message. blocks cmd sudo passwd testuser expected passwd: password updated successfully differs on rocky/alma the message is `passwd: all authentication tokens updated successfully.` a too short/simple password triggers a warning but is still accepted (as root). v03 title add to a group text create the `labteam` group, add `testuser` with **-ag** and paste the `id` output. blocks cmd sudo groupadd labteam
sudo usermod -ag labteam testuser
id testuser expected uid=1001(testuser) gid=1001(testuser) groups=1001(testuser),1002(labteam) differs if the group exists you get `groupadd: group 'labteam' already exists`; continue. if `labteam` is missing next to the primary group, check the letters `-a` and `-g`. v04 title lock the account text lock `testuser` and show its status. blocks cmd sudo usermod -l testuser
sudo passwd -s testuser expected testuser l 2026-11-12 0 99999 7 -1 differs on rocky/alma the status is shown as `lk`. to unlock: `sudo usermod -u testuser`. v05 title password policy text paste the `chage -l` output; force a password change at first login. blocks cmd sudo chage -d 0 testuser
sudo chage -l testuser expected last password change                : password must be changed
password expires                    : never
... differs the output must contain the `last password change` line; the value may be `password must be changed` or a date. if `chage: command not found`, the `shadow-utils` (rocky) or `passwd` (ubuntu) package is missing. v06 title userdel keeps the home text delete the account without `-r`; then show that the account is gone but its home directory remains. blocks cmd sudo userdel testuser
getent passwd testuser
ls -ld /home/testuser expected drwx------ 2 1001 1001 62 nov 12 10:00 /home/testuser differs `getent` prints nothing; the account is deleted. the home directory's owner now shows as a number (1001) instead of a name; that means an ownerless directory. on `user is currently used by process`, end the user's session. v07 title cleanup text clean up the now unneeded test directory and group. type the full path in the commands. press \  when finished. blocks cmd sudo rm -r /home/testuser
sudo groupdel labteam
ls /home expected student differs `groupdel: group 'labteam' does not exist` means it is already gone. if you notice you mistyped the path, do not press enter; be sure of the full path `/home/testuser`. quiz : { what does `sudo usermod -g devs alice` (without `-a`) do? options adds alice to devs and keeps the others removes all of alice's supplementary groups and leaves only devs deletes the alice account locks alice explain -g replaces the supplementary group list; without `-a` (append) old groups such as wheel are lost. : { what happens after `userdel alice` (without `-r`)? options the home directory is deleted too nothing happens the account is deleted but the home directory stays the account is only locked explain the records are removed; `/home/alice` and its files stay on disk. deleting them needs `-r`. : { how do you cut an account's access immediately without deleting it? options usermod -l userdel -r passwd -d chmod 000 /home explain `usermod -l` disables password login; the account and data stay and `-u` brings it back. : { membership in which group gives sudo rights on rocky/alma? options wheel sudoers admin root explain on the rhel family the sudo group is `wheel`; on debian/ubuntu it is `sudo`. summary `sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash name` creates an account; `passwd` sets a password; `chage -d 0` forces a change at first login. when adding to a group always use `usermod -ag`; forgetting `-a` removes the old groups. `usermod -l` locks, `-u` unlocks; locking is the safe first step before deleting. `userdel` keeps the home directory, `userdel -r` deletes it permanently; back up and snapshot first. glossary term wheel meaning the administrator group that grants sudo on the rhel family (`sudo` on debian). term /etc/skel meaning template files copied into a new home directory. term locked account meaning an account whose password login is disabled (`usermod -l`). term ownerless directory meaning a directory that still belongs to the uid of a deleted user. term snapshot meaning a restorable point-in-time image of a vm.

4.3.title: Switching identity: su, sudo, and sudoers
objectives: Explain that root has UID 0, the difference between `su -` and `sudo`, and which password each command asks for.
Run one administrative command with `sudo` and inspect your permissions with `sudo -l`.
Open a full root login shell with `sudo -i`, close it with `exit`, and avoid staying root unnecessarily.
Know that `/etc/sudoers` defines privilege policy and must only be edited with `visudo`.
4.3.text: title switching identity: su, sudo, and sudoers lead learn when and how to use root privileges: prefer one-command sudo and manage its policy safely with visudo. objectives explain that root has uid 0, the difference between `su -` and `sudo`, and which password each command asks for. run one administrative command with `sudo` and inspect your permissions with `sudo -l`. open a full root login shell with `sudo -i`, close it with `exit`, and avoid staying root unnecessarily. know that `/etc/sudoers` defines privilege policy and must only be edited with `visudo`. sections identity title who is root? su and sudo body on linux, **root** is the superuser with uid 0. root can manage system files and other accounts; a wrong command can cause serious damage. stay in your normal account for everyday work and use administrator privileges only when needed. `su - user` switches to the target account and asks for that account's password. `su -` switches to root, but root password login may be disabled on systems such as ubuntu. the `-` loads the target user's login environment (for example, `home` and profile). `sudo command` lets an authorized user authenticate with their own password and run only the specified command as another user, usually root. a sudo rule can also be configured not to ask for a password. running one command with sudo is safer than keeping a root session open. commands cmd whoami what shows the current effective user name. where when checking which account will run a command. why prevents acting as the wrong user, especially after changing privileges. example whoami cmd what shows the uid, primary gid, and group memberships. where when checking which group grants sudo access. why verifies user and group identities together. example }, { su - what opens root's login session; it requires the root password. where only when the root account is enabled and a longer admin session is truly needed. why loads the login environment; every command in the session runs as root. example su - nosim cmd sudo command what runs one permitted command as another user. where when a specific administrative action is needed from a normal account. why keeps both the privilege and its scope limited. example sudo whoami cmd exit what leaves an open su or sudo login session. where when the administrative work is finished. why avoids staying in a root shell longer than necessary. example exit tip no characters appear while typing a password at the terminal; that is expected. enter your own password only at a trusted sudo prompt. sudo title one command and administrator sessions body `sudo whoami` prints `root`; plain `whoami` prints your own account. sudo elevates only that command, so your shell remains a normal user when the command ends. `sudo -l` lists the commands your account may run. `sudo -u user command` runs one command as a specified user when the policy allows it. the rules depend on the distribution and organization; membership in `wheel` is common on rocky/alma and `sudo` on ubuntu/debian. `sudo -i` opens root's login shell; `whoami` then prints root and `home` is `/root`. `sudo -s` opens a root shell that keeps more of the current environment. both are full, high-risk sessions: keep them short and use `exit` to leave. sudo may cache authentication for a while; `sudo -k` invalidates that cache. commands cmd sudo -l what lists the commands and rules available to your account through sudo. where before investigating your permissions or an access error. why shows the machine's actual policy rather than assumptions. example sudo -l cmd sudo -u user what runs one command as the specified user. where when checking how a service or job behaves under another account. why tests the target account's permissions without opening a root session. example sudo -u nobody id nosim cmd sudo -i what opens an administrator shell with root's login environment. where for a brief, controlled session that needs several admin commands. why loads root's home and startup environment. example sudo -i nosim cmd sudo -k what invalidates the cached sudo authentication. where when leaving a shared terminal or requiring authentication again immediately. why prevents a previous authentication from being reused by subsequent commands. example sudo -k nosim warn a forgotten command inside `sudo -i` still runs as root. prefer `sudo command` for short tasks; after leaving a root shell, use `whoami` to verify you returned to your normal account. policy title sudoers: manage privilege policy safely body `/etc/sudoers` and files in `/etc/sudoers.d/` define who may run which commands as which target users. never edit these files directly with `nano`, `vim`, or `echo`: a single syntax error can break all sudo access. use `sudo visudo` to inspect and edit the policy. to open a separate rule file, use `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/name`; `visudo` checks the syntax before saving. for example, `alice all=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx` permits only that command. `nopasswd` removes the password prompt, for example `alice all=(root) nopasswd: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx`. use it only when truly needed, with the full command path and a narrow scope. granting unrestricted access with `all` or opening a general-purpose shell without a password is not a safe rule. check the result with `sudo -l`. commands cmd sudo visudo what edits sudo policy with locking and syntax validation. where when adding or changing a sudoers rule. why reduces the risk of saving a malformed file and breaking sudo access. example sudo visudo nosim cmd sudo visudo -f what safely edits the specified sudoers file. where when creating a separate sudoers.d rule supported by the distribution. why keeps rules separate from the main file and validates their syntax. example sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/alice nosim cmd sudo visudo -c what checks the syntax of sudoers files. where after verifying a policy change. why confirms that the file can be read and parsed. example sudo visudo -c nosim cmd sudo -l what shows the active sudo rules. where when checking whether a policy change applies to a user. why lets you compare the written rule with the effective permissions. example sudo -l danger `nopasswd: all` lets a user run every command without a password. limit the rule to the required user, exact command path, and necessary arguments; write it with `visudo` and verify it with `sudo -l`. workflow title a safe administrator workflow body first verify the target and its impact from your normal account; when elevated access is required, run only the necessary command with sudo. if it fails, do not blindly add `sudo`: inspect `id`, `sudo -l`, and the file permissions. when the work is done, leave any root session with `exit`. never put passwords in command history, edit sudoers directly, or run an unfamiliar command as root. on a real vm, take a snapshot before changing system policy. commands cmd sudo -l what verifies the scope of your permissions before acting. where before starting an administrative task. why helps catch a missing or overly broad rule. example sudo -l cmd sudo whoami what safely verifies that a command runs as root. where when learning how sudo behaves. why shows that the privilege switch applies only to the command. example sudo whoami cmd sudo visudo -c what checks the syntax of the sudoers configuration. where after a policy change. why catches a broken rule before it is relied upon. example sudo visudo -c nosim tip apply least privilege: grant no more than the required user, target account, command, and arguments. tasks t01 text show your current account with `whoami`. hint if you are not root, your own user name appears. t02 text inspect your uid and group memberships with `id`. hint find the `uid=`, `gid=`, and `groups=` fields. t03 text run `sudo whoami` and verify that the command runs as root. hint if sudo permits it, the output is `root`. t04 text run `sudo id` and observe that the uid and groups differ from your normal account. hint an effective uid of 0 identifies root. t05 text show the owner and permissions of root's home directory with `sudo ls -ld /root`. hint `-d` lists the directory itself; sudo allows you to inspect another user's directory. t06 text read the permissions of the sudo policy file with `sudo ls -l /etc/sudoers`; do not change its contents. hint this task only lists file metadata. t07 text predict: what will `whoami` print in your normal account? run it to check. hint without sudo, it prints your own user name. t08 text predict: what will `sudo whoami` print? run it to check. hint if permitted, the command runs as root. t09 text debug: `~/sudoers.bad` contains a dangerous rule granting everyone every command without a password. replace the file with this narrowly scoped example: `student all=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx`. this is only a draft; do not copy it into the real sudoers file. hint use `echo 'student all=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx' > ~/sudoers.bad`. (`>` and `>>` → module 3.2.) t10 text mini project: write these commands in order to `~/admin_runbook.txt`: list permissions, check nginx status, and clear the password cache: `sudo -l`, `sudo systemctl status nginx`, `sudo -k`. hint use `>` for the first line and `>>` for the rest. (`>` and `>>` → module 3.2.) t11 text challenge: write a rule allowing only an nginx restart to `~/sudoers_rule.txt`: `alice all=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx`. hint this is a draft; applying it requires `sudo visudo -f`. (`>` and `>>` → module 3.2.) t12 text challenge: write the steps to check permissions and then restart the permitted service, in order, in `~/service_plan.txt`. hint write `sudo -l` followed by `sudo systemctl restart nginx`. t13 text ticket #4310: a new rule file is needed for alice. without changing any real file, write the safe edit command into `~/ticket_4310.txt`. hint use `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/alice`. t14 text ticket #4311: alice should be able to restart nginx without a password for this one operation only. write the visudo command followed by the narrowly scoped rule into `~/ticket_4311.txt`. do not apply this draft to a real system. hint use `nopasswd` for `/usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx` only, not `nopasswd: all`. (`>` and `>>` → module 3.2.) : { this section inspects privilege policy on a real system; it does not change configuration. take a vm snapshot if possible. enter your password only at the terminal's sudo prompt. tasks v01 title inspect your normal identity text show your normal account and group memberships with `id`. blocks cmd expected uid=1000(student) gid=1000(student) groups=1000(student) differs user names and uids vary by distribution; your own values are expected. ubuntu commonly uses the `sudo` group; rocky/alma commonly use `wheel`. v02 title use sudo for one command text run `sudo whoami` and verify that the effective user is root. blocks cmd sudo whoami expected root differs no characters appear while typing the password; that is expected. a `not in the sudoers file` error means your account has not been granted permission; ask an administrator. v03 title verify the effective uid text run `sudo id -u` to verify that the privileged command runs with uid 0. blocks cmd sudo id -u expected }],  : [ if the command is denied, inspect permissions with `sudo -l`. v04 title read your sudo permissions text list commands permitted for your account with `sudo -l`; do not change any rules. blocks cmd sudo -l expected user student may run the following commands differs the user name and rules vary by distribution. if the output includes `nopasswd`, note which exact command it covers; do not change the rule. v05 title check sudoers syntax text run `sudo visudo -c` to verify that the current sudo configuration parses. this command does not edit the files. blocks cmd sudo visudo -c expected /etc/sudoers: parsed ok differs a distribution may also check included files; expect a `parsed ok`-style line for each file. if an error appears, do not edit the file directly; report it to the system administrator. quiz : { what is the main difference between `sudo command` and `su -`? options both always require the root password `sudo` runs one permitted command; `su -` opens the target account's login session `su -` only reads files `sudo` permanently turns the user into root explain `sudo` grants privilege for a command; `su -` switches to another account's login shell. : { why use `visudo` to edit the sudo policy file? options it encrypts the file it creates the root account it checks syntax and reduces the chance of saving a broken rule it adds all users to the sudo group explain `visudo` locks the file while editing and checks its syntax before saving. : { which sudo rule follows least privilege? options grant one user only the exact command they need give everyone `nopasswd: all` share the root password with the team run every command in a permanent root shell explain limit access to the right user and required command; avoid broad `all` rules. : { if `su -` rejects the root password on ubuntu, what is a likely explanation? options linux has no root account sudo is always disabled the terminal does not support root sessions the root account may be locked for password login; an authorized user should use `sudo` explain ubuntu installations often lock the root account; an authorized user uses sudo for administration. summary root has uid 0. `su -` opens the target account's login session; `sudo command` runs one permitted command with elevated privileges. `sudo -l` shows actual permissions; `sudo -i` opens a full root login shell and should be closed with `exit` when finished. edit sudoers policy only with `visudo` and validate its syntax with `visudo -c`. keep `nopasswd` and especially `all` rules narrow; grant only the required user, command, and arguments. glossary term root meaning the account with uid 0 and system-wide administrative privileges. term sudo meaning a tool that lets an authorized user run a specific command as another user. term meaning a tool for switching the current session to another user account. term sudoers meaning the policy defining sudo permissions by user, target account, and command. term visudo meaning a tool that edits sudoers files with locking and syntax validation. term nopasswd meaning a sudo rule option that removes the password prompt for specified commands.

4.4.title: Permission Basics
objectives: You read the type character, the three permission triplets, owner and group in `ls -l`.
You explain that r, w, x mean different things for files and for directories.
You know that deleting a file depends on the w+x permission of the **parent directory**, not of the file.
You set permissions with `chmod` (octal and symbolic) and change ownership with `chown`/`chgrp`.
You show by calculation that `umask` is a bit mask, not a subtraction.
4.4.text:
title permission basics lead read `ls -l` output and manage file and directory permissions correctly with `chmod`, `chown` and `umask`. objectives you read the type character, the three permission triplets, owner and group in `ls -l`. you explain that r, w, x mean different things for files and for directories. you know that deleting a file depends on the w+x permission of the **parent directory**, not of the file. you set permissions with `chmod` (octal and symbolic) and change ownership with `chown`/`chgrp`. you show by calculation that `umask` is a bit mask, not a subtraction. sections read title reading ls -l output body `ls -l` prints one line per file: `-rw-r----- 1 student devs 120 nov 12 10:00 report.txt`. the first character is the **type**: `-` file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link. the next nine characters are three triplets: **owner (u)**, **group (g)**, **others (o)**. each triplet is `rwx` for read, write, execute; a missing permission shows as `-`. the two names after the number are owner and group (`student devs`); the `1` before them is the hard link count. the system checks in order: if you are the owner, only the owner triplet applies; otherwise, if you are in the group, the group triplet applies; otherwise the others triplet. **root** and processes with relevant capabilities can bypass many discretionary access-control (dac) checks; other controls such as selinux or a read-only mount may still deny access. `id` shows your groups. a new group membership only reaches your process after a fresh login (or with `newgrp`). commands cmd ls -l what lists files with type, permissions, owner, group, size and date. where first stop for any permission problem. why shows at a glance who may do what. example ls -l cmd ls -ld what shows the permissions of the directory itself (not its contents). where when checking directory permissions. why `ls -l shared` lists the contents; for the directory itself you need `-d`. example ls -ld shared cmd stat what shows file details; permissions in octal and symbolic form. where when you want to verify the octal value. why no need to convert between `ls -l` and octal in your head. example stat secret.txt cmd what shows user and group ids. where for the question 'why can't i access this?'. why determines which triplet applies to you. example }],  split the permission string into groups of three: `rw- r-- ---` means owner reads and writes, group reads, others nothing. meaning title r, w, x: on files and on directories body **on files:** `r` reads the content, `w` changes the content, `x` runs the file as a program. new files are **never created executable**; for `./script.sh` you first need `chmod +x`. **on directories:** `r` lists the names, `x` allows entering and reaching entries by name (`cd`, `cat vault/data.txt`), `w` allows creating, deleting and renaming entries. `w` alone is useless; **w needs x too**. to reach a path you need **x on every directory** along it. **key rule:** to delete or move a file, the file's own permissions do not matter; you need **w+x on the parent directory**. file permissions only control reading and writing the content. so a `644` file inside a `555` directory cannot be deleted, and neither can a `777` file there. commands cmd cat what reads file content; needs r on the file and x on the directories in the path. where when testing read permission. why unauthorized reads stop with `permission denied`. example cat secret.txt cmd what deletes a file; success depends on w+x of the parent directory. where when understanding delete failures. why the directory permission decides, not the file permission. example rm locked/old.txt cmd what enters a directory; needs x on the directory. where for access problems. why without x you cannot get in. example cd vault tip when you say 'i can't delete it', don't look at the file; look at the **directory** with `ls -ld .`. warn `chmod -r 777` is not a fix. it gives everyone write and execute rights, hides the real cause and opens a security hole. first find the real reason with `ls -l` and `id`. chmod title chmod: changing permissions body in octal notation you add **r=4, w=2, x=1**: `7`=rwx, `6`=rw-, `5`=r-x, `4`=r--, `0`=---. the three digits are for owner, group, others. common values: `644` (regular file), `755` (program and directory), `600` (private file), `700` (private directory), `664` and `775` (group work). in symbolic notation you write who (`u`, `g`, `o`, `a`), operation (`+`, `-`, `=`) and permission (`r`, `w`, `x`): `chmod g+w,o-rx shared`. **capital `x`** sets x only on directories and on files that are already executable; `chmod -r u=rwx,go=rx data` makes directories 755 and previously non-executable files 644, while preserving x on files that were already executable. only the **owner** (or root) may change permissions; on someone else's file you get `operation not permitted`. commands cmd chmod 640 what sets octal permissions: owner rw-, group r--, others ---. where when you define permissions in one step. why the result is explicit and repeatable. example chmod 640 notes.txt cmd chmod +x what adds the execute permission. where when making a script executable. why changes only x, leaves other bits (subject to umask). example chmod +x script.sh cmd chmod g+w,o-rx what symbolic: group gains write, others lose read and execute. where for small corrections. why changes only the bits you name. example chmod g+w,o-rx shared cmd chmod -r u=rwx,go=rx what fixes a tree recursively: files 644, directories 755. where for bulk corrections. why thanks to `x`, files don't get needless x. example chmod -r u=rwx,go=rx data tip look at the target with `ls -l` first; with `-r`, double-check the end of the path. danger running `chmod -r` with a wrong value on `/` or `~` breaks the system or your home (e.g. ssh key permissions, sudo). in the vm take a **snapshot** first and work only inside the practice folder. owner title chown and chgrp: owner and group body every file has an owner and a group. **only root may change the owner** (`sudo chown`). a regular user may only set a file's group to a group they belong to; in the simulator we use `sudo chgrp` for that. `chown alice:devs report.txt` sets owner and group together. a typical team setup: group `devs`, mode `660` on files or `770` on directories; only `devs` members get access. finer rules (per-user permissions) use acls (`getfacl`/`setfacl`); those come in later modules. commands cmd sudo chown what changes the owner (and optionally the group). where when handing a file over to another user. why only root can do this. example sudo chown alice:devs report.txt cmd sudo chgrp what changes only the group. where when assigning a group to a shared directory. why keeps the owner and controls group access. example sudo chgrp devs team.txt tip be careful with `chown -r` on real systems too; verify the path with `ls -ld` first. umask title umask: default permissions body new files **start** from `666`, new directories from `777`; `umask` removes bits using a **mask**: **new mode = base & ~umask**. this is not subtraction. examples (file, base 666): umask `022` → `644`; `027` → `640`; `077` → `600`; `002` → `664`. the difference shows when the umask has bits the base lacks: for `025`, `666 & ~025 = 642`, while subtraction would give `641` (wrong). for `001` the result is `666`, subtraction would give `665`. because x is not in the base, files are never created executable. `umask` is **per process**: it applies only in that shell and the programs started from it. to make it permanent, put it in `~/.bashrc` (user) or `/etc/profile` (system). commands cmd umask what shows the current mask in octal (e.g. `0022`). where to understand
