options the command does not work only root may use it it changes the owner it gives everyone full access and hides the real cause explain 777 grants everyone read, write and execute and weakens security. first find the cause with `ls -l` and `id`, then grant only the minimum needed. summary `ls -l`: type character + owner/group/others triplets; r=4, w=2, x=1. on directories: r=list, w=create/delete/rename (with x), x=enter/access; deleting a file depends on w+x of its parent directory. `chmod` works in octal (`640`) or symbolic (`g+w`, `u=rwx`); only root can `chown`. umask is a mask, not a subtraction: new mode = base & ~umask (file 666, directory 777). `chmod -r 777` is not a fix; apply the principle of least privilege. glossary term permission triplet meaning a separate rwx set for owner, group and others. term octal mode meaning permissions written as the sum r=4, w=2, x=1, e.g. 644. term umask meaning bit mask that defines which permission bits are removed from new files and directories. term owner meaning the user the file belongs to; may change permissions. term group meaning a set of users sharing permissions, e.g. devs. term traverse permission meaning the x bit on a directory; allows passing through the path and access by name.

4.5.title: Special Permissions
objectives: You recognise the setuid (4), setgid (2) and sticky (1) bits and the leading digit in an octal mode.
You read the letters `s`, `S`, `t`, `T` in `ls -l` output correctly.
You build a team folder with `2775` and explain why new files keep the group.
You protect shared writable folders such as `/tmp` with the sticky bit (`1777`).
You know why setuid is dangerous and audit setuid files with `find`.
4.5.text:
title special permissions lead setuid, setgid and the sticky bit: what they do where plain rwx permissions are not enough (passwd, shared team folders, /tmp). try them on your own vm, then reinforce in the simulator. objectives you recognise the setuid (4), setgid (2) and sticky (1) bits and the leading digit in an octal mode. you read the letters `s`, `s`, `t`, `t` in `ls -l` output correctly. you build a team folder with `2775` and explain why new files keep the group. you protect shared writable folders such as `/tmp` with the sticky bit (`1777`). you know why setuid is dangerous and audit setuid files with `find`. sections bits title the three special bits and octal notation body normal permissions are written with three digits (`755`). in the four-digit form the **leading digit** carries the special bits: `4` = setuid, `2` = setgid, `1` = sticky. they add up: `3` = setgid + sticky, `6` = setuid + setgid. a leading zero (`0755`) means no special bit. `ls -l` shows the bits in the x position: `s` in the owner slot (setuid), `s` in the group slot (setgid), `t` in the others slot (sticky). if the x permission underneath is **missing**, the letter becomes uppercase: `s` or `t`. an uppercase letter means 'bit set, but not executable', which is usually a mistake. the meaning differs for files and directories: setuid and setgid on a file mean 'run with the owner's/group's privileges'; setgid and sticky on a directory mean 'inherit the group' and 'restrict deletion'. commands cmd stat what shows the mode as four-digit octal and as letters. where when verifying special bits. why the line `access: (2775/drwxrwsr-x)` gives both notations side by side. example stat prog_c cmd ls -ld what shows the permissions of the directory itself (not its contents). where when checking a team folder or `/tmp`. why without `-d` it lists the contents instead of the directory's own mode. example ls -ld /tmp cmd chmod 4755 what sets a four-digit octal mode; the leading digit is the special bit. where when you want to set a special bit together with the other permissions. why you know the exact result, but old special bits are overwritten too. example chmod 4755 prog_a tip symbolic mode is safer: `chmod g+s team` only adds setgid and leaves the other permissions alone. warn on files, a three-digit `chmod 755 notes.txt` **clears** the special bits. on directories gnu `chmod` keeps setuid/setgid; to remove them use `chmod g-s team` or the five-digit `chmod 00755`. check with `ls -ld` afterwards. setuid title setuid: run with the owner's privileges body when an executable file has **setuid** (`4000`), the program runs with the privileges of the **file owner**, not the person who starts it. the best-known example is `/usr/bin/passwd`: owned by root, shown as `-rwsr-xr-x`. an ordinary user can change their own password because the program, running as root, may update `/etc/shadow`. `sudo` and `mount` work on the same principle. this power is risky. a small bug in a setuid-root program (or a setuid shell, editor or interpreter) hands root to everyone. that is why you must know your setuid files and audit them regularly. two notes: the linux kernel **ignores** setuid on **shell scripts** (`#!/bin/bash`); `chmod u+s` on a script does not grant root, it only misleads. also, setuid does nothing on file systems mounted with `nosuid` (e.g. many usb sticks, or a separate `/tmp` partition). commands cmd chmod u+s what adds setuid in the owner x slot (`s`). where rarely on real systems, only for audited, compiled programs. why a (very carefully used) way to let normal users perform one privileged task. example chmod u+s backup.sh cmd ls -l /usr/bin/passwd what shows the mode of a real setuid program: `-rwsr-xr-x root root`. where to see what setuid looks like. why the `s` in the owner x slot is setuid. example ls -l /usr/bin/passwd nosim cmd find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null what lists all setuid files on the system (`-perm -4000` = this bit is set). where during security audits and hardening. why an unexpected setuid file can be a sign of compromise. example find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null nosim tip familiar names like `passwd`, `sudo`, `mount`, `su` are normal. an unknown setuid file, or one under `/home` or `/tmp`, needs investigation. danger never run `chmod u+s /bin/bash` (or on vim, python, find, cp) on a real system. it gives every user a root shell and is a classic privilege escalation. at most try it on your isolated test vm, after a snapshot, and undo it afterwards. setgid title setgid: a team folder that inherits the group body on files, **setgid** (`2000`) runs the program with the group's privileges; in practice its main use is on **directories**. in a directory with setgid, every new file and subdirectory gets the **directory's group** instead of the creator's primary group. new subdirectories inherit the setgid bit too, so the rule holds across the whole tree. without it: alice drops a file into the `devs` folder, the file belongs to group `alice`, and teammate bob cannot edit it. with setgid the group stays `devs`. for members to be able to **write** group files you also need `umask 002`; with `022` a new file is `rw-r--r--` and the group cannot write. the simulator does not implement group inheritance; it only sets the bit and shows it in `ls -l` and `stat`. you will see the real behaviour in the vm task. commands cmd chmod g+s what adds setgid in the group x slot (`s`). where to turn an existing folder into a team folder. why switches on group inheritance without touching other permissions. example chmod g+s team cmd chmod 2775 what setgid + `rwxrwxr-x`: owner and group full, others read. where when setting up a team folder. why the standard team-folder mode in one command. example chmod 2775 team cmd umask 002 what keeps the group write bit on new files in this shell. where before you work in the team folder. why setgid gives the right group, umask lets the group write. example umask 002 tip on a directory, `rwxrwsr-x` is fine: group `s` (x present + setgid). with `rwxrwsr-x` the group lacks x and cannot enter the folder; fix it. warn `umask` only affects the current shell. to make it permanent add it to the user profile (e.g. `~/.bashrc`); system-wide it is a separate configuration. sticky title sticky bit: restrict deletion in shared folders body in a folder everyone can write to (`777`), **anyone can delete or rename other people's files**, because the right to delete depends on the write permission of the directory, not of the file. the **sticky bit** (`1000`) changes that: only the file owner, the directory owner or root may delete or rename. the classic example is `/tmp`: mode `1777`, shown as `drwxrwxrwt`. everyone creates files, but nobody deletes someone else's. sticky matters on **directories**; on files it has no effect on modern linux. the simulator does not enforce the deletion protection; you check that the bit is set and appears as `t`. you will try the real protection in the vm with alice and bob. commands cmd chmod +t what sets the sticky bit on a directory; `t` appears in the others x slot. where on shared, world-writable drop or exchange folders. why stops users from deleting each other's files. example chmod +t inbox cmd chmod 1777 what sticky + `rwxrwxrwx`: the same mode as `/tmp`. where when creating a folder everyone may drop files into. why the standard shared-folder mode in one command. example chmod 1777 drop tip an uppercase `t` (`drwxrwx--t`) means sticky is set but others lack x. for a private team folder `1770` can look like this on purpose. recipe title recipe: team folder and what comes next body a real team folder is built like this: (1) create the folder, (2) set its group to `devs`, (3) set `2775` (`2770` if outsiders must not read), (4) members work with `umask 002`. because root creates the folder, you need `sudo`. if you also want sticky, use `3775` / `3770`: new files belong to the group, and members cannot delete each other's files. the method has limits: permissions of new files depend on the umask, and you cannot write per-user rules. that is what **default acls** (`setfacl -d`) are for, a topic of later modules. for now remember that a setgid folder is the foundation of teamwork without acls. commands cmd sudo mkdir /srv/project what creates the shared folder under `/srv` with root privileges. where when setting up a permanent team workspace. why a normal user cannot write to `/srv`; sudo is required. example sudo mkdir /srv/project nosim cmd sudo chgrp devs what sets the folder's group to `devs`. where before giving the team permissions. why this is the group setgid will pass on. example sudo chgrp devs team cmd chmod 2775 what completes the team folder's permissions. where after setting the group, before opening it for use. why the group can write and new files get the group `devs`. example chmod 2775 team warn group first, then mode: setting `2775` before the group is `devs` makes the wrong group inherited. at the end `ls -ld` should show `drwxrwsr-x ... devs`. tasks t01 text look at the permissions of `/tmp` with `ls -ld /tmp`. which letter is at the end? hint `drwxrwxrwt`: the final `t` is the sticky bit. t02 text add setuid to `backup.sh` with one command: `chmod u+s backup.sh`. hint 755 + setuid = 4755; see the `rws` with `ls -l backup.sh`. t03 text step by step: set the group of `team` to `devs` with `sudo chgrp devs team`, then apply `chmod 2775 team` and verify with `ls -ld team`. hint expected: `drwxrwsr-x student devs`. t04 text step by step: look at `drop` with `ls -ld drop`, make it sticky with `chmod 1777 drop`, and run `ls -ld drop` again. hint first `drwxr-xr-x`, then `drwxrwxrwt`. t05 text predict: `prog_a` has mode 4755. how do the owner permissions look in `ls -l prog_a`? guess first, then run it. hint x present and setuid set: lowercase `s`. t06 text predict: `prog_b` has mode 4644. how do the owner permissions look? verify with `ls -l prog_b`. hint owner has no x but setuid is set: uppercase `s`. t07 text predict: `prog_c` has mode 2755. what does the `access:` line of `stat prog_c` show? hint leading 2 = setgid; in letters the group x slot shows `s`. t08 text debug: someone left setuid (4755) on the shell script `legacy/tool.sh`. the kernel ignores it on scripts, but it fails an audit. return it to the normal mode `755`. hint see `rws` with `ls -l legacy/tool.sh`, then `chmod 755 legacy/tool.sh`. t09 text debug: the folder `inbox` is `777` and users delete each other's files. fix it to `1777` without touching the existing permissions. hint `chmod +t inbox` adds only sticky. t10 text mini project: set the group of `proj` to `devs`, apply `2770` (outsiders locked out), run `umask 002` and create `proj/plan.txt` with `touch`. hint order: `sudo chgrp devs proj`, `chmod 2770 proj`, `umask 002`, `touch proj/plan.txt`. t11 text mini project: create the folder `upload`, set `1777`, put `a.txt` inside and give the file to alice with `sudo chown alice:devs upload/a.txt`. (in reality bob could not delete it.) hint order: `mkdir`, `chmod 1777`, `touch`, `sudo chown`. t12 text challenge: make the folder `release` look like this: group `devs`, setgid set, owner `rwx`, group `r-x`, others nothing. hint octal: special 2, owner 7, group 5, others 0. t13 text challenge: which of the three scripts in the folder `audit` have a special bit? find them and make all of them plain `755`. hint look for `s` with `ls -l audit`. `chmod 755` also clears special bits. t14 text ticket #4501 — the finance team shares the folder `finance`. files must always belong to group `devs`, the group must be able to write, and outsiders must not get in. also create the subfolder `finance/2026`. hint group `devs`, mode `2770`: new files get `devs`, others have no access. t15 text ticket #4502 — a developer gave `bin/deploy.sh` setuid so it 'runs as root'. setuid does not work on scripts and is risky. remove setuid, set the group `devs` and the mode `750`. hint `chmod 750` clears the special bit as well. in practice you grant privileges with a `sudo` rule. t16 text ticket #4503 — a new folder `dropbox` is needed: group `devs`, new files belong to the group, members must not delete each other's files, outsiders cannot enter. put a `readme.txt` inside containing the text `uploads only`. hint setgid + sticky = 3, then `770`: `3770`. `echo uploads only > dropbox/readme.txt`. (`>` and `>>` → module 3.2.) : { work on your own ubuntu/rocky/alma vm. the tasks use `/srv` and the temporary users `alice` and `bob`; **take a vm snapshot first**. the first two tasks are read-only, tasks 3–5 create users and folders on the system, and the last one cleans up. do them in order (3 → 4 → 5). tasks v01 title see the special bits text look at the permissions of `/tmp` and of real setuid programs and paste the output. blocks cmd ls -ld /tmp
ls -l /usr/bin/passwd /usr/bin/sudo

options makes the folder read-only gives files root privileges only the file owner, directory owner or root may delete encrypts files automatically explain the sticky bit prevents deleting or renaming other people's files in a world-writable folder. : { `ls -l` shows `-rwsr--r--`. what does it mean? options setuid is set but the owner has no execute permission setgid is set and the group can execute the file has the sticky bit the file is encrypted explain an uppercase `s` means the bit is set but the underlying x permission is missing; usually a misconfiguration. : { which command lists all setuid files on the system? options `ls -l /etc/setuid` `chmod -r u+s /` `find / -perm 4755 -name suid` `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null` explain `-perm -4000` finds files with the setuid bit set; `2>/dev/null` hides permission errors. summary in four-digit modes the leading digit is: setuid `4`, setgid `2`, sticky `1`; they add up. `s`/`t` in the x slot, uppercase `s`/`t` means x is missing. setuid runs a file with the owner's privileges (`passwd`); the kernel ignores it on scripts; a wrong setuid-root is a serious vulnerability. setgid folder: new files get the folder's group; team recipe `chgrp devs` + `chmod 2775` + `umask 002`. sticky folder (`/tmp`, `1777`): only the owner or root deletes. audit setuid files regularly with `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null`. glossary term setuid meaning on executables, the program runs with the owner's privileges; octal `4000`. term setgid meaning on files, run with group privileges; on directories, pass the group to new entries; `2000`. term sticky bit meaning on directories, only the file/directory owner or root may delete; `1000`. term privilege escalation meaning a normal user gaining root-like privileges without permission. term umask meaning a mask that decides which permission bits are removed from new files. term nosuid meaning mount option; setuid/setgid are ignored on that file system.

5.1.title: Process Basics
objectives: You explain what a process is, what PID and PPID mean and why PID 1 is special.
You list processes with ps aux, ps -ef and ps -o, and find them with pgrep.
You show parent/child relations with pstree and ps --forest and look into /proc/<pid>.
You recognise process states (R, S, D, T, Z) and know what a zombie is and what it is not.
5.1.text:
title process basics lead look at the running system with a microscope: what a process is, who started it and what state it is in. objectives you explain what a process is, what pid and ppid mean and why pid 1 is special. you list processes with ps aux, ps -ef and ps -o, and find them with pgrep. you show parent/child relations with pstree and ps --forest and look into /proc/<pid>. you recognise process states (r, s, d, t, z) and know what a zombie is and what it is not. sections concept title what is a process? body a program on disk (for example `bash`) is just a file. when you start it, the kernel loads it into memory and it becomes a **process**. hundreds of processes run at the same time. every process has a unique number, the **pid**. it also knows who started it: the **ppid** (parent pid). processes give birth to each other: your shell starts `ps`, `ps` is the child of the shell. at the top is **pid 1**, the first process of the system, today usually `systemd`. all others descend from it. the shell knows its own pid: `$$`. in the simulator it always prints 4242. commands cmd echo $$ what prints the pid of the current shell. where in scripts and when you need your own pid, e.g. for /proc/$$. why you can inspect your own process without searching for it. example echo $$ cmd what lists only the processes of your current terminal. where for a quick look: normally just `bash` and `ps` itself. why the smallest snapshot; shows pid, terminal, cpu time and command. example }],  `ps` is a **snapshot**, not a live view. for a live view you use `top` (next modules). title reading with ps body `ps` exists in two styles. `ps aux` is **bsd style** (no dash): all users, with %cpu and %mem. `ps -ef` is **unix style** (with dash): all processes with a **ppid** column. `ps aux` has no ppid column; for relations use `ps -ef` or `-o`. with `-o` you choose the columns yourself: `ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd`. this is the cleanest way for scripts and the best way to read exactly what you need. on rocky/alma/ubuntu `ps` is already installed (package `procps` / `procps-ng`). commands cmd ps aux what all processes of all users, with user, %cpu, %mem, state and command. where when you ask who is using the system and how much. why most common overview; combine with `grep` or `sort`. example ps aux | head -n 10 nosim cmd ps -ef what all processes in unix format, including the ppid column. where when you want to know who the parent is. why shows relations; ppid 1 means the process hangs directly under init/systemd. example ps -ef | head -n 10 nosim cmd ps -o what shows exactly the columns you list. where in scripts and for focused questions. why short, readable and stable output. example ps -o pid,ppid,stat,comm cmd ps -p what shows only the process with the given pid. where when you know the pid and want to check it. why no grep needed; combine with `-o`. example ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd -p $$ tip `ps aux | grep sshd` also finds the grep process itself. `pgrep` avoids that. warn never rely on column positions in `ps aux` for the command field: it contains spaces. use `ps -o` in scripts. tree title trees and searching: pstree and pgrep body `pstree` draws the family tree: systemd at the root, then services, your ssh session, your shell and your commands. `ps -ef --forest` shows the same with a ppid column. `pgrep` searches by name and prints only pids. it is made for scripts: `pgrep -x sshd` prints the pid if `sshd` runs and exits with 1 if not. `pstree` comes from the package `psmisc`, which is not always installed. rocky/alma: `sudo dnf install psmisc`. debian/ubuntu: `sudo apt install psmisc`. `pgrep` belongs to procps and is always there. commands cmd pstree -p what shows the process tree with pids. where to understand who started whom. why at a glance: everything hangs under pid 1 (systemd). example pstree -p | head -n 15 nosim cmd ps -ef --forest what the ps list in tree form with ppid. where when psmisc is not installed. why a tree plus all columns of `ps -ef`. example ps -ef --forest | head -n 20 nosim cmd pgrep -l what finds processes by name and prints pid and name. where in scripts, to check whether a service runs. why cleaner than `ps | grep`; `-x` matches the exact name. example pgrep -l sshd nosim cmd pgrep -a what prints pid and the complete command line. where when several processes have the same name. why you see the arguments and can pick the right pid. example pgrep -a bash nosim tip package install: rocky `sudo dnf install psmisc`, ubuntu `sudo apt install psmisc`. proc title inside /proc/<pid> body `/proc` is a **virtual filesystem**: it does not live on disk, the kernel generates it. every process has a directory `/proc/<pid>/`. that is the source `ps` itself reads from. useful files: `status` (name, state, pid, ppid, uid), `exe` (link to the program), `cwd` (working directory), `fd/` (open files), `cmdline` (the command line). as a normal user you can read your own processes; for others some files are restricted. `/proc/self` always means the process that reads it. so `cat /proc/self/status` shows the status of `cat`. commands cmd cat /proc/$$/status what shows name, state, pid, ppid and uid of your shell. where for details that ps does not show. why the raw source: state and ppid lines tell the story. example head -n 9 /proc/$$/status nosim cmd ls -l /proc/$$/exe what a link to the executable of the process. where when you ask which binary really runs. why uncovers renamed or deleted programs. example ls -l /proc/$$/exe nosim cmd ls /proc/$$/fd what lists the open file descriptors (0, 1, 2 ...). where when debugging open files. why 0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr; more means open files. example ls -l /proc/$$/fd nosim tip `cat /proc/self/status` is a quick test that /proc works, also in wsl. states title states, zombies and signals body the **stat** column shows the state: `r` running, `s` sleeping (waiting, interruptible), `d` uninterruptible sleep (usually waiting for disk/network; cannot be killed), `t` stopped (ctrl+z), `z` **zombie**. extra letters: `s` session leader, `+` foreground, `<` high priority. a **zombie** is a process that has already finished. only its entry in the process table remains, because the parent has not yet read the exit status (`wait`). a zombie uses no cpu and almost no memory, and **you cannot kill it, not even with `kill -9`**, because it is already dead. the fix: the parent must collect it, or you stop/restart the parent; then init adopts and reaps the orphan. signals: `kill` sends a signal, default `sigterm` (15, polite request, the program can clean up). `sigkill` (9) cannot be caught; the kernel ends the process immediately without cleanup. **pid 1** is special: signals without a handler are ignored for it, even sigkill from user space. that protects the system from an accidental kill. load average (`uptime`) shows runnable processes over 1/5/15 minutes. read it **relative to the number of cores** (`nproc`): load 4.0 is full on 4 cores and overload on 2. commands cmd ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,cmd what all processes with state and parent. where when looking for zombies (stat z) or stuck processes (d). why pipe to `grep` or `sort` for a quick filter. example ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,cmd | head -n 10 cmd uptime what shows uptime and the load average of 1, 5 and 15 minutes. where as the first look at 'is the server slow?'. why compare the load with the number of cores. example uptime cmd nproc what prints the number of cpu cores. where to read the load average correctly. why load 2.0 is fine on 8 cores and busy on 2. example nproc nosim cmd kill -15 what sends sigterm (polite stop) to a pid. where first choice to end a process. why the program can save data and clean up. example kill -15 4242 nosim cmd kill -9 what sends sigkill; the process is ended immediately. where only if sigterm did not work. why last resort; no cleanup, data can be lost. example kill -9 4242 nosim tip order for stopping: `kill -15`, wait a few seconds, check with `ps -p pid`, and only then `kill -9`. warn check the pid twice before you kill. `pkill name` and `killall name` kill **all** processes with that name, including ones you did not mean. danger do not kill processes you do not know, especially not as root: `kill -9` on `sshd`, `systemd-journald` or a database can lock you out or corrupt data. practise only with your own `sleep` processes. tasks t01 text list the processes of your terminal with `ps`. which two do you see? hint just `ps`, no options. you see `bash` and `ps`. t02 text print the pid of your shell with `echo $$`. hint two dollar signs. in the simulator it is always 4242. t03 text run the all-process view in bsd style: `ps aux`. hint no dash for `aux`. (`ps -ef` is accepted too.) t04 text choose your columns with `ps -o pid,ppid,comm`. hint columns separated by commas, no spaces. t05 text read only the header line of the snapshot with `head -n 1 ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`. which column is the cpu usage? hint `ps_snapshot.txt` is a saved `ps aux` output in `~/lab`. the column is %cpu. t06 text show all processes of alice in the snapshot: `grep alice ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`. which program is busy? hint look at the %cpu column; the process is `python3 worker.py`. t07 text count the processes of alice: `grep alice ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt | wc -l`. hint `wc -l` counts lines after the pipe. (`wc` → module 2.6; `|` → module 3.2.) t08 text find the zombie in the snapshot with `grep defunct ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`. which pid and which user? hint zombies show stat `z` and `<defunct>`. it is pid 1701 of bob. t09 text `~/lab/proc_status.txt` is a copy of `/proc/1701/status`. find the parent: `grep ppid ~/lab/proc_status.txt`. hint ppid is the pid of the parent; you must deal with it, not with the zombie. t10 text predict first: how many lines does `ps | wc -l` print? then run it to verify. hint header plus bash plus ps = 3. t11 text predict first: is the 1-minute load average low? run `uptime` to verify. remember: read load relative to `nproc`. hint look at the three numbers after 'load average:'. t12 text sort the snapshot by cpu, highest first, and show two lines: `sort -k3 -nr ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt | head -n 2`. hint `-k3` = third column, `-n` numeric, `-r` reverse. (`sort` → module 3.5.) t13 text mini project: write the pids of all root processes into `~/lab/root_pids.txt`. filter with `grep ^root`, squeeze spaces with `tr -s ' '`, pick column 2 with `cut -d' ' -f2`, redirect with `>`. hint one pipe: `grep ^root ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt | tr -s ' ' | cut -d' ' -f2 > ~/lab/root_pids.txt`. (`grep` → module 3.4; `tr/cut` → module 3.5; `>` → module 3.2.) t14 text debug: `~/lab/fix.txt` says `kill -9 1701`. that is wrong, a zombie cannot be killed. overwrite the file with the better command: signal the parent, e.g. `kill -s sigchld 1500`. hint `echo \  > ~/lab/fix.txt`. the parent pid is 1500 (see t09). (`>` → module 3.2.) t15 text challenge: find the process with the highest cpu usage in the snapshot using `sort`. write the **polite** stop command for it into `~/lab/decision.txt` (do not run it). hint it is pid 1620. polite means signal 15: `echo \  > ~/lab/decision.txt`. (`>` → module 3.2.) t16 text ticket #5110 — the server is slow. alice's job is suspected. write the user, pid and command of the busiest process into `~/lab/report.txt`. hint use `sort` or `grep` on the snapshot; then `echo \  > ~/lab/report.txt`. (`sort/grep` → module 3.4/3.5; `>` → module 3.2.) t17 text save your shell pid to a file: `echo $$ > ~/lab/mypid.txt`. hint `>` writes the output of `echo` into the file. (`>` → module 3.2.) : { run these steps on your own vm (ubuntu, rocky, alma or wsl). steps 1 to 4 only read. step 5 stops a process: take a **snapshot** first and only touch your own `sleep` process. tasks v01 title your own process text print the pid of your shell, then show its pid, ppid and state with ps. paste the output. blocks cmd echo $$
ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd -p $$ expected 2100
    pid    ppid stat cmd
   2100    2050 ss   -bash differs the numbers differ on your system; `ppid` must be in the header. in a terminal started via ssh the parent is `sshd`, in a desktop terminal it is the terminal program. v02 title ps aux and ps -ef text compare both styles. which one has a ppid column? blocks cmd ps aux | head -n 5
ps -ef | head -n 5 expected user  pid %cpu %mem ... command
root    1  0.0  0.3 ... /usr/lib/systemd/systemd
uid   pid  ppid  c stime tty time cmd
root    1     0  0 08:00 ?   00:00:02 /usr/lib/systemd/systemd differs on wsl1 or in a container pid 1 may be `init` or something else. only `ps -ef` has ppid; `ps aux` has %cpu and %mem. v03 title process tree text install `psmisc` if needed and look at the tree. who is at the root? paste the first lines. blocks cmd # rocky/alma: sudo dnf install -y psmisc
# ubuntu/debian: sudo apt install -y psmisc
pstree -p | head -n 8
ps -ef --forest | head -n 15 expected systemd(1)-+-sshd(412)---sshd(2050)---sshd(2090)---bash(2100)-+-pstree(2200)
           |-crond(650)
... differs `pstree: command not found` means psmisc is not installed; use the install line above. on wsl you may see `init(1)` or `sessionleader` instead of systemd. v04 title look into /proc text read the status of your shell directly from /proc and show where the program lives. blocks cmd head -n 9 /proc/$$/status
ls -l /proc/$$/exe
ls -l /proc/$$/fd expected name:	bash
umask:	0022
state:	s (sleeping)
...
ppid:	2050
...
lrwxrwxrwx 1 student student 0 ... /proc/2100/exe -> /usr/bin/bash differs the `name:`, `state:` and `ppid:` lines must exist; the order of other lines can differ. `exe` may show `/bin/bash` on some systems (a link to /usr/bin). v05 title start and stop a process safely text **snapshot first.** start your own `sleep` in the background, find it with pgrep, stop it politely with sigterm and check that it is gone. never use `pkill` or `kill -9` on unknown processes. blocks cmd sleep 600 &
pgrep -l sleep
kill -15 $!
sleep 1
pgrep -l sleep || echo gone expected [1] 2300
2300 sleep
[1]+  terminated   sleep 600
gone differs `$!` is the pid of the last background process. if `pgrep` still prints a line, another `sleep` is running; check with `pgrep -a sleep` before you kill anything. quiz : { which pid has the first process of a linux system (today usually systemd)? options 100 explain pid 1 is started by the kernel; all other processes descend from it. it also ignores signals it has no handler for, even sigkill from user space. : { what is true for a zombie process (stat z)? options it uses a lot of cpu it waits for disk i/o it is finished; the parent has not collected the exit status, and `kill -9` does not help it was stopped with ctrl+z explain a zombie is already dead; only its table entry remains. the parent must call wait, or you restart the parent. : { what does `$$` mean in the shell? options the pid of the current shell the pid of the last background job the exit code of the last command the number of processes explain `$$` is the shell's own pid. the last background pid is `$!`, the exit code is `$?`. : { which command shows a ppid column by default? options ps aux uptime ps -ef explain `ps -ef` (unix style) shows ppid. `ps aux` (bsd style) does not; for it use `ps -o pid,ppid,...`. summary a process is a running program with a pid; its parent has the ppid; pid 1 (systemd) is the ancestor of all. `ps aux` (bsd) shows cpu/mem, `ps -ef` shows ppid, `ps -o` chooses columns, `pgrep` finds by name. `pstree` (package psmisc) and `ps -ef --forest` show the tree; `/proc/<pid>` is where the kernel exposes the details. a zombie (z) is dead and cannot be killed; fix the parent. use `kill -15` first, `kill -9` last, never on unknown processes. read the load average relative to `nproc`. glossary term process meaning a running instance of a program with its own pid and memory. term pid / ppid meaning process id and the id of its parent process. term zombie meaning a finished process whose exit status has not yet been collected by its parent (stat z). term signal meaning a message to a process, e.g. sigterm (15) or sigkill (9). term /proc meaning virtual filesystem through which the kernel exposes process and system information. term load average meaning average number of runnable processes over 1, 5 and 15 minutes; read it relative to the cpu cores.

5.2.title: Resource Monitoring
objectives: You read the load average relative to the number of CPU cores (nproc).
You tell free memory from available memory and understand buff/cache.
You check disk usage with df and du and find big folders.
You find the top CPU and memory consumers with top, htop and ps.
5.2.text:
title resource monitoring lead read cpu, load, memory and disk with uptime, free, df, top and friends, and find out what is slowing the system down. objectives you read the load average relative to the number of cpu cores (nproc). you tell free memory from available memory and understand buff/cache. you check disk usage with df and du and find big folders. you find the top cpu and memory consumers with top, htop and ps. sections load title load and cpu: uptime, nproc, lscpu body when a server feels slow, look at the **load average** first. `uptime` shows three numbers: the average load of the last **1, 5 and 15 minutes**. the same values live in `/proc/loadavg`. a load number alone means nothing. read it **relative to the number of cores** (`nproc`). on a 4-core machine a load of 4.0 means fully used, 8.0 means processes are waiting in line (saturation). rule of thumb: load below the core count is fine, load above it means overload. compare the three values: 1 min higher than 15 min means the load is rising now; 1 min lower than 15 min means it is calming down. commands cmd uptime what shows the time, how long the system has been up, logged-in users and the load average (1, 5, 15 min). where as the very first look at a slow server. why one line tells you if the machine is busy and in which direction it is going. example uptime cmd nproc what prints the number of available cpu cores (threads). where together with uptime to judge the load. why load 4.0 is fine on 8 cores but saturated on 2 cores. example nproc nosim cmd lscpu what shows cpu details: model, sockets, cores, threads, mhz. where when you need to know what hardware the vm or server really has. why confirms how many cores you have and whether they are virtual. example lscpu nosim cmd cat /proc/loadavg what raw load data: three load values, running/total tasks and the last pid. where in scripts, or when uptime is not installed. why it is the source that uptime and top read from. example cat /proc/loadavg nosim tip quick check: if the first load value divided by `nproc` is above 1, the cpu is saturated. memory title memory: free, /proc/meminfo, vmstat body `free -h` shows ram and swap in readable units. do not panic about a small **free** value: linux uses unused ram as cache (**buff/cache**) and gives it back when programs need it. the column that matters is **available**: it estimates how much memory new programs can get without swapping. low *available* plus heavy swap use means real memory shortage. details are in `/proc/meminfo` (`memtotal`, `memfree`, `memavailable`). `vmstat` shows memory, swap, i/o and cpu in one table. columns `si`/`so` (swap in/out) above zero for a long time and a high `wa` (waiting for i/o) are warning signs. commands cmd free -h what shows total, used, free, shared, buff/cache and available ram and swap in human-readable units. where when the system is slow and you suspect full ram. why looking at available instead of free prevents false alarms. example free -h cmd cat /proc/meminfo what prints the detailed kernel memory statistics. where for scripts or when you need exact values like memavailable or swapfree. why it is the source behind free. example grep memavailable /proc/meminfo nosim cmd vmstat 1 5 what prints a cpu, memory, swap and i/o line every second, five times. where to see trends over a few seconds instead of one snapshot. why shows swapping (si/so) and i/o wait (wa) that top hides at first glance. example vmstat 1 5 nosim tip ignore the first line of `vmstat`; it shows averages since boot. the following lines are live. disk title disk: df, du, iostat body a full disk causes strange errors: services crash, logs cannot be written. `df -h` shows usage per filesystem, `du` shows which folder uses the space. workflow: `df -h` finds the full filesystem, then `du -sh /var/*` or `du -h /var | sort -h | tail` finds the big folders. `sort -h` understands sizes like 4k, 12m, 3g. `iostat` comes from the **sysstat** package and shows disk activity. high `%util` and `await` mean the disk is the bottleneck. commands cmd df -h what shows size, used, available and percentage per mounted filesystem. where as the first check for 'no space left on device'. why you see which mount point is nearly full (use%). example df -h cmd du -sh what shows the total size of a folder (-s summary, -h readable). where to measure a single folder such as your home or /var/log. why answers 'how big is this?' with one line. example du -sh ~/documents nosim cmd du -h | sort -h what lists sizes of all subfolders, sorted from small to large. where to find the biggest folders; add `| tail -n 5` for the top five. why finds the space hog quickly. example du -h /var/log | sort -h | tail -n 5 nosim cmd iostat -x 1 3 what extended disk statistics every second, three times (needs the sysstat package). where when the system is slow but cpu and ram look fine. why shows whether the disk is saturated (%util, await). example iostat -x 1 3 nosim tip install sysstat: ubuntu/debian `sudo apt install sysstat`, rocky/alma `sudo dnf install sysstat`. warn `du` on `/` can run for minutes and load the disk. limit it to one folder, for example `du -h /var | sort -h | tail`. procs title processes: top, htop, ps body `top` is the live task manager of the terminal. the header shows load, tasks, cpu and memory; below is the process list. in `top`: `p` sorts by cpu, `m` by memory, `q` quits. `htop` is the colourful, easier version. it is not installed by default. ubuntu/debian: `sudo apt install htop`. on rocky/alma it lives in the **epel** repository: first `sudo dnf install epel-release`, then `sudo dnf install htop`. for scripts and logs use batch mode: `top -b -n 1` prints one snapshot and exits. `ps aux --sort=-%mem | head` lists the top memory consumers, `--sort=-%cpu` the top cpu consumers (the minus means descending). commands cmd top what live view of load, cpu, memory and processes; refreshes every 3 seconds. where to see right now who is using resources. why finds the pid of the problem process. example top nosim cmd top -b -n 1 what batch mode: prints one snapshot and exits. where in scripts, tickets and when piping to head or grep. why you can save or filter the output, for example `top -b -n 1 | head -n 15`. example top -b -n 1 | head -n 15 nosim cmd htop what interactive process viewer with colours, bars and mouse support. where daily work on servers and vms. why easier to read and to sort than top. example htop nosim cmd ps aux --sort=-%mem | head what lists processes sorted by memory use, highest first, first 10 lines. where when ram is nearly full and you look for the culprit. why shows user, pid, %cpu, %mem and command in a copyable list. example ps aux --sort=-%mem | head nosim cmd ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head what lists processes sorted by cpu use, highest first. where when the load is high. why finds the cpu hog without an interactive screen. example ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head nosim tip in `top` press `1` to see every core separately and `c` to see full command lines. triage title triage: a fixed order body when a ticket says 'the server is slow', follow the same order each time: **1.** `uptime` and `nproc` (load vs cores), **2.** `free -h` (available memory, swap), **3.** `df -h` (full disk), **4.** `top` or `ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head` (who is the culprit), **5.** `vmstat 1 5` / `iostat -x` (swap or disk bottleneck). decide: high load and high `us` cpu means a cpu problem. high load with low cpu but high `wa` means disk or network i/o. low available memory and swap activity means a ram problem. to practise on your vm you need load. use a time limit: `timeout 30 yes > /dev/null &` starts one cpu hog that stops after 30 seconds. see the vm section. tip write down the numbers before you change anything. a ticket answer like 'load 4.5 on 2 cores, python3 uses 85% cpu' is worth more than 'it is slow'. warn load generators such as `yes > /dev/null &` or `stress-ng` run until stopped. always use `timeout` and clean up with `pkill yes` afterwards. danger never start a load generator or kill processes on a production server. practise only on your own vm, and take a snapshot first. tasks t01 text show uptime and the load average with `uptime`. hint three numbers after 'load average:' are 1, 5 and 15 minutes. t02 text show memory in readable units with `free -h`. find the `available` column. hint -h means human-readable. t03 text show the disk usage of all filesystems with `df -h`. hint look at the use% column. t04 text find where the `free` program lives with `which free`. hint usually /usr/bin/free. t05 text the file `~/lab/loadavg.txt` is a copy of `/proc/loadavg`. show it with `cat ~/lab/loadavg.txt`. hint the first three numbers are the 1, 5 and 15 minute load. t06 text the machine has the number of cores in `~/lab/cores.txt`. read it with `cat ~/lab/cores.txt`, compare it with the 1-minute load 4.52, and write your verdict (`overloaded` or `ok`) into `~/lab/load_verdict.txt` with `echo`. hint load 4.52 on 2 cores is above the core count: `echo overloaded > ~/lab/load_verdict.txt`. t07 text in `~/lab/meminfo.txt` find the line `memavailable` with `grep memavailable ~/lab/meminfo.txt`. hint memavailable is the number that matters, not memfree. t08 text in `~/lab/top_snapshot.txt` show the cpu line with `grep cpu ~/lab/top_snapshot.txt`. hint `us` is user time, `wa` is i/o wait, `id` is idle. t09 text predict: which value will `free -h | grep mem` show in the `available` column? think first, then run it. hint look at the last column of the mem line. t10 text predict: how many lines does `grep -c java ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt` print? think first, then run it. hint -c counts matching lines. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t11 text predict: what does `cut -d ' ' -f 1 ~/lab/loadavg.txt` print? think first, then run it. hint -d sets the separator, -f 1 is the first field. (`cut` → module 3.5.) t12 text find the top cpu consumers in the snapshot: `sort -k3 -nr ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt | head -n 3`. which process is first? hint -k3 is the %cpu column, -n numeric, -r descending. (`sort` → module 3.5.) t13 text mini: save the top 2 memory consumers of `~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt` into `~/lab/top_mem.txt`. sort by column 4 with `sort -k4 -nr`, take two lines with `head -n 2` and redirect with `>`. hint `sort -k4 -nr ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt | head -n 2 > ~/lab/top_mem.txt` (`sort/head` → module 3.5/3.2; `>` → module 3.2.) t14 text debug: `~/lab/monitor_cmds.txt` lists the wrong commands (`nprocs` does not exist and `free -m` is not human-readable). rewrite the file with `printf` so it contains `cores: nproc`, `memory: free -h` and `disk: df -h`, one per line. hint `printf 'cores: nproc\nmemory: free -h\ndisk: df -h\n' > ~/lab/monitor_cmds.txt` (`>` → module 3.2.) t15 text mini: `~/lab/du_report.txt` has sizes in kb. save the 3 biggest entries into `~/lab/biggest.txt` with `sort -nr`, `head -n 3` and `>`. hint `sort -nr ~/lab/du_report.txt | head -n 3 > ~/lab/biggest.txt` (`sort/head` → module 3.5/3.2; `>` → module 3.2.) t16 text challenge: build `~/lab/report.txt` with three parts: the 1-minute load from `~/lab/loadavg.txt` (use `cut`), the `memavailable` line from `~/lab/meminfo.txt` (use `grep`, append with `>>`) and your verdict `overloaded` (use `echo`, append). hint the first command uses `>`, the others `>>`, so nothing is overwritten. (`>/>>` → module 3.2.) t17 text ticket #5201 — the server linux-lab is very slow. in `~/lab/top_snapshot.txt` is the output of `top -b -n 1`. find the process with the highest cpu use and write its name and its user into `~/lab/culprit.txt`. hint look at the first process line with `head -n 9 ~/lab/top_snapshot.txt`, then `echo \  > ~/lab/culprit.txt`. (`>` → module 3.2.) quiz : { which memory value tells you how much ram new programs can really get? options free shared available buff/cache explain free is only unused ram. linux also uses ram as cache; available includes the part it can give back, so it is the right value. : { a 4-core machine shows a 1-minute load of 8.0. what does that mean? options everything is fine the cpu is saturated: processes wait in line the disk is full the system has just started explain load is read relative to the cores. load 8 on 4 cores means twice as many runnable tasks as cores. : { how do you install htop on rocky linux? options sudo apt install htop sudo dnf install htop directly, always works sudo yum remove htop sudo dnf install epel-release, then sudo dnf install htop explain on the rhel family htop is in the epel repository, so enable epel first. apt is for debian/ubuntu. : { which command lists the top memory consumers? options ps aux --sort=-%mem | head df -h uptime nproc explain ps with --sort=-%mem sorts by memory descending; head shows the first lines. summary read the load average (1/5/15 min) relative to `nproc`; load above the core count means saturation. `free -h`: look at available, not free; buff/cache is reusable. `df -h` finds the full filesystem, `du -sh` and `du -h | sort -h` the big folders. `top`, `htop` (epel on rocky/alma), `top -b -n 1` and `ps aux --sort=-%mem | head` find the culprit. `vmstat` and `iostat` (sysstat) reveal swap and disk bottlenecks. test load only on your own vm, with `timeout`, after a snapshot. glossary term load average meaning average number of tasks running or waiting for cpu/i-o over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. term saturation meaning load is higher than the core count; work waits in a queue. term buff/cache meaning ram used for file caches; the kernel frees it when needed. term available meaning estimate of memory that new programs can use without swapping. term swap meaning disk space used as an emergency extension of ram; slow. term epel meaning extra packages for enterprise linux: additional repository for rhel, rocky and alma. term i/o wait (wa) meaning share of time the cpu waits for disk or network. : { run these on your own vm (ubuntu, rocky, alma or wsl). monitoring commands are harmless; only the last task creates load. take a snapshot before it. tasks v01 title load and cores text show the load average and the number of cores. is the 1-minute load below the core count? paste the output of `uptime`. blocks cmd uptime
nproc

5.3.title: Process Control
objectives: You explain that `kill` sends signals and distinguish SIGTERM from SIGKILL.
You verify a PID and command line before targeting a process.
You understand `pkill`, `nice`, `renice`, and their permission limits.
sol: echo 'verify PID; send SIGTERM; wait; use SIGKILL only if needed' > ~/lab/escalation_plan.txt
echo 'PID 2210 is python3; inspect it and request SIGTERM first' > ~/lab/ticket_5301.txt
echo 'Mistake: pkill -f with a short pattern can match unrelated processes' > ~/lab/pitfalls_5301.txt
5.3.text:
title process control lead stop processes safely with signals, target them by pid or name, and adjust cpu priority. objectives you explain that `kill` sends signals and distinguish sigterm from sigkill. you verify a pid and command line before targeting a process. you understand `pkill`, `nice`, `renice`, and their permission limits. sections signals title signals: kill, sigterm, and sigkill body `kill pid` sends **sigterm (15)** by default. it gives the process a chance to shut down cleanly and save data. if it does not respond, **sigkill (9)** is the last resort; a process cannot catch or ignore it. `kill` sends a signal; it does not always mean “kill.” verify the pid and command with `ps` or `pgrep` first. in particular, `kill -9` and targeting multiple processes can cause data loss. commands cmd kill -term pid what sends sigterm to the specified pid. where when closing an application or stopping it cleanly. why it gives the process a chance to clean up and save data. example kill -term 2210 nosim cmd kill -kill pid what immediately terminates the process through the kernel. where only as a last resort when sigterm does not work. why the process cannot catch it; unsaved work may be lost. example kill -kill 2210 nosim tip name the signal explicitly: `kill -term pid`. then check with `ps -p pid` to see whether the process exited. warn do not signal a process on a production server or under a process manager without verifying its pid. never target pid 1 or an unknown system process. target title find and target processes by name body `ps` gives you a process snapshot; `pgrep` searches for pids by name. `pkill` sends signals to matching processes. check `pgrep -a` first because a name match may affect more processes than expected. `pkill -term -x worker` targets only exact process-name matches. use `-f` to match the full command line only when needed; it carries a higher risk of matching too broadly. commands cmd pgrep -a -x worker what lists the pid and command for processes named exactly worker. where before sending a signal to verify the target. why it reduces the chance of targeting the wrong pid or a similarly named process. example pgrep -a -x sleep nosim cmd pkill -term -x worker what sends sigterm to processes named exactly worker. where when stopping a verified group of processes. why it requests a graceful shutdown without entering each pid. example pkill -term -x sleep nosim tip run the same match with `pgrep -a` before using `pkill` so you can review every target. danger `pkill -f` matches any part of a command line. do not use it with a short or generic pattern. priority title cpu priority: nice and renice body the nice range is **-20 to 19**: a higher value means a lower cpu priority. regular users can lower the priority of their own processes; raising it usually requires administrator privileges. `nice` starts a new command with a chosen value; `renice` changes the value of a running process. this affects cpu scheduling, but does not limit memory or cpu usage. commands cmd nice -n 10 command what starts a new command with nice value 10. where for background work such as backups. why it lets interactive work get cpu time more easily. example nice -n 10 sleep 60 nosim cmd renice 10 -p pid what sets a running process's nice value to 10. where when lowering the priority of a running background task. why it changes cpu priority without restarting the process. example renice 10 -p 2210 nosim tip nice value and process state are different; inspect them separately with `ps -o pid,ni,stat,comm -p pid`. tasks t01 text use `grep` to find user alice's processes in `~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`. hint the file starts with a `user` column; try `grep alice ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t02 text find the pid of the `python3` process in the snapshot. hint in the line from `grep python3 ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`, the second field is the pid. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t03 text predict how many lines contain `python3`, then verify with `grep -c`. hint `grep -c python3 ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt` counts matching lines. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t04 text save a graceful shutdown plan in `~/lab/term_plan.txt`: use `kill -term` for pid 2210. hint `echo 'kill -term 2210' > ~/lab/term_plan.txt` (`>` → module 3.2.) t05 text write an example in `~/lab/priority_plan.txt` that starts a backup with lower cpu priority. hint use the form `nice -n 10 ./backup.sh`. t06 text add pid verification and a wait after sigterm; mention sigkill only as a last resort. hint save your plan to `~/lab/escalation_plan.txt`. t07 text for ticket #5301, write a short note that pid 2210 is `python3` and sigterm should be tried first. hint write the note to `~/lab/ticket_5301.txt`. (`>` → module 3.2.) t08 text find the `java` line in `~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`; what is its pid? hint try `grep java ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t09 text predict: on how many lines does `alice` appear? then verify with `grep -c`. hint try `grep -c alice ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t10 text find the pid of the `bash` process. hint `grep bash ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`; the second field is the pid. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t11 text error prevention: write the step of checking matches with `pgrep -a` before `pkill` into `~/lab/pkill_check.txt`. hint `echo '...' > ~/lab/pkill_check.txt`; include `pgrep -a` in the text. (`>` → module 3.2.) t12 text write the `renice` command that sets pid 2210 to nice value 10 into `~/lab/renice_plan.txt`. hint format: `renice 10 -p pid`. (`>` → module 3.2.) t13 text common mistake: why is `pkill -f` risky? write a short note for ticket #5301 into `~/lab/pitfalls_5301.txt`. hint mention `pkill -f` in the note. (`>` → module 3.2.) : { run these commands only in your own test vm. do not signal an arbitrary pid; verify the process name and pid. tasks v01 title start a controlled process text start a short-lived test process, note its pid, and verify it with `ps`. stop it when done. blocks cmd sleep 300 &
echo $!
ps -o pid,ni,comm -p $! expected the pid and sleep command are visible. differs the shell may also print a job number; the pid is on the `echo $!` line. the pid will differ; do not expect a fixed number. v02 title try sigterm first text use the real pid of the test process you just started. send sigterm, wait briefly, and verify that it exited. blocks cmd kill -term pid
sleep 1
ps -p pid || echo 'process stopped' expected process stopped differs replace pid with the number from v01; do not run the literal word `pid`. if the process remains, verify the pid; do not signal another process. v03 title inspect the nice value text start a test process with lower priority, read its ni value in `ps`, and then stop your process. blocks cmd nice -n 10 sleep 60 &
ps -o pid,ni,comm -p $!
kill -term $! expected the ni column shows 10 and the command column shows sleep. differs column headings may be aligned differently by `ps`; the ni value should be 10. stop only the pid started by your shell. quiz : { which signal does `kill pid` send by default? options sigkill sigterm sigstop sighup explain sigterm is the default signal; it asks the process to shut down cleanly. : { when should sigkill be used? options for every application shutdown without checking the pid as a last resort when sigterm fails to change a nice value explain sigkill cannot be caught and leaves no time for cleanup, so use it only as a last resort. : { what happens when the nice value rises from 0 to 10? options cpu priority decreases the process must stop the memory limit increases the process becomes root explain a higher nice value means lower priority in cpu scheduling. : { what should you do before targeting a process with `pkill`? options try pid 1 send sigkill use a broad `pkill -f` pattern verify matches with `pgrep -a` explain reviewing the matches confirms the target and reveals possible side effects. summary `kill` sends sigterm by default; sigkill is a last resort. verify the pid and command with `ps` or `pgrep -a` before sending a signal. `nice` sets priority at launch and `renice` changes it for a running process; higher nice means lower priority. glossary term signal meaning a control notification the kernel sends to a process. term pid meaning the unique process identifier of a running process. term nice meaning a value that affects a process's relative priority in cpu scheduling.

5.4.title: Job Control
objectives: You distinguish foreground, background, and stopped shell jobs.
You manage the current terminal's jobs with `jobs`, `bg`, and `fg`.
You understand what `nohup` does and what it does not replace.
sol: echo 'fg %1; return with Ctrl+Z; kill %1 when finished' >> ~/lab/job_plan.txt
echo 'Check jobs -l; use nohup only if the job must outlive the session' > ~/lab/ticket_5401.txt
echo 'disown -h %2 detaches a job from SIGHUP' > ~/lab/disown_note.txt
echo 'Ctrl+Z stops the job; bg %1 resumes it in the background' > ~/lab/stop_plan.txt
echo 'Mistake: plain job number 2 is not %2; use kill %2 for job 2' > ~/lab/pitfalls_5401.txt
5.4.text:
title job control lead manage shell jobs in the foreground or background, cancel with ctrl+c, pause with ctrl+z, and use nohup when appropriate. objectives you distinguish foreground, background, and stopped shell jobs. you manage the current terminal's jobs with `jobs`, `bg`, and `fg`. you understand what `nohup` does and what it does not replace. sections signals title foreground, ctrl+c, and ctrl+z body a foreground command occupies the terminal. `ctrl+c` usually sends sigint to cancel it; `ctrl+z` sends sigtstp and **pauses** the job. a stopped job is not finished and may still hold resources. adding `&` to the end of a command starts it in the background. that does not make it independent of the terminal; closing the session can still affect it. commands cmd sleep 300 what waits for five minutes in the foreground and keeps the terminal busy. where to safely try how a foreground job behaves. why it demonstrates the difference between ctrl+c and ctrl+z. example sleep 300 nosim cmd sleep 300 & what starts the sleep command in the background. where when you want to keep entering commands in the terminal. why the shell prints a job number and pid. example sleep 300 & nosim tip do not forget a stopped job: find it with `jobs -l` and resume or stop it according to its purpose. jobs title jobs, bg, and fg body `jobs -l` lists jobs only in the current shell session. `bg %1` resumes a job in the background; `fg %1` brings it to the foreground. `%1` is the shell job number from `jobs`, not a pid. a background job may continue writing to the terminal. the shell reports when it finishes. do not guess the job number; check `jobs` first. commands cmd jobs -l what lists the current shell's jobs with their states and pids. where when looking for stopped or background jobs. why you can see the job number and state before choosing the correct job. example jobs -l nosim cmd bg %1 / fg %1 what resumes a selected job in the background or brings it to the foreground. where when resuming a job or reclaiming terminal control. why it changes how the same job interacts with the terminal. example bg %1 nosim tip `jobs` gives the job number; `ps` or `jobs -l` shows the pid. they are not interchangeable. nohup title session independence: nohup body `nohup` starts a command so that it ignores sighup, which can help it continue after a session closes. a common pattern redirects output to a file and starts the command with `&`. `nohup` is not a job monitor or service manager. use `systemd` for long-running production services; use `tmux` or `screen` for interactive work across disconnected ssh sessions. stop test jobs and inspect their output. commands cmd nohup command > job.log 2>&1 & what protects the command from sighup, redirects output to a file, and starts it in the background. where when a short, non-interactive job needs to outlive a session. why terminal output is retained and the shell is freed. example nohup ./backup.sh > backup.log 2>&1 & nosim cmd tail -n 20 job.log what shows the job's most recent output lines. where when checking progress or error messages. why you can inspect the log without bringing the job to the foreground. example tail -n 20 backup.log warn test only in your own vm with a short job. `nohup` does not stop the job automatically; track its pid and log file. tasks t01 text find the state of the `sleep` job in the snapshot. hint `grep sleep ~/lab/jobs_snapshot.txt` should show `stopped`. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t02 text show the current state of the `backup.sh` job. hint the line from `grep backup ~/lab/jobs_snapshot.txt` contains `running`. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t03 text predict how many jobs are stopped in the snapshot, then verify with `grep -c`. hint `grep -c stopped ~/lab/jobs_snapshot.txt` counts them. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t04 text save resuming job 1 with `bg %1` and then checking with `jobs -l` to `~/lab/job_plan.txt`. hint `echo 'bg %1; jobs -l' > ~/lab/job_plan.txt` (`>` → module 3.2.) t05 text add bringing the job to the foreground and cleaning it up when finished to the plan. hint add `fg %1` and `kill %1` to the file. t06 text write a nohup example to `~/lab/persistent_job.txt` that redirects output to `backup.log`. hint `nohup ./backup.sh > backup.log 2>&1 &` t07 text add a `jobs -l` check and a nohup note to ticket #5401 to assess whether the job is tied to the terminal session. hint save the short note in `~/lab/ticket_5401.txt`. (`>` → module 3.2.) t08 text find the `done` job in `~/lab/jobs_snapshot.txt`; what is its command? hint try `grep done ~/lab/jobs_snapshot.txt`. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t09 text predict: how many jobs are `running`? then verify with `grep -c`. hint try `grep -c running ~/lab/jobs_snapshot.txt`. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t10 text find the state of the `report` command. hint try `grep report ~/lab/jobs_snapshot.txt`. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t11 text write a `disown` note so the job does not receive sighup when the session ends into `~/lab/disown_note.txt`. hint include `disown` in the note. (`>` → module 3.2.) t12 text write the steps \  into `~/lab/stop_plan.txt`. hint include `ctrl+z` and `bg`. (`>` → module 3.2.) t13 text common mistake: a job number without `%` is read as a pid. write a note for ticket #5401 into `~/lab/pitfalls_5401.txt`. hint include `kill %2` in the note. (`>` → module 3.2.) : { run the examples in your own test vm. a shell job belongs to that shell session; stop test jobs you no longer need. tasks v01 title stop a job text start `sleep` in the foreground. press `ctrl+z` while it runs, then check the shell job with the command below. blocks cmd sleep 300
# after pressing ctrl+z:
jobs -l expected [1]+ stopped sleep 300 differs the job number may not be 1; use your own `jobs -l` output. make sure your terminal emulator sends ctrl+z to the shell. v02 title background and clean up text first verify the job number with `jobs -l`. replace `%1` in the example with the correct number, resume it in the background, and then clean it up. blocks cmd bg %1
jobs -l
kill %1 expected the job appears as running. differs replace `%1` if your job number is different. `kill %1` signals this shell job; use it only for the test `sleep` job. v03 title a short nohup job text redirect the output of a short command with `nohup`, wait for it to finish, and read the file. blocks cmd nohup sh -c 'sleep 2; echo done' > ~/job-output.txt 2>&1 &
sleep 3
cat ~/job-output.txt expected done differs if the command is still running, wait a few seconds and run `cat ~/job-output.txt` again. if you get a path or permission error, make sure the destination is inside your home directory. quiz : { what does `ctrl+z` do to a running job? options permanently deletes it pauses it starts it as root closes the terminal explain ctrl+z usually sends sigtstp; the job pauses but is not complete. : { what does `%1` mean in `bg %1`? options the shell job number pid 1 one second the nice value explain the percent-prefixed number is the shell job number shown by `jobs`. : { what does `nohup` provide? options turns the job into a systemd service schedules the job automatically limits memory use helps protect against sighup explain nohup starts a command to ignore sighup; it is not a service manager by itself. : { what is the difference between a job number and a pid? options there is no difference only root has job numbers the job number belongs to the shell; the pid belongs to the process a pid exists only for background jobs explain a shell job number belongs to the current session; a pid identifies the system process. summary `ctrl+c` usually cancels a job; `ctrl+z` pauses it. `jobs`, `bg`, and `fg` manage the current shell's jobs; `%n` is a shell job number. `nohup` protects against sighup but does not replace a service manager; redirect output and monitor the job. glossary term foreground meaning an interactive job that owns terminal control. term background job meaning a job running in the shell without terminal control. term sighup meaning a signal processes may receive when a session or terminal connection closes.

5.5.title: Package Management
objectives: You know Debian-family systems use apt/dpkg and RHEL-family systems use dnf/rpm.
You can search, inspect, install, update, and remove packages.
You review changes before installation and protect critical packages.
cmds: sudo apt install package / sudo dnf install package
sudo apt update / sudo dnf check-update
sudo apt remove / sudo dnf remove
sol: echo 'sudo apt update before installing on Debian or Ubuntu' > ~/lab/install_plan.txt
echo 'sudo dnf install cowsay; sudo apt install cowsay' >> ~/lab/install_plan.txt
echo 'Remove only the test package; review the autoremove list before confirming' > ~/lab/cleanup_plan.txt
echo 'Check the distribution; use httpd on RHEL-family systems or apache2 on Debian-family systems' > ~/lab/ticket_5501.txt
echo 'apt search nginx; dnf search nginx' > ~/lab/search_plan.txt
echo 'rpm -qa on RHEL family; dpkg -l on Debian family' > ~/lab/query_plan.txt
echo 'Mistake: -y skips the confirmation; read the package list first' > ~/lab/pitfalls_5501.txt
5.5.text: title package management lead search, install, update, and remove software with your distribution's package manager; distinguish repositories from the installed package database. objectives you know debian-family systems use apt/dpkg and rhel-family systems use dnf/rpm. you can search, inspect, install, update, and remove packages. you review changes before installation and protect critical packages. sections families title distributions and package tools body package managers download software from signed repositories, resolve dependencies, and update the installed package database. ubuntu and debian use `apt` as the high-level tool and `dpkg` for lower-level queries; rocky, alma, and fedora use `dnf` and `rpm`. the package name for the same software can vary by distribution: apache http server is usually `httpd` on the rhel family and `apache2` on the debian family. identify the distribution and correct package name first. commands cmd cat /etc/os-release what shows the distribution name, version, and identifier. where before choosing a package command or service name. why it confirms whether the system is in the debian or rhel family. example cat /etc/os-release cmd apt search / dnf search what searches configured repositories by package name or description. where when you are unsure of the package name. why it reduces the chance of installing the wrong package. example dnf search nginx nosim tip choose `apt` or `dnf` for the system family; do not assume the same command is available everywhere. install title search, install, and update body before installing, inspect the package description and source. `apt update` refreshes package lists on debian-family systems; it does not upgrade packages by itself. `dnf check-update` checks whether updates are available. installing packages and system updates requires administrator privileges. read the confirmation prompt to see which packages will be installed, removed, or updated. cancel if critical, unexpected changes are listed. commands cmd sudo apt install package / sudo dnf install package what installs a repository package and its required dependencies. where after verifying the package name and source. why it keeps the package database consistent instead of placing downloaded files manually. example sudo dnf install cowsay nosim cmd sudo apt update / sudo dnf check-update what refreshes repository package information or checks for updates. where before debian-family installations or when checking for updates. why the package manager uses current repository information. example sudo apt update nosim tip `apt update` refreshes package lists; use `apt upgrade` separately to upgrade installed packages. remove title remove and verify packages body `apt remove` and `dnf remove` may affect dependencies when removing a package. `apt purge` also removes package configuration; `autoremove` finds dependencies that are no longer needed. review the proposed removals carefully. `dpkg -l` or `rpm -qa` lists installed packages. these lower-level tools are useful for queries, not installation; use `apt` or `dnf` to install or remove packages. commands cmd sudo apt remove / sudo dnf remove what removes a package through the package manager. where when a test package is no longer needed. why it updates the package database and dependencies in a controlled way. example sudo apt remove cowsay nosim cmd dpkg -l / rpm -qa what queries the list of installed packages. where when verifying whether a package is installed. why it reports the installation state from the package database. example rpm -qa | grep cowsay nosim warn installing or removing packages changes the system. practise only in your own vm; do not remove critical packages such as `kernel`, `systemd`, ssh, or networking tools. review the confirmation list. tasks t01 text find the high-level package manager for the rhel family in the package notes. hint the line from `grep rhel ~/lab/package_notes.txt` contains `dnf`. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t02 text find the high-level package manager for ubuntu/debian. hint the line from `grep ubuntu ~/lab/package_notes.txt` contains `apt`. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t03 text predict how many lines contain `package`, then verify with `grep -c`. hint `grep -c package ~/lab/package_notes.txt` (`grep` → module 3.4.) t04 text write in `~/lab/install_plan.txt` that ubuntu/debian should refresh repository lists before installing. hint record the command `sudo apt update`. (`>` → module 3.2.) t05 text add the `cowsay` installation command for both the rhel and debian families to your plan. hint `sudo dnf install cowsay` and `sudo apt install cowsay`. t06 text write a cleanup plan reminding you to review `autoremove` suggestions before removing a test package. hint save the note in `~/lab/cleanup_plan.txt`. t07 text for ticket #5501, note that you should identify the distribution and that the web package is named `httpd` or `apache2` depending on the family. hint write the note to `~/lab/ticket_5501.txt`. (`>` → module 3.2.) t08 text find the `debian` line in `~/lab/package_notes.txt`; what is the web package called? hint try `grep debian ~/lab/package_notes.txt`. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t09 text predict: on how many lines does `rhel` appear? then verify with `grep -c`. hint try `grep -c rhel ~/lab/package_notes.txt`.
