(`>` → module 3.2.) t12 text write the commands for listing installed packages (`rpm -qa`, `dpkg -l`) into `~/lab/query_plan.txt`. hint include `rpm -qa` in the note. (`>` → module 3.2.) t13 text common mistake: why should `-y` be used carefully? write a note for ticket #5501 into `~/lab/pitfalls_5501.txt`. hint include `-y` in the note. (`>` → module 3.2.) : { installing and removing packages changes your system. work only in your own test vm, never on a production system, and always read confirmation prompts. tasks v01 title identify the distribution text check the distribution identifier and which package tools are available. blocks cmd cat /etc/os-release\ncommand -v apt\ndnf --version expected the id= line identifies the distribution; apt or dnf is available for your family. differs you may not have both package managers; use the one for your distribution. id or id_like helps identify the distribution family. v02 title inspect a package before installing text first display information about the `cowsay` package. run only the command appropriate for your distribution. blocks cmd apt-cache policy cowsay expected candidate or package version cmd dnf info cowsay expected available packages or package information differs use apt-cache on debian/ubuntu and dnf on rocky/alma/fedora. if the package is not found, package lists may be stale or an enabled repository may not contain it. v03 title install a test package text install the small `cowsay` package only in your own test vm, using the command for your distribution. review the changes in the confirmation prompt. blocks cmd sudo apt install cowsay expected setting up cowsay or installation complete cmd sudo dnf install cowsay expected complete! or installed: cowsay differs run only one block: apt for debian/ubuntu, dnf for the rhel family. if the package cannot be found, check the repository and package name before proceeding. v04 title remove the test package text after the test, remove `cowsay` with the same package manager and verify the result. review the proposed removals before confirming. blocks cmd sudo apt remove cowsay expected removing cowsay or cowsay was removed cmd sudo dnf remove cowsay expected removing: cowsay or complete! differs use only the command for the distribution family where you installed the package. if unexpected important packages are listed, do not confirm; cancel with `n`. quiz : { which high-level package tool is commonly used on ubuntu and debian? options apt dnf rpm systemctl explain `apt` manages repositories and package installations on debian-family systems. : { what is the usual apache http server package name on the rhel family? options apache2 nginx httpd openssh explain it is usually httpd on the rhel family and apache2 on the debian family. : { what does `apt update` do? options upgrades the kernel refreshes package repository lists removes all packages reboots the system explain apt update refreshes local repository indexes; use apt upgrade to upgrade installed packages. : { what should you do at an installation confirmation prompt? options always confirm ignore critical packages press enter without reading the output review packages to be added or removed explain dependency resolution can change other packages; review the list before proceeding. summary ubuntu/debian: apt/dpkg; rocky/alma/fedora: dnf/rpm. verify your distribution and package names first. `apt update` refreshes package lists; installation and upgrades are separate operations. review proposed changes before removal and `autoremove`; protect critical system packages. glossary term repository meaning a software source where a distribution publishes packages and package information. term dependency meaning another package required for a package to install or run. term package manager meaning a tool that installs, updates, and removes packages and their dependencies.

5.6.title: Services and Logs
objectives: You check, start, stop and enable services with systemctl and know the difference between start and enable.
You know the service names on RHEL/Rocky and Debian/Ubuntu (sshd/ssh, httpd/apache2, firewalld/ufw).
You read a unit file ([Unit], [Service], [Install]) and create a custom unit with daemon-reload.
You read logs with journalctl and with classic files in /var/log, and you know logrotate and the persistent journal.
cmds: systemctl is-active sshd && systemctl is-enabled sshd
sol:
printf "sudo cp linux-lab-demo.service /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now linux-lab-demo.service
" > ~/lab/install_steps.txt

printf "systemctl status httpd
journalctl -u httpd -n 50 --no-pager
sudo systemctl enable --now httpd
" > ~/ticket_5610.txt
5.6.text:
title services and logs lead manage services with systemd and systemctl, write a simple unit file, and find the cause of problems in the journal and in /var/log. objectives you check, start, stop and enable services with systemctl and know the difference between start and enable. you know the service names on rhel/rocky and debian/ubuntu (sshd/ssh, httpd/apache2, firewalld/ufw). you read a unit file ([unit], [service], [install]) and create a custom unit with daemon-reload. you read logs with journalctl and with classic files in /var/log, and you know logrotate and the persistent journal. sections systemctl title systemd and systemctl body **systemd** is the first process (pid 1) of almost every modern distribution and manages **units**. the most common types are `service` (a daemon such as sshd), `target` (a group of units, like a run level) and `timer` (a scheduled job, modern cron alternative). `systemctl` is the control tool. **start** runs a service **now**, **enable** only makes it start **at boot**. they are independent: a service can be running but disabled, or enabled but stopped. `enable --now` does both at once. `reload` makes a service re-read its configuration without a restart (not every service supports it); `restart` stops and starts it. the state commands `status`, `is-active` and `is-enabled` only read and are always safe. changing a service needs root, so use `sudo`. all systemctl commands are real-vm only; the built-in terminal cannot run them, so in the simulator you only write the command down. commands cmd systemctl status what shows state, pid, boot setting and the last log lines of a unit. where first step with every service problem. why one command tells you whether it runs, whether it is enabled and what its last messages were. example systemctl status sshd --no-pager nosim cmd systemctl start / stop what starts or stops a service now; the boot setting does not change. where when testing a service or freeing a port. why immediate effect without a reboot. example sudo systemctl start chronyd nosim cmd systemctl restart / reload what restart stops and starts the service; reload only re-reads the configuration. where after editing a config file. why reload keeps connections alive; restart is the fallback. example sudo systemctl reload chronyd nosim cmd systemctl enable / disable what turns the start at boot on or off; the running state does not change. where for services that must always be available. why after a reboot the service comes up again without you. example sudo systemctl enable chronyd nosim cmd systemctl enable --now what enables the service for boot and starts it right away. where when installing a new service. why two steps in one; the most common form. example sudo systemctl enable --now chronyd nosim cmd systemctl is-active / is-enabled what prints only active/inactive or enabled/disabled; the exit code is usable in scripts. where in scripts and quick checks. why short answer, easy to test. example systemctl is-active sshd && systemctl is-enabled sshd nosim cmd systemctl list-units --failed what lists all units that are in failed state. where after a boot or when something is wrong with the system. why a fast overview of what is broken. example systemctl list-units --failed --no-pager nosim cmd systemctl mask what links the unit to /dev/null so it cannot be started at all, even by dependencies. where when a service must never run. why stronger than disable; undo with `unmask`. example sudo systemctl mask cups.service nosim tip in `systemctl status` the line `loaded:` shows enabled/disabled, the line `active:` shows the running state. warn never run stop, disable or mask on a service you do not know. stopping the wrong service can take a machine offline. danger **never stop, disable or mask sshd or the network service on a remote vm.** you cut your own connection and cannot reconnect. in this module only read ssh/cron/chronyd state. names title service names on different distributions body the same software has different unit names on different families. on rhel/rocky/alma the ssh service is `sshd`, on debian/ubuntu it is `ssh` (an alias `sshd` often works too). the web server is `httpd` on rhel and `apache2` on debian/ubuntu. the firewall is `firewalld` on rhel and `ufw` on ubuntu. the cron service is `crond` on rhel and `cron` on debian/ubuntu; the time service is `chronyd` (rhel) or `chrony`/`systemd-timesyncd` (ubuntu). if a name is not found, search with `list-unit-files`. `/etc/os-release` tells you which family you are on. commands cmd cat /etc/os-release what shows the distribution name and version. where before you use a service or log name. why id and id_like tell you whether you are on the rhel or the debian family. example cat /etc/os-release cmd systemctl list-units --type=service what lists the currently loaded services with their state. where when you want to know what runs on the machine. why you see real names instead of guessing. example systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager nosim cmd systemctl list-unit-files what lists all installed unit files with their boot setting. where when a name is unknown or a service is not loaded yet. why also finds stopped and disabled services. example systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --no-pager | grep -e 'ssh|cron|chrony' nosim cmd systemctl list-timers what lists timer units with next and last run. where when looking for scheduled jobs of systemd. why timers replace many cron jobs. example systemctl list-timers --no-pager nosim tip names that are common on one family may not exist on the other. use `ssh` or `sshd` with tab completion: `systemctl status ssh<tab>`. unitfile title unit files and a custom service body a service is described in a **unit file** with three parts. `[unit]` has the description and ordering, `[service]` says what is run (`execstart=` with the **full path**) and how (`restart=on-failure` restarts it after a crash), `[install]` says where it is hooked in when enabled (`wantedby=multi-user.target`). packages place their units in `/usr/lib/systemd/system` (on debian also `/lib/systemd/system`). **do not edit those.** your own units and overrides go to `/etc/systemd/system`, which has priority. after every new or changed unit file run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload`, so systemd re-reads the files. without it you get a warning or the old version keeps running. minimal example: `[unit]` `description=linux lab demo` — `[service]` `execstart=/usr/bin/sleep 3600` `restart=on-failure` — `[install]` `wantedby=multi-user.target`. the vm exercises build exactly this unit as `linux-lab-demo.service` and remove it again. commands cmd systemctl cat what prints the unit file including drop-in overrides. where when you want to see what a service really runs. why shows execstart and the file path without searching. example systemctl cat sshd nosim cmd systemctl edit what creates a drop-in override in /etc/systemd/system without touching the original. where when changing a packaged service. why survives package updates; daemon-reload happens automatically. example sudo systemctl edit chronyd nosim cmd systemd-analyze verify what checks a unit file for syntax errors. where before you start a new unit. why finds typos like exec_start or a relative path. example systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/linux-lab-demo.service nosim cmd systemd-analyze blame what lists units by the time they needed during boot. where when the boot is slow. why shows the slowest units at the top. example systemd-analyze blame --no-pager | head -n 10 nosim tip typical unit errors: `execstart=sleep 3600` (relative path, needs `/usr/bin/sleep`), a typo in a key name, a missing `[install]` (then `enable` says there is no installation config). warn do not copy unit files into /usr/lib/systemd/system and do not delete units of the system. work only with your own `linux-lab-demo.service` in /etc/systemd/system. journal title journalctl and the kernel log body systemd collects all messages in the **journal**. `journalctl` reads it. combine filters: `-u` for a unit, `-b` for the current boot, `-p err` for the priority error and worse, `--since` for time, `-n 50` for the last 50 lines, `-f` to follow live (end with ctrl+c). `journalctl -xe` jumps to the end with extra explanations; it is what systemctl suggests after a failed start. in scripts and when pasting output use `--no-pager`. by default the journal may be kept only in memory (`/run/log/journal`) and is lost at reboot. for a **persistent journal** create `/var/log/journal` (or set `storage=persistent` in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`) and restart journald. on ubuntu it is persistent already; on many rhel systems it is not. `journalctl --disk-usage` shows how much space the journal uses. `dmesg` prints the kernel ring buffer (hardware, drivers, disk errors); on some systems it needs `sudo`. commands cmd journalctl -u what shows the log of one unit. where when a service does not start or behaves wrongly. why only the messages of this service, not the whole system. example journalctl -u sshd --no-pager nosim cmd journalctl -f what follows new log lines live. where while you restart a service or reproduce an error. why you see the reaction immediately; leave with ctrl+c. example journalctl -u sshd -f nosim cmd journalctl -b what shows only the current boot (`-b -1` the previous one). where after a reboot or crash. why cuts out old noise. example journalctl -b --no-pager | tail -n 20 nosim cmd journalctl -p err what filters by priority: err and everything worse. where for a quick list of real problems. why hides info and debug messages. example journalctl -p err -b --no-pager nosim cmd journalctl --since what shows entries from a point in time (`--until` for the end). where when you know roughly when it happened. why keeps output small. example journalctl --since \  --no-pager nosim cmd journalctl -n 50 --no-pager what prints the last 50 lines without the pager. where for quick checks and for pasting into tickets. why no scrolling in less, easy to copy. example journalctl -n 50 --no-pager nosim cmd journalctl -xe what opens the end of the journal with explanations. where right after a failed start. why systemd itself suggests it in the error message. example journalctl -xe --no-pager nosim cmd journalctl --disk-usage what shows the disk space used by the journal. where when /var fills up. why read-only and safe. example journalctl --disk-usage nosim cmd journalctl --vacuum-time what deletes journal entries older than the given time. where when the journal uses too much disk space. why frees space, but the old logs are gone for good. example sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=2weeks nosim cmd dmesg what prints the kernel messages. where for disk, usb, network card or memory problems. why the kernel reports hardware issues here first. example sudo dmesg | tail -n 20 nosim tip combine filters: `journalctl -u sshd -p err --since \  --no-pager`. warn `--vacuum-time` and `--vacuum-size` delete logs permanently. do not run them on a vm whose logs you still need for an investigation. classic title classic log files, rsyslog and logrotate body besides the journal there are text logs in `/var/log`, written mostly by **rsyslog**. the names differ: on rhel/rocky `/var/log/messages` (general) and `/var/log/secure` (login and sudo); on debian/ubuntu `/var/log/syslog` and `/var/log/auth.log`. these files are readable only by root or the `adm` group, so use `sudo`. typical tools: `tail -f` follows a file, `grep -i error` searches it, `less` scrolls through it (`/word` searches, `q` quits). combine them: `sudo grep -i error /var/log/messages | tail -n 20`. **logrotate** keeps logs from growing forever: it renames, compresses and deletes old files by rules in `/etc/logrotate.conf` and `/etc/logrotate.d/`. a rule has the log path and options like `weekly`, `rotate 4` (keep 4 old copies), `compress`, `missingok`, `notifempty`. it is started daily by a timer or cron. the simulator has the files of a rhel machine, so you can practise reading logs here. commands cmd ls /var/log what lists the log files and folders. where to find out which logs exist. why file names differ by distribution. example ls /var/log cmd sudo cat /var/log/secure what reads a log that only root may read (ubuntu: `/var/log/auth.log`). where when you investigate logins and sudo. why shows who logged in and who failed. example sudo cat /var/log/secure cmd tail -f what shows the end of a file and follows new lines. where while a service is running or being tested. why live view; leave with ctrl+c. example sudo tail -f /var/log/messages nosim cmd grep -i what searches lines case-insensitively; `-c` counts them. where to find errors in a big log. why reduces thousands of lines to the relevant ones. example grep -i error /var/log/messages cmd less what shows a file page by page; `/word` searches, `q` quits. where for long logs. why scrolling without flooding the terminal. example less /var/log/messages cmd logrotate -d what debug mode: shows what logrotate would do without doing it. where after writing a new rule in /etc/logrotate.d. why tests the rule safely. example sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.conf nosim tip to count the errors: `grep -ci error /var/log/messages`. to see only the last lines of a long search: add `| tail -n 5`. warn never delete or truncate a log file with `rm` or `> file` while a service writes to it; let logrotate do it. deleting evidence also makes later troubleshooting impossible. tasks t01 text list the log files of the machine with `ls /var/log`. hint look for `messages` and `secure`. t02 text you cannot run systemctl here, so write the command you would use on a vm to show the state of sshd into a file: `echo \  > ~/answer_status.txt`. hint the file is checked for `systemctl status sshd` (or `ssh`). t03 text find the error lines in the general log with `grep -i error /var/log/messages`. hint `-i` ignores upper/lower case, so error is found too. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t04 text count how many lines contain `error` (ignore case) with `grep -ci error /var/log/messages`. hint `-c` prints the number instead of the lines. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t05 text read the login log, which only root may read: `sudo cat /var/log/secure`. hint without sudo you get permission denied; `student` is in the wheel group. t06 text the file `~/lab/systemctl_status.txt` is saved output of `systemctl status`. show its `loaded` line with `grep loaded ~/lab/systemctl_status.txt`. is the service enabled? hint in the `loaded:` line look for `enabled` or `disabled`. t07 text `~/lab/failed_units.txt` is a saved `systemctl list-units --failed`. write only the unit names into `~/lab/failed_names.txt`: `cut -d\  -f1 ~/lab/failed_units.txt | grep service > ~/lab/failed_names.txt`. hint `cut -d\  -f1` takes the first column, `grep service` drops the header and the summary line. (`cut` → module 3.5.) t08 text write the journalctl command for the last 50 lines of the sshd log without pager into `~/answer_journal.txt`, e.g. `echo 'journalctl -u sshd -n 50 --no-pager' > ~/answer_journal.txt`. hint `-u` unit, `-n 50` last 50 lines, `--no-pager` no less. t09 text `~/lab/logrotate_demo.conf` is a logrotate rule. show the `rotate` line with `grep rotate ~/lab/logrotate_demo.conf`. how many old copies are kept? hint `rotate 4` means four old copies; `weekly` means a weekly rotation. t10 text predict: which messages are the last two lines of `/var/log/messages`? guess first, then check with `tail -n 2 /var/log/messages`. hint `tail -n 2` prints the last two lines; the newest entry is at the bottom. (`tail` → module 2.6.) t11 text predict: how many lines of `~/lab/journal_sample.txt` contain the word `failed` (case-sensitive, so failure does not count)? guess first, then verify with `grep -c failed ~/lab/journal_sample.txt`. hint read the file first with `cat ~/lab/journal_sample.txt` if you want to count by eye. t12 text predict: who owns `/var/log/secure` and who may read it? check with `ls -l /var/log/secure`. hint mode `-rw-------` means only the owner (root) can read and write. t13 text debug: `~/lab/broken1.service` would not start, because the key is misspelled and the command has no full path. rewrite the file (for example with `printf` and `>`) so that it has `execstart=/usr/bin/sleep 3600`. hint `cat ~/lab/broken1.service` shows the error; the key must be `execstart`, the path `/usr/bin/sleep`. t14 text debug: `systemctl enable` would complain about `~/lab/broken2.service` because it has no `[install]` section. append `[install]` and `wantedby=multi-user.target` with `printf` and `>>`. hint `printf \  >> ~/lab/broken2.service`. (`>>` → module 3.2.) t15 text mini project: create `~/lab/linux-lab-demo.service` with `[unit]` (description), `[service]` (`execstart=/usr/bin/sleep 3600`) and `[install]` (`wantedby=multi-user.target`). then write the three vm steps (copy to `/etc/systemd/system/`, `daemon-reload`, `enable --now linux-lab-demo.service`) into `~/lab/install_steps.txt`, one per line. hint use `printf` with `\n` for line breaks. the steps file only contains text; nothing is installed. t16 text challenge: build an incident report `~/lab/incident.txt`. first write all error lines of `/var/log/messages` (case-insensitive) into it, then append the content of `/var/log/secure`. the report needs at least 4 lines. hint `grep -i error ... > file`, then `sudo cat ... >> file` (the redirect is done by your own shell, so the file in your home is fine). (`grep` → module 3.4; `>/>>` → module 3.2.) t17 text ticket #5610 — a customer reports that the web server does not come up after a reboot. write the three commands you would run on a rhel vm into `~/ticket_5610.txt`, one per line: show the state (`systemctl status httpd`), read its log (`journalctl -u httpd -n 50 --no-pager`) and enable and start it (`sudo systemctl enable --now httpd`). hint use one `printf` with `\n` between the lines. on ubuntu the name would be `apache2`. : { these tasks run on your own vm. most are read-only. task 4 creates a harmless unit that runs `sleep 3600`. **take a snapshot first** and never stop or change sshd or the network service on a remote vm. use `sshd`, `crond`, `chronyd` on rhel/rocky and `ssh`, `cron`, `chrony` on ubuntu. tasks v01 title read service state text check ssh, cron and your time service without changing anything. paste the output. blocks cmd # rocky/rhel
systemctl status sshd --no-pager
systemctl is-active crond chronyd
systemctl is-enabled sshd
# ubuntu
systemctl status ssh --no-pager
systemctl is-active cron
systemctl is-enabled ssh expected ● sshd.service - openssh server daemon
     loaded: loaded (/usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service; enabled; ...)
     active: active (running) since ...
active
active
enabled cmd systemctl list-units --failed --no-pager expected 0 loaded units listed. differs `unit sshd.service could not be found` on ubuntu: use `ssh` instead of `sshd`. if `chronyd` is not found, your system uses `systemd-timesyncd` (ubuntu); try `systemctl status systemd-timesyncd`. failed units in the list are not an error of this exercise; just note them. v02 title read the journal text read the journal with filters and check how much space it uses. paste the output. blocks cmd journalctl -b -n 10 --no-pager
journalctl -p err -b --no-pager | tail -n 5
journalctl --since \  --no-pager | wc -l
journalctl --disk-usage expected ... linux-lab systemd[1]: started ...
1234
archived and active journals take up 48.0m in the file system. differs `permission denied` or a hint about the `systemd-journal` group: run the commands with `sudo`. `-- no entries --` for `-p err` is good news: there were no errors. if the journal only has the current boot, it is not persistent yet (see `ls /var/log/journal`). v03 title classic logs and dmesg text read the end of the general and the login log, then the kernel log. use the file names of your family. blocks cmd # rocky/rhel
sudo tail -n 5 /var/log/messages
sudo tail -n 5 /var/log/secure
# ubuntu
sudo tail -n 5 /var/log/syslog
sudo tail -n 5 /var/log/auth.log
# both
sudo dmesg | tail -n 5
ls /etc/logrotate.d expected nov 12 10:01:02 linux-lab systemd[1]: ...
nov 12 10:02:11 linux-lab sudo[2101]: student : tty=pts/0 ; ...
[ 12.345678] ... differs `no such file or directory` for syslog/messages: the other family's file name, or rsyslog is not installed. the journal has the same data. on ubuntu, `dmesg` without sudo may be blocked; use `sudo dmesg`. v04 title create your own service text create `linux-lab-demo.service`, load it, start it and look at its state and log. **snapshot first.** the unit only runs `sleep 3600`. blocks cmd sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/linux-lab-demo.service > /dev/null <<'eof'
[unit]
description=linux lab demo

[service]
execstart=/usr/bin/sleep 3600
restart=on-failure

[install]
wantedby=multi-user.target
eof
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start linux-lab-demo.service
systemctl status linux-lab-demo.service --no-pager
systemctl is-enabled linux-lab-demo.service
journalctl -u linux-lab-demo.service -n 5 --no-pager expected ● linux-lab-demo.service - linux lab demo
     loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/linux-lab-demo.service; disabled; ...)
     active: active (running) since ...
disabled
... systemd[1]: started linux lab demo. differs `failed to start ... no such file or directory`: check the path with `which sleep`; on some systems it is `/bin/sleep`. `is-enabled` says `disabled` because you used start only; that is the difference between start and enable. if `sudo` is missing the heredoc, copy the file in two steps: write it in your home and `sudo cp` it to /etc/systemd/system/. v05 title remove your service again text stop and remove only `linux-lab-demo.service`, then check that systemd no longer knows it. do not touch any other unit. blocks cmd sudo systemctl stop linux-lab-demo.service
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/linux-lab-demo.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl status linux-lab-demo.service --no-pager expected unit linux-lab-demo.service could not be found. differs if you also ran `enable`, run `sudo systemctl disable linux-lab-demo.service` before the `rm`. `unit ... not found` or `inactive (dead)` both mean the service is gone or not running. check the file name in `rm` twice: it must be exactly the demo file. quiz : { what is the difference between `systemctl start` and `systemctl enable`? options they are identical start runs it now, enable makes it start at boot enable runs it now, start makes it start at boot start installs the package, enable removes it explain start acts now, enable only changes the boot setting. `enable --now` does both. : { which pair is the web server service on (rhel, ubuntu)? options apache2, httpd nginx, httpd httpd, apache2 httpd, ssh explain rhel/rocky use `httpd`, debian/ubuntu use `apache2`. the same applies to sshd/ssh and firewalld/ufw. : { which command shows only errors of the current boot? options journalctl -b -p err journalctl -f journalctl --vacuum-time=1d systemctl status -b explain `-b` limits to the current boot, `-p err` to priority error and worse. : { you created /etc/systemd/system/linux-lab-demo.service. what do you do first? options reboot the machine mask the unit delete the files in /usr/lib/systemd/system run systemctl daemon-reload explain daemon-reload makes systemd read the new or changed unit file. summary `start`/`stop` act now, `enable`/`disable` act at boot, `enable --now` does both. names differ: sshd/ssh, httpd/apache2, firewalld/ufw, crond/cron; check with `/etc/os-release`. a unit has `[unit]`, `[service]` (`execstart` with full path, `restart=`), `[install]`; own units go to `/etc/systemd/system` followed by `daemon-reload`. `journalctl -u`, `-b`, `-p err`, `--since`, `-n 50 --no-pager`, `-f`, `-xe` find the cause; `--disk-usage` shows the size. classic logs: rhel `messages`/`secure`, debian/ubuntu `syslog`/`auth.log`; logrotate rotates them by `/etc/logrotate.d` rules. never stop sshd on a remote vm; never delete or vacuum logs you still need. glossary term systemd meaning the init system (pid 1) that starts and supervises services. term unit meaning an object managed by systemd: service, target, timer, mount and more. term target meaning a group of units that describes a system state, e.g. multi-user.target. term timer meaning a unit that starts another unit on a schedule; alternative to cron. term daemon-reload meaning makes systemd re-read unit files after you changed them. term mask meaning links a unit to /dev/null so that it cannot be started. term journal meaning systemd's binary log database, read with journalctl. term rsyslog meaning the classic syslog daemon that writes text logs to /var/log. term logrotate meaning tool that rotates, compresses and deletes old log files by rules.

6.1.title: Network Basics — ip, ss, DNS, Ports
objectives: You read the IP address, prefix and default gateway with `ip a` and `ip r`.
You see which service listens on which port and interface with `ss -tulpn`.
You know the name resolution chain: `/etc/hosts` → `/etc/resolv.conf` → DNS server.
You read the firewall (firewalld / ufw) first and change it without locking yourself out.
You diagnose "no internet" layer by layer (address → gateway → IP → name).
sol: grep LISTEN ~/net/ss.txt | tr -s ' ' | cut -d' ' -f5 | cut -d: -f2 | sort -n | uniq > ~/net/ports.txt
6.1.text:
title network basics — ip, ss, dns, ports lead read your network identity: address, gateway, port and name. almost every command in this module is read-only. objectives you read the ip address, prefix and default gateway with `ip a` and `ip r`. you see which service listens on which port and interface with `ss -tulpn`. you know the name resolution chain: `/etc/hosts` → `/etc/resolv.conf` → dns server. you read the firewall (firewalld / ufw) first and change it without locking yourself out. you diagnose \  layer by layer (address → gateway → ip → name). sections addr title address and routing: ip a, ip r body every network interface (`eth0`, `ens3`, `enp0s3`, `lo`) has an **ip address** and a **prefix**. `192.168.1.42/24` means: the first 24 bits are the network, the rest identifies the host (`/24` = `255.255.255.0`). `lo` is the loopback interface (`127.0.0.1`): the machine itself, it never leaves the host. if the destination is not on the local network, the packet goes to the **default gateway**. the line `default via 192.168.1.1` in `ip r` tells you which. use the modern `ip` command instead of the old `ifconfig` and `route`; it exists on rocky/alma and ubuntu/debian alike. interface names vary by distribution and vm; your output may show `ens3` or `enp0s3` instead of `eth0`. commands cmd ip a what lists all interfaces with their ip addresses and state (up/down). where to learn the machine's address or verify an interface is up. why first stop in network trouble; without an address nothing above it works. example ip a nosim cmd ip -br a what shows the same information as a short one-line-per-interface table. where for a quick look at which interface has which address. why saves you from reading long output; it fits on the screen. example ip -br a nosim cmd ip r what shows the routing table; the `default via` line is the gateway. where when investigating why you cannot reach outside networks. why without a default route no packet leaves the local network. example ip r nosim cmd grep default what filters lines by text; here it finds the gateway in saved route output. where when you want a single line out of long output. why the same filtering works on `ss` output; in the simulator you practise with sample files. example grep default ~/net/routes.txt tip chain it with cutting: `grep default ~/net/routes.txt | cut -d' ' -f3` returns just the gateway address. warn changing an interface address by hand with `ip addr add/del` can cut your connection (including ssh) instantly. in this module we only read. ports title ports and listening services: ss body the ip address selects the machine, the **port** selects the service on it: `22` ssh, `80` http, `443` https, `53` dns. a running service **listens** (listen) on a specific address and port. `ss -tulpn` letters: `t` tcp, `u` udp, `l` listening only, `p` process name, `n` numeric output (no name lookup). you need `sudo` to see process names. **watch the local address:** `0.0.0.0:22` means reachable on every interface. `127.0.0.1:5432` is reachable only from the machine itself. a database listening on `0.0.0.0` may be exposed to the network, which is a security finding. `ss` replaced the old `netstat -tulpn`; the options are nearly the same. commands cmd ss -tulpn what lists listening tcp/udp sockets with ports and processes. where to answer \ why a service may look running yet listen on the wrong address, so connections fail. example sudo ss -tulpn nosim cmd ss -tln what shows only tcp listeners, without process info (no sudo needed). where for quick checks or in scripts. why short and unprivileged; enough to see whether a port is open. example ss -tln | grep 8080 nosim cmd curl -i what fetches only the response headers of a web server. where to test whether the service really answers over http. why a port can be open while the application does not answer; a code like `200` or `301` shows it does. example curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080 nosim tip filter `ss` output: `ss -tln | grep listen | wc -l` counts how many tcp ports listen. warn do not port-scan servers you do not own. it is unethical and noticeable; work on `127.0.0.1` of your own vm. dns title name resolution: hosts, resolv.conf, dns body a name (`example.com`) is turned into an ip in this order: first `/etc/hosts` is checked, then the **dns server** listed in `/etc/resolv.conf` is asked (the order is set by the `hosts:` line in `/etc/nsswitch.conf`). `/etc/hosts` holds local, hand-written mappings: `192.168.1.50 intranet.lab`. great for tests, but it only affects that machine. `/etc/resolv.conf` is usually generated by networkmanager or systemd-resolved; hand edits can be overwritten on reboot. on ubuntu you often see `127.0.0.53` in it; `resolvectl status` shows the real server. **key distinction:** if `ping 1.1.1.1` works but `ping example.com` does not, your network is fine and the problem is dns. commands cmd cat /etc/hosts what shows local name-to-address mappings. where when a name goes to an unexpected address. why `/etc/hosts` is read before dns; a wrong line overrides all resolution. example cat /etc/hosts cmd cat /etc/resolv.conf what shows the dns servers (`nameserver`) and search domain (`search`) in use. where first file to check when names do not resolve. why a wrong or unreachable `nameserver` line breaks all name resolution. example cat /etc/resolv.conf cmd getent hosts what resolves a name the way the system really does (hosts + dns). where to test what applications will see. why it also honours `/etc/hosts`, so it is more accurate than tools that only query dns. example getent hosts localhost nosim cmd resolvectl status what shows per-interface dns servers on systemd-resolved systems. where on ubuntu and newer rocky/alma when `resolv.conf` does not tell enough. why reveals the real dns server behind `127.0.0.53`. example resolvectl status nosim tip back up before changing: `sudo cp /etc/hosts /etc/hosts.bak`. warn one wrong `nameserver` line breaks all name resolution. on a production machine configure dns via networkmanager (`nmcli`) or netplan instead of editing `/etc/resolv.conf`. firewall title firewall: firewalld and ufw body even if a service listens, the **firewall** may block the port. rocky/alma/rhel use `firewalld` (`firewall-cmd`), ubuntu/debian use `ufw`. in firewalld changes are **runtime** by default: effective immediately but lost on reload or reboot. to make them permanent add `--permanent` and run `--reload`. ufw rules are permanent automatically. **read** first: `firewall-cmd --list-all` or `ufw status verbose`. then change. selinux (rocky) and apparmor (ubuntu) are a separate layer; opening the port does not always mean the service may use it, but that is outside this module. commands cmd firewall-cmd --list-all what shows allowed services and ports of the active zone. where on rocky/alma/rhel when a port is not reachable from outside. why you see at a glance which services or ports are allowed; read-only and safe. example sudo firewall-cmd --list-all nosim cmd firewall-cmd --add-port what opens a port; without `--permanent` it is runtime only. where when you must expose a service to the outside. why try at runtime first and make permanent once it works; mistakes disappear with a reload. example sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp --timeout=300 nosim cmd ufw status verbose what shows the firewall state and rules on ubuntu/debian. where when auditing rules on an ubuntu server. why `inactive` means the firewall is off; `active` shows the default policy. example sudo ufw status verbose nosim tip on rocky a rule added with `--timeout=300` disappears after 5 minutes; if you make a mistake it heals itself. warn when changing the firewall over ssh keep a second ssh session open and use `--timeout` first. before `ufw enable` allow ssh with `sudo ufw allow 22/tcp`. danger applying a rule remotely that closes the ssh port or sets the default policy to `deny` locks you out. take a vm snapshot first (module 0.2) and keep console access ready. diagnose title diagnosis ladder: bottom to top body solve \  **layer by layer**; the first failing step is where the problem is: (1) is the interface up with an address? (2) does a ping to the gateway work? (3) does a ping to an outside ip (`1.1.1.1`) work? (4) does the name resolve? (5) does the service listen and does the firewall allow it? `ping` uses icmp; some networks block icmp, so a failed ping does not always mean no connectivity. also try the real service with `curl -i`. constant `ping` needlessly burdens the target; limit the count with `-c 3`. commands cmd ping -c 3 what sends 3 icmp packets to the target and measures the reply time. where to test gateway, outside ip and name separately. why shows which layer is broken, one at a time. example ping -c 3 1.1.1.1 nosim cmd cut -d what splits a line into fields by a delimiter and takes the field you want. where to pull one value such as address, port or prefix out of output. why you pass the value into a file or the next command without copying by hand. example echo 192.168.1.42/24 | cut -d/ -f2 cmd sort -n | uniq what sorts lines numerically and removes duplicates. where when producing a clean list of listening ports. why gives a tidy, duplicate-free list for reports and comparison. example sort -n ~/net/ports.txt | uniq tip write your findings into a report: `hostname > ~/net/report.txt`, then append with `>>`. it makes pasting into a support ticket easy. tasks t01 text read the sample route file: `cat ~/net/routes.txt`. which line names the gateway? hint the `default via ...` line. t02 text show only the listening (listen) lines of `~/net/ss.txt`. hint `grep listen ~/net/ss.txt` t03 text read the local name mappings with `cat /etc/hosts`. hint look for the `localhost` line. t04 text find the default route with `grep default ~/net/routes.txt`. what is the gateway address? hint the address after the word `via`. t05 text write only the gateway address into `~/net/gateway.txt`. hint `grep default ... | cut -d' ' -f3 > ~/net/gateway.txt`; field 3 is the gateway. (`grep` → module 3.4; `cut` → module 3.5; `>` → module 3.2.) t06 text write the number of listening (listen) lines into `~/net/listen_count.txt`. hint a pipeline like `grep listen ... | wc -l > file`. (`wc` → module 2.6.) t07 text write the externally exposed listeners (listen lines that are not `127.0.0.1`) into `~/net/exposed.txt`. hint pipe two `grep`s together; use `-v 127.0.0.1` in the second. (`grep` → module 3.4.) t08 text predict: which process listens on port 8080? then verify with `grep 8080 ~/net/ss.txt`. hint look at the `users:((...))` part at the end of the line. t09 text predict: which address and prefix does `eth0` carry? verify with `grep 192 ~/net/ipa.txt`. hint the `inet` line has the form `address/prefix`. t10 text predict: what does `echo 192.168.1.42/24 | cut -d/ -f2` print? run it and check. hint the field after the `/` character: the prefix length. t11 text debug: the `nameserver` in `~/net/resolv.conf` is invalid. rewrite the file so it has two lines: `nameserver 192.168.1.1` and `nameserver 1.1.1.1`. hint `printf 'line1\nline2\n' > file` writes two lines; look at the error with `cat` first. (`cat` → module 2.6.) t12 text debug: the script `~/net/check_ports.sh` does not run. find the cause, fix it and run the script. hint check permissions with `ls -l`; `chmod 755`, then `~/net/check_ports.sh`. (`chmod` → module 4.4.) t13 text mini report: write the host name, the gateway address and the number of listening services (3 lines, in that order) into `~/net/report.txt`. hint use `>` in the first command and `>>` in the following ones; `hostname` gives the host name. (`>/>>` → module 3.2.) t14 text hard: from the listen lines of `ss.txt` write only the port numbers, numerically sorted and without duplicates, into `~/net/ports.txt` (one port per line). hint `grep listen | tr -s ' ' | cut -d' ' -f5 | cut -d: -f2 | sort -n | uniq > file` (`tr/cut/sort/uniq` → module 3.5.) t15 text hard: write the firewalld plan for opening 8080/tcp permanently into `~/net/fw_plan.txt` as two lines: first the command containing `--permanent --add-port=8080/tcp`, then `firewall-cmd --reload`. (you write the plan, you do not run it.) hint `echo 'command' > file`, use `>>` for the second line. use quotes. (`>/>>` → module 3.2.) t16 text ticket: users cannot reach the name `intranet.lab`. the internal server's address is `192.168.1.50`. add this mapping to `~/net/hosts` (do not delete existing lines). hint `echo '192.168.1.50 intranet.lab' >> ~/net/hosts` t17 text ticket: a security audit wants proof that postgresql (port 5432) listens only on the local address. save the relevant `ss.txt` line into `~/net/audit.txt`. hint `grep 5432 ~/net/ss.txt > ~/net/audit.txt`; the line must contain `127.0.0.1:5432`. (`grep` → module 3.4.) : { these steps run on your own vm and only read. outputs are specific to you; ips and interface names may differ. if a command is missing, install `sudo dnf install iproute bind-utils` on rocky or `sudo apt install iproute2 dnsutils` on ubuntu. tasks v01 title address and gateway text read your interfaces and route and paste the output. blocks cmd ip -br a
ip r expected lo      unknown  127.0.0.1/8
ens3    up       192.168.1.42/24
default via 192.168.1.1 dev ens3 proto dhcp metric 100
192.168.1.0/24 dev ens3 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.42 differs the interface may be called `eth0`, `ens3` or `enp0s3`; what matters is the address and the `default via` line. if there is no `default` line the machine has no gateway; check the vm's network mode (nat/bridge). v02 title listening services text list which services listen and find ssh. blocks cmd sudo ss -tulpn
ss -tln expected netid state  local address:port process
tcp   listen 0.0.0.0:22         users:((\ ,pid=812,fd=3))
... differs without `sudo` the process name (`process` column) stays empty. if `ss` is missing install `iproute`/`iproute2`; if there is no `listen` line the service is not running. v03 title name resolution chain text read hosts and resolv.conf, then resolve a name the way the system does. blocks cmd cat /etc/hosts
cat /etc/resolv.conf
resolvectl status | head -n 15
getent hosts localhost expected 127.0.0.1 localhost
nameserver 127.0.0.53
...
::1             localhost differs if `resolvectl` is missing (old or minimal system) skip that line; `resolv.conf` is enough. seeing `nameserver 127.0.0.53` on ubuntu is normal; the real server is listed in `resolvectl status`. v04 title diagnosis ladder text ping the gateway, an outside ip and a name, 2 packets each. replace `192.168.1.1` with your own gateway. blocks cmd ping -c 2 192.168.1.1
ping -c 2 1.1.1.1
ping -c 2 example.com expected 2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss differs if the ip answers but the name does not, the problem is dns (`/etc/resolv.conf`). if none answer, check address/gateway with `ip a` and `ip r` first; some networks block icmp, so also try `curl -i https://example.com`. v05 title create your own listener and see it text start a temporary web server on `127.0.0.1` only, see it with `ss`, test it with `curl`, then stop it. blocks cmd python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1 &
sleep 1
ss -tln | grep 8080
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080
kill %1 expected listen 0 5 127.0.0.1:8080 0.0.0.0:*
http/1.0 200 ok differs if `python3` is missing it needs installing; you can skip and paste your `ss -tln` output instead. if the port is busy use `8081`. when done, verify with `jobs` that no background job remains. v06 title read the firewall (do not change it) text read your distribution's firewall state. add no rule for now. before changing rules take a vm snapshot (module 0.2) and keep a second ssh session open. blocks cmd # rocky / alma / rhel
sudo firewall-cmd --state
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
# ubuntu / debian
sudo ufw status verbose expected running
public (active)
  services: cockpit dhcpv6-client ssh
# or: status: inactive differs the command that does not belong to your distribution prints `command not found`; that is normal, run the other one. `not running` or `inactive` means the firewall is off; you do not need to change that in this lab. quiz : { which command shows the default gateway? options `ip a` `ip r` `ss -tulpn` `cat /etc/hosts` explain `ip r` shows the routing table; the `default via ...` line is the gateway. `ip a` shows addresses, `ss` listening ports, `/etc/hosts` name mappings. : { in `ss -tulpn` output a database listens on `127.0.0.1:5432`. who can connect to it? options everyone on the network only those with a firewall rule only the machine itself nobody explain `127.0.0.1` is the loopback address; the service is reachable locally only. exposed to the outside is `0.0.0.0` or an external interface address. : { in which order is a name usually resolved? options first `/etc/hosts`, then the dns server in `resolv.conf` first the dns server, then `/etc/hosts` only the dns server first the gateway, then `/etc/hosts` explain the `hosts:` line in `nsswitch.conf` sets the order; by default the file (`/etc/hosts`) comes first, then dns. : { what happens if you run `firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp` without `--permanent`? options the rule stays forever the rule only applies after a reboot the command is rejected the rule applies immediately but is lost on reload or reboot explain the default is the runtime configuration: effective at once, not persistent. to make it permanent you need `--permanent` and `--reload`. summary `ip a` shows addresses, `ip r` the routes and the default gateway. `ss -tulpn` shows listening services; `127.0.0.1` is local only, `0.0.0.0` is every interface. name resolution: `/etc/hosts` → `/etc/resolv.conf` → dns server. read the firewall first; in firewalld separate runtime from permanent, and over ssh use `--timeout` and a second session. diagnosis: address → gateway → outside ip → name → service and firewall. glossary term ip address meaning the address of an interface on the network, e.g. 192.168.1.42. term prefix / subnet mask meaning separates the network and host part of an address; /24 = 255.255.255.0. term gateway meaning the router address to which packets for destinations outside the local network are sent. term loopback meaning the machine itself: the `lo` interface, 127.0.0.1. term port meaning a number that selects a service on a machine; 22 ssh, 80 http, 443 https. term listen meaning a service waiting for connections on a specific address and port. term dns meaning the system that translates names into ip addresses. term nameserver meaning a dns server defined in `/etc/resolv.conf`. term runtime / permanent meaning temporary (until reload) and persistent configuration in firewalld. term icmp / ping meaning a simple network protocol that measures reachability and latency.

6.2.title: SELinux — Labels, Booleans, AVC
objectives: You read the SELinux modes (enforcing, permissive, disabled) and explain why disabling it permanently is a bad idea.
You read file labels with `ls -Z` and fix them persistently with `chcon`, `semanage fcontext` and `restorecon`.
You manage booleans with `getsebool` and `setsebool -P` and resolve AVC denials with `ausearch` and `sealert`.
You read the Debian/Ubuntu equivalent, AppArmor, with `aa-status` and tell complain from enforce mode.
sol: echo 'wrong type user_home_t, correct type httpd_sys_content_t, fix with restorecon' > ticket.txt
6.2.text:
title selinux — labels, booleans, avc lead selinux gives every file and process a label. when a service fails, the culprit is often a wrong label; learn to find the cause instead of switching selinux off. objectives you read the selinux modes (enforcing, permissive, disabled) and explain why disabling it permanently is a bad idea. you read file labels with `ls -z` and fix them persistently with `chcon`, `semanage fcontext` and `restorecon`. you manage booleans with `getsebool` and `setsebool -p` and resolve avc denials with `ausearch` and `sealert`. you read the debian/ubuntu equivalent, apparmor, with `aa-status` and tell complain from enforce mode. sections modes title what selinux is, modes body classic permissions (rwx) look at the owner. **selinux** is an extra layer: every process and file has a **label (context)** and the policy says which label may do what to which. a label looks like `user:role:type:level`; the **type** field matters most in daily work (e.g. `httpd_t`, `httpd_sys_content_t`). there are three modes: **enforcing** (violations are blocked and logged), **permissive** (only logged, not blocked; for debugging) and **disabled** (off). rhel/rocky/alma default to enforcing. debian/ubuntu use **apparmor** instead. commands cmd getenforce what prints the running selinux mode. where first check when a service misbehaves. why narrows down whether selinux is involved. example getenforce nosim cmd sestatus what shows mode, policy type and the mode in the config file. where when you need a general summary. why you see the difference between running and persistent mode. example sestatus nosim cmd setenforce 0 what switches to permissive for now (resets on reboot). where to test temporarily whether selinux is the cause. why if the problem vanishes in permissive, selinux is the culprit; turn it back on with `setenforce 1`. example setenforce 0 nosim cmd /etc/selinux/config what file holding the persistent mode (`selinux=enforcing`). where when setting the mode persistently across reboots. why if you write `disabled`, labels go stale and re-enabling needs a long relabel. example cat /etc/selinux/config nosim tip troubleshooting order: `getenforce`, test with `setenforce 0`, read the log, fix, then `setenforce 1`. warn do not make `setenforce 0` or `selinux=disabled` a habit. use permissive for a temporary test and the right label or boolean for a lasting fix. labels title labels: ls -z, chcon, semanage, restorecon body `ls -z` shows a file's label. the web server (`httpd_t`) can only read web-typed files such as `httpd_sys_content_t`. if you `mv` a file from your home directory, it keeps the old `user_home_t` label and access is denied. `chcon` changes the label immediately but **not persistently**: `restorecon` or a relabel wipes it. the lasting way has two steps: first write the rule into the policy with `semanage fcontext`, then apply it with `restorecon`. commands cmd ls -z what lists the selinux label of files. where when looking at the file type after a denial. why you compare the expected type with the actual type. example ls -z /var/www/html nosim cmd chcon -t what changes a file's type temporarily. where for quick experiments. why proves the label fixes the problem; but it is not persistent. example chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/web/index.html nosim cmd semanage fcontext -a what adds a persistent labeling rule for a path pattern. where when using a non-standard directory (e.g. /srv/web). why the rule stays in the policy and survives a relabel. example semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t \ nosim cmd restorecon -rv what restores labels to what the policy says (-r recursive, -v verbose). where after `semanage fcontext` or after moving files. why applies the rule to the real files. example restorecon -rv /srv/web nosim tip a file copied with `cp` takes the label of the target directory; a file moved with `mv` keeps its old label. run `restorecon` after moving. warn do not run `restorecon -r /` or other huge paths; it takes long and can surprise you. look first with `-n` (dry run). booleans title booleans body switches that turn common behaviors on and off without rewriting the policy are called **booleans**: `httpd_can_network_connect` lets the web server connect to the network, `httpd_enable_homedirs` opens home directories. `setsebool` alone changes the **running** state and is lost on reboot. add `-p` to make it persistent. enable only what you need; every boolean is a hole in the wall. commands cmd getsebool -a what lists all booleans and their states. where when searching for the right switch (`| grep httpd`). why the right boolean saves you from fiddling with labels. example getsebool -a | grep httpd nosim cmd getsebool what shows the state of one boolean. where to verify before and after a change. why you see that the change took effect. example getsebool httpd_can_network_connect nosim cmd setsebool -p what turns a boolean on/off persistently. where when a service must reach the network or home directories. why without `-p` the setting is lost on reboot. example setsebool -p httpd_can_network_connect on nosim cmd semanage boolean -l what lists booleans with descriptions and persistent/running state. where to learn what a boolean does. why the description keeps you from enabling the wrong switch. example semanage boolean -l | grep httpd_can_network nosim tip a new port may need more than a boolean: add it to the service type with `semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888`. warn pick the narrowest boolean; broad switches like `httpd_unified` grant a lot. avc title avc denials: ausearch, sealert, audit.log body when selinux blocks something, an **avc** (access vector cache) record lands in `/var/log/audit/audit.log`. it has the source label (`scontext`), target label (`tcontext`), class (`tclass`) and the blocked permission (`{ read }`). if `permissive=1`, the access was not blocked, only logged. reading order: who (`comm`, `scontext`), what (`name`, `tcontext`), what it tried to do (`{ ... }`). then fix: wrong label means `restorecon`, a behavior permission means a boolean, a new port means `semanage port`. generating a module with `audit2allow` is the last resort. commands cmd ausearch -m avc -ts recent what searches the audit log for recent avc records. where right after a denial. why finds the relevant records without wading through the raw log. example ausearch -m avc -ts recent nosim cmd sealert -a what analyzes the log and suggests a fix (setroubleshoot package). where when you want a cause and fix summary. why often suggests the right `restorecon` or `setsebool` command. example sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log nosim cmd grep avc what filters avc lines in the audit log. where without ausearch or when inspecting a log copy. why the simplest method that works everywhere. example grep avc lab/audit.log cmd grep -c denied what counts denied records. where to measure the size of the problem. why tells you whether it is one repeated denial or many sources. example grep -c denied lab/audit.log tip without auditd, records may appear in `journalctl -t setroubleshoot` or `dmesg`. warn do not load a module with `audit2allow -m` for every avc. try the label and the boolean first; objectives: You check whether firewalld is running and read the default and active zones.

title firewalld — zone, service, port lead listening is not the same as reachable: learn to read firewalld, change rules safely (runtime vs permanent) and meet ufw, the debian/ubuntu counterpart. with `ss` you see that a program listens. whether others can reach it depends on the firewall in between. **firewalld** (rocky/alma/rhel/fedora) sorts every network interface into a **zone**: a trust level with its own list of allowed services and ports. `public` is the usual default; `trusted` allows everything, `drop` silently discards everything. a **service** is a predefined bundle (`ssh` = 22/tcp, `http` = 80/tcp, `https` = 443/tcp). a **port** is an explicit number such as `8080/tcp`. use a service when one exists, a port for non-standard numbers. always read before you change: first the state, then the zone, then the whole list. commands cmd firewall-cmd --state what prints running or not running. where as the very first check on a rocky/alma vm. why if the daemon is stopped, all other firewall-cmd commands fail. example sudo firewall-cmd --state nosim cmd firewall-cmd --get-default-zone what shows the zone used for new interfaces. where before adding any rule. why rules without `--zone` go to the default zone. example sudo firewall-cmd --get-default-zone nosim cmd firewall-cmd --get-active-zones what lists zones that currently have interfaces or sources. where when you wonder which zone really handles your traffic. why the default zone can differ from the active one on an interface. example sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones nosim cmd firewall-cmd --list-all what shows services, ports, rich rules and interfaces of a zone. where before and after every change. why verify first, change, verify again. example sudo firewall-cmd --list-all nosim tip `--list-all` shows the runtime state. add `--permanent` to see what is stored on disk. runtime title runtime vs permanent, --reload, --timeout body firewalld has two configurations. **runtime** is active right now and is lost on `--reload` or reboot. **permanent** is written to disk and survives reboots, but `--permanent` alone does **not** change the running firewall. typical safe workflow: test in runtime with `--timeout`, check, and only then write it permanently and run `--reload`. `--reload` applies the permanent configuration and **discards runtime-only rules**. a good test: if a rule works in runtime and you want to keep it, use `firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent`. commands cmd firewall-cmd --add-service=http --timeout=60 what adds a runtime rule that disappears after 60 seconds. where for tests, especially over ssh. why if you made a mistake, it fixes itself. example sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=http --timeout=60 nosim cmd firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http what writes the rule to disk only; not active yet. where for rules that must survive a reboot. why runtime and permanent are separate lists. example sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http nosim cmd firewall-cmd --reload what loads the permanent configuration into runtime. where after `--permanent` changes. why activates permanent rules; runtime-only rules are dropped. example sudo firewall-cmd --reload nosim cmd firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent what saves the current runtime rules as permanent. where after you tested a rule and it works. why no need to type the rule twice. example sudo firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent nosim warn take a vm snapshot first (module 0.2). on a remote machine keep a **second ssh session open** while you change firewall use `--add-port=8080/tcp`. to close it again use `--remove-port` or `--remove-service`. remember: every `--permanent` change needs `--reload`. a port in the firewall does not start the program. check with `ss` that something listens. on rocky/alma with selinux a non-standard port may also need a label (module 6.2). commands cmd firewall-cmd --get-services what lists all predefined service names. permanently (after reload). where for apps on non-standard ports. why services only cover standard ports. example sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8080/tcp nosim cmd firewall-cmd --list-ports
