options it opens http immediately and for good it writes the rule to disk, active only after `--reload` it opens http for 60 seconds it removes http from runtime explain `--permanent` only changes the stored configuration. the running firewall changes after `--reload`. : { you are connected over ssh to a new ubuntu server. what must come before `ufw enable`? options `ufw reset` `ufw deny 22` `ufw allow openssh` `ufw delete 1` explain ufw blocks incoming traffic by default. without an ssh rule you lock yourself out. : { what does `--timeout=60` do with `--add-service`? options the runtime rule disappears after 60 seconds the rule is permanent for 60 days it waits 60 seconds before adding it it limits connections to 60 per minute explain timeout rules are runtime only and remove themselves — a safety net for tests. : { what happens to runtime-only rules on `firewall-cmd --reload`? options they become permanent they are kept they block all traffic they are discarded explain `--reload` reloads the permanent configuration and drops runtime-only changes. summary firewalld sorts interfaces into zones; `--list-all` shows what a zone allows. runtime is active now; `--permanent` is stored and needs `--reload`; `--reload` drops runtime-only rules. test with `--timeout`, verify before and after, keep a second ssh session and a snapshot. use services for standard ports and `--add-port` for the rest; rich rules limit a rule to a source network. on ubuntu: `ufw allow openssh` first, `ufw enable` second. glossary term zone meaning a trust level with its own allowed services and ports; each interface belongs to one zone. term service meaning a predefined firewalld bundle of ports, such as http = 80/tcp. term port meaning an explicit number plus protocol, for example 8080/tcp. term runtime meaning the configuration active right now; lost on reload or reboot. term permanent meaning the configuration stored on disk; applied by `--reload` or reboot. term --reload meaning loads the permanent configuration and discards runtime-only rules. term --timeout meaning makes a runtime rule expire automatically after the given time. term rich rule meaning a conditional rule with source, port, protocol and action. term ufw meaning uncomplicated firewall, the default front end on ubuntu. term lockout meaning losing your own ssh access because of a firewall change.

6.4.title: LVM — PV, VG, LV and Extending
objectives: You explain the PV → VG → LV layers and what each one does.
You build a pool with pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate and read it with pvs/vgs/lvs/lvdisplay.
You grow a volume and its filesystem together with lvextend -r, and you know XFS cannot shrink.
You practise only on file-backed loop devices in a snapshotted VM.
6.4.text:
title lvm — pv, vg, lv and extending lead no panic when the disk fills up: grow the volume. practise first in a safe loop-device lab. objectives you explain the pv → vg → lv layers and what each one does. you build a pool with pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate and read it with pvs/vgs/lvs/lvdisplay. you grow a volume and its filesystem together with lvextend -r, and you know xfs cannot shrink. you practise only on file-backed loop devices in a snapshotted vm. sections concepts title concepts: pv, vg, lv body with classic partitions the size is fixed. **lvm** (logical volume manager) pools disks and cuts volumes of any size from the pool. there are three layers: a **pv** (physical volume) is the lvm signature on a disk or partition, a **vg** (volume group) is the pool made of pvs, an **lv** (logical volume) is a volume cut from the pool that looks like a disk. order: disk → pv → vg → lv → filesystem (xfs/ext4) → mount. example names: pool `vg_data`, volume `lv_web`, path `/dev/vg_data/lv_web`. to read the state, these commands are enough; none of them changes anything. commands cmd pvs what lists physical volumes in a short table. where to see which disks belong to a pool. why the pfree column shows free space on the pv. example sudo pvs nosim cmd vgs what lists volume groups; vsize is the total, vfree the free space. where before extending, to check the pool has room. why if vfree is 0 you must add a pv with vgextend first. example sudo vgs nosim cmd lvs what lists logical volumes. where which volume is in which vg and how big? why gives a quick overview. example sudo lvs nosim cmd lvdisplay what shows details of an lv (path, size, status). where when inspecting a single volume. why lets you verify the lv path and lv size fields. example sudo lvdisplay /dev/vg_data/lv_web nosim cmd lsblk -f what shows disks, lvm layers, filesystems and mount points as a tree. where before every lvm operation. why makes sure you pick the right device. example lsblk -f nosim tip **read first, write second**: pvs, vgs, lvs and lsblk -f change nothing; run them before every command that does. safe-lab title safe lab: loop devices body never touch a real disk. you create a file with `truncate` and attach it with `losetup` as a **loop device** (`/dev/loop0`); lvm treats it as a real disk, but a mistake costs you at most one file. first **take a vm snapshot** (module 0.2). install the tools: on rocky/alma `sudo dnf install lvm2 xfsprogs`, on debian/ubuntu `sudo apt install lvm2 xfsprogs`. files live in `~/lvm-lab`; the loop number may differ, so use the `--show` output. commands cmd truncate -s 300m what creates a sparse file of the given size. where for a fake disk image. why a safe stand-in for a real disk. example truncate -s 300m ~/lvm-lab/disk1.img nosim cmd losetup -f --show what attaches the file to the first free loop device and prints its name. where when turning an image into a block device. why pvcreate only works on block devices. example sudo losetup -f --show ~/lvm-lab/disk1.img nosim cmd losetup -a what lists active loop devices and their files. where to confirm which loop belongs to which file. why prevents writing to the wrong device. example losetup -a nosim cmd losetup -d what detaches a loop device. where when cleaning up the lab. why the device must be released before the file is deleted. example sudo losetup -d /dev/loop0 nosim warn `pvcreate`, `vgcreate` and `mkfs` erase the target. check the device name with `losetup -a` before the command; never type real disk names like `/dev/sda` in this module. tip a sparse image shows 300m in `ls -lh` but uses almost no disk space. create title creating pv, vg and lv body the order is always the same: `pvcreate` → `vgcreate` → `lvcreate` → filesystem → mount. in the example below the variable `loop1` holds the `losetup` output. `lvcreate -l 200m` means a fixed size, `-l 100%free` means all remaining space. the rhel family defaults to **xfs**, debian/ubuntu usually to **ext4**; both work. commands cmd pvcreate what writes an lvm signature to the device, making it a pv. where before adding a disk to a pool. why a vg is built only from pvs. example sudo pvcreate $loop1 nosim cmd vgcreate what creates a vg from one or more pvs. where when building the pool. why volumes are cut from this pool. example sudo vgcreate vg_data $loop1 nosim cmd lvcreate what cuts a named lv from a vg. where when giving an application its own volume. why -n sets the name, -l the size. example sudo lvcreate -l 200m -n lv_web vg_data nosim cmd mkfs.xfs what creates an xfs filesystem on the lv (mkfs.ext4 for ext4). where when preparing a new volume for use. why without a filesystem it cannot be mounted. example sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vg_data/lv_web nosim cmd mount what attaches the volume to a directory. where before you start writing data. why files appear in the directory it is mounted on. example sudo mount /dev/vg_data/lv_web /mnt/web nosim danger `mkfs` destroys existing data. never run it on an existing lv or disk; first confirm with `lsblk -f` that the target is empty and a loop device. extend title extending: lvextend -r body when a volume fills up you need two steps: grow the lv, then grow the filesystem. `lvextend -r` does both. by hand use `xfs_growfs <mountpoint>` for xfs or `resize2fs <device>` for ext4; both can grow while **mounted**. if the vg has no free space (vfree), first make the new device a pv with `pvcreate`, add it with `vgextend`, then run `lvextend`. shrinking is **problematic**: xfs **can never shrink**; ext4 only when unmounted and after a backup. commands cmd lvextend -r what grows the lv and the filesystem in one go. where when extending a full volume online. why removes the risk of forgetting the second step. example sudo lvextend -r -l +100m /dev/vg_data/lv_web nosim cmd xfs_growfs what grows a mounted xfs up to the lv size. where when you did not use lvextend -r. why xfs takes the mount point as argument. example sudo xfs_growfs /mnt/web nosim cmd resize2fs what grows an ext4 filesystem up to the lv size. where when growing an ext4 volume by hand. why takes the device path as argument. example sudo resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_web nosim cmd vgextend what adds a new pv to an existing vg. where when vfree runs out. why grows the pool so the lv can grow. example sudo vgextend vg_data $loop2 nosim tip `-l +100m` adds to the current size, `-l 300m` sets the total size. to take all free space write `-l +100%free`. safety title persistent mounts, removal and warnings body to have the volume back after a reboot you need an `/etc/fstab` line: `/dev/vg_data/lv_web /srv/web xfs defaults 0 0`. a typo can break booting; back up the file before editing, then test with `sudo mount -a`. you do not need fstab in the loop lab. removal goes in reverse: `umount` → `lvremove` → `vgremove` → `pvremove` → `losetup -d`. these commands ask for confirmation and destroy data irrecoverably. always see the name first with `lvs`/`vgs`. commands cmd cat /etc/fstab what shows the filesystems mounted at boot. where when checking a persistent mount. why a wrong line can block booting. example cat /etc/fstab cmd lvremove what deletes an lv and its data. where only when cleaning up the lab. why there is no way back; umount first. example sudo lvremove /dev/vg_data/lv_web nosim cmd vgreduce what removes a pv from a vg. where when detaching a disk from the pool. why if the pv holds data, move it first with pvmove. example sudo vgreduce vg_data $loop2 nosim cmd pvremove what wipes the lvm signature from a device. where last step of the lab. why the device is no longer a pv; refused if still in a vg. example sudo pvremove $loop1 nosim warn `lvremove`, `vgreduce` and `pvremove` can destroy production data on a real server. take a snapshot/backup first and check the name twice. danger on a real system with a separate disk a wrong name loses everything. in this module use loop devices only; never try to shrink an xfs volume. the way is backup, recreate, restore. tasks t01 text read the sample output `~/lvm/vgs.txt` with `cat`. which vg has free space? hint `cat ~/lvm/vgs.txt` — look at the vfree column. (`cat` → module 2.6.) t02 text show only the `vg_data` volumes from `~/lvm/lvs.txt` using `grep`. hint `grep vg_data ~/lvm/lvs.txt` (`grep` → module 3.4.) t03 text back up before editing: copy `~/lvm/fstab.test` to `~/lvm/fstab.bak`. hint `cp ~/lvm/fstab.test ~/lvm/fstab.bak` (`cp` → module 2.4.) t04 text create `~/lvm/lab.sh`: first line `truncate -s 300m ~/lvm-lab/disk1.img`, second line `sudo losetup -f --show ~/lvm-lab/disk1.img` (append the second with `>>`). hint use `printf '...\n' > ~/lvm/lab.sh` for the first line, `>>` for the next ones. (`>/>>` → module 3.2.) t05 text append two lines to `lab.sh`: `sudo pvcreate /dev/loop0` and `sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/loop0`. hint `printf '...\n' >> ~/lvm/lab.sh` twice. t06 text append `sudo lvcreate -l 200m -n lv_web vg_data` and `sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vg_data/lv_web` to `lab.sh`. hint append with `>>`; `>` would reset the file. t07 text predict: what will `grep -c vg_data ~/lvm/lvs.txt` print? then run it to verify. hint `-c` counts matching lines. t08 text predict: what does `grep xfs ~/lvm/fs.txt` say about shrinking xfs? run it to verify. hint xfs grows but never shrinks. t09 text debug: the `lvextend` in `~/lvm/grow.sh` does not grow the filesystem. fix the line by adding `-r`: `lvextend -r -l +2g /dev/vg_data/lv_web`. hint rewrite the file with `echo '...' > ~/lvm/grow.sh`. t10 text debug: `~/lvm/fstab.test` has a wrong device name (`lv_wb`). fix the line to `/dev/vg_data/lv_web /srv/web xfs defaults 0 0`. hint first `cat ~/lvm/fstab.test`, then rewrite the single line. t11 text mini project: select the `vg_data` lines from `lvs.txt`, cut only the first column (lv name) and write it to `~/lvm/data-lvs.txt`. hint `grep ... | cut -d' ' -f1 > file` (`grep` → module 3.4; `cut` → module 3.5.) t12 text mini project: create `~/lvm/check.sh` containing `pvs`, `vgs`, `lvs` in that order. then make it executable (`755`). hint `printf 'pvs\nvgs\nlvs\n' > ...` then `chmod 755`. (`chmod` → module 4.4.) t13 text challenge: write to `~/lvm/runbook.txt` the commands `pvcreate`, `vgcreate`, `lvcreate`, `mkfs.xfs` and `lvextend -r` in that order, one per line. device `/dev/loop0`, vg `vg_data`, lv `lv_web`. hint one `printf` with `\n` separators works. t14 text challenge: how many lvs does each vg have in `lvs.txt`? squeeze spaces (`tr -s`), cut the vg column, then count with `sort` and `uniq -c`. hint `tr -s ' ' < file | cut -d' ' -f2 | sort | uniq -c` (`tr/cut/sort/uniq` → module 3.5.) t15 text ticket: `vg_sys` is full (vfree 0) and `lv_root` needs 5g more. write to `~/lvm/ticket-fix.sh` in order: new pv `/dev/loop1`, `vgextend vg_sys /dev/loop1`, `lvextend -r -l +5g /dev/vg_sys/lv_root`. hint three lines: `pvcreate`, `vgextend`, `lvextend -r`. t16 text prepare the mount point: create the directory `~/mnt/web` and put an empty `index.html` in it. hint `mkdir -p` and `touch`. (`mkdir/touch` → module 2.3.) : { do these tasks on your vm. **take a snapshot** first. use loop devices only; never type a real disk name. tasks v01 title read the current lvm state text without changing anything, list the existing disks and lvm layers. paste the output. blocks cmd lsblk -f
sudo pvs
sudo vgs
sudo lvs expected vg   #pv #lv #sn attr   vsize  vfree
rl     1   2   0 wz--n- <19.00g 0 differs if lvm is missing run `sudo dnf install lvm2` (rocky/alma) or `sudo apt install lvm2` (debian/ubuntu). if a default ubuntu install does not use lvm, empty output is normal; it still proves the commands work. v02 title build pv, vg and lv on loop devices text after the snapshot, create two fake disks, build a vg and lv, format with xfs and mount. paste the output. blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/lvm-lab
truncate -s 300m ~/lvm-lab/disk1.img
truncate -s 300m ~/lvm-lab/disk2.img
loop1=$(sudo losetup -f --show ~/lvm-lab/disk1.img)
loop2=$(sudo losetup -f --show ~/lvm-lab/disk2.img)
echo $loop1 $loop2
sudo pvcreate $loop1
sudo vgcreate vg_data $loop1
sudo lvcreate -l 200m -n lv_web vg_data
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vg_data/lv_web
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/web
sudo mount /dev/vg_data/lv_web /mnt/web
sudo vgs vg_data expected vg      #pv #lv #sn attr   vsize    vfree
vg_data   1   1   0 wz--n- 296.00m 96.00m differs the loop number may not be `/dev/loop0`; the `$loop1` variable handles that. if `mkfs.xfs` is missing on debian/ubuntu run `sudo apt install xfsprogs`, or use `mkfs.ext4`. in another terminal the variables are gone; find the names with `losetup -a` and type them by hand. v03 title grow the volume online text the first disk has 96m free: grow the lv by 90m, then add the second disk to the pool and grow again with the remaining free space. verify the size with `df`. blocks cmd sudo lvextend -r -l +90m /dev/vg_data/lv_web
df -h /mnt/web
sudo vgextend vg_data $loop2
sudo lvextend -r -l +100%free /dev/vg_data/lv_web
sudo lvs vg_data
df -h /mnt/web expected lv     vg      attr       lsize
lv_web vg_data -wi-ao---- 592.00m differs if `-r` fails check that the volume is mounted; grow by hand with `sudo xfs_growfs /mnt/web` (`resize2fs` for ext4). `insufficient free space` means vfree is used up; run `vgextend` first. v04 title clean up the lab text unmount, remove lv, vg and pvs in order, detach the loop devices and delete the images. if there were no errors, press \ blocks cmd sudo umount /mnt/web
sudo lvremove -y /dev/vg_data/lv_web
sudo vgremove vg_data
sudo pvremove $loop1 $loop2
sudo losetup -d $loop1 $loop2
rm ~/lvm-lab/disk1.img ~/lvm-lab/disk2.img expected logical volume \  successfully removed. differs on `target is busy` run `cd ~` first and leave no open shell inside `/mnt/web`. if `$loop1` is empty in another terminal, find the names with `losetup -a` and type them by hand. if unsure, revert to the snapshot. quiz : { what is the correct order of the lvm layers? options disk → lv → vg → pv disk → pv → vg → lv vg → disk → lv → pv lv → pv → disk → vg explain a disk becomes a pv, pvs form the vg pool, volumes (lv) are cut from the pool. : { which statement is true? options ext4 can never shrink xfs shrinks online xfs and ext4 shrink together xfs cannot be shrunk explain xfs only grows; to shrink it, back up, recreate and restore. : { what does `lvextend -r -l +100m /dev/vg_data/lv_web` do? options grows the lv and the filesystem grows only the vg shrinks the lv to 100m creates a new pv explain -r (resizefs) grows the filesystem together with the lv. : { what is the correct order when cleaning up the loop lab? options pvremove → vgremove → lvremove → umount lvremove → umount → pvremove → vgremove umount → lvremove → vgremove → pvremove vgremove → umount → pvremove → lvremove explain unmount first, then remove from the top down: lv, vg, pv. summary lvm: disk → pv → vg → lv → filesystem → mount. read commands: pvs, vgs, lvs, lvdisplay, lsblk -f. create: pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, mkfs, mount. grow: lvextend -r (vgextend first if needed). xfs cannot shrink; lvremove/vgreduce/pvremove destroy data. practise only on loop devices in a snapshotted vm. glossary term meaning physical volume: a disk or partition carrying an lvm signature. term meaning volume group: a storage pool made of pvs. term meaning logical volume: a volume cut from a vg and used like a disk. term vfree meaning free space in a vg not yet assigned to any lv. term loop device meaning a kernel feature that presents a file as a block device. term sparse file meaning a file that looks large but uses little real disk space. term lvextend -r meaning grows the lv and the filesystem on it together. term xfs_growfs meaning grows a mounted xfs filesystem. term resize2fs meaning resizes an ext2/3/4 filesystem. term fstab meaning the list of filesystems mounted at boot: /etc/fstab.

6.5.title: Bash Script 1 — Variables, Arguments, Conditions
objectives: You write a script with a shebang, make it executable with chmod +x and start it with ./script.sh.
You assign variables and know the difference between single and double quotes, read, $(command) and $(( )).
You read arguments with $1, $# and "$@" and check exit codes with $? and exit.
You make decisions with if/elif/else, [[ ]] and test, and you use set -euo pipefail as a safety net.
cmds: if [ -f "$1" ]; then echo exists; else echo missing; fi
sol:
printf '#!/bin/bash
if [ -z "$1" ]; then
  echo "Usage: need_arg.sh NAME"
  exit 1
fi
echo "Hello, $1"
exit 0
' > ~/bin/need_arg.sh
6.5.text:
title bash script 1 — variables, arguments, conditions lead write your first bash script, make it executable, and work with variables, arguments, exit codes and conditions. objectives you write a script with a shebang, make it executable with chmod +x and start it with ./script.sh. you assign variables and know the difference between single and double quotes, read, $(command) and $(( )). you read arguments with $1, $# and \  and check exit codes with $? and exit. you make decisions with if/elif/else, [[ ]] and test, and you use set -euo pipefail as a safety net. sections first title the first script: shebang and execute permission body a script is a text file with commands. the first line, the **shebang** `#!/bin/bash`, tells the system which interpreter runs the file. without the **execute bit** the file cannot be started directly: `./hello.sh` then gives *permission denied*. `./` means 'the file in this folder'. linux does not search the current folder for commands, so `hello.sh` alone gives *command not found*. in this module you create scripts with `printf` (or a heredoc on your vm) so you can see exactly what is in the file. commands cmd #!/bin/bash what the shebang: first line of the file, names the interpreter. where at the top of every bash script. why the script runs with bash and not with another shell such as sh. example printf '#!/bin/bash\necho \ \n' > ~/bin/hello.sh cmd chmod +x what sets the execute bit on a file. where once after you create a script. why without it `./script.sh` fails with permission denied. example chmod +x ~/bin/hello.sh cmd ./script.sh what runs an executable script by path. where when you start your own scripts. why the path (`./` or full path) tells the shell where the file is. example ~/bin/hello.sh cmd bash script.sh what runs a script with bash directly, no execute bit needed. where for quick tests and on volumes mounted noexec. why handy for debugging; the shebang is ignored. example bash ~/bin/hello.sh nosim tip put your own scripts in `~/bin`. on ubuntu and rocky this folder is added to `path` at login once it exists, so you can start them by name. warn never run a script you downloaded or do not understand. read it first with `cat script.sh`. be especially careful with `curl ... | bash` and with `sudo` on a first attempt. vars title variables, quoting and arithmetic body a variable is set with `name=value` — **no spaces around `=`**. you read it with `$name`. `name = value` does not work: bash thinks `name` is a command. **double quotes** `\ ` expand variables, **single quotes** `'...'` do not: `echo '$home'` prints the text `$home`. always quote variables (`\ `) so file names with spaces stay one word. `$(command)` inserts the output of a command, `$(( ))` calculates integers, `read` asks the user for input (vm only). commands cmd name=value what sets a variable (no spaces around the equals sign). where at the top of a script for settings and paths. why you change a value in one place instead of ten. example name=student; echo \ }, { $var\ what double quotes expand the variable, single quotes keep the text. where in every command that uses variables. why quoting protects against spaces and glob characters in values. example echo '$home' \ }, { read -r -p what reads a line of input into a variable. where in interactive scripts that ask questions. why `-r` keeps backslashes, `-p` shows a prompt. example read -r -p \  name nosim cmd $(command) what replaces itself with the output of the command. where to store output in a variable or use it in text. why lets scripts react to system state. example echo \ }, { $(( )) what integer arithmetic. where counters, sizes, simple calculations. why bash has no decimals; for those use `bc`. example echo $((6 * 7)) nosim tip a default value is written `${name:-default}`: it is used when `name` is empty or unset. args title arguments and exit codes body a script receives arguments: `$0` is the script name, `$1`, `$2`, ... are the arguments, `$#` is their number and `\ ` is the list of all of them, each kept as one word. quote `\ `, otherwise `my file` becomes two words. every command ends with an **exit code**: `0` means success, anything else means failure. `$?` holds the code of the last command. in a script you end with `exit 0` or `exit 1`. the simulator cannot run arguments in scripts reliably, so the real runs are in the vm section. commands cmd $0 $1 $2 what script name and the first arguments. where when the script needs input from the caller. why one script works for many files or names. example ./args.sh alice bob nosim cmd $# and \ what number of arguments and the list of all arguments. where to check the count or loop over arguments. why $@\ example ./args.sh \  bob nosim cmd ${1:-guest} what first argument, or `guest` if none was given. where for optional arguments. why the script does not break when the argument is missing. example name=\ nosim cmd $? and exit what `$?` is the last exit code, `exit n` ends a script with code n. where after commands you want to check, and at the end of scripts. why other scripts, cron and ci decide based on this code. example false; echo $? tip `grep` returns 1 when nothing matches. that is not an error in the program, just a 'no' answer: `grep carol ~/users.txt; echo $?` prints `1`. cond title conditions: if, elif, else body `if` runs a command and looks at its exit code. the command is usually `[ ... ]` (the same as `test`) or bash's `[[ ... ]]`. spaces inside the brackets are required: `[ -f \  ]`. useful tests: `-f` regular file, `-d` directory, `-x` executable, `-z` string is empty, `-n` string is not empty. for numbers use `-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge`, for text `==` and `!=`. `[[ ]]` is safer than `[ ]` (no word splitting) but exists only in bash, not in plain `sh`. short forms: `cmd1 && cmd2` runs the second only on success, `cmd1 || cmd2` only on failure. commands cmd if / elif / else / fi what runs different commands depending on a test. where whenever a script must decide. why scripts react to input and state instead of running blindly. example if [ -f \  ]; then echo exists; else echo missing; fi nosim cmd [ ] / test what tests files, strings and numbers; the result is the exit code. where in the condition of `if`, or alone with `&&` / `||`. why the portable form that works in every shell. example test -f ~/notes.txt && echo yes cmd [[ ]] what bash conditions with patterns and `&&` / `||` inside. where in scripts with `#!/bin/bash`. why fewer quoting traps than `[ ]`. example [[ $score -ge 50 && -n $name ]] && echo ok nosim cmd && and || what chains commands by success or failure. where for short checks on one line. why quick alternative to a full `if`. example test -d ~/documents && echo dir || echo nodir tip check first, act second: `[ -f \  ] || { echo \ ; exit 1; }` stops early with a clear message. strict title safe scripts: set -euo pipefail and debugging body by default bash **continues after errors**. the line `set -euo pipefail` at the top changes that: `-e` stops at the first failing command, `-u` treats an unset variable as an error, `-o pipefail` makes a pipe fail if any part fails. to debug use `bash -n script.sh` (syntax check only) and `bash -x script.sh` (prints every command with a `+` before running it). `shellcheck` finds typical mistakes before you run the script. install it with `sudo apt install shellcheck` on debian/ubuntu or `sudo dnf install epel-release && sudo dnf install shellcheck` on rhel/rocky. on hardened systems a script can fail although `chmod +x` was done: the folder may be mounted `noexec`, or selinux (rhel/rocky) / apparmor (ubuntu) may block it when a service starts it. then use `bash script.sh` for a test and look at the audit/journal logs. commands cmd set -euo pipefail what strict mode: stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipes. where second line of almost every script. why errors are not silently ignored, so the script does less damage. example set -euo pipefail nosim cmd bash -n / bash -x what `-n` checks syntax, `-x` traces each command. where when a script misbehaves. why you see exactly which line and which values are used. example bash -x ~/bin/hello.sh nosim cmd shellcheck what static analysis of shell scripts. where before you share or schedule a script. why finds quoting bugs and typos early. example shellcheck ~/bin/vars.sh nosim cmd ${var:?message} what aborts with a message if the variable is empty or unset. where before destructive commands that use a variable. why prevents `rm` from running on the wrong path. example rm -r \ nosim tip print first, delete later: replace `rm` with `echo rm` in a test run and check the paths with your eyes. warn only `-e` is no 6.6.title: Bash Script 2 — Loops, Functions, Pitfalls
objectives: You write repeated work with `for` and `while`.
You read a file safely line by line with `while IFS= read -r`.
You route arguments and menus with `case` and structure code with functions and `local`.
You clean up with `mktemp` and `trap` and prevent the empty-variable disaster with `"${DIR:?}"`.
You find script errors with `shellcheck`, `bash -n` and `bash -x`.
cmds: for i in 1 2 3; do echo "n=$i"; done
while IFS= read -r host; do echo "$host"; done < servers.txt
case "$1" in start) echo go ;; *) echo usage ;; esac
for h in "${hosts[@]}"; do echo "$h"; done
sol:
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash
while IFS= read -r host; do
  echo "checking $host"
done < ~/lab/servers.txt
' > ~/scripts/readlines.sh

printf 'hosts=(web01 web02 db01)
for h in "${hosts[@]}"; do
  echo "$h"
done
' > ~/scripts/arr.sh

printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash
for f in ./*.txt; do
  echo "$f"
done
' > ~/scripts/list_files.sh

printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
DIR=/home/student/tmpwork
trap "echo cleanup done" EXIT
rm -rf "${DIR:?}/"*
' > ~/scripts/cleanup.sh

printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash
check_host() {
  local h=$1
  echo "check $h"
}
while IFS= read -r host; do
  [ -n "$host" ] || continue
  check_host "$host"
done < ~/lab/servers.txt
' > ~/scripts/check_all.sh
6.6.text:
title bash script 2 — loops, functions, pitfalls lead do not do the same work a hundred times: build loops, case and functions, clean up temporary files with trap and write safe scripts without quoting traps. objectives you write repeated work with `for` and `while`. you read a file safely line by line with `while ifs= read -r`. you route arguments and menus with `case` and structure code with functions and `local`. you clean up with `mktemp` and `trap` and prevent the empty-variable disaster with `\ you find script errors with `shellcheck`, `bash -n` and `bash -x`. sections loops title loops: for and while body a script is more than commands running in order. if you do the same work for several servers or files, you use a **loop**. `for` runs once per item in a list, `while` runs as long as a condition stays true. the source of the list must be safe: file patterns (`./*.txt`), fixed lists or `\ `. never feed the output of `$(ls)` into a loop; names with spaces get split. **note:** the built-in simulator cannot execute loops; you write them into script files and run them in your vm. commands cmd for what runs the commands once for each item in the list. where when running the same check on several servers or processing the files of a folder. why shortens repeated code and reduces mistakes. example for i in 1 2 3; do echo \ ; done nosim cmd while what repeats the commands as long as the condition is true. where when waiting for something or reading files. why you do not need to know the number of rounds in advance. example while [ -e /tmp/lock ]; do sleep 1; done nosim cmd echo {1..5} what brace expansion: produces 1 2 3 4 5 (no spaces inside the range). where for number ranges or numbered series of files. why makes short lists without a loop; also used in `for i in {1..5}`. example echo {1..5} cmd break / continue what `break` ends the loop, `continue` jumps to the next round. where when skipping empty lines or leaving once the item is found. why avoids needless work and nested `if` blocks. example [ -n \  ] || continue nosim tip if a file pattern matches nothing, `./*.txt` stays literal. put `[ -e \  ] || continue` at the start of the loop body. readfile title reading a file line by line body the correct pattern for line-by-line reading is `while ifs= read -r line; do ... done < file`. `ifs=` keeps leading and trailing spaces, `-r` does not interpret backslashes. do not write `for line in $(cat file)`: lines are split at spaces and every word becomes a round. the redirection `done < ~/lab/servers.txt` makes the file the input of the loop. commands cmd while ifs= read -r what reads input line by line and puts each line into a variable. where with server lists, logs or csv files. why reads safely without altering spaces or backslashes. example while ifs= read -r host; do echo \ ; done < servers.txt nosim cmd done < file what redirects the loop's input from a file. where on the last line of a `while read` block. why a pipe (`cat | while`) runs in a subshell and variables vanish after the loop; a redirection does not. example done < ~/lab/servers.txt nosim cmd wc -l what prints the number of lines. where when you want to know how many rounds the loop will run. why you compare your expectation with the real number. example wc -l ~/lab/servers.txt warn if the last line does not end with `\n`, `read` may skip it. if needed, add `|| [ -n \  ]`. case title branching with case body `case` compares a value with patterns and is far more readable than a long `if/elif` chain. each branch starts with `pattern)` and ends with `;;`; `*)` runs when nothing matches. the block closes with `esac`. typical uses: branching on the first argument (`$1`) as in `./menu.sh start`, or acting differently by the prefix of a server name. commands cmd case ... esac what branches a value according to patterns. where in service scripts (start/stop/status) and menus. why readable; you catch unknown input with `*)`. example case \  in start) echo go ;; *) echo usage ;; esac nosim cmd $1  $@  $# what first argument, all arguments and the number of arguments. where when passing values to the script from outside. why the script becomes reusable; `\ ` preserves arguments with spaces. example echo \ nosim cmd chmod +x what gives the script execute permission. where before running it as `./menu.sh`. why without the permission you get `permission denied`. example chmod +x ~/scripts/menu.sh tip combine several patterns with `|`, for example `start|restart)`. functions title functions, local and arrays body a **function** names repeated code: `name() { ...; }`. in bash variables are **global** by default; without `local` inside a function you overwrite variables from outside. `return` only gives an exit code of 0–255. for text use `echo` and capture it with `$(function)`. an **array** collects several values under one name; always write `\ ` in loops so elements with spaces stay intact. commands cmd name() { ...; } what gives a block of code a name that you call later. where when the same check runs in several places in the script. why structures the code, ends repetition and makes testing easier. example log() { echo \ ; } nosim cmd local what limits a variable to the function. where for temporary variables inside functions. why you do not accidentally overwrite a variable of the same name outside. example local msg=$1 nosim cmd arr=(a b c) what defines an array with three elements. where for lists of servers or options. why the list lives in one variable; `${#arr[@]}` gives the count. example hosts=(web01 web02 db01) nosim cmd ${arr[@]}\ what expands each element as a separate quoted word. where when building a `for` loop over an array. why elements with spaces are not split. example for h in \ ; do echo \ ; done nosim tip arrays exist only in bash, not in `sh` (dash). put `#!/usr/bin/env bash` on the first line. cleanup title safe scripts: set, mktemp, trap body create temporary files not with a fixed name but with `mktemp`: the name is unique and unpredictable. with `trap ... exit` the cleanup function runs however the script ends (error, ctrl+c, normal); `kill -9` is the exception. `set -euo pipefail` makes the script stricter: stop on errors (`-e`), stop on undefined variables (`-u`), do not hide failures inside pipelines (`pipefail`). commands cmd mktemp -d what creates a temporary directory with a unique name and prints its path. where when the script needs intermediate files. why prevents collisions and attacks through predictable names. example tmp=$(mktemp -d) nosim cmd trap cleanup exit what runs the `cleanup` function when the script ends. where with temporary directories, lock files or connections. why everything is cleaned up even after an error. example trap cleanup exit nosim cmd set -euo pipefail what stops the script on errors, undefined variables and pipeline failures. where in the first lines of the script. why you stop at once instead of silently continuing wrongly. example set -euo pipefail nosim danger if you delete inside `trap`, the same rule applies: write `rm -rf \ `. if `tmp` is empty, `rm -rf $tmp/` really becomes `rm -rf /`. test first with `echo rm -rf \ }, { pitfalls title pitfalls and debugging body the most common mistake is the **unquoted variable**: `touch $f` with `f=\ ` creates two files (`my` and `notes.txt`). rule: always quote variables as `\ the most dangerous line is `rm -rf $dir/*`: if `dir` is empty it becomes `rm -rf /*`. `\ ` stops the script with an error on an empty or undefined value. show the path with `echo` before deleting. debugging: `bash -n` checks the syntax without running, `bash -x` shows every command with a `+` prefix, `shellcheck` finds common traps. commands cmd $var\ what quotes the variable; no word splitting and no glob expansion. where every time you use a variable. why file names with spaces stay in one piece. example touch \ }, { ${dir:?}\ what aborts with an error if `dir` is empty or undefined. where with `rm -rf` and other destructive commands. why prevents an empty variable from deleting the path `/`. example rm -rf \ nosim cmd shellcheck what statically analyses the script and reports traps with a code (sc2086). where after writing a script, before committing. why catches unquoted variables and similar mistakes without running anything. example shellcheck ~/scripts/bad.sh nosim cmd bash -n what checks only the syntax without running the script. where when you suspect a missing `done`, `fi` or `esac`. why harmless; no command runs. example bash -n ~/scripts/loop.sh nosim cmd bash -x what prints every command with its expansions and a `+` prefix. where when the script behaves unexpectedly. why you see what the variables really contain. example bash -x ~/scripts/loop.sh nosim tip run a destructive command first with `echo` in front: `echo rm -rf \ `. if the output is right, remove the `echo`. warn install shellcheck on ubuntu/debian with `sudo apt install shellcheck`, on rocky/alma via epel: `sudo dnf install epel-release`, then `sudo dnf install shellcheck`. tasks t01 text create `~/scripts/loop.sh` with `printf`; its first line should be `#!/usr/bin/env bash` (redirection `>`). hint `printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n' > ~/scripts/loop.sh` — the `\n` at the end is the line break. t02 text how many servers are in `~/lab/servers.txt`? count with `wc -l` and guess how many rounds a loop would run. hint `wc -l ~/lab/servers.txt` prints the line count. (`wc` → module 2.6.) t03 text append with `>>` (without overwriting) a `for i in 1 2 3; do ... done` loop to `loop.sh`: three lines with `printf`. hint inside single quotes the shell does not expand `$i`. use `\n` for line breaks. t04 text make `loop.sh` executable (mode 755). hint `chmod 755 ~/scripts/loop.sh` or `chmod +x`; check with `ls -l` for `-rwxr-xr-x`. (`touch` → module 2.3.) t07 text write `~/scripts/arr.sh`: it defines the array `hosts=(web01 web02 db01)` and prints it with `for h in \ ; do ... done`. hint inside the single-quoted `printf`, `\ ` is written as is. t08 text guess the output of `./scripts/count.sh | wc -l` before running it: how many lines? then run it and verify. hint the script contains three `echo` lines; look with `cat scripts/count.sh`. (`cat` → module 2.6.) t09 text set an empty variable with `dir=` and run `echo \ `. which path would it delete? guess, then verify. hint the empty `$dir` vanishes; only `/` remains. that is why you write `\ },  : { `~/scripts/hello.sh` does not run (`permission denied`). fix it and run it. hint `ls -l ~/scripts` shows the permissions; `chmod +x` adds them; then `~/scripts/hello.sh`. (`chmod` → module 4.4.) t11 text the line `rm -rf $dir/*` in `~/scripts/clean.sh` is dangerous. rewrite the file: keep `dir=/home/student/tmpwork`, and make the delete line use `\ *`. hint look with `cat ~/scripts/clean.sh`; then rewrite the three lines with `printf`. t12 text `~/scripts/list_files.sh` contains `for f in $(ls *.txt)`, which splits names with spaces. rewrite the file with a glob: `for f in ./*.txt; do`. hint look at the content with `cat`. rewrite four lines with `printf`; keep `$f` inside single quotes. t13 text create `~/scripts/menu.sh`: `case \  in` with branches `start)`, `stop)` and `*)`, ending with `esac`; then make it executable. hint write the file with one `printf`, then `chmod 755`. every branch ends with `;;`. t14 text write `~/scripts/safe.sh`: a temp directory with `mktemp -d`, a `cleanup()` function, `trap cleanup exit` and a `log()` function that uses `local`. hint first `tmp=$(mktemp -d)`, then `cleanup() { rm -rf \ ; }`, and `trap cleanup exit` at the end. t15 text which servers logged an `error` in `~/lab/app.log`? write the unique, sorted server names to `~/lab/failed_hosts.txt`. hint `grep error`, then `cut -d' ' -f4`, `sort -u`; redirect the output with `>` into the file. bash -x loop.sh 2>&1 | head -8
dir=\ 
echo rm -rf $dir/* expected + for i in 1 2 3
+ echo n=1
n=1
...
rm -rf /bin /boot /etc ... differs lines starting with `+` are the `bash -x` trace; several `+` signs mean nested commands. the last line is only `echo`, so nothing is deleted; it just shows that the empty variable becomes `/*`. quiz : { what happens with `rm -rf $dir/*` when `dir` is empty, and which notation protects? options nothing happens; add `rm -i` only the home directory is deleted; use `sudo` it tries to delete `/*`; `\ ` protects it errors out; `chmod 000` is enough explain the empty variable disappears and the command becomes `rm -rf /*`. `${dir:?}` stops the script on an empty value. : { which pattern reads a file safely line by line? options `for l in $(cat file); do ... done` `while ifs= read -r l; do ... done < file` `cat file | for l; do ... done` `ls file | read l` explain `for` with `$(cat)` splits lines into words. `while ifs= read -r` reads the line unchanged. : { what does `local x=1` do inside a function? options makes `x` a constant passes `x` on to child processes defines `x` system-wide makes `x` valid only inside the function explain `local` limits the scope to the function; a variable of the same name outside is left untouched. : { when does `trap cleanup exit` run? options however the script ends (including errors); except after `kill -9` only on ctrl+c before the first line of the script only if `cleanup` returns 0 explain the exit trap runs on normal exit, on errors and on most signals; sigkill cannot be caught. summary `for` runs once per list item, `while` as long as the condition is true; choose a safe source. read files with `while ifs= read -r line; do ... done < file`, not with `$(cat)`. `case ... esac` routes arguments and menus readably; `*)` is the default branch. use `local` in functions; walk arrays with `\ create temporary files with `mktemp` and clean up with `trap cleanup exit`. quote every variable; write `\ ` when deleting and test with `echo` first. `bash -n`, `bash -x` and `shellcheck` show errors without running or step by step. glossary term loop meaning a construct that repeats a block of commands: `for`, `while`. term word splitting meaning splitting an unquoted variable at whitespace. term ifs meaning the characters the shell uses to separate words (field separator). term case meaning multi-way branch that compares a value with patterns. term local meaning keyword that limits a variable to a function. term array meaning a bash variable holding several values under one name. term trap meaning defines a command to run on a signal or at exit. term mktemp meaning creates a temporary file or directory with a unique name. term shellcheck meaning static analysis tool for shell scripts. term bash -x meaning trace mode that prints every command with its expansions before running it.

6.7.title: systemd Timers — The Modern Alternative to Cron
objectives: You write a `.service` file (`Type=oneshot`, `ExecStart`) and a `.timer` file (`OnCalendar`, `Persistent=true`).
You verify a time expression with `systemd-analyze calendar` before it ever runs.
You install and monitor a timer with `daemon-reload`, `enable --now`, `list-timers` and `journalctl -u`.
You read a cron line (`30 2 * * *`) and write the equivalent timer.
You know user timers (`systemctl --user`) and how to decide between cron and a timer.
6.7.text:
title systemd timers — the modern alternative to cron lead schedule the work; the system runs it for you. you will write a service and a timer, verify the time expression, watch the run with journalctl and compare it with cron. objectives you write a `.service` file (`type=oneshot`, `execstart`) and a `.timer` file (`oncalendar`, `persistent=true`). you verify a time expression with `systemd-analyze calendar` before it ever runs. you install and monitor a timer with `daemon-reload`, `enable --now`, `list-timers` and `journalctl -u`. you read a cron line (`30 2 * * *`) and write the equivalent timer. you know user timers (`systemctl --user`) and how to decide between cron and a timer. sections why title why timers? comparison with cron body running a script by hand is easy; real automation means running it **at the right time**. the classic way is **cron**: five time fields and a command on one line. the modern way is a **systemd timer**: two files, one saying **what** runs (`backup.service`), the other **when** it runs (`backup.timer`). a cron line: `30 2 * * * /home/student/bin/backup.sh` = every day at 02:30. fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. the timer's advantages: output goes to the **journal** (`journalctl -u`), `persistent=true` catches up a missed run at boot, `randomizeddelaysec` spreads load, and `systemctl list-timers` shows the next run. in this module you write the files in the simulator and check their content; `systemctl` and `journalctl` only work on a real vm. cron's advantage is simplicity: one line, available everywhere. commands cmd crontab -e what opens your own cron table in an editor. where for simple one-line scheduled jobs. why the reference point: you recognise the old job before moving it to a timer. example crontab -e nosim cmd crontab -l what lists the current cron lines. where when taking inventory of jobs to migrate. why you see which jobs to convert to timers. example crontab -l nosim cmd printf (cron line) what writes a cron line to a file: `minute hour day month weekday command`. where to practise cron syntax and keep it in a file. why you get used to the right field order. example printf '30 2 * * * /home/student/bin/backup.sh\n' > backup.cron cmd systemctl list-timers what lists active timers with their next and last run times. where when verifying a timer is really scheduled. why you catch a silently idle timer immediately. example systemctl list-timers --all nosim tip for a simple one-off user job, cron is enough. choose a timer when you want logs, dependencies, catch-up and monitoring. service title the service unit: what runs? body the service file defines the command. for scheduled jobs use **`type=oneshot`**: the command runs and finishes. `execstart` requires an **absolute path**; write `/usr/local/bin/backup.sh`, not `backup.sh`. system units go to `/etc/systemd/system/` (root needed). you cannot write there in the simulator; use the `~/units/` folder instead, the content to copy is identical. make the script executable first: `chmod +x`. note: a `.service` does not need an `[install]` section; scheduling belongs to the timer. to test by hand, `sudo systemctl start backup.service` is enough. commands cmd printf > backup.service what writes the service unit line by line. where in `~/units/` in the sim, under `/etc/systemd/system/` on the vm. why you create the file reproducibly without opening an editor. example printf '[unit]\ndescription=nightly backup\n\n[service]\ntype=oneshot\nexecstart=/home/student/bin/backup.sh\n' > backup.service cmd cat what shows the content of the file you wrote. where after every write. why you spot typos (`type=oneshot`, path) before starting. example cat backup.service cmd chmod +x what gives the script execute permission. where for every script called by `execstart`. why without it the service fails with `203/exec`. example chmod +x backup.sh cmd systemd-analyze verify what checks the unit file's syntax and paths. where before `daemon-reload`. why catches a wrong path or typo without running anything. example systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/backup.service nosim tip run the unit once by hand with `sudo systemctl start backup.service`; if it works, scheduling it is safe. warn on rhel/rocky (selinux) a service may be unable to run a script under `/home` (`203/exec`, `permission denied`). put the script in `/usr/local/bin`; on debian/ubuntu (apparmor) this is rarer, but the same path is recommended. timer title the timer unit: when does it run? body a timer file contains the time in `[timer]` and the line `wantedby=timers.target` in `[install]`. the name matches the service: `backup.timer` → `backup.service`. **`oncalendar=`** is calendar time: `*-*-* 02:30:00` every day at 02:30, `mon *-*-* 08:00:00` every monday at 08:00; `hourly`, `daily`, `weekly` are shortcuts. **`onbootsec=`** waits after boot, **`onunitactivesec=`** after the last run. **`persistent=true`**: a run missed while the machine was off happens right at the next boot. **`randomizeddelaysec=`** delays the start randomly, so many machines do not hit a shared resource at once. commands cmd oncalendar= what defines calendar-based time. where for jobs at fixed times such as nightly or weekly. why it is the readable counterpart of cron's five fields. example printf '[timer]\noncalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00\n' | cat cmd onbootsec= / onunitactivesec= what waits a relative time after boot or after the last run. where for jobs like \ why solves interval-based jobs that have no calendar. example printf '[timer]\nonbootsec=10min\nonunitactivesec=1h\n' | cat cmd persistent=true what catches up a missed run at the next boot. where on laptops, vms or machines switched off at night. why gives anacron-like safety, which cron lacks. example printf '[timer]\noncalendar=daily\npersistent=true\n' | cat cmd randomizeddelaysec= what adds a random delay to the start. where on many servers running at the same time. why prevents sudden load spikes on a shared repository or network. example printf '[timer]\noncalendar=daily\nrandomizeddelaysec=5min\n' | cat cmd systemd-analyze calendar what interprets a time expression and shows the next elapse. where before and after writing a timer. why a wrong expression silently never runs; here you see it at once. example systemd-analyze calendar \ nosim tip lists like `mon,fri *-*-* 08:00` and `*-*-* *:00/15:00` (every 15 min) work; test them all with `systemd-analyze calendar` first. manage title install, start, monitor body the order is fixed: write the files → `systemd-analyze verify` and `calendar` → `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` → `start` the service by hand and check `journalctl` → `enable --now` the **timer** → verify with `list-timers`. `enable --now` applies to the **timer** (`backup.timer`), not the service. if you forget `daemon-reload` after a new or changed file, systemd keeps using the old state. read the output with `journalctl -u backup.service`; `-f` follows live, `--since today` filters the day. a failed run shows a `failed with result` line. commands cmd sudo systemctl daemon-reload what makes systemd re-read the unit files. where after every new or changed .service and .timer. why without it systemd sees an old file or none at all. example sudo systemctl daemon-reload nosim cmd sudo systemctl start backup.service what runs the service once, right now. where to test the job itself before enabling the timer. why you find errors without waiting for the timer. example sudo systemctl start backup.service nosim cmd sudo systemctl enable --now backup.timer what enables the timer at boot and starts it immediately. where for every permanent timer. why it also runs after a reboot. example sudo systemctl enable --now backup.timer nosim cmd systemctl list-timers what shows the next and last runs. where after installing and when troubleshooting. why the next column proves the timer is really scheduled. example systemctl list-timers backup.timer nosim cmd journalctl -u what shows the log entries of a unit. where when reading successful and failed runs. why one searchable record instead of cron's mailbox. example journalctl -u backup.service --since today nosim warn a service running as root can do great harm with a script that deletes or moves files. dry-run the script with `echo` first, verify the path, then schedule it. a wrong `oncalendar` gives no error; it simply never runs. danger over ssh never stop or disable `sshd` or network services with `systemctl`; you lock yourself out. experiment only with your own units and take a vm snapshot before important changes (module 0.2). user title user timers and the migration decision body you can schedule without root: **user units** live in `~/.config/systemd/user/` and are managed with `systemctl --user` (no `sudo`). they stop when you log out; to keep them running use `loginctl enable-linger student`. decision: one-line job, output irrelevant → **cron**. need logs, dependencies (run when the network is up), catch-up (`persistent`), random delay or resource limits → **timer**. both can coexist; when migrating, comment out the old cron line, verify the new timer, then delete. on debian/ubuntu packages often ship timers instead of cron (`apt-daily.timer`); on rhel/rocky something like `dnf-makecache.timer`. `systemctl list-timers --all` is full of ready examples. commands cmd mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user what creates the user units folder. where before your first user timer. why systemd looks for user units here. example mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user cmd systemctl --user daemon-reload what makes systemd re-read user units. where after writing the user files. why you follow the same flow without `sudo`. example systemctl --user daemon-reload nosim cmd systemctl --user enable --now notes.timer what enables and starts a user timer. where for personal jobs in your own home. why no root needed, so the risk is small. example systemctl --user enable --now notes.timer nosim cmd loginctl enable-linger what keeps user units running while you are logged out. where on a server where a user timer must continue in the background. why otherwise the timer stops when you log out. example sudo loginctl enable-linger student nosim tip a user timer is the safest place to experiment: if you make a mistake only your own account is affected, not the system. tasks t01 text create the folders `~/bin` and `~/units` with one command: `mkdir -p ~/bin ~/units`. hint `mkdir -p` accepts several paths. (`mkdir` → module 2.3.) t02 text read the cron sample file: `cat ~/sample/crontab.txt`. it has three job lines. hint lines are: minute hour day month weekday command. t03 text write `~/bin/backup.sh` with `printf`: first line `#!/bin/bash`, second line `echo backup done`. hint `printf '#!/bin/bash\necho backup done\n' > ~/bin/backup.sh` t04 text make `~/bin/backup.sh` executable (mode 755). hint `chmod 755 ~/bin/backup.sh` or `chmod +x`. (`chmod` → module 4.4.) t05 text write `~/units/backup.service`: in `[service]` put `type=oneshot` and `execstart=/home/student/bin/backup.sh`. hint separate lines with `\n` in one `printf` and end with `> ~/units/backup.service`. (`>` → module 3.2.) t06 text write `~/units/backup.timer`: under `[timer]` `oncalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00` and `persistent=true`, under `[install]` `wantedby=timers.target`. hint use single quotes in the sim so the shell does not expand `*`. t07 text predict: how many lines in `~/sample/list-timers.txt` contain `timer`? then verify with `grep -c timer ~/sample/list-timers.txt`. hint the header has no lowercase `timer`; there are two timer lines. t08 text predict: which time does the `next elapse` line in `~/sample/analyze.txt` show? look with `grep 'next elapse' ~/sample/analyze.txt`. hint the expression was monday 08:00; find the next monday. t09 text debug: `~/broken/broken.timer` does not work. it has a typo `oncalender` and the `[install]` section is missing. rewrite the file with `oncalendar=daily`, `persistent=true` and `wantedby=timers.target`. hint start with `cat ~/broken/broken.timer`. spelling: calen**d**ar. t10 text debug: `execstart=report.sh` in `~/broken/report.service` is a relative path; systemd rejects it. rewrite the file so it contains `execstart=/home/student/bin/report.sh` (keep `type=oneshot`). hint see the current lines with `cat`, then `printf ... > ~/broken/report.service`. t11 text mini project (user timer): create the folder `~/.config/systemd/user`. `notes.service` must contain `execstart=/usr/bin/touch /home/student/notes.txt`; `notes.timer` must contain `oncalendar=hourly` and `wantedby=timers.target`. hint three commands: `mkdir -p`, one `printf` for the service, one for the timer. t12 text mini project (cron comparison): write two cron lines to `~/units/backup.cron`: `30 2 * * * /home/student/bin/backup.sh` and `0 8 * * 1 /home/student/bin/report.sh`. hint use `>` for the first line and `>>` for the second. t13 text challenge: for a `cleanup` job write `~/units/cleanup.service` (`execstart=/home/student/bin/cleanup.sh`, `type=oneshot`) and `~/units/cleanup.timer`. timer: 10 minutes after boot (`onbootsec=10min`), then every hour (`onunitactivesec=1h`), random delay up to 5 minutes (`randomizeddelaysec=5min`), `wantedby=timers.target`. hint it is an interval timer, not a calendar one: do not use `oncalendar`. t14 text ticket: \  write only the `failed` lines of `~/sample/journal.txt` to `~/units/failed.txt`. hint `grep failed ... > ...` (`grep` → module 3.4; `>` → module 3.2.) t15 text ticket: \  write `~/units/report.timer` (`oncalendar`, the setting that catches up a missed run, `wantedby=timers.target`). hint monday 08:00 = `mon *-*-* 08:00:00`; catch-up = `persistent=true`. t16 text count how many lines the journal sample has with `wc -l ~/sample/journal.txt`. hint look at the number at the start of the output. : { on your vm (ubuntu or rocky/alma) go through these in order. **take a snapshot** first (module 0.2). you write units under `/etc/systemd/system/`; only touch your own `backup.*` files. if something goes wrong, stop it with `sudo systemctl disable --now backup.timer`. tasks v01 title write the script and service text first put the script in `/usr/local/bin`, then write the service file and show its content. keep the script in `/usr/local/bin` because of selinux. blocks cmd sudo tee /usr/local/bin/backup.sh > /dev/null <<'eof'
#!/bin/bash
echo \ 
eof
sudo chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/backup.sh expected (no output) cmd sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/backup.service > /dev/null <<'eof'
[unit]
description=nightly backup

[service]
type=oneshot
execstart=/usr/local/bin/backup.sh
eof
cat /etc/systemd/system/backup.service expected [unit]
description=nightly backup

[service]
type=oneshot
execstart=/usr/local/bin/backup.sh differs if you get `permission denied`, `sudo` is missing; `sudo` must come before `tee`. the `eof` line of the heredoc (`<<'eof'`) must stand alone at the start of its line. v02 title write the timer text write a timer that runs every night at 02:30 and catches up missed runs, then paste its content. blocks cmd sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer > /dev/null <<'eof'
[unit]
description=run backup nightly

[timer]
oncalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00
persistent=true
randomizeddelaysec=5min

[install]
wantedby=timers.target
eof
cat /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer expected [timer]
oncalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00
persistent=true
... differs the file must be called `backup.timer`: same name as the service, different extension. the quoted heredoc (`'eof'`) stops the `*` from being expanded. v03 title verify text verify the time expression and the unit files without running anything; paste the output. blocks cmd systemd-analyze calendar \ 
systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/backup.service /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer expected normalized form: *-*-* 02:30:00
    next elapse: fri 2026-11-13 02:30:00 cet
(verify: usually no output = no problem) differs if `verify` prints nothing, there is no problem. on older versions the `next elapse` text may differ slightly; the `normalized form` line still appears. v04 title install and schedule text run `daemon-reload`, enable the timer and see it scheduled with `list-timers`. `backup.timer` must appear in the output. blocks cmd sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now backup.timer
systemctl list-timers backup.timer expected next                        left     last passed unit         activates
fri 2026-11-13 02:30:00 cet 16h left n/a  n/a    backup.timer backup.service differs if you see `unit backup.timer not found`, you skipped `daemon-reload` or the file name/path is wrong. because of `randomizeddelaysec`, next may be a few minutes after 02:30. v05 title run by hand, read the journal text start the service once by hand and find the `backup done` line in its journal. blocks cmd sudo systemctl start backup.service
journalctl -u backup.service --no-pager -n 10 expected systemd[1]: starting backup.service - nightly backup...
backup.sh[1234]: backup done
systemd[1]: backup.service: succeeded. differs on rocky/rhel the last line may read `deactivated successfully.`; that is fine. if you see `failed with result 'exit-code'`, the script path or permission is wrong (`chmod 755`, `ls -z` for selinux). v06 title user timer and cleanup text set up a user timer without `sudo`, see it in the list; then stop it and the system timer. if no errors, press \ blocks cmd mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user
printf '[service]\ntype=oneshot\nexecstart=/usr/bin/touch %h/notes.txt\n' > ~/.config/systemd/user/notes.service
printf '[timer]\noncalendar=hourly\n\n[install]\nwantedby=timers.target\n' > ~/.config/systemd/user/notes.timer
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now notes.timer
systemctl --user list-timers expected next ... unit        activates
... notes.timer notes.service cmd systemctl --user disable --now notes.timer
sudo systemctl disable --now backup.timer expected removed ...notes.timer symlink differs if you get `failed to connect to bus`, run it in your normal login session, not via `sudo su`; `--user` needs a non-root session. `%h` means the home directory inside a unit; the `printf` is single-quoted so the shell does not expand it. quiz : { which file defines **when** a job runs? options `backup.service` `backup.timer` `multi-user.target` `/etc/fstab` explain the timer defines 'when', the service defines 'what'; their names match. : { what does `persistent=true` do? options delays the job randomly deletes the timer at reboot catches up a run missed while the machine was off at the next boot runs the job as a user instead of root explain persistent stores the last run time on disk; a missed run is made up at boot. : { you wrote a new `.timer` file. what must you do before `enable --now`? options `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` `reboot` `crontab -e` nothing, systemd sees it automatically explain systemd caches unit files; `daemon-reload` is required after a change. : { where do you read a service's output and error lines? options from `/var/spool/cron/` with `crontab -l` `systemctl status` alone is always enough `journalctl -u backup.service` explain systemd writes output to the journal; `-u` filters by unit. summary a timer is two files: `.service` defines what runs, `.timer` defines when. `type=oneshot` and an absolute `execstart` path are the standard for scheduled jobs. `oncalendar` is calendar time, `onbootsec`/`onunitactivesec` an interval; `persistent=true` catches up missed runs. order: file → `systemd-analyze calendar/verify` → `daemon-reload` → manual `start` → `enable --now` → `list-timers`. read output with `journalctl -u`; the cron line `30 2 * * *` = every day at 02:30. user timers work without root via `~/.config/systemd/user` and `systemctl --user`. glossary term timer unit meaning a `.timer` unit that starts a service at a given time. term service unit meaning a `.service` unit that defines the command to run. term oneshot meaning `type=oneshot`: the command runs and finishes; suited to scheduled jobs. term oncalendar meaning calendar-based time expression, e.g. `*-*-* 02:30:00`. term persistent meaning `persistent=true`: catches up a missed run at the next boot. term randomizeddelaysec meaning adds a random start delay to avoid load spikes. term daemon-reload meaning makes systemd re-read its unit files. term journal meaning systemd's log store, read with `journalctl`. term cron meaning the classic scheduler; `crontab` lines use five time fields. term linger meaning `loginctl enable-linger`: keeps user units running while logged out.

6.8.title: Final Project — Small Company Server
objectives: You plan the whole server first and take a VM snapshot before you change anything.
You build users alice, bob, carol, the groups staff and admins, and a shared directory /srv/company with setgid.
You publish a site with nginx, label it correctly (SELinux) or check AppArmor, and open ports 80/443 without locking yourself out of SSH.
You automate a backup with a script and a systemd timer.
You verify every step with a checklist and write a delivery report.
6.8.text:
title final project — small company server lead combine everything on one server: users, shared directory, web site, firewall, backup, timer, and a verified delivery report. objectives you plan the whole server first and take a vm snapshot before you change anything. you build users alice, bob, carol, the groups staff and admins, and a shared directory /srv/company with setgid. you publish a site with nginx, label it correctly (selinux) or check apparmor, and open ports 80/443 without locking yourself out of ssh. you automate a backup with a script and a systemd timer. you verify every step with a checklist and write a delivery report. sections plan title 1. plan and safety first body the target: a small company server called `linux-lab`. three people work on it: **alice** (admin), **bob** and **carol**. everything lives under `/srv/company`: `shared` (team files), `admin` (admins only), `web` (the site), `backup` and `scripts`. **work in the vm, never on a production machine.** this project creates users, changes permissions, selinux labels, firewall rules and systemd units. before you start, take a **snapshot** (module 0.2). if a step goes wrong you roll back in seconds. the built-in terminal cannot run `useradd`, `nginx`, `firewall-cmd` or `systemctl`. so the simulator tasks rebuild the **files** of the project (permission tree, script, unit files, report) under `~/srv/company`, while the vm tasks do the real thing in `/srv/company`. order of work: 1) plan + snapshot, 2) users and directories, 3) web, 4) firewall, 5) backup + timer, 6) verify + report. rhel/rocky and debian/ubuntu differ in only a few commands; both are shown. commands cmd cat /etc/os-release what shows distribution name and version. where before you choose dnf or apt commands. why tells you which variant of the guide applies. example cat /etc/os-release cmd getenforce what prints the selinux mode: enforcing, permissive or disabled. where rhel, rocky, alma, fedora. why you must know the mode before testing the web label; keep it enforcing. example getenforce nosim cmd sudo aa-status what shows which apparmor profiles are loaded and in which mode. where debian and ubuntu. why ubuntu uses apparmor instead of selinux; here you only check it. example sudo aa-status nosim cmd what shows user id and group memberships. where when you check who may use the shared directory. why group membership decides access to `/srv/company/shared`. example id student warn take a vm snapshot now and name it `before-company-project`. do not run this project on a real server that others use. tip keep a notes file while you work. every command you run becomes a line in your delivery report later. users title 2. users, groups and the shared directory body create the groups `staff` (alice, bob, carol) and `admins` (alice only). use `useradd -m -g` for the users. deleting users is **not** part of this project (`userdel -r` would remove home directories). a shared directory needs two things. **setgid** (`chmod 2770`) makes new files inherit the directory group `staff`, so bob can edit carol's files. mode `770` keeps everybody else out. optionally add a **default acl** (`setfacl -d -m g:staff:rwx`) so new files are group-writable even with a strict umask. use least privilege: `web` is `755` (nginx must read it), `scripts` is `750`, `backup` is `700`. in the simulator you practise the same modes with `chmod` on `~/srv/company`; a normal user cannot `chgrp` there, so the group part is vm only. commands cmd sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -g staff alice what creates a user with home directory, shell and extra group. where once for each of alice, bob, carol. why real accounts with their own home directories. example sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -g staff alice nosim cmd sudo chgrp staff /srv/company/shared what sets the owning group of the directory. where on the shared and admin directories. why group ownership is what setgid passes on to new files. example sudo chgrp staff /srv/company/shared nosim cmd chmod 2770 what sets rwx for owner and group, nothing for others, plus the setgid bit. where on the shared and admin directories. why new files inherit the group; outsiders get no access. example chmod 2770 ~/srv/company/shared cmd sudo setfacl -d -m g:staff:rwx what sets a default acl that new files in the directory inherit. where on the shared directory (package `acl`). why group stays writable even if a user has umask 077. example sudo setfacl -d -m g:staff:rwx /srv/company/shared nosim cmd ls -ld what shows the directory itself, not its content. where to verify mode and group. why `drwxrws---` means setgid is active (the `s`). example ls -ld ~/srv/company/shared tip a capital `s` in `drwxr-s---` means setgid is set but the group has no execute bit; fix the mode. warn never fix permission problems with `chmod 777`. everybody could then change or delete the files. web title 3. web site with nginx, selinux and apparmor body install nginx and let it serve `/srv/company/web`. we add a server block named `company.local` in `/etc/nginx/conf.d/company.conf` (works on both families) and test with a `host:` header, so the default site does not interfere. **rhel/rocky:** selinux labels every file. a new directory under `/srv` gets a generic label, so nginx gets **403 forbidden** although the unix permissions are fine. the fix is the right label: `semanage fcontext` stores the rule, `restorecon` applies it. do not use `setenforce 0` as a shortcut; that switches protection off for the whole system. **debian/ubuntu:** there is no label to set. apparmor is active but nginx is normally not confined by a profile; you only check the status with `aa-status`. a 403 there is a normal permission problem (check the directory modes up
